God promised everything to the son as an inheritance and through the Son he created the universe."

God's external counsel or other words, God's plan for the universe with regards to Christ is that what Christ has already accomplished is central to God's plan. God ordained salvation in him and Christ wont fail. God had foreknowledge and a purpose in mind. This is clear in Ephesians 1:4,11 "Even before he made the world, God loved us and chose us in Christ to be holy and without fault in his eyes, furthermore because we are united with Christ, we have received and inheritance from God for he chose us in advance and he makes everything work out according to his plan."

God the Father promised to fulfill His kingdom plans for creation and humanity through the Son. The Son promised to become incarnate as a human being descended from God's chosen line of Davidic kings and to fulfill all the terms set forth in the prior covenant of redemption. He would die an atoning death for fallen humanity and all those who turned to him in repentance and faith would be redeemed from the presence of corruption and guilt of sin. In addition to these promises, both the Father and the Son agreed to send the Holy Spirit to apply the benefits of salvation to those the Son would save.

There are four things that Jesus specifically did to accomplish redemption for sinners. The 1st is His inauguration of the kingdom of God. Jesus taught that he had brought the kingdom of God to earth in His day. This can be found in Matthew 12:28. Secondly, His obedience to the Father. Jesus lived a life of perfect obedience to the Father, even unto his death on the cross. The third was his resurrection. By rising from the dead, Jesus conquered death itself. Lastly, His ascension. This was important because one, his ascension into heaven showed his enthronement as King and two, it allows Jesus to complete his sacrifice in the heavenly temple and to remain in the Father's presence interceding for his people.

At least three crucial events will take place when Jesus initiates the consummation. The first will be the general resurrection. This is where everyone that has died will be resurrected. This includes both the wicked and the righteous and they will be given new bodies. The second event is the last judgement. After the general resurrection has occurred, Jesus will exercise his authority and power as King by destroying all his enemies and blessing all His faithful people at the last judgement. The last event is the renewal of creation. Just as Jesus will judge humanity and purge the unbeliever, he will also purge and renew creation itself.

The identity of the Authorship of Hebrews is a difficulty as the it is not revealed in the letter. Earlier most of the Scholars believed of Paul's authorship. But Scholars also suggested Barnabas, Luke, Apollos and even Clement of Rome as authors. Origen commented' only God knows the truth of the matter'. 
Due to this fact , Hebrews was avoided from Marcionite canon and Muratorian canon. But by the end of patristic period the majority of the interpreters in the eastern and western Church come to recognize Hebrews as part of Canon. They generally agreed Pauline authorship. 
Theme like Melchizedek, Tabernacle, Christ as High priest distinguishes Hebrews from other Pauline letters.  Tee strong reason for doubting Pauline authorship is the way of Hebrews distanced himself from the first generation of Jesus' followers. Paul mentions in letters that he received the gospel from the Lord. Gal 1:11,12. But in Hebrews 2:3 contrasts this thought and says the salvation was announced by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard him. Also it is the opinion of the Scholars that it was a Hellenistic Jew who wrote it because of the quotes from Septuagint. The vocabulary and style shows the evidence of a mastery of the language. So Pauline authorship is questioned by most of the critical Scholars.

The Book of Hebrews does not identify the audience by name, city or region, but he wrote to an audience familiar to him. He shows his intent to visit them. 13:19-24. Following are the five important factors about the audience. 
1. Jewish: A good portion of the original audience were Jewish. Hebrews 1:1. Here the author referred, how God revealed himself to Israel in the Old Testament. 
2. Hellenistic: The content of Hebrews indicates that the audience was familiar with theological teachings that were more common among Jews living outside of Palestine. People like Clement referred the place as Rome on the basis of Hebrews 13:24. 
3. Immature: Hebrews 5 : 12 address them as spiritual babes; though they were supposed to be teachers. They need to be taught the elementary truths of the word. 
How ever the book contains most advanced , sophisticated theological teachings in the entire NT. 
4. Persecuted: It become evident in the book that the original audience had already faced persecution in the past. Some were suffering in the present. 10:32-35. Also there is a warning of expected persecution in future. 
5. Near Apostacy: They were in danger of turning away from Christ. 10: 26-27. They were warned of Apostacy and judgement if they turn away from Christ.

The author of Hebrews had many literary devices to express his exhortations of which Rhetorical device appears common. 
1. Synkrisis: this is a rhetorical device used in Hebrews 7:111-28 where a detailed comparison between two or more things expressed. The author described an eight point comparison between Melchizedek and Christ: their parentage, genealogy, birth, death, office, actions, status and achievements. 
2. Exempla: These are list of examples or illustrations that follow onw after another to build arguments. This is seen in Hebrews 11. 
3. Qolwahomer: This is a Hebrew expression which is well known in Greeco - Roman and Rabbinical traditions. It can be translated ' light t heavy or ' less to great' or 'simple to complex'. An example of this thought is  seen in Hebrews 10:28-29. 
With these literary styles the author was expressing the seriousness of the situation and convincing them to make right decisions.

The original audience of the book of Hebrews were believers of long enough for the author to say ' by this time you ought to be teachers". But they needed to be taught elementary truths of God's word all over again. 
However the book contains some of the most advanced, sophisticated theological teachings in the entire NT. Balancing these two facts is a difficult task. The early Christians adopted a practice of reading and explanation of the scripture from synagogue practices of first centaury. Just as in the synagogue, elders used to teach the scripture to the congregations.
So the author of Hebrews wrote some of the most theologically sophisticated NT writings because he expected Church leaders to teach this to the congregation. 
According to Hebrews 5:11, it is vivid that the original audience were slow in understanding the truths of the scripture and obeying their leaders Hebrews 13:17 underlines this fact.

To challenge the false doctrine and to accomplish the goal of calling his audience to faithful service to Jesus, the author organized his exhortations to five major divisions. 
1. The supremacy of Christ over Angelic Revelations. 1: 1-2:18. Refuting all Jewish false teachings about the angels as superior beings, the author was establishing the superiority of Christ over them.
2. Jesus is above Moses and his authority. 3:1- 4:13. The local Jewish community called for Christians to return to Moses' teachings and his ways. Here the author affirmed his point that Jesus was even greater than Moses, the faithful servant, because he was God's royal son. 
3. Melchizedek's priesthood 4:14 -7:28. Here the author argued that Jesus was the supreme royal priest after the order of Melchizedek. Local Jewish community had the idea that Melchizedek will appear the great high priest in the last days. So the author presented Jesus as the true royal priest appeared in the last days. 
4. Supremacy of the New covenant in Jesus 8: 1- 11:40. The teachings of the local Jewish community raised doubt about the Christian claim of new covenant made by Jesus. The author affirmed that Jesus is the mediator of the New covenant promised by Jeremiah. 
5. Practical perseverance. 12:1- 13:25. In the light of so many challenges to their from the local Jewish community and else where, the author wrote to inspire and energize his audience. Exhorted them to remain faithful, reminding promises and blessings in Jesus.

The book of Hebrews quotes, refer to or alludes to the OT nearly 100 times. More than quoting simple historical facts, the author focused on theological beliefs affirmed by the scriptures. 
1. Affirmed the declaration that every King in David's dynasty called God's son. Hebrews 1:5.
2. Angels are described as Serving spirits. Hebrews 1:7
3. God ordained human beings to be lower than angels only until the end when mankind will rule with Christ. Hebrews 2:6-8. 
4. Quoting from Isaiah 8:6, the author describes that the blessings of God's vindication will be shared among the members of Abraham's family. Hebrews 2:13.
5. Promises of Abraham was permanent and extending to the NT times. Hebrews 6:13-14.
6. Deuteronomy 4:24 is quoted in Hebrews 12;29 to describe God as the consuming fire to strengthen his teaching that God is still a consuming fire in Christ. 
By all these references and quotations from OT, the author of Hebrews insisted that certain theological outlooks established in the OT continued to be true in the NT times.

A number of Jewish writings from Qumran as well as books like Ephesians and Colossians, indicate hat Jewish communities in the first centaury often exalted angels as powerful glorious creatures who brought divine revelations to inferior human beings. 
The author of Hebrews responded to this challenge of exaggerated honor for angels. 
The author stated in Hebrews 1;1-14 that his audience should follow Jesus because Jesus is God's supreme source of Divine revelation. Hebrews 1:5-14, the author explained that Jesus is greater than angels because he alone is God's messianic son. Angels are just spirits sent to serve the saints. 
In Hebrews 2:1-4, the audience are exhorted to pay careful attention to the great message of salvation announced by Jesus because more judgement will come if it is rejected. 
Hebrews 2:5-9 explains the supremacy of Christ as who now rules over angels.  in Hebrews 2:10-18, the author demonstrated that Jesus is Abraham's descendent, and will share his glory with Abraham's children, not with angels.
By all these explanations the author substantially proven the superiority of Jesus over angels.

The term New covenant is derived from Jeremiah 31:31 where the prophet predicted that God would grant a covenant of final renewal to Israel and Judah. In eight ways this covenant is described in Hebrews. 
1. Hebrews 8:1-13 introduces the idea that Jesus mediates the New covenant as the Royal high priest in heaven. The Levitical priesthood failed to accomplish the purpose but the New covenant is based on a better promise through Christ. 8:6
2. Jesus' heavenly priesthood is superior to the Levitical priesthood. Sacrifices of the earthly tabernacle could not fully resolve the problem of sin but had to be repeated. But Jesu did away with sin once for all because his blood is sprinkled in man made sanctuary. 
3. Hebrews 10:1-18 compare and contrast the Old and New covenants and declare that the animal sacrifices needed because Jesus brought final forgiveness of sin through his sacrifice. 
4. Jesus has opened the way in to the most holy place. Hebrews 10:19-23
5. There is severity of punishment upon them that deny the salvation through Christ. Hebrews 10:24-31.
6. The audience are exhorted not to throw away their confidence through Christ. !0;32-35.
7. Hebrews 10:36-39 warns that God does not take pleasure in those who withdraw from living by faith. 
8. Hebrews 11 gives a long list of saints and explained, they would share with the audience in being made perfect when Christ returns. 
By all these references and explanations the author established the superiority of the New Covenant in Christ.

The famous theologian Thomas Aquinas insisted that the literal sense of Scripture was foundational to all its other senses. Unlike his other contemporaries , he insisted that every legitimate spiritual interpretation was rooted in the literal senses of a passage. He also taught that nothing necessary to faith was communicated as a spiritual meaning without being taught elsewhere in Scripture in the literal sense. Although Aquinas efforts to anchor spiritual meanings in the literal meaning of the Bible may seem like common sense to us ,his pint of view wasn't adopted by everyone. The church authorities asserted that they had special God -given insights into every spiritual meanings that had no connection to the literal meaning f the Bible. Not all scholars would agree that Aquinas always followed these principles as he interpreted the scriptures.

Biblical elaborations are places where one part of Scripture directly or indirect,y comments on an aspect of the meaning of another passage in scripture. These elaborations always record with and confirm original meaning as all Scripture is inspired and infallible.
Three types of elaborations used are :
1: as repetition of a facet of the original meaning
2: as a clarification of things that weren't entirely apparent  or well understood
3:as an expansion of the meaning of  particular passage.
The first Biblical elaboration is primarily a repetition of the words as in You shall not murder (Exo20:13) and in Deu5:17 again You shall not murder. This repetition confirmed  the commandment and reminded God; people of the terms if his covenant.
The second type of elaboration was clarification as we see in numbers 35:20-25. Here we see a clarification that provides information that was important to understand the commandment against murder.
The third type of elaboration was expansion , in which Scripture provides addition all information about the passage or topic it references.

The more we study the Scriptures , the more we see that the Bible elaborates on Itself over and over. The prophets and Psalmists regularly refer back to Moses, law. Jesus continually referred back to the old testament. And New testament writers did it the same again and again. But Biblical elaborations confirm other parts of the bible by repeating them, clarifying them and expanding them under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.  so, as we explore the meaning of Scriptures , we must acknowledge and submit ourselves to all places where the Scripture elaborate on themselves. And the legitimate applications of Scripture must be derived from and consistent with the Bible's original meaning and elaborations. As our applications are not inspired by God, we can make mistake s, so our applications must be subject to improvement and modification.

The writer, the document and the audience are three  interdependent guides to meaning. If we fail to account for their interdependence , its very easy to fall into error.
 1: INTENTIONAL FALLACY-If we overemphasize the author, we often fall into intentional fallacy. An intentional fallacy relies too heavily on what we think we know about a writer and his intentions , and de-emphasizes the things we learn about the document and the audience.
2: GRAPHIC FALLACY: when we overemphasize the document to the reclusion of contextual considerations of document and audience. the word graphe means writing.this is a fallacy because the same document can mean very different things on who wrote it or for whom  it was written
3: AFFECTIVE FALLACY: A third type of interpretive mistake we can make is over emphasizing the audience. It focuses too heavily on the how Scripture effects  the audience. This happens when an interpreter speculates too much about the mindset of the audience and fails to pay attention to the writer and audience.

The word synchronic derives from two Greek words the preposition sun which means 'with' or 'together with' and the noun' chronos' which means 'time'. When the word synchronic is applied to historical events, it describes occurances that took place 'together in time' or 'at the same time.' We will use the term synchronic to indicate how biblical theologians often explore sets of events in old testament history that happened at the same time. 
just as a movie director conveys his whole film by breaking it down into small series which tells a portion of old story although it being all one unit. Similarly synchronic studies takes an approach in synchronic synthesis biblical theologians concentrate their attention on particular  periods of time in the old testament as if they were scenes in a movie rather than on the flow of its entire history.

Synthesis means combining different components of something into a whole. We describe the ways different components of theology revealed in a particular period of history fit together in a coherent logical structure. Critical theologians believed that logic was a primary feature of what they call the Greek mindset, but it was foreign to the Hebrew mindset. Based on a number of linguistic and cultural assessments, they argued that the Greek focused on abstraction and logical order, much like systematic theology. and by contrast they suggested that the Hebrew mindset looked at everything in terms of historical dynamics. from this point of view, the old testament did not focus on logical systems or on theological relationships between beliefs. and for the this reason, to synthesize old testament theology was to misread the Hebrew bible and to force it into a Greek framework.

Poets of the old testament were interested in two different worlds that tell us about history. Old testament poetry often conveyed information about the revelatory acts and words of God in the past, present and future. Old testament poets also focused on the world of their readers which we will call 'their world'. They focused on their world by designing their texts to influence the lives of their original readers in particular ways. 
Old testament narratives were designed to have many different influences. They were doxological, leading readers to praise and worship God. They were theological, explaining truth about God. Some were political, focusing on current national events as well as polemical, opposing false teachings. They were moral, explaining how God's people should leave. They were motivational, encouraging every kind of faithful response. They were designed to teach early readers about their lives.

Modern evangelical often make the mistake of expecting Old testament narratives to be like modern journalistic historical writings. Old testament stories were only as comprehensive as suited the didactic purposes of their writers. They did not include every significant fact. Consider an example from the book of Chronicles when the writer of Chronicles composed his history of Solomon's life in 2 Chronicles 1-9, he followed the record of 1 kings 1-11 fairly closely. But he omitted every negative dimensions of Solomon's Reign. In  the second place, Old Testament authors were only as precise as their didactic purposes required. They were only as precise as they needed to be to reach their didactic goals like in example, Gen 1;7, where Moses wrote about earth's atmosphere.
Old testament narratives are not objective by Modern Standards.

We must say that trustworthy historical accounts must be comprehensive, precise and objective. that is to say that it will include every significant fact about a situation to give a balanced account. They will report details with exacting precision, or will at least acknowledge that they haven't. and they will avoid all subjective evaluations that may prejudice readers. Yet, the authors of Old Testament narratives did not completely follow these modern ideals. Now they did not propagate religious fantasies. Nor did they present historical errors or fabrication as fact. But they did write in ways that where determined largely by their didactic purposes and not by our modern sensibilities.

English term "diachronic" derives from the two Greek words; first, the preposition "dia" which often means 'through' or 'throughout' and second the Greek noun "chronos" which means time. Diachrony is a concern with the passage of time. In the case of biblical theology the term 'diachronic' points to the ways Old Testament theology transformed, changed, or developed through time. It will help to see how Diachronic approaches to the Old Testament relate to synchronic synthesis, how it stands in contrast with synchronic synthesis. A diachronic approach however, is much more concerned with changes that occurred in theological structures. It asks questions like, ''what changes in theology occurred as God acted and spoke in different ways during this period of time?"

The term "development" instead of simply speaking of diachronic changes to suggest two main ideas. First, changes in Old testametical structures always move toward fulfilling God's purposes for history. and Second, we speak of development because theological changes only occur through God's providential involvement in history. The scriptures affirm that everything in history including shifts in theology always accomplish unfailing purposes for his creation. 
Divine purposes from one end to another the scriptures affirm that everything in history including shifts in theology always accomplish God's unfailing purposes for his creation. 
Divine Providence; while are right to speak of changes in Old testament theology as developmental because they fulfill God's purposes, we must also keep in mind how complex this development was. God revealed himself through His actions and His words in many different ways and for this reason developments in old testament theology also took place in many different place. 
At the same time, some theological developments that took place in old testament often appear to us as random or inexplicable.

The six Old testament covenants fall into three main categories; First the universal covenants with Adam and Noah, second the national covenants with Abraham, Moses and David and third, the new covenant predicted by old testament prophets.
Universal Covenant is the covenant as ''universal'' because they were made between God and all of humanity. The covenant with Adam refers to the governance of divine- human relations established in the opening chapters of Genesis. 
National covenant; God established national covenant with his special people Israel the covenants with Abraham, Moses and David. The covenant with Abraham emphasize promises for numerical promise of Israel and possession of promise Land, from which Israel was to spread God's blessings to the entire world. and for this reason Abraham's covenant maybe covenant of promise. Similarly, covenant with Moses was known as covenant of law and covenant with David was known as covenant of Kingship.
New Covenant: The new covenant was designed to govern God's people when God fulfilled promises to reestablish his people after exile and to spread his kingdom through them to the ends of the earth. For this reason we may speak of the new covenant as ''the covenant of fulfillment''.

God disclosed himself during the Old testament in two main ways: through act revelation and word revelations. This twofold concept of revelation has characterized biblical theology of the new testament as well. On the other hand, the new testament many revelatory acts of God such as Christ's earthly ministry and the ministry of the holy spirit in the first century church. I t also foretells acts of God that will take place in the future such as the glorious return of Christ. But on the other hand, the new testament also reports word revelations associated with the act of God. God the Father spoke; Christ also spoke, and at times, angels and humans by the Spirit of God revealed God's word as well. The new testament contains all three kinds of word revelation as well. The Gospels report how God spoke through the word of Jesus to reflect Jesus' earlier actions.

The period of creation begins with the creation week and ends with humanity's fall into sin and expulsion from the Garden of Eden teaches that the Son was at the father's side during creation, and that the father created the world by or through Him. These facts are taught in places like john 1:1-3 and Hebrews 1:12. God filled the empty world in 6 days and revealed some of the basic dimensions of his eternal purpose for the world. God ordered and filled the universe in ways that pleased Him.
 1-3 days: Formed the world. Separated light from darkness, sky from sea, dry land from water and created vegetation. 
4-6 days: Created sun, moon, and stars, fishes and other creatures of the sea birds to inhabit the air and all the animals that live in the earth.
 He created the universe to be his special kingdom.

The theological term 'eternal counsel' often called eternal decree, refers to God's plans for the universe which we have set before his work of creation. God's eternal counsel is mentioned in places like Acts 2:23, Romans 8:28-30, 1 peter 1:2.
Different theological traditions have different beliefs about the nature and extent of God's plans. Some believe that God's eternal plan includes every detail of History. Others believe that God has fixed certain things and others. But we all agree that what Christ accomplished is central to God's plan- that God ordained salvation in Him and that Christ won't fail. Foreknowledge: God's knowledge prior to creation of events that would occur in the course of history. Regarding his foreknowledge, God said that from beginning that is before he created the world, he knew that was still to come. And regarding his purpose, he said,''My purpose will stand, and i will do all that I please.'' 
Purpose; God created the universe in order to display and increase hi glory through Christ. 
Covenant to Redemption: God's eternal decree regarding his glorious Kingdom.

God's promises are immutable. They can never change, and he will never break them. Whatever God promises, he will certainly fulfill. The first was the covenant of redemption in which they promised to redeem fallen humanity. Second is ''covenant of grace''. This solemn arrangement was made between the Father on the one hand and the Son and redeemed humanity on the other hand. And it governs the entire period of redemption, beginning immediately after humanity's fall into the sin and coming to its ultimate fulfillment when Jesus returns in glory.

Jesus redeeming work: his inauguration of the kingdom of God; his obedience to the Father; his resurrection; Inauguration of Kingdom; God's people longed for the day when God would bring his kingdom to earth. Jesus brought the kingdom of God to earth in his day. This was the day when humanity's original mandate would finally be fulfilled. God would completely restore his creation, and his will would be done on earth just as perfectly as it is already done in  heaven. 
Obedience; Jesus lived a life of perfect obedience to the father, culminating his death on the cross. And by his obedience, he won the blessing that Adam had lost. 
Resurrection; Jesus' bodily Resurrection was critical to his work of redemption. By raising from the dead, Jesus conquered death itself and secured the everlasting physical life of everyone that has faith in Him.

General Resurrection: At Christ's return, everyone that has ever died, will be resurrected. Both the wicked and the righteous will be given new bodies that will endure forever. This is clearly taught in John 5;28,29, where Jesus spoke these words:
A time is coming when all who are in their graves, will hear the Son's voice and come out- those who have done good will rise to live and those who have done evil will rise to condemned. Believer's bodies will be free from corruption and presence of sin. Bodies of unbelievers will continue to be plagued by the effects of sin.
Last Judgement; Immediately after general resurrection, Jesus will exercise his authority and power as king by destroying all his enemies and blessing all his faithful people at the last judgement. Every human being will be included in the last judgement.
Renewal of Creation: Just as Jesus will judge humanity and purge the unbelievers from it, he will also purge and renew the creation itself.

Peter's apostolic confession confirmed that Jesus was the Christ. His affirmation of Jesus' anointing to the office of Christ was direct revelation from God. Peter's confession as the spokesman for the apostles was more than that. It was an authoritative prophetic revelation from God. As such, it was an infallible confirmation of that fact that Jesus really was the Christ.
Transfiguration: Jesus took 3 disciples to a mountain to pray while Moses and Elijah appeared to Jesus. God's voice was heard from heaven affirming that Jesus was his son. And when Peter suggested that the disciples build shelters for them singled out Jesus as being worthy of the greatest honor and obedience.This was significant because Moses was the lawgiver and Elijah was the faithful prophet, it meant Jesus  stood in continuity with the law and prophets and that He was fulfilling the expectations set by the greatest leaders of Israel's past. it also meant that he was the final Davidic heir who was bringing God's kingdom to the earth.

Jesus fasted for 40 days in the desert before being tempted by Satan. Jesus overcame temptation to bring salvation to his people.
1] Obedience: As we see in the temptation he suffered, Jesus obeyed God both by keeping the requirements of his law and by submitting the Father's plan for His life. And his obedience prepared him for his work as Christ. 
2] Sympathy: Jesus didn't give into temptation but still felt it acutely. He recognized that the things Satan offered him, where desirable and weakened condition from fasting must have amplified his longing for them. This experience caused him to grow in compassion and understanding for us as we suffer and struggle with temptations.
3] Impeccability: means inability to sin. Jesus never sinned. He never succumbed to temptation, or has a evil thought or desire or said a sinful word. because Jesus is impeccable, his obedience and sympathy are increased.

Crucifixion was a form of death penalty used in the ancient roman empire. Jesus' crucifixion was unique, of course, because it also served as an atoning offering for sin. 
When we speak of the imputation of our sin to Jesus on the cross, God counted Jesus as if he had personally committed every sin imputed to him. Once our sin was reckoned to his account, God viewed him as being guilty of all the sins that were assigned to him. Christ's role as our substitute is reflected in the fact that bible often refers to him as our sacrifice. It's also why he is called our ransom. 
Human death is always a divine judgement against sin. Jesus' death was also a divine judgement against sin. Before laid our guilt on Him, Jesus couldn't' die. But once our sin was imputed to him on the cross, his death became not only possible but necessary.

Plan of redemption: God's plan to redeem humanity and the rest of creation depend on him, fulfilling his covenant promises to establish his kingdom on the earth under the kingship of a descendant of David, otherwise known as the Christ.
Jesus resurrection was a critical step that enabled God to fulfill his covenant promises.
Blessings of Salvation: The new testament associated Jesus resurrection was a wide variety of blessings we receive as a part of salvation. It results in our justification, which is the forgiveness of our sins. Its the source of regeneration of our spirit, and it opens the door for our eternal inheritance. It produces good works and a true witness to Christ in pour bodies and lives. And it's the source of future bodily resurrection of believers, when will have glorified bodies just like the one Jesus has.

"Creation Ordinances" is moral requirements established by God's works of creation. Bible relates the true story of creation in order to explain how humanity was actually designed to function within the world. Creation Ordinances are explicit such as God's command to be fruitful and multiply in Genesis 1:28. But others are implicit such as our obligation to keep the sabbath holy. The creation accounts don't say explicitly that human being should rest every 7th day, but in the ten commandments in Exodus 20:11, Moses clarified that God's pattern of working six days and resting on the seventh obligated human being to do the same. So as we think about the significance and role of humanity is both natural and helpful to start with our creation.

The book of Genesis contains two accounts of creation. One is Genesis 1;1-2:3 and the other is in Genesis 2:4-25. Together these accounts give us a general picture of how and why God created us. In the first creation account in genesis 1:2, we're told that the creation was originally formless and empty. Then, in the rest of the chapter we were told that God spent six days forming and filling the universe. A this point, humanity was clearly distinguished from the rest of creation. Human beings were created in God's image and given authority over his other creatures.
2. Gen 2:4-25- God;s work on the sixth day when he created the land, animals and humanity. Here, we're told that God formed the animals from the dust. He also made the first man Adam in the same way. In order to give him a helper, God created the first women, Eve to be his wife, creating her from his ribs. This made Eve unique amongst all.

The Bible clearly teaches Adam and Eve were created to be superior to the rest of the God's earthly creatures. But the real proof of Adam and Eve's superiority over the rest of creation is found in the fact that God created them in His image and appointed to rule over creation on his behalf. God created humanity to reflect his glory and his attributes in ways that other creatures couldn't. Human beings are likeness of God. Our very existence points to God's power and goodness and because no other earthly creature is God's image, no other creature carries this much honor or inherent dignity. God appointed our first parents to rule over every other creature he had made. Its our job to administer God's rule over the earth. God has delegated the administration of His creation to us, and not to any other animals

"Likeness"- a statue, a sketch, the appearance or sound of something compared to another: having a similar form. "image" and "likeness" both describe a model or sketch of greater reality. Scripture affirms that God alone is God. We're God's images and likenesses because we rule over the earth as God's servant kings and are endowed with the necessary qualities and abilities to perform our duties.

Our definition of Christian ethics focuses on God and His blessings rather than on terms like good or evil, or right or wrong. Those things that receive God's blessings are good and right, whereas those things that do not receive his blessing are wrong and evil.
1.DIVINE NATURE- God himself is the ultimate standard of right and wrong,of good and evil.God is not accountable to any standard outside himself.
2 DIVINE ACTIONS-God's actions demonstrates the standard of morality. God shows his approval by bestowing blessings. He shows his hatred by withholding blessings and pouring out curses. Many times the Bible communicates right and wrong by recording God's reactions rather that by explicitly labeling things good or evil.

Obedience to God's commands must be done with proper motive.Unless a work is done with right motive , it is not a work that God will reward with blessings. 

1.FAITH
Only believers who are indwelled by the Holy Spirit can do works that God rewards with blessings.
Only believers have hearts that are purified by faith. Saving faith motivates good works. This is the faith possessed by believers and only by believers. Unless our attempts to seeks God's blessings are founded on faith, we cannot please God and therefore cannot be rewarded by Him.
2. LOVE
Our works are useless if they are not motivated by love.
Works and even spiritual gifts that produce beneficial results merit no reward if they are not motivated by love.
Love is an aspect of every law God requires us to obey . If we do not act in love, no work we do can conform to his standard.Our love mist be both for God and neighbor.

THREEFOLD CRITERIA
Westminister Confession of faith says" Works done by ungenerate men may be things which God commands and of good use both to themselves and others , yet because they proceed not from an heart purified by faith, nor are done in a right manner , according to the word; nor to a right end , the glory of God;they are therefore sinful and cannot please God.
The threefold criteria are
1.PROPER MOTIVE
Unless a work is done with right motive , it is not a work that God will reward his blessings.Only believers are hearts are purified by faith. saving faith motivates good works. Our works are useless if they are not motivate by love Our love must be both for God and neighbor
2. PROPER STANDARD
In order for works to be good , they must be done according to the standard of Word of God, God's revelation.All commands of scriptures are designed to guide us.
3. PROPER GOAL
Good works may have any number of innumerate goals. Everything in the Christian life should be done in a way that honors God and brings Him glory. God approves of works intended to bring him glory and He condemns works that disregard or oppose his glory

Sin is any want of conformity unto or transgression of the law of God. Adam and Eve were created sinless. To continue in God's covenant blessings and avoid covenant curses they needed to remain loyal to the terms of God's covenants. The serpent tempted eve to eat the forbidden fruit and she gave it to Adam and he ate it. God cursed Adam and Eve because of their disloyalty. "the fall"- the events from the serpent's temptation through God's judgement when Adam and Eve's sin caused humanity to fall out of God's favor and blessings. Consequences of the fall- Gen 3:16-19- Eve- Pain in childbirth, strife in her relationship with Adam, death
Adam- difficulty subduing and cultivating the earth, death.

The authorship of human sin refers to who is ultimately to blame for it. Adam and Eve tried to blame to someone else for their sin. Adam explicitly blamed Eve and implicitly blamed God who had created her. (Gen 3:12). Eve blamed the serpent. (Gen 3:13). God punished each one.: the serpent for deceiving the women, Eve- for being deceived, eating the fruit and misleading her husband. Adam- for being misled and eating the fruit. 
The serpent was the ultimate author of sin because it was the first to come up with the idea to sin and the first to try to cause humanity to sin. Adam and Eve freely chose to sin and in this sense, authored human sin. God isn't culpable or guilty or of compelling anyone to sin. (1 john 1:5). God hates sin and can't be tempted by sin.(james 1:13)

In term original sin refers to the consequences of humanity's first sin. Original sin- The condition to which Adam's natural descendants are born as a result of Adam's fall into sin. 
Corruption- Humanity's relationship to sin: posse non peccare (the ability not to sin)- Adam and Eve's original sinless state
non posse non peccare (the inability not to sin)- Adam and Eve's corruption removed their capacity to please God and to merit his blessings. Every part of our human nature has been completely affected by sin, our bodies, our minds, and our hearts.
Concepts- Sin has damaged our capacity for conceptual thought and caused us to believe that false ideas are true.
Behavior- Adam and Eve's sin served as the model for all the behavioral sins that have plagued humanity's sins. God has given fallen humanity over to its sinful appetites.
Emotions- Sin prevents us from loving God and our neighbors as we should and from manifesting other righteous emotions. Apart from God's saving grace, we have no ability to please God.

God the Son, the second person of the trinity joined the covenant as its mediator. As the mediator, the Son intercedes for God's covenant people. He reconciles us to God by taking the blame and punishment for our sins. He preserves the integrity of the covenant and the lives of his people by suffering the covenant curses on our behalf. Similarly, through his obedience to the covenant's requirements of human loyalty, the Son earns the covenant blessings for himself. And then shares them with the sinners he redeems. The Son's mediation provided forgiveness and salvation for the old testament saints on the basis of his promised future work. The Son's mediation of the covenant of grace centered around his incarnation as Jesus his life of perfect faith and obedience, his death on the cross, his resurrection from the dead and his ascension to heaven. As mediator of covenant of grace, he fulfilled the covenant of works on our behalf and guaranteed that we would receive its blessings.

The covenant of grace was administered by various covenant representatives: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and Jesus. 
Adam: The covenant of grace was instituted with Adam immediately after he fell into sin. The Adamic administration provided humanity the immediate opportunity to reconcile our relationship with God. 
Noah: The covenant confirmed with Noah after the flood explicitly incorporated all the terms of Adam's administration. The Noahic administration expanded the covenant blessings by adding God's promise never again to destroy the earth with flood waters. 
Abraham: Under Abraham, the covenant included the previous terms and added God's promises to turn Abraham's descendants into a mighty nation and to bless all nations through them. IN the Abrahamic administration, the nation of Israel was charged with expanding God's kingdom throughout the earth. 
Moses: With the Mosaic administration, God confirmed his promises to Abraham provided structure for Israel gave it the first codified version of the law redirected Israel to build his kingdom throughout the world.
David: In the Davidic administration God confirmed the Mosaic administration revealed that the greatest covenant blessings would be fulfilled under the kingship of David and his dynastic heirs. 
Jesus: Jesus' administration is typically referred to as the "new covenant". In it, God established a permanent, unbreakable covenant in which his people would receive all his covenant blessings.

1. CLAIM OF AUTHORITY-
In the earliest history recorded in the Bible , God spoke directly to humanity and his speech carried authority. All things were created by the power of his word. In the days of Moses  ,God encoded his spoken word in the written form . His spoken word is the basis for his written word. God's written word is his authoritative covenant document that his people are obligated to obey. Jesus frequently appealed to scripture to justify and explain his actions. Because Scriptures carries  God's authority, we are morally obligated to conform all our choices, actions thoughts and feelings to it. We must keep the breadth of Biblical instruction . The letter clearly identifies a man named 'James' as the author. Two men named James had enough authority in the early church to write a letter like this: James, son of Zebedee and James the brother of Jesus- leader of the early church in Jerusalem. Critical scholars still offer at least three arguments for this objection. Three arguments by scholars for
 1) Psuedonymity: No relation to Jesus- there is no mention of the author's relation to Jesus but Jude never mentioned his blood ties in his epistle either. 
2) Hellenistic culture- the book gives evidence that the author was aware of Greek culture. Many Jews in Palestine had knowledge of Hellenistic philosophy and religion. 
3) Inconsistencies- some ideas in the epistle don't match James' theological outlooks in other new Testament books(Acts 21:17-25, Galatians 2:12). James position on the law is actually consistent with his theology in Acts and Galatians.

James identifies his readers as ''the twelve tribes scattered among the nation''(1:2) and believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ (2:1). These verses indicate that James' original audience was made up, primarily of Jewish Christians who lived outside of Palestine. It is possible that these were members of the Jerusalem church scattered throughout Judea and Samaria following Stephen's Martyrdom. James vocabulary supports the idea that his original readers were Jewish followers of Jesus. "Synagoge"- reference to Jewish gatherings. "Kurios Saboth"- from a common Old Testament name for God of Israel. There were also many Gentiles converts to Judaism who attended synagogues (Acts 8, 10)

James lived and ministered in Jerusalem until he was martyred in AD 62. His audience was most likely scattered throughout Judea and Samaria, as far as Phoenicia, Antioch and Cyprus. Date- The earliest likely date for the letter's composition is AD 44. He became a significant leader of the early church in Jerusalem, by the time Peter was released from prison in AD 44. The latest possible of composition for the epistle is AD 62, when he was matryed. Two reasons to think that the date of composition was earlier in this timeline: James' use of the word: 'Synagogue"- James may have written before Christians were forced out of the synagogues. 
Purpose- No mention of Jewish- Gentile controversies- it's likely that they hadn't yet become a factor for James' audience. He called his audience to pursue wisdom from God, so that they would joy in their trials. These trials appear to have led some to abandon their loyalty to Christ and pursue "friendship with the world".

James' epistle reflects a long history of wisdom literature stemming from the Old Testament; Job, Ecclesiastes, Proverbs."wisdom psalms", prophetic wisdom sayings. James also reflects the contents of influential wisdom books outside of Scripture: (5:11) to promote perseverance. Beyond this, James touched on topics such as speech, the treatment of widows and orphans, poverty, and favoritism. These topics reflect numerous parallels with the content of the book of Proverbs. 
The wisdom of Sirach (e.g James 1:5, and Sirach 1:26). The wisdom of Solomon. In addition to these types of wisdom literature, much of Jesus' instruction recorded in the Gospels is characteristic of wisdom teaching in Israel. And interpreters have noted a number of similarities between James' writing and Jesus' instruction.

First words about the wisdom began with a call to joy. James 1:2- Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sister, whenever you face trials of many kinds. This passage may seem odd to us, especially because it addresses people who were facing " trials of many kinds". But James' appeal to consider this pure joy is not as unusual as we might think. The phrase "pure joy" comes from the Greek expression pasan charan that may be translated unmitigated joy." This kind of encouragement fits well with other wisdom literature of James' day. Many times wisdom writings encouraged those who suffered to consider themselves blessed. Jesus, for instance, closed the beatitudes in Matthew 5:12 with the call to "rejoice and be glad" in the face of persecution. It's often difficult to see the benefits of suffering so James told his readers to pursue wisdom from God(1:5). Wisdom strengthens our confidence that God has ordained for us the blessing of eternal salvation.

The majority of interpreters reject Pauline authorship. 
First, Anonymity: this book is anonymous and it was Paul's practice to name himself in his epistles. In fact, as 2 Thessalonians 2: 2 makes clear, Paul was deeply concerned that forgeries had spread under his name. So, it seems unlikely that he would have failed to identify himself had he written Hebrews. 
Second. Themes, the book of Hebrews emphasizes subjects that don't receive much, if any, attention in Paul's letter. For instance, author of Hebrews mentioned Melchizedek three times. He drew attention to the Old Testament tabernacle. And he dealt at length with Christ as the high priest. Taken together, these themes distinguish the book of Hebrews from books that we know were written by Paul. 
Third. Generation: the strongest reason for doubting Pauline authorship is the way the writer of Hebrews distanced himself from the first generation of Jesus' followers.

The author wrote to a specific audience with whom he was personally familiar. 
1. Jewish- the author referred to the Old Testament Israelites as "our forefathers". It's no wonder, that from as early as the time of tertullian, who lived from AD 155-230, the title attached is "Pros Hebraious","For the Hebrews". 
2. Hellenistic- Hebrews contains theological teachings that were common among Jews living outside of Palestine. The content of Hebrews indicates that the audience was familiar with theological teachings that were more common among Jews living outside of Palestine than among more traditional Jewish circles within Palestine.
3. Immature- The original audience may have remained theologically immature because they didn't respect their leaders. In heb 5.11- the author reprimanded his audience for being ''slow to learn''. 
4. Persecuted- As we read, it is evident that original audience has already faced persecution in the past, some in the present, perhaps more severely in future.
5. Near Apostasy- as the audience faced persecution, some of them were near apostasy. Rather than simply being discouraged or weakened by sufferings, they were in danger of turning away from Christ entirely.

Hebrews employs many literary devices that were associated with persuasive oratory or urgent debate in 1st century:
1. One rhetorical device called synkrisis is a detailed comparison between two or more things designed to convince audience to affirm speaker's point of view, For eg, Heb 7:11-28. Rather than asserting his belief, author gave a compelling eight point comparison between Melchizedek and Christ. 
2. Another one is exempla. Exempla are lists of illustrations or examples that follow one after the other to build a persuasive argument for a paticular point of view. This technique appears in familiar list of faithful in Heb.11
3. Third is known as Hebrew expression qol wahomer. This expression is well known from both Greco- Roman and rabbinical traditions and can be translated "light to heavy" "less to great" etc. This argument says that because simple premise is true then surely the more difficult conclusion must also be true.

In Hebrews 5.12 it says of the need of "milk" is an expression used for immature believers. The one who needs milk is compared to a spiritual baby and is unskillful in the word of righteousness. Those who are known to the basic principles of the oracles of God, are compared to the one who can have strong meat which is they have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.

1. Factual Backgrounds- the book of Hebrews quotes refers to or alludes to the old testament nearly 100 times. The author of Hebrews incorporated historical facts into his presentation of the christian faith. (Hb 7:2). 
2. Theological outlooks- the author focused on theological beliefs affirmed by the Hebrew scriptures. God's son, angels are serving spirits, lower than angels, God's oath to Abraham, God as a consuming fire.
3. Moral Obligation- Old testament moral requirements were to remain as standards in New Testament times: not to rebel, not to be discouraged, adhere to righteousness, confidence in God( Hb 13:6)
4. Eschatological Predictions- the author used several old testament eschatological predictions to show that God's final judgement and blessings are fulfilled in Christ: angels will worship, current arrangement destroyed, universal sovereignty, royal priesthood from God, no further sacrifices etc.
5. Dynastic ideals- the author referred to a number of dynastic ideals that were established for David's lineage in the Psalms. Jesus is the perfect fulfillment of the ideas of David's house, royal son to rule nations, vindication shared with Israel, devotion of body to God. (Hb10.5, Ps 40.6-8)

The author of Hebrews wrote that his audience should follow Jesus because Jesus is God's supreme source of divine revelation. The author acknowledge that God spoke through angels throughout Old Testament history. But Jesus brought revelation that was far superior to any revelation given through angels. In Hb 1:5-14, Jesus is greater than angels because He alone is God's messianic son. Jesus fulfilled ideals for David's house, fulfilled David's prediction of victory of God's messianic son over all God's enemies. By Contrast, he noted that angels are nothing more than spirit sent to serve those who inherit salvation in Christ. 
In 2:1-4, the author exhorted of the great message of salvation by Jesus and reminded them that violating messages from angels received punishment from God. 
Hb. 2:5-9, supports belief in the supremacy of Christ by explaining that Jesus is now ruler over angels and in the future all believers will reign over them with him. And finally, Heb 2:10-18, author demonstrated that Jesus is Abraham's descendant. And Jesus will share his Glory with Abraham's descendants not with angels.

The author of Hebrews explained the supremacy of Christ as God's ordained high priest by discussing how the new covenant is superior to the old. First, Hb 8:1-3 introduces the idea that Jesus mediates the new covenant as the royal high priest in heaven. In Heb. 9:1-28, He elaborated on the fact that Jesus' heavenly royal priesthood is superior to the Levitical priesthood. He began this section by mentioning the arrangements of Moses earthly tabernacle revealing features that resemble God's heavenly sanctuary. Jesus brought final forgiveness of sin. Jesus died as a ransom to set his people free from judgement. The author ends his portion by stating that Christ will return but not to bear sin again. He called his audience to remember the past and not throw away their confidence. He reminded that they had willingly and joyfully suffered in the past because they Knew they had better and lasting possessions in the world to come.

God's plan to redeem humanity from the corruption and consequences of sin was made before he created the Universe.
 ( Ephesians 1:3-4 ,3:11 which speaks of God's eternal purpose historically accomplished by Jesus
 2 Thessalonians 2:13 says that we were chosen for salvation from beginning .
 2 Timothy 1:9,10) speaks of grace that was given to us before the beginning of time.
Ephesians 1:11 says that our redemption was determined before the creation of the world.
in Ephesians 1:11,Romans 8:29,30 and Ephesians 1:5 the Greek word 'Proorizo' is used ,this term is most commonly translated as predestination .
So from above references we all agree that God's decision to save sinners was made as part of his eternal counsel, before the foundation of the world.

God's eternal plan of redemption involves the work of all three persons of the Trinity.
THE FATHER- originated the agreement because of his desire to redeem fallen human beings from the course of sin (Ephesians 3:10,11). According to Paul it was the Father's eternal purpose to accomplish our redemption through Christ.
THE SON- agreed to add a perfect human nature to his perfect divine nature to die on behalf of sinners.(2 Timothy 1:9) Paul said that we received grace in the Son before the beginning of time
THE HOLY SPIRIT agreed to enable and empower the Son's work and to apply salvation to those whom the Son redeemed .(2 Thessalonians 2:13)

COVENANT OF GRACE-The covenant relationship God established with humanity after our fall into sin that provides forgiveness and redemption on the basis of God's mercy in Christ
FULFILLMENT-The covenant of grace fulfills part of God's eternal plan for history
The Father fulfilled his eternal decree in to covenant of grace by sending the Son and the/Spirit to work,appointing the son to the office of Messiah(John 5:36), giving the Son his powerful spirit without limit.( John 3:34),and preparing the Son's perfect human nature.
The Son fulfilled his eternal agreement to redeem humanity by veiling his divine glory, adding a full human nature, to his full divine nature,living a perfect life and dying an atoning death(Philippians 2:5-8)
The Holy Spirit fulfilled His part in God's eternal counsel by enabling and empowering the Son's incarnation and subsequent work, empowering Christ's death on the cross and his resurrection, regenerating our spirit, empowering us to resist sin ,giving us spiritual gift and securing our salvation

God the Son joined the covenant of grace as its mediator as
1. He intercedes for God's covenant people
2. He reconciles us to God by taking the blame and punishment for our sins
3. He preserves the integrity of the covenant and the lives of his people by suffering the covenant curses and earning the covenant blessings
The Son began to mediate the covenant of grace when it was first made, back in the Garden of Eden ,when God first offered redemption to Adam and Eve. And He continues to mediate ever since.
Jesus ' role us our fully divine and fully human covenant mediator is what enabled him to atone for our sin  by dying in our place and because this solution to human sin will always be available in the covenant of grace, there will never be a need for divine providence to introduce another covenant, another covenant representative or another mediator.

ADMINISTRATIONS;
The covenant of grace was administered by various covenant representatives:
1. ADAM-  The Adamic administration provided humanity the immediate opportunity to reconcile our relationships with God(Gen 4:25,26)
2. NOAH- The Noahic administration expanded the covenant blessing by adding God's promise never again to destroy the earth with flood waters.
3. ABRAHAM- In the Abrahamic administration the nation of Israel was charged with expanding God's kingdom throughout the earth (Romans 4:13)
4. MOSES- In Mosaic administration God confirmed his promise to Abraham,provided structure fir the nation of Israel,gave Israel the first codified version of the law,redirected Israel t build his kingdom through out world .
5. David-In the Davidic administration , the Mosaic administration was confirmed,it was revealed that the greatest covenant blessings would be fulfilled under the kingship of /David and his dynastic heirs.
6. Jesus- In the New Covenant God established a permanent unbreakable covenant in which his people would receive all his covenant blessings.

Distance:
the information we receive about the distant things is fallible, but we need to rely strongly on the Holy Spirit to help us evaluate our imagination.

Ethics is the study of moral right and wrong, the study of what is good and evil. Christian ethics is; theology viewed as a means of determining which human persons acts and attitude receive God's blessing and which do not. 
Our definition focuses on God and his blessing rather than on terms like good or evil, or right or wrong. Those things that receive God's blessings are good and right, whereas those things that do not receive his blessings are wrong and evil. 
1. Divine Nature- God himself is the ultimate standard of right or wrong, of good and evil. God is not accountable to any standard outside himself. 
2. Divine Action- God's actions demonstrate the standard of morality. God shows His approval by bestowing blessings. He shows his hatred by withholding blessings and pouring out curses.

Unless a work is done with a right motive, it is not a work that God will reward with blessings.

Middle ages mistake: because the bible is inspired by God, it communicates in extraordinary ways that exceed human comprehension. Ordinary- The bible communicates in ordinary human language, using all the normal conventions of human communication. Moral laws are typically thought to convey God's ethical standards and are usually identified with the Ten Commandments. Civil Laws provide for the governing of society, especially during the period of Israel's theocracy. Ceremonial laws. in turn, are those which provide instruction for worshiping God. Frequently, these are most closely associated with the Old Testament sacrificial system, and tabernacle and temple administration. There are basic types of revelation; general revelation, which comes to us through the creation in general and existential revelation, which comes to us through persons, remember that God reveals his will to us in all three of these ways. Even though special, general, existential revelation differ in some respects, they all communicate content in the form of facts. These facts include everything that God reveals about our situation, such as events, people, objects, ideas, duties, actions- even God and his revelation. 
It is possible to speak of the facts that God's revelation communicates in countless ways. In addition to speaking about facts in general, we will also speak of goals and means. Goals are the intended or potential outcomes of thoughts, words, and deeds. They include everything we  might think, say, or do, and any tool or method that we might use in order  to accomplish our objectives.

God is our ultimate fact, our ultimate ethical environment. In order for us to know our obligations before God, he must first reveal himself to us. God's character is our ultimate norm or standard. Correspondingly, from the situational, perspective, God is our ultimate fact, our ethical environment. The reality of God's existence rules over every ethical question and obligates us to live by the standard of his character. God is the supreme authority over all creation. His authority is absolute, and his character is the perfect expression of his will. So, when he reveals his character is the perfect expression of his will. So, when he reveals his character, that revelation is the means through which God exercises control much like human governments exercise control through their laws. And just as human beings obey civil laws because they bow to the government's authority, all creation must obey God's laws by bowing to his authority.

Goals- goal in ethics, we have in mind the expected outcomes of our endeavors. In many ways, this is no different from the way that we set goals to accomplish anything else in life. They can be things we hope to accomplish immediately, or things we plan to do in the distant future. Our goals give direction to our actions. Special, general, and existential revelation each teach us important generic facts, each type of revelation also provides us with goals that we must adopt in Christian ethics. Existential revelation also helps  us to discern good goals from evil goals, especially through our consciences. And in the case of believers, the Holy spirit is another source of existential revelation, moving within us so that we pursue good goals and shun evil ones.

The strategy of rigor results from mistaken beliefs about the Bible's similarity to modern world and about its clarity. This strategy gives little or no consideration to the ways that the facts, goals, and means of Scripture differ from those in the modern world. The strategies has some consequences too. Firstly, it destroys Christian freedom by prohibiting behaviors that are wrong under certain conditions, but good under other conditions. The classic example of this are Paul's discussions of food that had been sacrificed to idols in 1 Corinthians 8-10, and in Romans 14. 
Second, a strategy of rigor also inspires despair in believers by turning God's word into a heavy burden. God gave his word to his people to bless them, not to oppress them. And there are many, many places in Scripture that state this idea. example is Mark 2;27 and in Romans 9;4,5. 
A good corrective is to realize  that modern situations are sufficiently different from biblical situations so that we cannot simply mimic the application we find in the scripture.

Jesus spoke about the kingdom of God in the sermon on the mount found in Mt 5-7. Three specific times when Jesus spoke of the kingdom of God as the goal of ethics during his sermon about earthly needs. In each of these sections, Jesus indicated that the kingdom of God must be the main priority of our lives. 
1. Beatitudes- Christian ethics- viewed as means of determining which human person, acts and attitudes receive God's blessing and which do not. So, which the beatitudes, Jesus began his Sermon by encouraging people to live ethically. Jesus set forth the blessings and ethics in terms of kingdom of God. Jesus specifically set forth the blessings of god's kingdom as the reward or goal that was to motivate his listeners to live ethically. 
2. Lord's Prayer- Jesus indicated that all creatures in heaven already obey God's will. but Jesus instructed us to pray that all creatures on earth would obey the divine king in the same way. 
3. Earthly needs- Jesus made it very plain that the ultimate goal of the christian life, the greatest end toward which we are to strive is the glorification of God through the triumph of his Kingdom.

1. Kings- Kings were expected to protect and provide for their people, treat them with kindness, rule wisely to benefit their people. God is frequently presented as the suzerain or supreme emperor over all creation. God was king in a special way over Israel in the old testament and the church in the new testament.
2. People- in old testament often Abraham and his descendants and in New testament generally the church. They populate the whole world, improve the world as Go had improved the Garden of Eden. God ruled directly over all humanity. He intended the world to be his kingdom. The people that God has called to himself; when God create the world, he set up humanity as his vassal kings. 
3. Covenants- God administered his kingdom through covenants. His covenants expressed God's goodwill toward his people , listed the people's obligations towards God, and stated the consequences of obedience and curses for disobedience.

Historical phases- creation; initial peace, fall- rebellion, redemption- final peace
1. Initial peace- Adam and Eve were obedient servants. As a result, there was peace between God and humanity. All the components of the covenant worked properly to favor humanity. And at first, Adam and eve were blessed with close fellowship with God and continued to live in the Garden of Eden where life was easy and blissful.
2. Rebellion- Humanity violated one of their covenant obligations. As a result, they received the covenant curses. Instead of turning to God in repentance and keeping our covenant obligations, we continued to rebel and to perpetuate the covenant curses. But God did not abandon us to rebellion and curse. Instead he determined to bring final peace to his kingdom and to return blessings to  his people.
3. Final Peace- God began to restore peace to his kingdom immediately after humanity's fall into sin. Protoevangelion- God offered to send a redeemer to rescue humanity from the curse of sin. Therefore, God was working towards the goal of full redemption and success of his kingdom. But he did not restore his kingdom to the glory it had displayed during the initial peace days.

God is the ultimate fact in our situation because he gives existent and meaning to every other fact. 
a. Authority- God's right to rule derives from the fact that he is the creator and sustainer of all creation. Absolute- He has complete and total freedom on his creation. Exclusive- God's authority is always superior to creaturely authority. Exhaustive- He has authority on everything in every detail. 
b. Control- God powerfully governs everything that exists. Sovereign- He has an unlimited ability and right to control the creation. 
moral- Creation is conducive to morality. He provides the means and the opportunity to avoid sin. 
c. Presence- 1. Covenant King- Our first parents were vassal kings whose job it was to spread God's kingdom throughout the earth. 2. Modern Christians, often pay little attention to angels and demons the fact is that angels and demons have significant impact on the things that happen in our lives. Inhabitants- Scripture teaches that God has also populated the universe with a vast number of spiritual persons known as angels and demons. Both angels and demons are intelligent, rational human beings that have wills and personalities. All prenatural beings were originally angels. 
a. Angels- They serve as God's loyal messengers and agents. They communicate his word to human beings and interact with humanity. By observing God's salvation of humanity, angels learn more about Lord's glory and are better able to praise him.
b. Demons- They are fallen rebellious angels. They are able to interact with the natural realm which they do in order to harm us.

The details of the natural world are nearly limitless.
1. Creation- Human beings are of central importance upon the earth, part of nature, lords and rulers over nature. God has called human beings to govern the world- to administer it in a way that promotes life and growth, turning the world into a kingdom that is fit for him to inhabit. 
2. Fall- When Adam and Eve fell into sin, God cursed both the human race and the earth, subjecting them to corruption. Nature is the recipient of God's cursing. The earth still proclaims God's goodness and majesty, and God uses it to provide many good things.
3. Redemption- In redemption, the effects of the fall are reversed. The natural realm becomes an instrument of redemption, a recipient of redemption.

Both angels and demons in our ethical environment have impact on our lives. Angels serve as God's loyal messengers and agents. They communicate his word to human beings, and they interact with humanity on God's behalf. Eg, in 2 Kings 19:35 we learn the angel of the Lord slew 185,000 Assyrian troops in one night to halt Sennacherib's invasion of Judah. another one is, Psalms 91:11-12 teaches that angels also work to prevent God's faithful followers from stubbing their toes. 
Demons are also able to interact with the natural realm which they do in order to harm us. In New testament the most common way demons attack us is by tempting them into idolatry. Another one is temptation and harming us. For eg, in Job 1-2 we find that Satan, the chief of demons was permitted to destroy Job's possession and health and to kill his children.

Humanity was created to reflect God's goodness. 
1. Image- God, the great king over all creation appointed human beings to be his living images. He created us with qualities that reflected his own perfections. But we were created without flaw and without sin, in conformity to the standard of his character. 
2. Blessing- Whatever God blesses and approves id good, and whatever God curses and condemns is evil. God blessed Adam and Eve because they had the innate attribute of goodness. 
3. Cultural Mandate- God appointed humanity: to be his vassal kings on earth and to fill, subdue and rule it for his glory. God indicated that humanity was not only physically capable of accomplishing this task but morally capable as well.

The Fall has prevented human beings from obtaining a proper knowledge of God's commands.
1. Access to Revelation- The Fall limits the Holy Spirit's work of illumination and inward leading. Illumination: a divine gift of knowledge or understanding that is primarily cognitive. Inward leading: a divine gift of knowledge or understanding that is primarily emotive or intuitive. God reveals himself in ways that bless those who love him and that curse those who hate him.
2. Understanding of Revelation- Moral understanding depends on more than mere cognition, involves the whole person. Instead of accepting true knowledge from God, we believe that lies that our sinful hearts invent. 
3. Obedience to Revelation- There is a sense in which knowledge and obedience are essentially the same thing. Obedience leads to Knowledge- obedience is a prerequisite for knowledge.
4. Redemption- Redemption began immediately after the fall, when God extended mercy to Adam and Eve, did not immediately eradicate all the effects of the Fall.

The term imagination simply refers to our ability to form mental images of things that are beyond our experience. It may seem strange to think imagination as a way of acquiring ethical knowledge. But our imaginative abilities are vital to learning and thinking about God, the world and ourselves. First, a form of creativity. Second, the ways imagination enables us to think about subjects that exist in different periods of time. And third, how imagination allows us to think about things that are separated from us by physical distance. 
1. Creativity- Imagination is involved in everything that we make or create. It helps us to form and to recognize moral patterns and analogies.
2. Time- Imagination can help us think about things that do not exist at the moment we are thinking about them. Without our ability to imagine the future, we would not be able to apply God's word to our lives. 
3. Distance- When people and things are so distant from us that they are not currently part of our experience, we have to use our imagination to think about them.

A. Reason- we evaluate the information we have received. Our intellect comes from God, and the Holy Spirit helps us use it rightly. It has an important role to play in our decision-making process. Reason is the capacity to make logical interferces and to judge logical consistency. 
B. Conscience- Every time sensory data is processed mentally, we are exercising reason to some degree. Scripture uses reason and it regularly calls on us to do the same. Conscience is the God given ability to discern good and evil. It can give true affirmation that our behavior is pleasing to God, rightly condemn us a guilty and encourage us to repent. 
C. Emotions- The solution to sin's corrupting influence is to rely on the power of the Holy Spirit who works within us as we strive to conform our conscience to God's word.

Will is the capacity for making decisions, volition and ability to make choices. Our will is affected by our fallen nature. For the Christian, the Holy Spirit enables us to make decisions that please God. Indwelling sin many persuade us to make sinful decisions. Our will maybe active or passive. It also functions in a passive, unconscious way when we respond by reflex. 
Our will is involved in each and everything we choose to think, say or do. It is the faculty we use to make every decision in our lives. We must will what God's Word commands and we must allow the Holy Spirit  working within us to influence our will in positive ways.

Our words are the commentaries on our wills, for when we speak we make, as it were a dissection of our own hearts. Out of the good treasure of his heart, a good man would bring forth, not harsh but kindness, gentleness, compassion filled works and out of  the evil treasure, the hypocrite  would only bring forth bitterness, and harsh surmises. Therefore, as it says in Psalms 19.14 let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in thy sight, we should pray that our life be pleasing and commitments be to God alone.
