The famous theologian Thomas Aquinas, who lived from around 1225 to 1275, championed a much more responsible approach to Quadriga. Unlike many of his predecessors and contemporaries, he insisted that the literal sense is the singular meaning of Scripture. He also taught that nothing necessary to faith was communicated as spiritual meaning without being taught elsewhere in scripture in the literal sense. Not all scholars would agree that Aquinas always followed these principles as he interpreted the scriptures, but nevertheless he insisted the principle that every sense of a passage of scripture must be tied to its literal meanings. The meaning of scripture is multifaceted. Each passage's meanings has many smaller parts of aspects that contribute to the singular unified meaning we've called its literal sense. But the most responsible approach to the richness of scriptures is to ensure that everything we say about a biblical passage is tied to its grammar set within the historical context of the ancient world.

Biblical Elaborations are places where one part of scripture directly or indirectly comments on an aspect of the meaning of another passage in scripture, these elaborations always accord with and confirm original meaning.
1] The first biblical elaboration of this passage is primarily a repetition of these exact words in Deuteronomy 5, where Moses reminded the nation of Israel of the content of Ten Commandments. In Deuteronomy 5.17, scripture again says, You shall not murder. This repetition confirmed the commandment and reminded God's people of the term of his covenant. 
2] The second type of elaboration is clarification, and we find clarification of commandment against murder in Numbers 35. In that chapter, Moses distinguished between murder and accidental manslaughter.
3] The third type of biblical elaboration was expansion, in which scripture provides additional information about the passage or topic it references. We find an expansion of commandment against murder in Matthew 5, where Jesus criticized the rabbis of his day for wrongly limiting the commandment's scope

Interpretation is simply trying to understand what the text says, in short, hermeneutics. Interpretation that does not somehow relate what is being displayed or described to something within the personality or experience of the visitor will be sterile. The aim of interpretation is not instruction, but provocation. It should stimulate people into form of action. Thus we should also prevent it from being misapplying in our sphere of influence too. We should first ask for the guidance of the Holy Spirit to help us think correctly, lest we distort the scriptures. The goal should be understanding the Author's Intended meaning and must follow principles derived from God's Word. It shouldn't be of what we're meaning it to be, thus preventing from misapplication.

The writer, the document, and the audience are interdependent guides to meaning. If we fail to account for their interdependence, it's very easy to fall into error. We need guidance from all of these sources so that our readings of Scripture aren't skewed by an imbalanced emphasis on just one or two. The three interpretive fallacies are 
Intentional fallacy- If we overemphasize the author, we often fall into an intentional fallacy. An intentional fallacy relies too heavily on what we think we know about a writer and his intentions, and de-emphasizes the things we learn about document and audience. 
Graphic fallacy- over emphasizes the document itself to the relative exclusion of contextual considerations like writer and audience. 
Affective fallacy- Overemphasizes the audience and focuses too heavily on how scripture affects the audience.

Normally a summary will come from a particular vantage point or emphasize a particular concept that appears in the passage. Since every passage has a complex meaning, summaries help us by narrowing our study, allowing us to focus on just a portion of what the passage has to say. Multiple legitimate summaries bring us closer and closer to the passage's full meaning. One student summarizes how characters developed in the story. One summarizes cultural values of the day. Another summarizes the events in chronological order. All of these responses are legitimate summaries of the presentation's meaning. But not the full meaning of the entire thing. So multiple summaries help us focus on individual aspects of meaning and allows us learn the whole picture. And taken together, it brings us closer and closer to the passage's full meaning.

God is immutable, meaning that he doesn't change. Since God is immutable. The biblical concept of divine immutability doesn't imply that God is inactive. But the God of Scripture is constantly interacting with his creation is real and meaningful ways. 

1. Eternal Counsel- Christian traditions understand God's eternal plan differently, everything God has done, is doing, and will do is part of a unified plan. God knows everything, and he is using that knowledge to direct history towards the ends for which he created it God's eternal counsel, or ultimate plan for history, is immutable and directs history toward the ends for which he created it.

2. Character - God reveals different aspects of his character more prominently at some times than others. Sometimes he displays his mercy, sometimes his wrath. Sometimes he reveals his omniscience and other times he hides it. But the full range of his attributes- his eternal nature- always stays the same. God's character, his essence, persons and attributes, never change.

3. Covenant Promises- Every revelation of God in scripture assumes that God will keep his covenant and his covenant promises. The original audiences were supposed to understand every passage of scripture in this light, and modern audiences should do the same. Where God hasn't made a promise, his words are best understood as threats of curse and offers of blessing.

There are at least three ways in which modern people are very similar to the people who first received the scriptures. First, all human beings, no matter when or where they live, are sinful images of God. Second, we suffer religious divisions. and third, humanity still includes the same classes of people. 
1. Sinful Images- God created humanity in his image, but we have fallen into sin. All recipients of scripture, whether ancient or modern, share the same sinful nature.
2. Religious Divisions- Both the original and modern audiences of scripture suffer religious divisions. Readers of scripture fall into one of three religious groups; Unbelievers- who refuse to submit to God. False believers- people who make superficial commitments to God. Believers- who make faithful commitments to God. 
3. Classes- the same classes of people exist for both the original and modern audiences. Many portions of scripture are directed toward particular classes. The connections we share with the classes of people that exist in every age can help guide our application of Scripture.

The developments between original and modern audiences should influence our application. We need to account for the epochal developments of redemptive history when we apply the Bible to modern life. 
The Bible's perspective on world history in three stages; 
Creation- the progressive nature of God's rule over creation has resulted in periodic developments that create discontinuity between the various epochs mentioned in scripture. When God first made the world. But theologians also commonly identify epochs according to God's various covenants throughout the Bible, especially those associated with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and David in the Old Testament, and with Jesus in the New Testament. 
Fall- when humanity first committed sin and was cursed by God. 
Redemption- the period following the fall, in which God redeems us from our sin. Soon after Adam and Eve fell into sin, God began a long slow process of redemption. And throughout the millennia, he had mercifully built his kingdom of redemption within and alongside the cursed creation.

Significant theological changes are the basis for identifying epochal divisions. Each epoch is period of time characterized by substantial and long lasting transitions in Old Testament theology. Time doesn't pass in sharply segmented periods. So, transitions between epochs generally took place gradually. And the epochs themselves often overlapped. The Old Testament reports many theological changes that took place throughout history. Theological changes occurred every time God altered his expectations regarding the concepts, behaviors and emotions of his people. And when the changes were significant enough, they became the basis for identifying epochal divisions. In similar way, theologians obviously tend to use theological criteria to delineate the epochs. But they still don't always agree on the divisions because theology within the Old Testament developed in different ways at different times. In a similar way, some parts of Old Testament theology advanced slowly, others proceeded at a medium pace, and others changed rapidly. And many of these parts did their growing at different times.

The divisions of the Old Testament make it clear that God wanted his people to apply theological themes in different ways at different times. And just as Old Testament believers weren't supposed to serve God as if they lived in earlier periods of history, New Testament believers should never apply the scriptures as if they live in earlier periods of history. Once God commanded a new way for sacrifice in worship, he expected his people never to return to the old ways. Christ's sacrifice has superseded every earlier form of sacrifice [Hebrews 8.13]
As people living under the new covenant, we follow Jesus the great son of David, as he leads his people into war against the forces of evil. Another striking example is the theme of leadership in battle. Imagine that you live in the period of David's dynastic covenant. You know that God has ordained the kings of Israel to lead his people into war against evil. The kings receive direction from God, and in turn direct the ways that you participate in war. 
God has always expected his people to serve him in ways that were appropriate to the covenant age in which they lived. So, understanding how Old Testament history divided into major covenant epoch is essential for applying the scriptures in our day.

Historical analysis is the study of Biblical literature, method of criticism of the Hebrew Bible ( Old Testament) and the New Testament that emphasizes the interpretation of biblical documents in the light of their contemporary environment.

Traditionally, faith and reason have each been considered to be sources of justification of religious belief. As both can purportedly serve this same epistemic function, it has been a matter of much interest to philosophers and theologians how the two are related and thus how the rational agent should treat claims derived from either source.  Some have held that there can be no conflict between the two - that reason properly employed and faith properly understood will never produce contradictory or competing claims. Others have maintained that faith and reason can be genuine contention over certain propositions or methodologies.

Biblical theology is in large measure a response to a cultural shift that be traced back to the 17th century. This is not to say that the concerns of biblical theology were entirely new, or belong only to the modern period. Christians have always explored the acts of God reported in Scripture. But in the modern period, significant cultural shifts took place that led theologians to emphasize interests as never before. 

Biblical theology is a Christian response to prominent intellectual movement in the modern period, often called modern historicism. In very general terms, modern historicism is the belief that history holds the key to understanding ourselves and the world around us. In this view, an adequate understanding of anything can only be gained by considering the place it occupies in history.

There are two common approaches to using scripture in modern Christianity. The task of interpreting scripture becomes a matter of discovering where in our theological system a particular passage fits. The usage of scriptures is for our won purpose. The bible may be viewed as authoritative, but it provides either confirmation of our preconceived ideas or divine advice for felt needs.

A theological reading or learning brings a map for a journey. The map may not give all the answers about a particular context but our reading sends us on a journey in which God in Scripture encounters us again and again. Reading scriptures is not about solving puzzles but discerning a mystery. Through scriptures, we encounter no less than the mysterious triune God himself.

Interest in the history of biblical interpretation is currently rising among students of the Bible. The rich history of its interpretation and that the history of biblical interpretation is marked to a great extent by the rich variety of distinct purposes of which biblical writings have been employed over the centuries. 

A veritable revolution in the biblical scholarship began toward the end of the renaissance among a group of Christian biblical scholars in Europe. On the model of leading classicists began to learn Hebrew and Greek and to consider the Bible from a similarly philological perspective.

The literature of the ancient Near East is very important to our purposes first because other premeval accounts were widely available to Moses, and second, because Moses actually interacted with other premeval accounts.
1. Availability- Many Nations in the near east had already written many myths and epics about premeval history. Moses was educated in the royal courts of Egypt. His writings indicate that he knew the literature of the ancient world. Moses wrote his own divinely- inspired and true account of the premeval period, he was quite aware of other literary traditions in the ancient Near East. 
2. Interaction- Moses wrote his history of the early times to counter falsehood with truth. His writings purposefully resembled other ancient Near Eastern writings to communicate God's truth in ways that Israel could understand. The Atrahasis Epic follows a basic threefold structure. Comparing Genesis with Atrahasis strongly supports the idea that Moses' formed his record with an intentional overarching structure.

Did God create the world in six ordinary days? Were the "days" of Genesis 1 great ages or epochs? Or is Genesis 1 a somewhat poetic, non-historical celebration of God's creative activity? All of these positions are acceptable within evangelical circles. Although my own view is that Genesis 1 teaches that God made the world as we know it today in six ordinary days, not all Bible-believing Christians hold to this view. This passage has three major steps, namely, a beginning, a middle, and an ending. 
Moses' creation account begins with 1:1-2. We may summarize the content of these verses as the "dark chaotic world." Chapter 1:3-31 form a middle section of the material which contains the so-called "six days of creation" or what we will cay the "six days of ordering" creation. Finally, 2:1-3 is the Sabbath Day, or as we will call it, the "ideal world."

The first portion of Genesis 1, we see a very important dramatic tension between the chaos covering the earth and the spirit of God. The opening of 1:1-2 sets the stage by giving a title in verse 1, and by describing the initial condition of the world in verse 2. The world is "formless and empty." Scholars believe that it meant that the world was uninhabitable, hostile toward human life, much like a desert or wilderness is inhospitable to human life. We see that an uninhabitable, dark, primordial, chaotic deep covered the entire earth. The second element in the dramatic tension also appears in 1:2. Moses wrote that "Spirit of God was hovering over the waters." The Hebrew term used here is merachefet which means to "fly above" or to "encircle above." So we see a very dramatic picture right at the beginning of this passage. On one side we see chaos on the earth; on the other side we see the spirit of God hovering above the chaos. In effect, God was ready to move into action to remedy the chaos which covered the earth.

Moses wrote to influence Israel to conform themselves to God's will. Other premeval accounts shared this same purpose. The cultures around Israel wrote their premeval accounts to justify their current religious and social programs. Their myths called the people to conform to creation ordinances of the Gods, the structures they had set for the universe. Moses focused on the ways Yahweh had created and ordered the world. Moses' policies and goals for Israel were true to God's design for the universe. Israel was moving toward God's ideal by going to Canaan. When God entered Sabbath rest, the tension between the chaos and God's hovering Spirit had been resolved. God had subdued the darkness, ruled over the chaotic deep, and delighted in his ideally ordered world. The creation story comes to an end with this delightfully peaceful vision of the universe in perfect harmony.

John 1:4-5 "In him was life, and that life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, but the darkness has not understood it." John continued to draw upon the themes of Genesis 1, especially the theme of the light which God brought to the dark chaotic world on the first day. John pointed to the incarnation of Christ as the light shining into the darkness of the world caused by sin. Followers of Christ find in Genesis 1 a portrait, an anticipation, of what God did in the first coming of Christ, the inauguration of the kingdom. Christ's appearance on earth was the beginning of God's final re-ordering of the world. We are right to place our faith in him and in him alone.

Flood of Deliverance- These chapters form a symmetrical five-step drama. 
1. Initial Covenant- The first step of this narrative also tells us that God spoke to Noah and revealed why he planned to destroy the human race. God planned to start over again by delivering Noah and his family. 
2. Enduring Covenant- God entered into a second covenant with Noah at the end of the flood narrative. God decided to give humanity the opportunity of a new order in the world. Noah was the mediator and God promised a covenant that flood won't destroy the earth and setting his bow was a sure sign.
3. Escape from Water- It appears in 7:1-16. Noah prepared the ark and brought animals of every kind into it. Noah, his family and the animals he had gathered were safely sealed in the ark. 
4. Exit to dry land- A dramatic counterpoint to the second step. After a waiting period, dry lands appeared God commanded Noah to leave the ark, just as he had previously ordered him to enter it. 
5. Divine Remembrance- The center or turning point of the narrative. God did not forget the covenant he made with Noah. he remembered the passengers of the ark, and moved on their behalf against raging flood.
 Moses' chief concern was to show that through Noah God brought humanity into a world of tremendous blessings.

1. Sons of Noah- Genesis 9.20-29 sets forth distinctions among the sons. Genesis 10:1-32 describes the distribution of Noah's sons and their descendants: 
Japhethites- North, Northeast, and northwest of Canaan, Hamites- Northern Africa
Canaan, son of Ham- land of Canaan, Israel's Promised Land, Shemites- Arabian Peninsula
2. Defeat of Babel- The story of the tower of Babel divides into five symmetrical dramatic steps.
a. Humanity Unified first steps of verses 1 &2 begins with vast majority of humanity together. 
b. Humanity's Plan- Second step of verses 3&4 reports a plan which the people had. They intended to build a city with great tower reaching heaven so that they will be famous for all time. 
c. Divine Investigation- in verse 5, where God investigated the city and its tower. Once God saw the city and the proud plans of its inhabitants, he determined to bring an end to the city of Babel. 
d. Divine Plan- Fourth step is verses 6 and 7 balances the human plan by reporting God's counterplan. God called his heavenly army to attack the city by confusing the language of the people and thereby to stop the construction of the city and its tower. 
e. Humanity Dispersed- in verses 8&9 where we learn that God dispersed humanity over the earth as he confused human language. Humanity move from being together with one language to being scattered and having many languages.

1. Connections- Moses established connections between the flood and his own day by pointing to connections between himself and Noah.
a. Violence- The work of both Noah and of Moses was to deliver from violence. In Genesis 6:13 Noah's flood came because there was violence in earth. In Exodus 1-2, Egyptians inflicted much violence on People of Israel.
b. Ark- Both Moses and Noah had been delivered from watery deaths by means of an ark, or tevah.
c. Covenants- Noah entered into covenant with God on behalf of entire human race. Moses led the people of Israel into a special covenant with Yahweh. 
d. Water Judgement- God delivered Noah and his family by taking them safely through flood that destroyed the wicked of earth, Moses brought Israel out of Egypt by passing through the waters of Red Sea, which destroyed the army of Egyptian oppressors. 
e. Wind- God sent wind to drive back the waters in both the days of Noah and the days of Moses.

The word eschatology comes from two Greek words: eschatos meaning "last" or "final"; and logos in this case meaning "study". So, "eschatology" is "the study of last things" or "the doctrine of last things". Broadly understood, eschatology covers the entire period of the last days that began with Jesus' life and ministry, and that will be completed when he returns.
Old Testament Expectation: God's kingdom was expected to unfold in three phases: the initial creation of the universe and its creatures; a long period of redemption necessitated by humanity's fall into sin; and finally, the everlasting eschaton- the ultimate state of the universe, after redemption is complete, when God's heavenly kingdom fills the earth.

Cultural Mandate: God's command to reproduce and create human culture throughout the world (Genesis 1:27-28). That means not only reproducing to create enough people to fill the world, but also creating human culture throughout the world. All Christian should know the story of humanity's fall into sin recorded in Genesis 3. God put Adam and Eve in the garden to work it and to take care of it. But Satan spoke through the serpent in the garden. He tricked Eve into eating the fruit from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, which God had forbidden. Then Eve gave the fruit to Adam and he ate it, too. Because of this sin, God cursed all humanity, and the great hope of his eschatological kingdom appeared to be lost. But God mercifully introduced a plan of redemption that would rescue individuals through personal salvation, and would restore the hope of his great messianic kingdom on earth. Proto-Euangelion (''first gospel")- the plan of redemption first introduced after the Fall (Genesis 3:15). God promised to redeem humanity from the curse of sin. Theological Developments, two great ages of Jewish eschatology: "this age" (olam hazeh)- characterized by sin, exile, suffering, and death; began at the Fall and corresponds to the age of redemption. And "the age to come" (olam haba)- future eschaton when God's kingdom would fill the earth; characterized by forgiveness, righteousness, peace and eternal life. Most first century Jewish sects agreed that the Messiah would lead an army of angels and faithful men to victory over Israel's enemies. Eschatology as "the study of last things" or "the doctrine of last things." We also said that eschatology covers the entire period of the last days, which began with Jesus' life and ministry and will be completed when he returns. Individual eschatology- the study of how individual human beings experience the events of the last days.

Present State- During the last days, or eschaton: believers ("the regenerate")- experience both hardships of  "this age" (e.g sin, death)and blessings of the "age to come" (e.g forgiveness, salvation) unbelievers ("the unregenerate")- experience mostly the hardships of "this age." 

Regenerate means recreated or reborn; It is the spiritually living of a person. 
Unregenerate is what is not recreated or reborn; it means that they are spiritually dead. Fallen human beings are born spiritually dead and remain in this state unless they are renewed or "regenerated" by the Holy Spirit.

Moral inability- no capacity to please God or merit his blessing. Augustine's states of moral ability: posse non peccare- the ability not to sin (Adam and Eve's moral state before the fall) 
non posse non peccare- the inability not to sin (Adam and Eve's moral after the Fall)
After the Fall, all of Adam and Eve's naturally generated descendants lost the moral ability to avoid sin . The unregenerate live under sin's control and remain in the state of spiritual death until God saves them. The unregenerate are morally incapable of doing works that God considers to be good (Luke 6:43-45; Romans 8:6-8).

1. Spiritual Life- The regenerate are those who have been born again (or regenerated) through the work of the Holy Spirit. The Bible teaches that to become regenerate, our souls must pass from death into life: "spiritual resurrection"- John 5:24; Ephesians 2:4-5; Colossians 2:13. "rebirth"- John 3:3-6;
2. Moral ability- the capacity to please God and merit his blessings. Our moral ability does not enable us to earn salvation, but it does empower us to obey God's will. Augustine's state of moral ability: posse non peccare- the ability not to sin, non posse non peccare- the ability not to sin. 
Even though we continue to struggle with sin, we also do good works because of the Spirit's influence.
3. Reconciliation to God- Through Christ's death, we've been brought into his household as heirs of his covenant promises (Romans 5:10). Because we're united to Christ: we share Jesus' status as God's favored Son. God credits Christ's perfections and righteousness to our account. No punishment remains for us- only blessings. Union with Christ is a fulfillment of God's eschatological promises.

Terms used for "hell" in Scripture: 
Sheol- home of unregenerate souls (Psalm 9:17)
Abaddon- "destruction" (Job 26:6, Proverbs 15:11)
Bowr- "pit"; a place of punishment (Isaiah 14:15-19)
Hades- place of punishment (Luke 10:15)
abussos- "abyss" prison for demons (Luke 8:31)
place for human souls, including Jesus' righteous soul (Romans 10:7)
Gehenna- universally identifies a place of fiery punishment, torment and destruction. It's mentioned in many passages, including Matthew 5:22. Gehenna is often described as bodily suffering, which associates it with the final state, rather than with the intermediate state. Suggesting that it's where unregenerate souls go during the intermediate state. Jesus described a rich man who died and was immediately tormented in Hades.

Regenerate souls continue to exist just like unregenerate souls do. But their experience is far different. Whereas unregenerate souls suffer a foretaste of their final punishment, regenerate soul enjoy a foretaste of their final blessings. 
1. Lord's presence- When the regenerate die, their souls are immediately taken into God's presence in heaven (Luke 23:43, Revelation 6:9). Regenerate souls are taken into Lord's presence regardless of whether or not their bodies rest in physical graves. Jesus, Paul and others believed they would enjoy each other's presence in heaven immediately upon their deaths. 
2. Fellowship- During the intermediate state, regenerate souls fellowship with other regenerate souls in heaven: Martyrs in heaven know and fellowship with each other and together appeal to God to hasten the final judgement. Hebrews speaks of a heavenly assembly that includes every regenerate person who has experienced physical death (Hebrews 11:40). 
3. Perfect Holiness- During the intermediate state, regenerate souls reach perfect holiness. Human holiness- moral purity and acceptability in God's presence. Augustine's states of moral ability: Scripture suggests that we lose the ability to sin when we enter the intermediate state (Hebrews 12:23). "The souls of believers are at their death made perfect in holiness, and do immediately pass into glory"

Jesus will descend from heaven as the victorious, conquering King over all creation. 
1. Personal - Jesus is coming back in person to finish his work. After Jesus' resurrection, he explained that he was going to send the Holy Spirit to empower the church for ministry (Acts 1:4-5). After Jesus' ascension, two angels appeared and told the apostles that Jesus would personally return in the future.
2. Physical- Jesus didn't  give up his humanity when he ascended into heaven; he has both a divine nature and human nature. Jesus has to return in his human nature in order to complete his work as the prophet like Moses. The New Testament consistently teaches that when Jesus returns, he'll appear in his glorified physical human body.
3. Visible- When Jesus returns in his glorified human body, we'll be able to see him. The New Testament explicitly states that Jesus will be seen when he returns (1 John 3:2, Revelation 1:7) and it will be an earth shattering event.
4. Triumphant - Jesus' first coming did not appear triumphant: born to a poor, humble family, with no political or military power and then condemned and executed as a criminal. He'll come with blazing fire and angelic armies and will be crowned with many crowns, and carrying an iron scepter to rule the nations. Everyone will bow before His power and authority (Philippians 2:9-11) .

The timing of Christ's return is divine mystery. Scripture mentions several circumstances that are precursors to Jesus' return. These circumstances create legitimate expectations for how the future may unfold, and they warn and encourage us as we prepare for Christ' arrival.
1. Demonic Opposition- A particularly terrible period of demonic opposition will precede Jesus' return (''the Great Tribulation"). In the Great Tribulation, demons will empower false prophets to perform misleading signs and wonders (Revelation 16:13-14)
2. Human Opposition- Many human beings will cooperate with the demonic opposition to God. For instance: two beasts with power to control societies and governments (Revelation 13).  "the false prophet" (Revelation 16:13, 19:20) "the man of lawlessness"(2 Thessalonians 2:1-10) False prophets and false Christs (Matthew 24:24) many antichrists (1 John 2:18).
3. Worldwide Evangelism- The kingdom will successfully present its gospel message to the nations (Matthew 24:14). Jesus associated the Great Commission with the entire continuation of the kingdom until the end of the age. When Jesus returns, the church will include members from every tribe, language, people and nation (Revelation 7:9).

Evangelical interpretive strategies exhibit four main tendencies with regard to the "signs of the times". 
Preterism- the precursors to Christ's return appeared in our past and will not be repeated in the future.
Futurism- the precursors to Christ's return haven't appeared yet, but will appear in the future. 
Historicism- the precursors to Christ's return are associated with actual people and events throughout history.
Idealism- the precursors to Christ's return are related to abstract concepts and general principles.
These interpretive strategies all can be used as tools to help us understand various aspects of Scripture. Each of these interpretive strategies has strengths and weaknesses, and evangelicals use all of these strategies to varying degrees.

Millennium is a period of one thousand years. The eschatological period of Christ's reign mentioned in Revelation 20:2-7. Evangelicals often disagree over where to place the millennium in the eschatological timeline. 
A. Historic Premillennialism- Premillennialism is a belief that Jesus will return before the millennium begins. Historic is this view has been held throughout church history. Basic views are: the church will go through the great tribulation just prior to Jesus' return. When Jesus arrives, he'll gather all living believers, bind Satan's influence and begin his earthly reign. Historic Premillennialists differ on whether the millennium will be literal one thousand years or a long unspecified length of time. Believers that remain alive when Jesus returns will be gathered to him in the air, and will immediately return to earth with Jesus as part of his victorious military parade and will live on earth during Christ's millennial reign. 
B. during millennium- Believers and unbelievers alike will enjoy earthly blessings, peace and prosperity. Unbelievers that have died won't be resurrected until end of millennium, but those living will still be on earth. The final judgement will come, and God's eternal reign over the new heavens and new earth will be fully realized.

Post Millennialism is a belief that Jesus will return after the millennium ends. 
Basic Views- During the millennium, Jesus is physically in heaven while he reigns spiritually on earth. The millennium is an age of success for the gospel that prepares the earth for Christ's return. 
Some postmillennialists believe the millennium stretches from Jesus' ascension to his return: others think it will be the last thousand years before he comes back. It will produce greater and greater success for the gospel and the church throughout the world.  Christ will successfully defeat his enemies before he returns. The millennium will be a time of increasing victory for Kingdom of God. Satan's rebellion will occur at the end of the millennium, and he will be defeated when Christ returns. The rapture will include resurrected and still living believers. Believers will meet the Lord in the air and immediately return with him as part of his victorious military parade. Jesus will render his final judgements on both believers and unbelievers and will usher in the new heavens and new earth, and the final state will begin.

Critical scholars have offered three arguments with regards to the authorship of the Epistle of James

1) They say that there is no mention of the author's relation to Jesus in the entire Epistle. They suggest that it's not possible that a brother of Jesus would write to the churches and not reveal his identity or relationship details when he identified himself

2) Some other critical scholars assume psedonymity, as the book gives insights into the Greek culture, whereas James was from Palestine. Some of the Greek phrases or terminology used in the book of James is more advanced.

3) The thrird view is that some of the views expressed in the epistle of James does not tally or match with  theological outlooks in the New Testament books. 

But when we study or analyze the epistle traditionally, these arguments against the book's authoriship are weak and substantial to prove otherwise.

The arguments in fact are more compelling to prove that James has written this epistle. Also because of this, most evangelical scholars rightly affirm that James the brother of Jesus was the author of the letter that bears his name.

General resurrection: called "general" because it includes all human beings that have ever lived. Called "resurrection" because the souls of the dead will be reunited with their reconstituted bodies. The general resurrection can be considered either one of the final events of the intermediate state or one of the first events of the final state which ends all temporary punishments of unregenerate souls
Early Controversies- Pharisees believed that there would be a general resurrection of the righteous and the wicked. Sadducees denied that there would be a general resurrection of the dead. 
The controversy is rooted in their understanding of scripture- Pharisees accepted the Old Testament as scripture where general resurrection is clearly taught (Isaiah 26:19, Daniel 12:2) and Sadducees accepted only the five books written by Moses. Jesus, Paul and the early church took the side of the Pharisees and strongly refuted the Sadducees (Mark 12:18-27). Paul said they rejected the truth and destroyed faith. Paul's opponents in Corinth found resurrection repulsive (1 Corinthians 15:12-34). 
In defending the resurrection of the regenerate, Paul removed any objection to the general resurrection.

Divine Authority is God's legal and moral right to carry out his will that it's perfectly within his rights to do it, and that he commits no wrong if he does it. God's divine authority in the general resurrection will divide into two parts: his authority over hell, and his authority over heaven.
1. Hell- When unregenerate souls suffer in hell during the intermediate state, they suffer because God is punishing them. And when they're drawn out of hell in order to face judgement, it's because God has summoned them into his court. God rules over hell and has complete over Satan, the demons, and the unregenerate souls he imprisons there (2 Peter 2:4,9).
2. Heaven- Heaven is God's throne room, where his authority and glory are manifested more openly than anywhere else (Isaiah 66:1, Matthew 5:34). The descriptions of God ruling from his throne in heaven appear to be literal (1 kings 22:19, 2 Chronicles 18:18).

The Epistle of James focuses a great deal of attention on wisdom as the way to find joy in trimes of trial. Many interpreters have considered it to be a book of wisdom.

Preceding the Epistle of James, there were alread wisdom writings in the Old Testament, including the books of Job, Ecclesiastes and Proverbs. James indebtedness to the Old Testament literature is evident when he takes the example of Job to proote perseverance. 

James touched on many topics, such as speech, the treatment of widows, orphans, poverty and favoritism. These topics reflect numerous parallels with the content of the book of Proverbs.

Much of Jesus instruction recorded in the gospel is characteristic of wisdom teaching in Israel, biblical scholars have noticed a number of similarities between the writing of James and instructions from Jesus

James book resembles wisdom literature in form and content. It focuses on important themes, by spending few verses on a particular topic and thereafter moving on to another. 

The most important point which is unique to James in terms of wisdom is that he links his wisdom very closely with the teachings of Jesus. 

James uses a wide range of practical illustrations to explain his point to the readers, referring to ships being guided by little rudders and farers that are patiently waiting, about merchants that are travelling. 

But the content of James is really carrying forward the way in which Jesus presents the kindom and the way the presence of the kingdom changes your life.

As part of the New Testament, James is an epistle written to the Church to gain practical wisdom.

1. Natural World- God uses eschatological events to alter how the natural world works in order to prepare it for his presence. God's curse on mankind included a curse on the earth itself (Genesis 3:17-18). Paul taught that the earth will be rescued through the resurrection of redeemed humanity (Romans 8:19-23). Just as creation was corrupted through God's curse on humanity it will be purged of corruption through humanity's redemption. 
2. Hell- the souls of regenerate will be removed from hell and returned to their bodies on earth so they can face God's judgement. The demons may be released either to fight in the rebellion or be summoned to judgement with the unregenerate. 
3. Heaven- Regenerate souls will return to earth in order to appear before God's judgement throne. We don't have bodies in heaven, so we aren't complete human beings there. Jesus' throne will be on earth, not in heaven and it's much better to remain in his presence. The new heaven and new earth will be even more wonderful.

1. Fallen Angels- Both 2 peter 2:4 and Jude 6, report that the demons used to be angels that held authority from God.  But they rebelled against him, and abandoned their heavenly homes and their authority. As a result, they're now chained in gloomy dungeons awaiting Christ's judgement. 
2. Unregenerate- Scripture teach that when the resurrected human race appears before Christ's judgement throne. At the final judgement, the Lord will separate the unregenerate from the regenerate and will condemn the unregenerate (Romans 2:5-8; Rev 11:18, 20:11-15). 
3. Regenerate- After Jesus separates the unregenerate from the regenerate, he'll also render judgement on the regenerate. We see this in many places, including Romans 2:7, Revelation 11:18, and again in Matthew 25, where Jesus compared the ungenerate to goats and the regenerate to sheep Matthew 25:33-34)

James suggested that those who want to have pure joy as they suffer trials must ask God for  insight and wisdom to help them understand how their trials will lead them to a better understanding that God intends us to have. In regards to methodology in terms of language study in general and of lexical semantics in particular. there are two foci of study; diachronic study and synchronic study. This is true of any language, ancient or modern, whether related to the New Testament or Old Testament or to neither. In other words, this is not an issue unique to biblical studies. 
In other words, the Diachronic study is what traces the historical development of a language from its earliest known form or usage up to the particular instance under consideration. To illustrate with lexical semantics, it is possible to trace the historical origin and development of a particular work.

The concept of Synthesis is not difficult to grasp. We use it often in daily life. Basically, it simply means combining different components of something into a whole. In many respects, this is what we do when we look at the scriptures with the synchronic synthesis in mind. We describe the ways different components of theology revealed in a particular period of history fit together in a coherent, logical structure. To grasp how synchronic synthesis involves assessing the logical structure of Old Testament theology at a particular time, we'll touch on two issues. First, we'll look at a popular denial of the Old Testament's logical character, and second, we'll offer an affirmation of its logical coherence.

poetry is a form of literary art that uses aesthetic and rhythmic qualities of language to evoke meanings in addition to prosaic ostensible meaning. Poetry has traditionally been distinguished from prose by its being set in verse. The prose is cast in a sentence, poetry in lines the syntax of proses is dedicated by meaning, whereas that of poetry is held across meter or the visual aspects of the poem,.

The defining feature of a narrative poem is its plot. Narrative poems feature an entire story, told by one narrator from beginning to end. Narrative poetry is one of the major categories of poetry but is distinguished from lyric poetry by its focus on plot over emotions. In practice, there is a crossover between these two types of poetry; poets often incorporate lyric elements into their narrative poems and vice versa.

A synchronic study of the Old Testament concentrates their attention on particular periods of time in the Old Testament. Unlike the modern journalistic historical writing,  biblical theologians exercise temporal flexibility when they divide Old Testament history into synchronic units. Sometimes they focus on relatively short, time frames, and other times they focus on longer periods of history.

For instance, in the relatively short story of Abraham's sacrifice of Issac in Genesis chapter 22, many things happen. But biblical theologians ask, " What theological outlooks characterized this part of Abraham's life" 

Biblical theologians also deal with a larger period of time, like Abraham's life in Genesis chapter 11 through chapter 25 a time that spanned around 175 years.

The word of God is given to people throughout history. Because God chose to speak to us in this way every book of the Bible has historical particularity. The word "trinity" simply means "tri-unity"- three in one. So, the doctrine of the trinity can be defined in this way: God is three divine persons in one divine essence. When we talk about trinity- we means that there's only one God, not three. God reveals who God is in terms of Father, Son and Holy Spirit- the three persons- not three people but the three persons of the one God. So, we have the Father who sends the Son, the Son who, After His death and resurrection, goes to the Father and they send the Spirit. And so we come up with terms like "essence"- God's essence is one; his person is three. The Bible talks about God as Father, and so we talk about this person of Father. It talks about God as son. It talks about about God as Holy Spirit too. When we say that God is one divine essence, we're affirming that he is the one uncreated creator. According to Romans 1:25 there is one uncreated creator, and all other things in the universe are a part of God's created order. The doctrine of the Trinity is concerned with persons of the Trinity within the one divine essence, or Godhead.

When we speak of three divine persons, we're referring to the distinct persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We can define the word "person" as "a distinct, self- aware personality existing in relationship with other persons." God's personhood is what we should define ours. One thing that we can pretty substantially rule out is the modern concept of person as a distinct ego, an individual self  consciousness attached to separated body and a particular personal name that no others share. The Father isn't just conscious of the Father as a self, but is conscious of himself in relation to the Son and in relation to the Spirit, and so too, the Son is conscious of himself as the one begotten eternally by the Father speaking and so forth.

Tritheism violates the biblical doctrine of divine simplicity- that God is indivisibly one- but the doctrine of God's threeness does not. This can be difficult to grasp until we recognize that although God is three divine persons, he is only one divine essence. And his essence cannot be divided into parts. He is indivisibly one. God's simplicity is a very interesting notion because, on one hand, the Bible says that God is inconceivable. That is, a man cannot analyze him and sort him out. And on the other hand, theology contains the concept of God's "simplicity." God has revealed himself as Trinity, but these three persons are one- they have one essence. That is, he cannot be broken down into what we'd call "parts." And God is one. So, in this sense, he is simple.

We see there in Colossians 1:15-17..we see there Paul explaining how Jesus Christ is God's image. He speaks of Jesus here as the first born over all creation, as the first created being. So, Paul is establishing for them, "we have one God and one Lord," and that Lord, Jesus. He is expecting the Corinthians to worship God the Father and God the Son, and that's how we can be confident that Jesus is part of creation as it happened, that Jesus is God, has always been God and that Paul, one of the earliest Christian authors, establishes the fact.

The scriptures are clear that Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity, is uncreated and eternal, just like God the Father. He is equal to the Father in power and glory, sharing equally in all the attributes of the Godhead. And the same thing is true of the Holy spirit as well. In fact, every Trinitarian formula found in Scripture mentions the Holy Spirit as an  equal member of the Trinity, together with the Father and the Son. The Trinitarian formulas of the New Testament help us to understand that the Holy Spirit is fully divine and fully personal. For example, In the Great commission Jesus commands us to baptize people in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And in Paul's benediction at the end of 2 Corinthians 13: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.." again there's a blessing in the name of the triune God, grace extended through the sacrifice of the Son, motivated by the love of God and applied to us by the Holy Spirit.  So, we see the Spirit is fully divine, equal with the Father and the Son, and fully personal, no less than the Father and the Son.

The doctrine of the Trinity teaches that there is one God- one divine essence- and all three members of the Trinity are equally and fully God. However, this biblical truth is not fully and explicitly revealed in the Old Testament. Instead, much of the Christian doctrine of the Trinity comes from the New Testament. Old Testament is incomplete revelation. God didn't reveal himself all at once. Now we are speaking of the third person of the Triune God that we come to know more fully in light of New Testament revelation, but just as much about God when we speak of him as the spirit of God in the Old Testament, as it is more revealed in New Testament passages like Matthew 28, Ephesians 4:1-6 & 2 Corinthians 13- where it is brought together in a clear way. New Testament is especially unfolding who is our Savior as the eternal Son of God but that's also true of the Holy Spirit as we see more a distinction of the Spirit in the New Testament.

Revelation chapters 1 and 4 say that the one who sits on the throne is God the Father. And John 1 tells us that the Lamb is the Word of God who became flesh- Jesus Christ, the son of God. Both these passages clearly teach Jesus' uncreated divinity. In Revelation 5, John used the imagery of both a lamb and a lion to describe Jesus. In Revelation 5, John is weeping because no one is worthy to open the scroll and he knows the scroll holds the secret to God's future. An angel announces that there is one who is worthy, Lion of the tribe of Judah, which is a symbol of royalty. Instead he sees a lamb, symbol of sacrifice, symbol of suffering. And there's a beautiful picture of Jesus who is the conquering King, he is the Messiah, who accomplishes salvation by suffering and dying as the sacrificial Lamb. So, the Lion who is the Lamb is the beautiful picture of who Jesus Christ is as Lord, as sovereign as King. So, a powerful picture of who Jesus is and how he accomplished our salvation. Revelation 5 places Jesus in the category of divine. He isn't one of God's creatures. Instead he's equal with God. And as God's divine Son, he will conquer all his and our enemies when he returns.

The first chapter of John, and the first verse in particular, has been used throughout the history of the church as proof that Jesus is God the Son, the second person of the Trinity. He is God and has been with God since the beginning. He's also involved in the creation of all things. And because he's involved in the creation of all things, he himself must be uncreated. He is the eternal and uncreated Creator. "What God was, the word was." in essence, what the Greek is doing is it's saying that in terms of his essence, in terms of what he is, the word is identical to God, and in the last few words of John 1:1, "and the word was God", say in the most concise way possible that the second person of the Trinity is equal in authority, in worship, in attributes as the first person of the Trinity, and yet they are not the same person. John 1:1 is a verse that affirms the deity of Christ. He is fully God himself, that he is a divine associate and he is fully God himself.

Searching and knowing is an attribute of a distinct, self aware personality who is in a loving relationship with other self aware personalities. This necessarily implies that the Spirit of God is a person, distinct from the person of God. If the Spirit of God were simply God's impersonal attribute or his impersonal force in action. In John 14-16, we read about Spirit doing things that only a person would do. He will advocate like Jesus, and the Spirit goes on to prosecute the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgement, just like Jesus did. The Spirit is like a witness just like we are witness. Jesus tells us what the Holy Spirit does..He teaches us, reveals all truth, guides us, comforts us, leads us and further we see the Holy spirit has emotions. He is grieved. Like Paul in Ephesians says that Don not quench the Spirit in 1 Thessalonians. So, the Spirit is identified as a distinct person.

And it is through his humanity- through his life, death and resurrection- that we are saved. And because the human Jesus is also the eternal God, equal in power and glory to the Father, we can trust that he is worthy and able to redeem us from our sins. Jesus has to a man is that he has to represent us. He must be tempted in every point like as we are. Because he is fully human yet without sin, he can be our complete substitute. Therefore the Scriptures are clear that Jesus is both God and man. He's the second person of the Trinity, God the Son. The three members of the Trinity are each eternal and uncreated. There was never a time when any member of the Trinity didn't exist. But the Father's relationship in the Trinity is unique. The Father is not begotten and doesn't proceed from any of the other members of the Trinity. He has never become incarnate, and the other two members of the Trinity have never sent him to do divine work. There's one God, yet they exist in some type of mysterious unity as one God, three persons. It's clear in New Testament that son gladly and joyfully submits to the Father and Spirit gladly and joyfully submits to Father and to the Son. They are always of one mind. They are always of one will and they work in an absolute perfect unity and harmony. So any idea that there's a disagreement among the Triune God is just a creation of man's imagination and nothing such can be found in God's revealed Word.

Just as the Father's relationship in the Trinity is unique, the Son's relationship is also unique. The Bible uses language that tells us that the Father "begat" the Son. Scriptures like Revelation 5:13,14 are clear that Son is eternal. He has always existed. Because of this theologians say that the Son is "eternally begotten" of the Father. New Testament uses the word "God", as first person and so when there's a father, there has to be a Son, and this relationship goes back to eternity. He's not a creature out of nothing but He's a Son begotten of his Father from eternity before all worlds. Son is of one substance with the Father, and through the Son all things were made, so that the Father, through the Son, made all things.

When we say that the eternal and uncreated Holy Spirit "proceeds" from His Father, we do not mean that the Spirit had a beginning. Just like the Father and Son, the Spirit is eternal, without beginning or end. So, Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father. This is the doctrine of Holy Spirit's "eternal procession". The Bishop of Constantinople said that the Holy spirit was created being like an angel and that he was subordinate to the Son. Constantinople reaffirmed Nicea, and added that Holy Spirit is Lord. He is life-giver. He is to be worshipped as the Father and the Son. And this is known as the Nicea Creed. By calling the Holy Spirit both "Spirit of God" and "Spirit of Christ," Paul implied that the Spirit not only proceeds from God, the Father, but also proceeds from Christ, the Son. Other passages that teach this same doctrine include John 16:13-15; 20:22 and Galatians 4:6.

In 589 A.D, a church council met in the western city of Toledo, Spain and among other things, attempted to solidify the doctrine of eternal procession. Here western theologians added the Latin term "filioque", meaning "and the Son," to the Nicene Creed of 381 AD. With this addition, creed clearly articulates that the Holy Spirit "proceeds" or "spirates" from the Father and the Son. They argued in the filioque clause that means "and from the Son"- they affirmed the double procession of the Holy Spirit and the Spirit proceeded from the Father and the Son. Many would say that it was a political matter but the truth was  that a big division came over the very issue of the trinity. And it is very clear that the issue that really divides the East and the West on this doctrine of the Trinity is this issue of the filioque or the double procession of the Spirit.

the word "Ontological" refers to being and existence. So, the theological term "ontological Trinity"- has to do with the existence and personal interaction of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit apart from their acts of creation and salvation. We refer to the fact that the three persons of the Trinity- Father, Son and Holy Spirit- are equal in substance, power and glory. And none of them are superior in this regard. The Father is God. The Son is God. The Holy Spirit is God. It means God in himself, God as present only to himself and what God in himself beyond all time and space, before creation, God within himself. The ontological Trinity is what from Scripture, we derive as to the relations within God himself beyond all creation. It is the same God at work in creation, but God in an inner life of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit relating to each other eternally.

Missions originated in the heart of God. It is not something we decide to do for God, but God reveals his purpose to us so that we may have a creative part in his mission. God's mission, however, is to redeem man from the clutches of evil and save him. Three basic purposes are;
1. To bring glory to God- In Ephesians, Paul stated three times that God's eternal plan is for his people to be to the praise of his glory (Eph 1:6,12,14). God stands as both the originator and the goal of the redemptive process. The glory of God is the ultimate goal of God's mission. God receives glory when man fully realizes the purpose of his existence, Eph 3:19)
2. To share the good news with the alienated
God's mission includes recreating man spiritually.  "We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works , which God prepared before ordained that we should walk in them" (Eph 2:10) God restores man's identity and his purpose for being. The mystery of God's mission is clear: "That the Gentiles should be fellow heirs, and of the same body and partakers of his promise" (Eph 3:6)
3. To display the wisdom of God to evil powers- Man becomes God's display of his wisdom to Satan and his evil beings: "In order that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known through the church to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" Redeemed man is the primary exhibit of God's grace. God seems to be depending on us to demonstrate his goodness, wisdom, and power. We do not understand what is at sake for God, but we are told that it is supremely important to him and us.

God's new strategy was to select one individual as his friend and partner. Christian, are elected in Christ and inherit the promises (Gal 3:13-16). God has called us and selected us to be one of his children. He expects us to walk in obedience to his commands and to serve him through serving the world. God intends for his people to be a disciplined people, holy priests and suffering servants to the world. Both Old and New Testament emphasize that God is forming a holy nation of servant priests. 
A disciplined people- The OT sketches God's efforts to form a holy people. Holy means to be separated unto God. God called Abraham to leave home and family to become a pilgrim people, and represent God's holiness to other nations of the world. They learned that righteousness of God demanded disciplined, obedient people. Israel was to be a parable and proclaimer of God's holiness.
A Nation of Priests- At the beginning of the covenant with Israel, God promised that they would be a kingdom of priests. God has decreed that they shall be called "priests of the Lord" and "ministers of our God". Priest were the models to the whole nation who represented God to man and Also represented man to God, They were a holy priest nation to whom God would reveal that they might transmit the revelation to other nations
A Servant People- the Lord of heaven and earth serves us and expects us to be servant people. We are to love like God, serve like God, and minister to all people like God. The servant passages of Israel clearly expresses the servant role of Israel and ultimately of Christ.

The incarnation- When God spoke at the beginning of time, the world was created, when God spoke by the Word in the incarnation, new humanity was created. The incarnation is the good news that the kingdom of heaven has come in Christ. Almost as startling as the incarnation was Jesus' becoming a servant. He served  man in the most menial ways. He fulfilled the intentions of the Father as stated in Isaiah. The graphic picture of his servant role is when Jesus took the towel and washed his disciples' feet. God, who became man, now stooped to serve man that man might catch the vision of serving. 

The Crucifixion- The self emptying of Christ climaxed with Gethsemane and Golgotha. Philippians 2:8 moves directly from Christ's incarnation to his crucifixion: "Being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even death to the cross." Jesus completely surrendered to the Father that the struggle centered on knowing the Father's will. He fulfilled the priestly role by his prayers and by death, positioned himself between sinful man and the Holy God as intercessor and represented man to God as well as God to man. By His death, satisfied the Father, subdued Satan and reconciled man to God.

The Resurrection- Jesus' resurrection proved that the evil forces of satan had been conquered throughout the cosmos. In his death and resurrection, Jesus "spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly" (Col 2:15). During these times the gospel is to be preached to all nations. Jesus gave the Great commission on basis of resurrection. The resurrection was the condition for world missions. The gospel all our lives may not realize what good news it is. 

The incarnation tells the masses that God cares; the crucifixion proclaims forgiveness of sin; the resurrection shouts that the victory has been won over sin, death, and Satan.

The mission of Holy Spirit who came to take Jesus' place, to inspire, to empower, and to guide them. 
The Inspirer of Missions- The mission of Christ could not be accomplished without the mission of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit came to make God's people into the body of Christ. He regenerates, sanctifies, teaches, guides, comforts, illuminates, and intercedes. But the most important ministry in relation to his mission is the filling of Christians for service. The Great Commission the Holy Spirit who inspires men to carry it out spontaneously. When God's people are revived, they witness. Result is that sinners coming to Christ has not been an outpouring of the Holy Spirit. 

The Empowerer of the Church- The power they received with the filling of the Holy Spirit was life changing and world changing because it was living, having authority spiritual power. Jesus used the word dunamis, from which we get the word dynamo and dynamite. Holy Spirit gives us the spiritual ability to make an impact on those hearing the testimony. The spirit filled believer never witnesses alone. The Holy Spirit works within the lost person to verify and to personalize the witness of the believer. He makes real the authority and the presence of Christ.

The Guide in Missions- As executor of Christ's will the Holy Spirit determines the course of missions. Holy Spirit thrust them farther into the fields. Acts 1:8 outlines the Spirit's movement: Jerusalem (Acts 2:! to 8:4); Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:5 to 12:25) and the remainder of the world. Holy Spirit redistributes the harvesters from an area where there are many laborers to other places to thrust them out into the world as flaming witnesses.

The church lives with two identities. First, it is the remnant that God has chosen, sanctified and commissioned to be blessing to the world. Second, it is the body of Christ that must fulfill his ministry in the world. 

Priest of God- The Calvary Principle
As God's chosen generation, we live in the election stream of God's great purpose. This part of the chapter explores what it means to be chosen to be priests. Formerly we were Christ less, homeless, promise less, hopeless and Godless (Eph. 2:12). Just as the veil in the Temple barred man from the holy of holies, so our sins had created a barrier that kept us separated from God and each other. Old Testament priests, as representatives of God, pronounced blessings on individual people; we bless all nations by who we are and what we do. The Old Testament priesthood was limited to the tribe of Levi; the New Testament priesthood includes all believers. We should be different in our thoughts, talks and walk. 

Servants of God- The incarnation Principle
The church as the body of Christ is incarnate in the world to become the suffering servant. It is not called out of the world but called to go into the world and love like Christ, forgive like Christ, and give itself to the world like Christ. But a more common application of the incarnation principle is to empty ourselves of earthly power and self importance. Proclamation grows most naturally out of life of service. His incarnation best illustrates the servant attitude. 

Sons of the King- The resurrection principle
From the time God created the world, his intention was to rule over obedient persons. The first church faced almost insurmountable odds. Obstacles like persecution, deception, discord and prejudice that cause the church not to fulfill its co-mission with God. Satan unleashed his attacks in ever increasing force and cunning, but the early Christian would not be silent. As children of King, we announce that kingdom has come. With joy we tell the good news that our Father owns everything.

AD 56 or 57 : Near the end of Paul's third missionary journey, Paul went to Jerusalem to deliver funds to the poor Christians who were enduring a famine. On their way they stopped in Miletus where Paul met with the the elders from the nearby church of Ephesus. During this meeting Paul revealed that the Holy Spirit had warned him that he would be imprisoned when he arrived in Jerusalem. Believers prophesied Paul's coming imprisonment. Paul knew these prophecies were to prepare him for his coming hardships.
The prophet Agabus bound his own hands and feet as a prophetic sign, warning that Paul would be arrested and bound if he continued to Jerusalem. Paul answered "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 21:12).
Paul understood that his coming imprisonment would be "for the name of the Lord Jesus."

Presumably, it was at this point that Paul delivered to the church the famine relief funds that he had collected during his third missionary journey. Paul hoped that the gift would make Jewish Christians more eager to receive the Gentiles as full brothers in Christ. Paul claimed that the Sadducees opposed him because he was Pharisee and that the gospel he preached agreed with the teachings of the Pharisees on many points. When Paul proclaimed to the Sanhedrin that he preached a gospel based on his vision of the resurrected Christ, he gained some sympathy from the Pharisees. Paul defended himself before the Sanhedrin, explaining why so many Jews had taken offense to his teachings. But the Sadducees did not back down, and the meeting became extremely violent. So, once again, Lysias took Paul into custody. Since Paul was a Roman citizen, he was transported to Caesarea Maritima. Felix: Governor of the Roman province of Judea.

Late AD 59: Paul was placed under the authority of a Roman centurion named Julius and put on a ship heading for Asia Minor. A violent storms blew their ship past Cauda, far out into the Mediterrean Sea. Eventually, the ship struck a reef near the Isle of Malta and was destroyed. Paul and everyone else from the ship were stranded in Malta for three months. Paul presented the people of with the gospel and performed miraculous healings. 
Early AD 60: Paul and his companions set sail for Italy. Paul arrived in Rome later that year, and was placed under house arrest. 
AD 60-62: Paul lived under house arrest in Rome. He was permitted to receive guests and to teach freely. "For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. Boldly and without hindrance he preached the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ" (Acts 28:30-31).

As we will see, Paul was not idle during his time in prison. Rather, he continued to serve actively as a minister of the gospel of Jesus Christ. Paul was an apostle. Jesus had personally called and trained Paul and appointed him to serve as his ambassador, his covenant emissary. Paul's appointed tasks were not put on hold when he was imprisoned. On the contrary, in God's providence prison was exactly so that Paul's imprisonment in Rome would provide the opportunity for Paul to spread the Gospel of Christ to the heart of the western world.

Paul's experiences of imprisonment were very important for Luke, the author of Acts. He dedicated nearly nine chapters to events related to this period in Paul's life.
1. Awareness of Suffering- Paul was aware that his service to Christ would bring severe hardship and suffering into his life. Paul was acutely aware of the difficulties that awaited him in his service to Christ and his gospel, and was willing even to be martyred. 
2. Awareness of Purpose- Paul was aware of the purpose of his suffering. The Lord also planned to use this suffering to promote the gospel. Imprisonment would be the means through which Paul accomplished his ministry. Paul presented his testimony to the mob that sought his death (Acts 22:1-21). He testified to the gospel and Christ's resurrection before the Sanhedrin, proclaimed the gospel to the Caesarean court- publicly at his hearing and privately to the governor Felix and his wife Drusilla, proclaimed the gospel to the new governor Festus. He regularly preached the gospel of the kingdom of God to all who came to see in Rome.
3. Awareness of Blessing-Paul was very aware of God's blessing on his ministry during this time. Paul received and interpreted visions to protect the lives of those on the ship that eventually crashed on the reef. He healed the sick. He ministered to the individual needs of the believers.

Paul's letters from prison share some important doctrinal foundations. Affirm the same gospel. Share a common way of presenting the gospel. Tend to emphasize the same aspects of that gospel. Common foundation: Jesus Christ is the conqueror  and ruler of all creation. 
1. Sovereignty- Christ has the strength and power to accomplish his will, and the legal authority and right to do. When Jesus ascended into heaven, God the Father vested him with sovereignty over all creation  with absolute power. Not everything in creation obeys him as it should. But Jesus has the right to command its obedience, and the power to make it obey. 
2. Honor- Christ's glory and value demand the responses of respect, emulation and worship. Jesus is God, and God is worthy of the highest honor imaginable. 
3. Determination- Christ is determined to return of Christ grew out of traditional Jewish views of the end times. Jesus revealed that this traditional Jewish conception was not entirely accurate. The age to come would replace the present age , but not at all once. Jesus reigns as king from heaven. He wants and plans to rule over inch of creation as fully and gloriously as he now reigns in heaven. Jesus must return in order to deliver our inheritance in the consummated kingdom.

When we believe in Jesus, we are united to him in a spiritual, though mysterious way. Paul frequently encouraged his readers through their sharing in Christ's kingship. Through our union with Christ: We are united to Christ's death. We are united to Christ in his resurrection and life. We are united to Christ in his ascension and kingship. We are seated with Christ in the heavenly places. Paul spoke of our union with Christ in order to encourage believers that they did not suffer alone, and that they did not suffer in vain.  Paul took comfort in the fact that when we suffer for the gospel , our union with Christ ensures that Christ suffers and sympathizes with us.

Paul had never actually visited the church in Colosse, but he cared deeply for them nonetheless. Paul's relationship with the Colossians from the details in Paul's letter to them as well as from his letter to Philemon, who lived in Colosse. For one thing, we read that Paul had an indirect relationship with Colossians through representatives, such as his Colossian friends Epaphras, Philemon, and Onesimus, and his messenger Tychicus. 
Paul and the Colossians corresponded with each other and ministered with each other. For instance, besides struggling in prison on their behalf, Paul prayed specifically for the Colossians. As he wrote in Colossians 1:9. Paul had friends that labored alongside him in gospel ministry including: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, Epaphras- Paul's fellow worker and prisoner, a faithful minister of Christ. Onesimus who was a slave who sought out Paul after fleeing from Philemon; ministered to Paul in prison. Paul had a fairly minimal personal relationship with the Colossian church. Even though Paul had not personally met most of the Colossian believers, they shared affection and affinity for one another, making their relationship real and substantial.

1) Greek Philosophy- Mysteries, Rites, Secret knowledge- secret wisdom "Philosophy" these words are typically applied to occult religions, especially those that were based on religious traditions such as =True mystery, wisdom and knowledge were found only in Christ, and not in pagan religions. False teachers in Colosse were enamored with beliefs and practices similar to those found in Greek religion. Paul objected to the ascetic practices in Colosse.
2. Jewish Law- In Colosse, their use and understanding of Jewish law departed both from traditional Judaism and from proper Christian practices. False teachings were using Jewish teachings and practices in corrupt ways. Paul wrote against abuses of the Mosaic Law, but he did not write against the law itself. 
3. Spiritual Beings- The false teachers in Colosse promoted the worship of spiritual beings. 
a. Angels- Ministering spirits- it is important to recognize their work. According to the false teachers, angels were cosmic powers. This exaggerated view of the power and influence of angels was not uncommon in the ancient world. 
b. Rulers and Authorities- Paul emphasized Christ's superiority over every power and authority in heaven and on earth. The false teachers attributed to these invisible rulers, actions and abilities that belong to Christ alone. 
c. Basic Principles- The basic principles were the basis for the philosophy of the false teachers. The false teachers appear to have combined: Jewish legalism, Pagan Religion, Christianity.

Paul's letters were: Personal and Pastoral
He was motivated by love and concern. Paul's letters were not just collections of authoritative teaching. For the churches and people to whom he wrote and Paul's letters were also "occasional." It was written to address specific issues in particular times and places.
Paul's letter to the Colossians, it is important for us to know something about the occasion that prompted Paul's writing. The background to Paul's letter to the Colossians from two directions: First,  some details of the his relationships with the Colossian church in general and with individuals within the church. and second, some of the problems in Colosse that concerned Paul.

In the main body of the letter the supremacy of Christianity over the religion of the false teachers. 
1. Supremacy of Christ- Christ is the image of invisible God. 
a. Image of God, Colossians 1:15- In some Greek philosophies, the universe was thought to be God's image, the greatest revelation of God. Paul pointed to Christ as the image of God. He adopted this Greek philosophical meaning of the term "image of God" to show that Christ was the ultimate revelation of God. 
b. Firstborn over all creation, Colossians 1:15- Paul mentioned that Christ is the firstborn over all creation. He associated Christ's status as "firstborn" with his authority and supremacy.
c. Agent of Creation, Colossians 1:16- Christ was the agent of creation, the one through whom God created the universe. Christ's priority as the agent of creation makes him far superior to everything within creation.
d. Supreme Lord, Colossians 1:18- Christ is the supreme Lord because God placed him as head over the church. 
e. God incarnate, Colossians 1:19- Christ is God is incarnate
f. Only Reconciler, Colossians 1:20- Christ is the only reconciler between God and man. Jesus Christ is the agent and the means through whom God is purging sin from the world, and making peace with humanity.

A. Reconciliation through the Christian Gospel, Colossians 1:21-23; 2:5- Paul and the Colossians had already experienced reconciliation through the gospel.
B. Altruism, Colossians 1:24- Paul suffered on behalf of the church and his sufferings benefitted the church by: Providing a powerful witness of the gospel, encouraging the church and completing the sufferings of Christ. 
C. Divine Commissions, Colossians 1:25- Paul had been appointed to his apostleship by the Lord himself. The false teachers relied on ideas that idolatrous human beings had invented. 
D. Revelation, Colossians 1:25-28, 2:2-4- The revelation Paul had received was superior to that attested by false teachers. Paul had spent three years in the desert of Arabia and in Damascus receiving revelations from God (Gal 1:15-18). 
E. Empowerment, Colossians 1:29-2:1- God gave power to Christ's ministers. The Holy Spirit gifted Paul with astounding gifts to advance the kingdom of God on earth: Words to speak, Opportunities to speak and Miracles to confirm his witness.
