A number of modern scholars have argued that Ephesians was written by one of Paul's students, but there are good reasons to accept Paul's authorship. The letter states that it was written by Paul. In Eph 1.1- Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints in Ephesus. Ephesians closely resembles Paul's other letters in both doctrine and language. The connections are especially strong with Colossians, which should not surprise us since Paul probably wrote them both at about the same time. According to Acts 19-21, Paul had planted the church in Ephesus, and had lived in Ephesus for two years. And even after that time, he had continued to maintained close relationships with its elders. It is simply unimaginable that the Ephesians would not have recognized this letter as a forgery.

Paul tailored his letter to address the specific problems of a relatively localized group of people whom he knew directly or personally. But in Ephesians he did something different: he responded to the problems of several churches in different locations, many of which he had never met.  The purpose is divided into two:
1. Kingdom of God- Christ's kingdom exists in the overlap of the ages: The present age- sin and death and the Age to come- God will pour out ultimate blessings and curses. Our divine King is using his power and authority: Citizenship, the most valuable and well-known citizenship in Paul's day was citizenship in the Roman Empire. Inheritance, Paul associated it with inheritance in Christ's kingdom; Military Service, Christians engage in spiritual warfare also implied citizenship in God's kingdom. Rule over Creation and Sources of our names were because we are a part of His Kingdom and An Ambassador. 
2. Challenges- A. Sinful Nature- Sin must not characterize the citizens of God's kingdom.
B. Racial Tension- Paul used the imagery of the God's kingdom to address tension between Jews and Gentiles in the church. 
C. Demonic Forces- The church- God's kingdom- is in a cosmic battle with the kingdom of darkness, ruled by Satan and his demons.

Paul's job as an apostle was to provide authoritative teaching and leadership to the church, and he did this partly by writing letters. But Paul didn't just want to spread sound doctrine or record it for posterity. First and Foremost, he wanted to minister to the church in his own day by applying sound doctrine. His letter were pastoral and caring, and they directly to the problems that the church faced in the first century. 
This means that as we study Paul's letter to the Ephesians, it helps to begin by asking questions like: To whom was this letter written? And what significant issues were they facing in life? Knowing the answers to the questions like these will help us make greater sense of Paul's teachings.

A section of praise to God appears next in 1:3-14. This is Paul's only canonical letter in which the salutation is followed by such a section of praise to God. Typically Paul followed his salutation with a personal reference or greeting. But as we have seen, there are no personal references of any type in the epistle to the Ephesians. We don't know for certain why Paul decided not to include any personal greetings. Maybe he thought that a section of praise would work better in a circular letter. or maybe he wanted to lay the groundwork for the doctrinal sections that followed. Some have seen this section as the beginning of a dialog of prayer that spans the first three chapters. Paul praised God for our inheritance in Christ. 
Prayer- The kingdom of God provides the context for Paul's prayer. He mentioned God's sovereignty when he spoke of: The Father's  "incomparably great power" and "mighty strength". Christ being enthroned above all other rulers and shares his inheritance with us, so that his inheritance is our inheritance too.

1. Citizenship- The body focuses on the contrast between the righteous kingdom of God and the sinful kingdom of demons and fallen humanity. 
a. In Kingdom of Darkness, the human race is sinful and fallen. 
b. In Kingdom of Light, God sovereignly determined to deliver people so they would inherit salvation.
c. In the nature of citizenship, God has fulfilled the Old Testament ideal of combining both Jews and Gentiles into one kingdom under God's sovereign rule. 
2. Administration- Just before his arrest in Jerusalem, Paul had warned the Ephesians elders that false teachers would arise from their own ranks. The apostles possessed: special grace from God that empowered them in their ministry, special revelation from God that taught them infallible truth. 
3. Code for Living- 
A. Ecclesiastical Order in the Kingdom- Paul portrayed the Lord as a victorious king returning from the battle.
B. Purifying the Kingdom- Believers within the kingdom of light have a new nature that they can rely on to overcome their sin. 
C. Domestic Order in the Kingdom- Proper relationships of authority must be maintained within all levels of Christ's kingdom.
D. Warfare of the Kingdom (6:10-20)
E. Final Greetings- Paul offered a closing blessings and indicated that Tychicus would deliver this letter

God requires that we help him expand and grow his earthly kingdom. The kingdom of God is a building, with each Christian being a stone in the structure. The goal of the building is to become God's dwelling, so that God will live in the midst of his people. When Paul taught that both Jews and Gentiles would live in God's presence as his Temple, he meant that God's kingdom was moving toward its final goal. The big picture: Honoring God, Living in his presence, Striving to increase Christ's glory rather than our own. We must be humble- no believer is more deserving of blessing than any other. We must embrace all believers as equals in the Kingdom of God. All believers collectively composing Christ's body. Like the metaphor of the Temple, the image of the body described the kingdom of God: Christ was seated as king in heaven. He ruled for the benefit of his people, the church. Paul's fullest use of the body imagery appears in Ephesians 4:1-6, where he argued for ecclesiastical order in the kingdom. These leaders are to guide the church toward two goals: Unity in the faith, Attaining to the whole measure of the fullness of Christ- to bring all of creation under the rule of Christ.

In the Bible, the gospel is cosmic in scope. It is the message that our divine King is using His power and authority to subject his enemies and to conquer sin, to redeem his people from their bondage and to establish them as rulers over the new earth. John The Baptist, Jesus and his disciples have all preached about the nearing Kingdom of God. "The time is fulfilled, and the Kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1.15)." The same gospel is being preached today also. In our understanding, people most often associate the "gospel" or  "good news" with things like the forgiveness of an individual's sins and the promise of an individual's everlasting life. And these are the wonderful aspects of our hope.

1. Philemon- Paul's partner in gospel ministry and the host of the local church. He seems to have had a significant history with Paul that formed a strong bond between the men. Paul meant that he had brought Philemon to faith, and owed Paul a great debt. But they knew each other very well. 

2. Onesimus- Onesimus was Philemon's slave, he was a member of Philemon's household. But unlike his master, Onesimus was not a believer, at least not initially. But after Onesimus left Philemon's household the apostle led him to faith in Christ and grew to love him greatly. Paul expressed his love for Onesimus, in Philemon 10-16 and because he had developed a fatherly love for him. 

3. Witness- Paul mentioned a number of other Colossians in his letter to Philemon: Apphia- as Paul's "sister" might simply indicate that she was a believer. It is more likely that she was a member of Philemon's household- probably his wife. Archippus, may have been the host of the local church met in Philemon's house. He was mentioned as person of some influence over Philemon, whether as a local pastor or a part of Philemon's household. Epaphras, Paul expected them to serve as familiar witnesses in his appeal to Philemon on Onesimus' behalf. He had a keen interest in making sure that Philemon would respond properly to Paul's letter.

"Onesimus" is derived from a Greek word meaning "useful" or "profitable." But Onesimus had been a useless or unprofitable slave. The initial problem in Philemon's household was that Onesimus had caused some loss to Philemon, whether intentionally or unintentionally, through negligence, sloth or malice. And this problem was compounded by the resulting tension between Onesimus and Philemon, including probably Philemon's anger and intent to discipline Onesimus, and Onesimus's fear. And finally, it culminated in Onesimus' flight from Philemon. Philemon may have assumed that Onesimus was a fugitive. But Onesimus' true motives remained to be seen.
Under Roman law, a master had the right to punish slaves severely, even with heavy beatings. Onesimus fled in fear. God had a positive reason for allowing the situation. The law permitted slaves to leave their masters temporarily to find an advocate or mediator. If Onesimus fled in order to ask Paul to be his advocate and mediator with Philemon, he was not a fugitive.

1. Onesimus' Petition- Scripture provides some details suggesting that Onesimus sought out Paul as his advocate. He knew where Paul was- the church at Colosse had sponsored Epaphras' mission to care for Paul in prison. He pursued  a meeting with Paul and pursued Paul's advocacy. Paul wrote to Philemon only after Onesimus had endeared himself to Paul: Paul converted Onesimus to Christianity. He ministered to Paul in prison. Some scholars conclude that Onesimus was seeking to start a new life far from Philemon, and encountered Paul only accidentally. 
2. Paul's Agreement- Philemon had the right to punish Onesimus. So, Paul defended Onesimus on the basis of mercy. Godly authority figures carry out appropriate punishments because it is the right thing to do. Onesimus initially stayed with Paul to convince the apostle of his good intent. During this time: Paul preached the gospel to Onesimus. The Holy Spirit brought Onesimus to faith in Christ. He might have remained with Paul without becoming a fugitive. Morally, this would not have been the best solution. The Christian values of charity and reconciliation demanded his return to Philemon.

Paul presented his petition to Philemon in verses 8-21. The petition represents the main purpose of the letter, namely advocating on behalf of Onesimus before Philemon. Paul had the authority to order Philemon to do the right thing. Instead, he wrote to Philemon in ways that elicited Philemon's sympathy and concern. Paul spoke as a weak, elderly man in need of help. 
Paul wanted Philemon to respond to this situation with genuine Christian love. Compassion for an elderly man in prison. Compassion for the newly converted brother in Christ who ministered to him, We will explore the petition in some depth, breaking it down into the following six elements:
An explanation of Paul's role as advocate in verses 8-10
An explanation of Onesimus's role as petitioner in verses 11-12
An explanation of Philemon's role as master in verse 14
An explanation of God's role as providential ruler of the universe in verses 15-16
Paul's petition itself in verses 17-20
 And Paul's statement of confidence that the petitions would be granted, in verse 21.

Paul said in Philemon 11-13, that Onesimus who was unprofitable in the past, but is now profitable to you and me, whom Paul has retained and in Philemon's absence, ministered him in the bonds of gospel. Paul appealed on the basis of mercy, because Onesimus had sinned and was guilty, hence Paul with mercy appealed for him. It is easier and better to appeal for mercy, as we all have sinned and have no right to make demands. God is extremely merciful and gracious to us. And in verse 12, "He is very dear to me but even dearer to you, both as a man and as a brother in the Lord." Paul's high praise of Philemon as a deeply loving Christian, as well as Paul's strong advocacy for Onesimus, it appears that Paul expected this to be the outcome.

Paul had planted the church in Philippi during his second missionary journey, around the year A.D 48 or 50. Many of Paul's activities in Philippi are recorded in Acts 16:12-40, it was in Philippi that Paul gained his first convert in Europe, the merchant woman, Lydia. And it was in Philippi that he was jailed for an exorcism he performed on a slave girl. He led the Philippian jailer to a profession of faith in Christ. The church was poor and not always able to help Paul financially. But, when they had opportunity, they gave to him generously. Paul referred to the Philippians as his "dear friends" (2:12, 4:1).

We approach Paul's letters to the Philippians, we have questions like: Who were the Philippians? What was happening in their lives and in Paul's life? And why did Paul write to them? The answers to questions like these will help us to understand Paul's authoritative teaching in this letter, and to apply it to our own lives. 
As we investigate the background to Paul's epistle to the Philippians, we will focus our attention on three matters: First, we will consider Paul's relationship with the Philippians. Second, we will mention some details pf Paul's suffering in prison and Third, we will explore the conditions in Philippi at the time Paul wrote to them.
Relationship- Paul had planted the church in Philippi during his second missionary journey, around the year AD 49 or 50. The church was poor and not always able to help Paul financially. But when they had opportunity, they gave to him generously. 
Suffering in Prison- Paul often suffered greatly. He did not always bear up well under these hardships. At times, he was depressed, even despairing. He spoke frequently of death as welcome relief from his suffering. 
Concern for Paul- As soon as the Philippians were able, they demonstrated their concern by sending: A gift to meet Paul's earthly needs. Epaphroditus to deliver the gift and minister to Paul.

Paul instructed the Philippians to remain faithful to Christ and to live exemplary lives even in midst of distressing circumstances. 
a. Importance of Perseverance:- God had planned the Philippians' sufferings as a means of blessing them. Paul wanted the Philippians to rejoice in the midst of suffering because of the blessings it produces.
b. Help for Perseverance:- It is much easier to endure suffering when we have real people helping us on a daily basis, and suffering right alongside us. Paul sent Epaphroditus back to them in order to ease their minds as well as to minister to them, planned to send Timothy to Philippi. Paul hoped that he would be released from prison, and would come to minister to the Philippians. 
c. Examples of Perseverance:- Paul was a positive example of perseverance in the faith: Mindset, Behavior Paul refused to rely on his earthly merits. He depended only on Christ's merit, which God credited to him by means of faith.
d. Challenges to Perseverance- Paul encouraged the Philippians not to falter in their faithfulness to God because of: False teachers, Conflict within the church and Personal hardship.

A. Salutation- Paul is the primary author of the letter. The letter also comes from Timothy. Philippians is Paul's only letter that never calls explicit attention to the apostolic authority. 
B. Thanksgiving- Paul presents a fairly standard statement of thanks, speaking of; the joy the Philippians have brought to him. His expectations for their ultimate salvation. 
C. Prayer- Paul's prayer is packed with statements that reflect the emphasis of the entire letter: Make proper judgements, perform good works, persevere in faith and practice, bring glory and praise to God.

Ethics is the science of morality. Its task is to examine the moral aspect of human nature and behavior, to clarify issues in moral decision making and moral dilemmas, and to facilitate the formation of moral character.  In Micah 6:8 we find a helpful definition of morality. It can be argued on the information found in that passage that morality asks four questions. Not what is normal, legal, or acceptable in a given culture, but what is good. Human beings are born with the rights, to which they have God-given rights. Immoral conduct consists of denying these rights to our fellow human beings. Our relationships and our inter-human conduct must be kind and compassionate.

In some ways, making biblical decisions requires to identify many factual details. And we also have to figure out how all these facts related to the ethical questions. Throughout many studies, biblical decisions have been that ethical judgement involves the application of God's word to a situation by a person.  This outlook on ethics has reminded us there are three major perspectives to be taken on every ethical issue. A focus on God's word, which we have called the normative perspective; a focus on the person, which we have called the existential perspective; and a focus on the situation, which we have called the situation perspective.  The importance of considering facts about God, the world around us and human beings when we make ethical decisions.

The Bible relates the true story of creation in order to explain how humanity was actually designed to function within the world. The Bible contain the appeal to the creation accounts to prove how the world is supposed to work and what role human beings are morally obligated to play. 
Theologians often refer these obligations as ' creation ordinances'. They are moral requirements established by God's work of creation.
Some times, creation ordinances are explicit. For example; God's command to be fruitful and to multiply is very vivid. It is a direct command to the human beings. But there are implicit ordinances like' keeping Sabbath day holy. The creation accounts don't say explicitly about keeping Sabbath. But in Exodus 20:11, Moses clarified that God's pattern of working six days and resting on the seventh. 
Thus the creation ordinances shed light on the rules and obligations for the function of creation on this earth. Violation of them will lead to Chaos and calamity.

The two accounts of creation ( Genesis 1:1-2:3 and 2:4-25)give us a general picture of how and why we are created. Both these accounts compliment each other. The first narrative give a picture of the whole creation process when the second is the kind of a window to the sixth day of creation. 
In the first account we see God giving form and shape to the formless and empty universe. First three days God did it by separating light and darkness, forming sky and the atmosphere and finally separating dry land and water. Next three days God filled the sky with heavenly bodies like sun, moon and stars on fourth day; birds in the sky and sea creatures on fifth day and on sixth day creating all living creatures on land and finally man. Man was made in God's image to represent and rule on his behalf. 
The second narrative concentrate more on creation of human race. Though animals also made from dust; only man was given the breath of God. In order to give a help mate to Adam, the first woman was made out of Adam's rib. Adam named he; which shows his authority in marriage but they were made equal in tasks assigned to them.
Thus the Bible contains the most unique accounts of creation compared to any other document available.

The Bible evidently says man as a superior being above all other creatures. According to Genesis 1:27, it is a separate act of creation. After making man God said' very good' where as ' good' is used in relation to other creations. The superiority is vivid in genesis 2:7, where we see only Adam receiving the breath of God.
The superiority of man is evident in the fact that he is made in the image and likeness of God. man is also appointed to rule over the creation on behalf of God. God created humanity to reflect his glory and attribute. Man is given a superior role to administer God's rule over earth. Adam exercised this authority by naming all creatures. later the scripture confirms human superiority by putting him almost on the level of angels ( psalms 8:5).
Though we see many people deny and destroy the distinction between human and animals; supporting evolution theory; we know that the humans are mentally superior to the animals. Humanity was created to be superior to the rest of creation in both dignity and authority.

India is a pluralistic society with different religious beliefs and cultures. The major religion Hinduism itself is pluralistic in relation to the myths on creation and origin of man. Though there are variations with different accounts, they have something common in them.
Hinduism believe creation as eternal and go through a process of creation and destruction. So beginning refers to the beginning of a phase. 
Concerning the origin of man, the major concept is Brahma created human and whole life. He created man of his soul. One of the stories mention that Brahma split in to two to create man and woman. According to the "Matsya purana', sage Manu was the first man created by Brahma. He was born through the union between Brahma and Shatrupa.( goddess). The rest of the race was born from the union of Manu and Ananti. 
Rigveda has a different account of human origin which says human race was born from the five children ( Four male and one female)of lord prajapati; as Brahma was earlier called.
Hinduism also talk about cycle of rebirths. The theory evolution has a greater place in Hindu mythology of creation and human origin.
The biblical record of human origin is totally different from the Indian or Hindu concept. The union of god and goddess, process of evolution and cycle of rebirths are in contrast with the biblical concept of God making man in his own image and likeness.

God made man with a purpose and entered in to a covenant relationship. garden of Eden as a sanctuary, a precursor to the Tabernacle or Temple; Adam and Eve had a priestly ministry to fulfill. As Adam and Eve were chosen to look after the garden, the old Testament priests were chosen to look after the tabernacle/ Temple. As priests represented God in the Temple; Adam and Eve represented God in the Garden of Eden. 
God appointed Adam and Eve to rule over the creation on his behalf. The great King of heaven ordained humanity as his royal vassals to expand his Kingdom beyond the initial boarders his dwelling In the garden through multiplying and replenishing the whole earth. Ultimately the humanity was to turn the whole planet in to God's earthly sanctuary as an extension of his heavenly Kingdom. 
God's covenant with Adam and Eve is binding to humanity. We are supposed to fulfill our priestly duty to serve God, worship him, cultivate and guard creation and to turn the whole world in to a sanctuary. Also we are supposed to exercise the divine authority given to us as the children of God. 
We fulfill the priestly responsibility in the Church through rendering sacrifices of praise and Obedience obedient to him proclaiming his goodness. By preaching the gospel and manifesting the power of the Holy Spirit, we exercise the divine authority and establish the Kingdom of God. As we are supposed to represent and rule on behalf of God; in different capacity we represent God in life and spiritual disciplines and exercise divine authority in establishing the Kingdom of God on earth through establishing his Church. Thus both in life and ministry we fulfill the priestly and royal responsibility assigned to us.

SIN is any want of conformity or transgression against the law of God
Disdain and complete disregard for God's law were central to humanity's first sin and they continue to characterize human race.

When God created the first human race - Adam and EVe, they were sinless, they had no predisposition to sin and no reason to sin. God had given them authority to rule over other creatures that God had created. Clearly God had given them clear prohibition - they were forbidden to eat the fruit of the tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. There were 99% possibilities and probabilities to obey God and 1% prohibition to round it up to 100%. But unfortunately Adam and Eve fell for that 1% to round the negativity to 100%, leaving aside every other probability in obeying God - and hence disobeyed the very first covenant made with humanity represented through Adam and Eve. 

In Genesis 3:1-7, the serpent tempted Eve to eat the forbidden fruit, and she gave some of it to Adam and he ate too. Immediately they realized they were naked and felt shame. that's the origin of sin in the human race. 

God confronted Adam and Eve and cursed them because of their disloyalty. These events are summarized as The Fall of mankind, sin caused humanity to fall out of God's favor and blessings. 

As a result of the fall, God judged man and women and indeed the whole of creation. Mankind experienced death because of the sin.

Adam and Eve sinned and their sin was the origin of sin in the human race.

The idea of authorship of human sin is important since many opponents of Christianity have accursed God of authorizing humanity's fall into sin.

After Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit, God judged the serpent, Adam and Eve. In the course of that judgement, Adam and Eve both tried to shift the blame to someone else. Adam was the first one to try to shift the blame to someone else. 

Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent - 

Adam didn't deny eating the fruit, but he did attempt to avoid being held responsible. First he blamed his wife, who had givem him the fruit to eat. And second he blamed God, since God had created Eve. 

Both Adam and Eve tried to arguie that the blame or authorship of their sin should be placed on someone else. And they tried achieving this to avoid punishment. But God didnt agree with their reasoning. 

As far as God was concerned Adam and Eve were guilty as they chose to disobey his command.

From scripture we can understand that the ultimate author of sin was the serpent, as it was the first character to come up with the idea to sin and first one to try to cause humanity to  sin. But Adam and Eve also contributed free choices to this event and in this sense authored human sin.

Both Adam and Eve knew God's command and freely chose to disobey him. There was no compulsion from any internal and external power. Their minds and choices were their own. In this way, humanity was culpable for their sin, and God was not.

Original sin refers to the consequences of humanity's first sin. Adam's disobedience negatively impacts every human being that naturally descends from him. 

Original sin, is sin that at bottom a person has possessed since he was born And a person cannot evade this sin. Every person who is born must accept this because people are born from a sinful lineage.

When they sinned they lost ther sinless ability and retained only the ability to sin. The corruption they suffered removed their capacity to please God and to merit his blessings and left them only with the ability to sin.

Jesus and Paul compared this state of moral corruption to being slaves of sin. We all remain in this state of corruption until God saves us. 

Jesus compared this corrupt state to a bad tree that can only produce bad fruit. He didn't mean that unsaved fallen humanity never does anything outwardly good. 

The mind of sinful man is death, as their mind is hostile to God.

Fallen humanity, our corruption extends to every facet of human nature, every faculty of our human nature gets affected.

CONCEPTS
Due to sin both Adam and Eve's concepts were corrupted they disobeyed God and believed the lies of the serpent. But the most terrible thing about these corruption is that they were passed on to all human beings.
Sin has damaged humanity's capacity for conceptual thought and caused us to believe that false ideas are true. Sin has made us insane in many ways, we don't value what God and we commit ourselves to evil

BEHAVIORS
Adam and Eve's behavior was probably the most obvious aspect of their sin they ate the forbidden fruit. Humanity sinned and God has given us over to our sinful appetities.
Behaviroal pattern was completely affected. Humanity was filled with every kind of wickedness and disobedience against God and with other humans.

EMOTIONS :
Love is an emotion that motivates us to bedience. Sinful corruption affects our emotions preventing us from loving God and our neighbors preventing us from ma

God told Adam that if he ate the fruit of the Tree of the knowledge of good and evil he would die. 

After the sin God cursed Adam to physical death. As covenant head of the entire human race, his rebellion against God affected our entire human race and fell under the shoadow of his guilt and consequently under the curse of death.

Paul said that all sinned because God reckoned Adam's guilt not only to Adam, but to the rest of natural humanity too.

Adam didn't die immediately when God cursed him, not physically though, but he died spiritually when he was cursed and his descendants are spiritually dead as well.

Paul says in Ephesians that we are dead in our sins and our transgressions in which we used to live when you followed the ways of this world.

As natural descendants of Adam and Eve, the fallen nature was automatilly passed on to  the descendants - all the character of the fallen nature is manifested in all of humans which originated at the Fall of mankind. Human beings suffer immediate spiritual death. But worst if we never come to faith in Christ. If we are redeemed from sin's curse by God's grace, we will continue to suffer both spiritual and physical death. The curst of death and sin is very real.

But by God's grace we can over come sin's influence if we trust in the salvation that was appointed by God, by faith in the Lord Jesus Christ who will enable us to overcome all the sins and curses due to the fall of mankind.

When God created Adam and Eve he gave them the full liberty and choice either to obey God or to disobey Him. God who in his foreknowledge knew everything beforehand. But both Adam and Eve knoews God's command and freely chose to disobey him. There was no compulsion from any internal or external power. Their minds and choices were their own, in this way humanity as a whole was culpable for their sin. Sin was passed on to the descendants.

Sin crept into humanity through the disobedience of one man. Furthermore the fallen nature of mankind was evident in all facets of human nature. Violenece, wickedness and self interest preceded over all other relationships, resulting in pain, sorrow and death Sin took the precedence over everything else and damaged man's relationship with God and also reflecting in the behavior pattern with the rest of the humans.

Though God is love, yet God gave mankind the free choice or will power to chose their paths whether in obedience or disobedience, thereby going through the consequence of sin and pain and death.

But inspite of all the curses and disobedience God's love was evident in Genesis 3:15 wherein God also promised a future redemption for all of mankind. 

There was a ray of hope for all humans to go through the plan of salvation that God himself had authorized.

Though our God is a loving God, yet he allows all humans to go through a process. God allows us to learn through our mistakes and in the process have faith not in our own abilities but to blindly trust in God's path of salvation and beliefs. 

All humans have to go through this life cycle, where the main turning poing it whether to Obey God or Disobey God - accordingly we will meet our destiny. 

Our choices and decisions determine our destiny in life. If we are willing to be governed by a loving God or whether we choose to rebel against God and his will,

But in all these processes of life that we go through all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, but there is hope if we believe in the salvation that God has appointed for us, we are freely justified through the redemption in Christ Jesus.

Having faith in God and his promises we are able to overcome Sin, Pain and even Death and get ready for the eternity that God has prepared for us.

This journey of ours in this world is temporary and we look forward to spend our entire eternity with God.

The office of the image of God is rooted in the authority God gave to humanity to rule over his creation on his behalf.( genesis 1:27-28). So we hold the office of delegated ruler. In theological terms we are God's vassal regents - his administrative deputies or in ancient near eastern terms, his servant or vassal kings. 
Human beings are physical representatives that remind all creation of God's power, authority and goodness. And through us, he manifest his rule over the world and all its creatures.
The nature of our role is first introduced in Genesis 1: 27-28. " Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and over every living creatures that moves on the ground. Just after the creation of man, God commanded his office and explained the nature of his role on the earth.

The first thing scripture tells about humanity is that we are the image and likeness of God. The term likeness further defines that we are not exact copies of God. So it is a representational dynamic, not a static copy of him. 
The Hebrew words for Image and likeness are not identical. Image can be a curved or cast idol. By contrast likeness never represent an idol. It describes the appearance or sound of one thing by comparing it to another. 
Although not identical, the meaning of image and likeness overlap because they both describe a model or sketch of a greater reality. In a similar way human beings are images and likeness of God because we model God's power, authority and goodness. Many theologians argue that collective meaning while image points to our similarity with God, Likeness distinguishes between God and humanity, to avoid wrong assumption that we are exactly like God. 
Our office as the image of God elevates all humanity to the level of royalty; with a task of administering God's reign on earth. This gives us great dignity, but still under divine authority.

It is understood that image of God included the capacity to think rationally. Man used his rationale to give appropriate names to the animals in Genesis 2:19-20. Some of these rational abilities we lost by fall, as evidenced in many biblical passages that speak human of being irrational and insane at times. According to Deuteronomy 29: 2-3, the mind of Israel could not understand the significance of the miracles of God performed for them. In John 8, Jesus referred the unbelievers as the children of the devil who is the father of lies. As a result they believe lies and are incapable of accepting the truth. "The gentiles live in futility of their thinking. They are darkened in their understanding and separated from the life of God because of the ignorance that  is in them due to the hardening of their hearts. ( Ephesians".  (4:17-18)
Our fall in to sin damaged our ability to think and to understand the world from God's perspective; though it was not destroyed completely.  Paul told in Colossians that the restoration of our rational abilities is an aspect of the image of God being renewed in us. 
Through Christ God begins to restore the lost image of God in man by which we are able to think and understand more correctly, so that, our thought and reason become more aligned with his.

The three aspects of covenant relationship with God are : 1. Our obligation to reflect God's Character. 2. Our duty to promote pure worship. 3. Our responsibility to build God's Kingdom. 
Man is supposed to reflect the pure, holy and righteous character of God. 1 Peter 1:15-16. Ass fallen man fell short of reflecting God's character; we rely entirely on Christ's perfect holiness for our standing before God. 
Any form of false worship especially of idol is prohibited in scriptures. Moses reminded that God had not revealed himself in a physical form to protect the purity of worship. He wanted Israel's relationship with God pure through worship, unadulterated by the idolatrous theology and practice of the surrounding nations. 
When God commanded to fill the earth, he was instructing us to place the images of himself every where through out the world and demonstrate God's rule every where they go. The scripture says fallen human beings as against God's kingdom and belongs to the enemy Satan's Kingdom ( Ephesians 2: 1-2). Until we come to the faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, we continue to struggle against God's Kingdom. Nevertheless, all human beings are tasked with building God's Kingdom especially the spiritual kingdom in the New Testament perspective.

As the image of God, man was created to protect,  felicitate and  rule the world and all the creation on his behalf. But man lost his image and accordingly his authority and failed to fulfill his responsibility  towards God and the creation. but God in his mercy reinstated man to relationship with him. But in Christ Jesus and through the Covenant of grace only man is perfectly restored to perfect relationship with God to fulfill God given responsibilities. 
As  ministers of the New Testament, primarily we are entitled to represent God or Jesus Christ in reflecting our Character to the world. In a lost world of sin and Chaos; We are appointed as light in the darkness. 
Secondly we are supposed to maintain true worship of God according to the scriptures. It's our responsibility to convince the world of their futile ways of false worship and lead them to the true worship and right relationship with God .
And ultimately our responsibility is to expand the Kingdom of God through the preaching of the gospel of Jesus Christ. The devil's Kingdom is defeated and Christ's Kingdom is established through turning people from their wicked ways and to the saving knowledge of Jesus Christ. We use God given authority and the power of the Holy Spirit to establish God's Kingdom, His Church. 
In my ministry I try to reflect God's character, to establish true worship and to establish God's Kingdom through preaching the gospel by using the divine authority vested on me.

According to west minister shorter catechism, sin is any want of conformity, or transgression of, the law of God. 
Adam and Eve were created sinless. In their covenant relationship with God; they were given responsibilities. In addition they were given prohibition; not to eat the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil. Covenant blessings were promised for obedience and covenant curses for disobedience. 
Sadly, deceived by the serpent, man disobeyed God and God confronted him and cursed them for their disloyalty.( Genesis 3: 1-24). The theologians describe the whole episode as the 'fall" with the idea that Adam and Eve's sin caused humanity to fall out of God's favor and blessings. 
Because of the covenantal curse God did not end the obligation of Adam and Eve but made it painful and harder.  Even worse Adam and Eve would both experience death because of their sin. 
There fore we see the origin of sin in human race through the disobedience of Adam and Eve in the  garden of Eden.

By 'authorship of sin' we mean the person who is ultimately caused and to be blamed for the original sin. Christianity is attacked by opponents blaming God as the author of sin and claim such God is not worthy to be worshiped and man should not be punished for sin. 
The scripture clearly speaks of the root of sin. Adam and Eve tried to argue that the ultimate blame, or the authorship of their sin, should be put on some one else. But their reasoning was not sufficient for God not to punish them. God punished serpent for deceiving the woman; Eve for mistrusting God and being deceived; and Adam for misled by Eve and eating fruit. 
 in this account we might say that the ultimate author of sin was the serpent because it was the first character to come up with the idea of sin; and the first one to try to cause humanity to sin. 
The scripture emphatically says that God is not culpable or guilty of sin. 1 John 1:5 says ' God himself is the ultimate standard of good and evil. There is no ultimate moral standard out side him that can judge. Besides this scripture portions like Deuteronomy 25:16, Psalms 5:4 James 1:13 make clear that God cannot be tempted by sin. God is free from sin and he hates sin. 
According to Augustin Adam and Eve were empowered to avoid sin completely. But they also had the ability to sin. According to the evangelical thinking, the fallen angel authored sin by taking the form of a serpent ands deceiving Eve and Adam, causing them to transgress the command of God.

In traditional systematic theology, the term 'original sin' refers to the consequences of humanity's first sin.  It is the condition in which Adam's natural descendants are born as a result of Adam's fall in to sin. 
Man lost his original ability not to sin by fall. The corruption Adam and Eve suffered removed their capacity to please God and to merit his blessings. They were left with only the ability to sin and merit God's curse. 
By means of faith and repentance God restored their ability to avoid sin but unfortunately this was not extended to the descendants. The generation were born with the moral corruption to being slaves to sin. 
Sin is pervasive in our lives. It corrupts every part of humanity's being- Body, soul, minds, desires, thoughts and everything else. And as a result also it corrupts everything that flows from our being - everything we think, do and feel. When we come to the faith in Christ, god renew us in ways that restore our ability to please him in all these areas. 
Sin has damaged human capacity for conceptional thought, and caused us to believe that false ideas are true. we don't value what God value and we commit ourselves to evil Ephesians 4:17-18.
Adam's sin served as the model for all the behavioral sins that have plagued humanity since then. This sinful behavior caused God to destroy the entire human race with a flood. Romans 1:29-32.
The sinful corruption also affect our emotions, preventing us from loving God and our neighbors as we should . Also it prevents us from manifesting other righteous emotions that flow from this love. This affected the social and family relations as well. Pervasive corruption is one of the terrible consequence of man's fall.

Adam was warned of death penalty if they eat the fruit of the prohibited tree in the garden. after the fall God, cursed man with physical death. As the covenant head, Adam's guilt passed to rest of humanity. ( Romans 5: 12-17).
The scripture does imply that Adam died spiritually when he was cursed, and that his natural descendants are spiritually dead before they come to faith.  Ephesians 2:1-2. Spiritually dead means to engage in sin and live against the spiritual kingdom of God, separated from the presence and fellowship of God. 
All fallen human beings share this spiritually dead condition until we receive spiritual life in Christ. Paul explained this in Romans 8:10. As a result of Adam's sin, human race is born spiritually dead; and eventually suffer physical death. But by faith in Christ we are redeemed from sin and made alive in spirit. By God's grace we can struggle against sin's completely escape it in future.

It is a natural question raised by common people that how a loving God allow sin and pain and death in to the world. The Bible makes it  clear that God mad made man with freedom of choice. Man originally had the ability not to sin. He was also waned of the covenantal curses which will follow their disloyalty.  But unfortunately man chose to sin mistrusting God and disobeying his command. As a result of sin man had to suffer the covenantal curses as a consequence of his sin instead of enjoying covenantal blessings. 
God is righteous and he cannot cancel the consequence of sin. But postponed the physical death which had to effect immediately. So God in his everlasting love and mercy restored Adam and Eve to himself and allowed them to continue in their covenantal obligations. 
Also God promised the redeemer and replaced the covenant of grace in place of the covenant of works to redeem humanity through his son Jesus Christ. As man was unable to fulfill the covenantal requirement God himself fulfilled them in Christ and opened the way for man's redemption. 
So it is not God who caused sin , pain and death but was the choice of man. But God found solution for it in Christ Jesus.

Hermeneutics is a common word in theological  and biblical studies. the word hermeneutics derives from the family of Greek terms , the name, the  ' hermes' the mythological messenger of the god. the family of Greek words related to the hermeneu, which means  interpret or explain. when we refer to hermeneutics we have in mind the interpretation or explanation of some kind of message or communication. biblical hermeneutics is the study of interpreting the meaning and the significance of the scripture. when we read the scripture , then we are involved ourselves in hermeneutics at least informally. informal approaches to the bible are of great value , and these lessons will build on what most of us already understand. one particular aspect of biblical hermeneutics is that we try to see to relate all the data of scripture together under the assumption that they don't contradict one another, but rather they speak - while of the variety of God's revelation, they also speak one in agreement with itself.

Biblical authors themselves often interpreted other scriptures with an orientation toward factual and logical analysis. Romans 4:3 to 5says what does the scripture says ? Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. Paul carefully analyze the meaning of the word "credited or reckoned" as the Greek term Logizomi may be translated . from his knowledge of Greek, he argued that, wages are not credited as gift , but as an obligation. but then he noted that, for anyone who trust god their faith not works, is credited as righteousness. so he conclude on the base of these reasoning that Genesis 15:6 indicates that Abraham was granted righteousness as a free gift through faith. 
Here Apostle Paul handles Genesis 15, with meticulously factual and logical analysis. as this example ,illustrates, time and again biblical authors presented this kind of careful interpretation of scriptures. 
And their approach to scripture, indicates that scientific biblical hermeneutics is firmly rooted in scriptures themselves.

Devotional hermeneutics focus primarily on the divine authorship of scripture. 2 Timothy 3:16 tells us the scripture were inspired by God, or more literally were God-breathed. this fact makes biblical hermeneutics distinct from general hermeneutics. we must interpret the scriptures devotionally as the living word of God himself. time and again Biblical authors indicates that the followers of Christ are to read the Scripture as the word of God, in the presence of God, in ways that bring about extra ordinary and even supernatural experience of God. The covenant of grace has its root in God's eternal plan of history, which theologians refer to as his ' eternal counsel' or 'eternal decree'. God planned to redeem sinners through Christ's death on our behalf which was made before the creation of the universe. Ephesians 3:11 speaks of God's eternal purpose, historically accomplished by Christ. 2 Thessalonians 2:13 says that we were chosen for salvation ' from the beginning'. 2 Timothy 1:9-10 speaks of the grace that was given to us' before the beginning of time. " The Lord and Father of Jesus Christ.... chose us in him before the creation of the world.." Ephesians 1:3-4.  Ephesians 1:11 says that we are predestined according to his plan. It means that God's eternal decree of salvation was fore ordained. There are differences of opinion regarding predestination of specific people but all agree that God's decision to save sinners was made as part of his eternal counsel, before the foundation of the world.

God's eternal plan of redemption involves the work of all three persons of Trinity. The Bible says it was Father's plan to save us ( Eph. 3:10-11). According to Paul it was father's eternal purpose to accomplish our redemption through Christ. ( Ephesians 1:4, @ Thessalonians 2:13, 1 Peter 1:20)
Correspondingly the son agreed to add a perfect human nature to his perfect divine nature, so that he could die on behalf of sinners.  2 Timothy 1:9 says that we received grace in the son before the beginning of time. John 17:4-5 supports this perspective. 
The Holy Spirit agreed to enable and empower the son's work, and to apply salvation to those whom the son redeemed. 2 Thessalonians 2:3
 All three persons of Trinity were and are involved in our salvation. The father planned, chose us and gave us his son. And the son has come and taken human nature, offered himself as the sacrifice and rose again fulfilling God's righteousness. The Holy spirit brings our stony hearts to life, make them tender to God's word, give us the ability to believe and trust in Christ.
The father is the planner, the son is the accomplisher and the Holy spirit is the applier of our salvation.

Covenant grace is the eternal plan of God to redeem fallen humanity through the atonement made by his son Jesus Christ. God eternally decreed it and fulfilled it in the covenant of grace by sending the Son and the spirit to do the work. He also appointed the Son to the office of Messiah or Christ which was necessary for redemptive work. Acts 2:36, John 5:36; 6:38. 
Jesus became incarnate for the specific purpose of dying on the cross to save us from sins. Philippians 2:5-8.  According to Hebrews 2:13-17, the son had come to die as an atonement for the people  that father had previously given him, in fulfilment of their eternal counsel. Romans 8:3-3, Galatians 4:4-5.
The Holy spirit fulfills his part in eternal counsel through enabling and empowering the son's incarnation. 
Amidst all the tragedies and untoward incidents, the believer is assured eternal redemption through Jesus Christ which is the eternal counsel of God fulfilled through the covenant of grace.

The covenant of works took the form of a typical Suzerain - vassal treaty; where God was Suzerain and Adam served as the head or representative of God's vassal people. But in addition to these parties, God the son joined covenant as the mediator. As the mediator, the son intercedes for the covenant people. He reconciled us to God by taking both the blame and the punishment for our sins. He suffered the covenant curses and earned the covenant blessings. through obedience and loyalty and shares them with the sinners he redeems. 
The son began to mediate the covenant of grace from the garden of Eden and continued to mediate ever since. No one was ever saved through works but by grace. The old testament ordinances were symbols that God's people performed in faith Colossians 2:17.
As mediator of the covenant of grace, Jesus fulfilled the covenant of works on our behalf. , and guaranteed that we should receive its blessings. Redemption is possible under the covenant of grace because Jesus is not just our representative but he is also our mediator, both God and man. Hebrews 9:15, 1 Timothy 2:5-6. The unique providence of God through Jesus Christ makes the redemption possible; and no other covenant or mediator sufficed the demands for the redemption of mankind.

When we evaluate actions from a moral point of view, we can do this in two very different ways. We can consider them as morally right or wrong, but we can also judge them as morally good or bad. Scripture shows that God intends His law to function in three ways, which Calvin crystalized in classic form for the church's benefit as the law's threefold use. 
Its first function is to be a mirror reflecting us both the perfect righteousness of GOd and our own sinfulness and shortcomings. The law is meant to give knowledge of sin, and by showing us our need of pardon and our danger of damnation to lead us in the repentance and faith of Christ.
A second function is to restrain evil, Though the law cannot change the heart, it can to some extent inhibit lawlessness by its threats of judgement. Thus it secures civil order and serves to protect the righteous from the unjust.
Its thrid function is to guide the regenerate in to the good works that God has planned for them. The law tells God's children what will please their heavenly father. The Christian is free from the law as a system of salvation, but it under the law of Christ as a rule of life.

Theologian Thomas Aquinas insisted that the literal sense of Scripture was foundational to all its other senses. In his /summa Theologica , he insisted that every legitimate spiritual interpretation was rooted in the literal sense of a passage. He also taught that nothing necessary to faith was communicated as spiritual meaning without being taught elsewhere in Scripture in the literal sense.
In Renaissance scholars begin to study classical  literary, philosophical, and religious texts in their original languages. in the medieval church most believers affirm that God 's full intent in Scripture was known through a four fold Approach. The model following the literal, analogical, and the allegorical. The Quadriga or the four fold sense of
scripture has a long and ancient history and tradition within Christian Church.
But scholars like William Whittaker says , they don't reject the idea of Quadriga, that there's four meaning, but we reject the idea that there is four meaning s or sense of to scripture. 
There's just one and its historical, literal and grammatical.
During the Renaissance, Protestants continued develop the idea that had been championed by Aquinas. they said that all the spiritual aspect of a text that were intended by the author for his original audience are actually aspects of its literal sense. they believed that Scripture's original sense or meaning  is both singular and complex.

The writer , the document and the audience are interdependent guide s to meaning, if we over emphasize the author, we often fall in to a intentional fallacy. it relies too heavily on what we think we know about a writer and his intentions and de-emphasizes the thinks we learn about the documents and audience. we might make unwanted assumptions about the author's intentions by speculating about what he was thinking when he wrote.
A second type of mistake  we make is over emphasizing the document. this kind of error , is often called a graphic fallacy. the term graphic , comes from the Greek word, graphe which means writing. graphic fallacy overemphasizes the document itself.  we might commit this fallacy by thinking that we can sufficiently grasp the meaning of a passage  merely by analyzing its vocabulary, grammar and stricture without regard to its author or original audience
a third type of interpretive mistake we make is over emphasizing the audience. its called an affective fallacy, because its focus too heavily on how scripture effects its audience. the fallacy is often committed when an interpreter speculates too much about the mind set of the original audience and fails to pay enough attention to the writer and the document.

The historical analysis is concerned with the " Acts of God' found in the Bible.  Historical analysis looks at the scripture as a window to history, exploring historical events lying behind the Bible.  " Biblical Theology is the theological reflection drawn from the historical analysis of Acts of God reported in scripture. The Holy Spirit has lead the Church to pursue the exegesis of the scripture in three mail ways such as, Literary analysis, Historical analysis and thematic analysis. The Bible reports of many different kinds of historical events, but biblical theology primarily asks, 'what do the scriptures say that God has done? '.

Factual historical analysis is concerned with how the events reported in scripture fit within the larger enviornment of the ancient near east. A factual approach to historical analysis is concerned with question like the date of Exodus, circumstances for Israel's monarchy, evidence of certain battles. The goal is to establish reliable account of the facts of history. 
Biblical theologians are more interested in the theological significance of the Acts of God. According to Thomas Aquinas, theology has two main concerns: any thing that refers directly to God and anything that describes other subjects in relation to God. Theological reflection teach us about God himself and what do mighty acts of God reveal about the charecter and will of God. 
Both these analysis go hand in hand but differs in the area that when the factual historical analysis gives us the information and facts about divine acts in history; theological historical analysis gives the insight of God, his purpose, charecter and will in the event.

The Christian theologians have always tried to fulfill the great commision by reformulating Christian theology in ways that communicate well with their contemporary cultures. Significant cultural shifts happened in the 17th century that led theologians to emphasis historical interest as never before. The enlightenment of 17th century can be root of the cultural shifts of modern era. 
Biblical theology is a Christian response to a prominent intellectual movement in the modern period, often called ' modern historicism'. For instance, avalanches of archiological discoveries shed much light on the ancient cultures of the world. The science of geology became a endeavor to discern the age and development of the earth. Even biology became historical in its focus on many biologists began to view their field in terms of Darvinian evolution. Similar shifts towards modern took place in nearly every academic discipline including theology.

Many modern Christians without denying the value and importance of scientific research, continued to hold that the scripture are true in all that they claim, including history. 
Modern Evangelical Theologian Charles Hodge defined biblical theology as an exegetical discipline, the study of the facts of scripture. And also he defined systematic theology as the discipline that takes the facts discerned in biblical theology and arranges them in relation to each other. In contrast with the critical theologians, Hodge believed in the authority of the scripture. He taught that Christians are obligated to base systematic theology on the findings of the biblical theology. Followed by Benjamin B Warfield, it was explained that the teachings of scripture were already logically organized in the Bible itself. 
He argued that the Bible never contradicts itself; all of its teachings are harmonious; though the authors described theology in different perspective and style. Thus they described systematic theology as an effort to bring all the theologies of the Bible in to a unified system. 
Geerhardus Vos agreeing to Hodge and Warfield, went further to say that the various theologies of the scripture had a common focus on the history of redemption. 
The efforts of such theologians to establish the authenticity of biblical theology and the initiative to connect with systematic theology harmoniously has caused modern Christians to approach scriptures through biblical theology.

Scholars generally recognize three languages as original biblical languages: Hebrew, Aramaic, and Koine Greek. The Old Testament was originally written almost entirely in Hebrew, with a few short elements in Aramaic.  The Vulgate is usually credited as being the first translation of the Old Testament into Latin directly from the Hebrew Tanakh rather than from the Greek Septuagint. Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Maccabees, and Baruch are included in the Vulgate and are purely Vetus Latin translation.  The Adamic language, according to Jewish tradition, is the language spoken by Adam in the Garden of Eden. Biblical languages are studied more widely. The very first translation of the Hebrew Bible was into Greek.

According to the Bible, God revealed the Ten Commandments to the Hebrew leader Moses at Mount Sinai. These commandments, which have been preserved in the Old Testament in Exodus 20: 1-7 and Deuteronomy  5:6-21, established a code of ethical conduct.  God gave Moses the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai to serve as principles of moral behavior for the human race. The 10 Commandments are commonly divided into two parts. Because the commandments establish a covenant, it is likely that they were duplicated on both tables. Jesus said: Don't think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn't come to destroy, but to fulfill.

Mosaic laws are divided into three categories: moral, civil, and ceremonial.  These were specifically given for the culture of the Israelites, which includes everything from murder to restitution and dietary restrictions. Second, are ceremonial laws.  In the view of Westminister Divines, only the moral laws of the Mosaic Law, which include the Ten Commandments and the commands repeated in the New Testament directly apply to Christians today. The law of Christ is a New Testament phrase that most likely refers to the two commandments which are mentioned by Jesus "you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.

If Jesus did not come to abolish the law, does that mean all the Old Testament laws still apply today? God's laws were given to help people love God with all their hearts and minds. Throughout Israel's history, however, these laws had often been misquoted and misapplied. By Jesus's time, religious leaders had turned the laws into a confusing mass of rules. When Jesus talked about a new way to understand God's law, he was actually trying to bring people back to its original purpose. Jesus did not speak against the law itself but against the abuses and excesses to which it had been subjected. Some of those in the crowd were experts at telling others what to do, but they themselves missed the central point of God's laws. Jesus made it clear that obeying God's laws is more important than explaining them. It's much easier to study God's laws and tell others to obey them than to put them into practice.

The word 'Synchronic' derived from two Greek words 'sun' and 'chronos' which means ' together with' and 'time' respectively. So the meaning can be derived as 'together in time or ' at the same time'. The term ' synchronic' is used to indicate how biblical theologians often explore sets of events in Old Testament history that happened in time. 
As a movie is divided in to different scenes which tell a portion of the large story; the old Testament history is approached with similar approach. 
in Synchronic synthesis, biblical theologians concentrate their attention on particular periods of time in the OT as if they were scenes in a movie rather than on the flow of its entire history. Biblical theologians when they apply synchronic approach some times, they focus on relatively short time frames and other time on long term periods of history. For example some times, the sacrifice of Issac is dealt seperately from Abraham's story; other time his life as a whole story. Some times biblical theologians treat the whole OT as a synchronic unit, to know what God did and said in the OT period.

'Synthesis' simply means 'combining different components of some thing in to a whole'. In this approach, we describe the ways different components of theology revealed in a particular period of history fit together in a coherent, logical structure. 
By the middle of the 20th century critical theologians began to deny the logical character of the OT. Based on a number of linguistic and cultural assessments they argued that the Greeks focused on abstraction and logical order, much like systematic theology.  And by contrast they suggested that the Hebrew mind set looked everything in terms of historic dynamics. From this point of view, the OT did not focus on logical systems or on theological relationships between beliefs.
But in contrast to the denial, the logical character of OT is affirmed because of two reasons. Primarily, recent studies have largely discredited the kinds of contrast between Greek and Hebrew minds; but concluded they were very similar to each other. Secondly, the OT theology displays substantial concern for logic and rational thought. 
Though the OT theology does not employ the standards of formal western philosophical traditions; God's revelation in scripture were not random, disconnected or contradictory.

The poets of the OT were interested in two different worlds that tell us about history. First they gave attention to 'the world' they wrote about. In the first place poetry often opened windows to the past as they provided objective facts about God's acts and words. Eg: Song of Moses and Miriam in Exodus 15. 
Secondly OT poetry provided windows to contemporary historical information from the writer's own time. Eg: Psalms 1:1- Meditation of the law. 
Thirdly OT poets turned their readers attention towards the future. Isaiah 40:1-11, return of exiles. In one way or other the OT poetry often conveyed information about the revelatory acts and words of God in the past, present and future. 
Like poets, the authors of narratives also stood between two worlds. On the one side, they wrote about world that was the subject of their 'text' or 'the world'. Narrative, largely focus on the past, only rarely mention the present or the future. 
On the other side the authors of the narratives also dealt with their ' world', the world in which their readers lived.  They wanted their readers to think, act and feel in certain ways within their own worlds in the light of past events. 
The OT narratives were doxological, theological, poetical, polemical, moral and motivational. They were didactic, designed to teach early readers about their lives.

Since the enlightenment in the 17th century, historians expect OT narratives to be like modern journalistic historic writings. Three modern standards that are often mistakenly applied to OT narratives are : primarily, historical accounts should be comprehensive. But the OT authors felt no compulsion to include every significant fact because it was written with a didactic purpose. Though they did not meet the criterion of comprehensiveness in good history writing; their narratives are true and authoritative records of the past. 
Secondly, the OT authors were only as precise as their didactic purpose required. They were only precise as they needed to reach their didactic goals. The lack of modern precision does not mean that the accounts are untrue. 
Thirdly the OT narratives are not objective by modern standards. God inspired OT authors to shape the opinions of their readers. This goal influenced what they omitted, what they included and how they described them. 
The OT narratives were not designed to meet modern standards of history writing. They only present fully reliable historical information that will enable us to construct synchronic synthesis of OT theology.

The Term ' Diachronic' derives from two Greek words; 'dia' means ' through' or ' through out' and 'Chronos' which means ' time'. Diachrony is a concern with the passage of time. In biblical theology, the term 'diachronic' points to the ways Old Testament theology transformed, changed or developed through time.
Diachronic approaches to the Bible concentrate on how theological structures progressively unfolded through time. This is in contrast with the synchronic synthesis. Though these approaches differs, they are also interdependent. So biblical theologians move back and forth between synchronic and diachronic work in variety of ways. Both these approaches are necessary to understand the theology of the Old Testament properly.

We use the term development to suggest two main ideas. First, changes in Old Testament theological structure always move toward fulfilling God's purposes of history. Secondly, we speak of development because theological changes only occur through God's providential involvement in history.
Divine purposes; The scripture affirms that everything in history including shifts in theology, always accomplish God's unfailing purposes for his creation Isaiah 46:10. It fulfills the long term and short term goals of God in history. And ultimately it leads to God's glory and establishment of his Kingdom. 
Divine providence: Though the Old Testament theological development often appears like a road seen from distance, actually on a close look, the road of the Old Testament is filled with steep inclines, fast descents, and sharp turns to the left and right. These abrupt shifts are caused by God's providence, his complex involvement with his creatures.

The covenants with Adam and Noah known as universal because they were made between God and all humanity. The theological structure of the covenants tell us much about the relationship between God and all people. 
Following the universal covenants, God established national covenants with special people Israel: the covenants with Abraham, Moses and David. God narrowed down his covenantal attention to just one ethnic group establishing Israel to lead the rest of humanity in service to God.
The people of Israel were promised by the prophet about a New and final covenant God would make with his people Jeremiah 31:31. This covenant is also known as the covenant of fulfilment. The New covenant charectarises every particular theological structure from Christ's first coming to his glorious return. 
 We see the six major divine covenants so permeated the theology of the times in which they were revealed that they provide us with ways of understanding the different emphases of major historic epoch in the Old Testament. Adam's covenant introduces the age of foundations; Noah's covenant began an age of natural stability; Abraham's covenant established promises for Israel; Moses' covenant introduced God's law; David's covenant emphasized Kingship and the New covenant brought all of these earlier covenants to their ultimate fulfillment.

In a broad sense biblical theology applies the term' Typology' to any diachronic development of topics in OT theology. In a narrow sense, we can summarize the meaning of typology as follows: ' Biblical typology is the study of diachronic developments between theological structures closely associated with significant persons, institutions and events in scripture'.
In simple language typology is the study of types in three important passages NT writers spoke of particular theological structures in the OT as Types of the theological structures of the NT faith. 
I Romans 5:14, Paul declared Adam as ' a pattern of the one to come'. Paul observed that Adam was a type of Christ. 
In 1 Peter 3:20-21, Christian baptism is presented as a NT counterpart to Noah's flood. Colossians 2:17 speaks of OT ceremonial law as a shadow of the things to come, which is fulfilled in Christ.

The aspects of Old Testament worship, like sacrifice, temple, Passover are types of the things to come. When we apply these aspects of Old Testament worship and practices, they should be presented as the shadow of the things to come. They were types of things to come and to be fulfilled in Jesus Christ as the messiah. 
Old Testament sacrifices foreshadowed the great sacrifice or atonement to be made by Jesus in the fulness of time. The old Testament temple was a shadow of the heavenly Tabernacle through which Jesus had to enter through with his own sacrifice. It also depicted the New Testament believer who is the living temple of God. The Passover meal also was fore shadow of the true pass over lamb, Jesus Christ who is to be sacrificed for the redemption of mankind. 
In every aspects of Old Testament worship we see the fore shadow of Jesus Christ, the mediator who reconcile God and man. In this perspective we need to apply them in the Church services today under the New covenant.

On the one hand the NT reports many revelatory acts of God, such as Christ's earthly ministry and the ministry of the Holy spirit in the first century Church. It also foretells the acts of God, like the glorious return of Christ. 
Also the NT reports word revelations associated with the Acts of God. God the father spoke; Christ also spoke and at times angels and humans by the spirit of God, revealed God's word as well. 
The NT records report both the actions and words of Jesus, the Apostles and other Christians in The NT because God reveals himself through the intersections between his actions and his words. The NT biblical theologians have drawn attention to the two fold manner in which God revealed himself. Old and New Testaments biblical theology, both focus on God's act and word revelation.

In the development of OT theology, each time God reveals himself acting or speaking in history, to one degree or another, his new revelations reconfigured existing theological structure. 
As NT history moved forward, theological structures underwent diachronic changes. But because diachronic changes in NT history were not as dramatic as changes in the OT. NT biblical theologians have shifted their attention in a new direction. Instead of focusing on different historical periods, they have tended to treat the entire period of NT history as a whole. The theological unity created by the NT brief history, uniform circumstances and single covenant makes it difficult to do extensive diachronic study. So instead of dividing the history of God's NT act and word revelations in to small segments, they have focused on the ways, different NT authors provided different perspectives on the entire period.

The OT eschatology also developed in significant ways over time. These diachronic developments in the OT set the stage for what the NT biblical theologians have discovered about eschatology in the New Testament as well. 
Old Testament eschatology began in seminal form in the days of Adam and was refined further in the days of Noah. In Abraham's time, Israel's blessings to the world became the means by which God would bring history to its ultimate end.  Moses connected this hope with Israel's glorious return from  exile. The covenant with David set his dynasty and Jerusalem at the center of these glorious last days after exile. And also there was a brief period of hope, Israel's continuing rebellion caused the OT to end with the hope of the eschaton postponed to the distant future. Upon these background developed the New Testament eschatology.

Biblical theologians have demonstrated that in one way or another every NT teaching was shaped by Jesus' three phase view of last days. 
First, the NT authors spoke of the entire period as the last days. Hebrews 1:1-2. Second, NT writers designated the extended period of Church history as the last days. 2 Timothy 3:1-5. Third, the NT authors described the consummation of the Kingdom at Christ's return as the ' last days'. John 6:39.
The NT writers believed that all revelations from God from time to time of Jesus' earthly ministry until his return in glory took place in the last days. Jewish religious leaders and general Jewish population raged against Christianity precisely because of the Christian outlook on the messianic last days. Christians believed that Messiah had already come, but in a way that unexpected. Such a messianic scenario was utterly contrary to what Jews believed in that day. This brought a break between first century Judaism and Christianity. And for these reasons NT authors were deeply pre occupied with Jesus' three phase eschatology.
