It was once believed that the Apostles' Creed was written by the twelve Apostles in the first Century. But there is no evidence. In the writings of the early Christians there are many lists of essential doctrines that resembles the Apostles' creed. The writings of the Church fathers like Origen and Irenius indicated the existence of written rules of faith; to preserve the faith. They included the affirmation of important doctrines, as well as moral teachings and traditions. 
Some ancient doctrinal lists are in the form of creed which were often recited in liturgical settings. In early centuries each congregation had its creed, summarising essential biblical truth. By the third or fourth century, some creeds rise to prominence and being used in multiple churches. 
The Roman creed was one among the prominent. This creed is so similar to the Apostles' creed. Many Scholars believe Apostles' creed as a later version of Roman creed. 
Regardless of its origin, the churches especially wester churches began widely using it. In the early centuries its wordings varied from Church to church. But in the eighth century the wordings was generally standardized in to the form that we recognize and use today.

The early church relied on scripture as the basis for all its doctrine and practice. But they still depended on the traditional teachings of the church to summarize and protect the teachings of the scripture. 
Bit it was necessary to formulate concise, clear statements on what the church believe, especially because of the false teachings. Also the scripture are very long and literacy was limited; so it was necessary for people to understand and comprehend the faith without reading the entire Bible. The canon of scripture was formally listed around 397 AD; so the authoritative faith of the Church was passed through creeds. The Apostles' creed still summarizes the essential teachings of the Bible in a simple way. The problem of human infallibility also made important for the Church to record its rule of faith in written form.
The goal of preserving the Church's traditional teaching was to ensure that the churches did not stray from the original meaning of the scripture, in order that believers would rightly understand the teachings of the Apostles, that they would firmly grasp and live by the words of Christ.

Christian faith affirms that there is only one God, and that this God exists in three persons, namely the person of the father, the son and the Holy Spirit. The mention of these three name together and on equal terms implies that while the father, the son and the Holy Spirit are all distinct persons, they are only one God. Apostles' creed does not mention the term 'Trinity' or spell out its details, but people understood God as one and in three persons. 
The Trinity is commonly stated this way: God has three persons, but only one essence. By the term 'person' we mean a distinct, self aware personality. And by the term ' essence' we are referring to God's fundamental nature of the substance of which he consists. 
Regarding father, the creed ascribes to him the attribute of being Almighty, the maker of heaven and earth. The creed describes more about the earthly life and ministry of Jesus Christ; The incarnation, life, suffering, death, burial, resurrection, ascension in to heaven and finally his role as a judge.
 Of the Holy Spirit , the creed says the he caused the virgin Mary to become pregnant with Jesus. The creed also associates the Holy spirit with the Church, and with our experience of salvation both now and in future.

Since first century there were people who refuse to participate in the visible church activities while believing in Christian doctrines. Hebrews 10:25. But the scripture teaches that the Church is important and necessary for Christians. Christians are supposed to form an actual, physical community, and this community is extremely important to every believer. It is not to be limited to spiritual fellowship, but to function as a family or neighborhood. 
The creed affirms the fact that Christ appointed his church to protect and proclaim the gospel and other truths of the Bible. Jude 3 - 4 mentions that part of Church's job is to content for faith, to protect the truths and beliefs that have been entrusted to it against those who promote false teachings and practices. The Church cannot abandon this call, but keep trying to preserve doctrine in the Church as we believe' I believe in the Church'.

In Ephesians 2:19-21 Paul spoke of the church as a building founded on the Apostles and prophets. Without a solid, true foundation, the church could not be built in a way that honored God. 
In a similar way, Christian theology must be founded on true doctrines and principles if it is to honor God and be useful to his people. Just as Jesus Christ is the corner stone of the Church, his teachings are the corner stone of Christian theology. And just as the Apostles and prophets became the Church's foundation, by introducing Christ to the world, the Apostles' creed is foundational to theology because it introduces us to the teachings of the Apostles recorded in scripture. 
The Apostles creed functions as a doctrinal standard because it presents several of the biggest, most important ideas of Christianity. Using the creed as a standard helps us remain faithful to scriptures amidst false teachings.
Also the Apostles' creed provides a logical basis for all that we believe. First, it helps us to see the relationship between the various different beliefs in our theological systems. And second, it helps us to think about doctrines that are more remote from scripture in ways that harmonize these less central ideas with our fundamental beliefs.

The scripture clearly says that the polytheistic belief is part of human sin and alienation from true one God. Romans 1:20-23. Many passages asserts God's singularity. 
It is clear from the scripture that all monotheistic religions like Judaism and Islam, do not worship same God. They disagree over his character, divine actions and even over his nature. Such monotheistic religions deny the Trinitarian faith of the Bible. 
Instead of using 'Yahweh', the Apostles' creed use 'God' which indicates that the God of Christianity is the only one deserves to be called God as we read in 1 Kings 8:60. Though the other religions believe that they worship actual gods, the Bible says they worship imaginary beings or even demons- inferior, created spirits who ruled by the Christian's God. 1 Corinthians 10:20. 
The Bible insists that only the Christian's God is true, divine and he will only judge the world; and only He has the power to judge us.

By 'simplicity' it means the essence of God that we have in mind- his fundamental nature, the substance that makes up his being. Theologians use this in a technical way to mean that God's essence is not a composite of different substances but a unified whole consisting of only one substance. 
When theologians say that God has a simple, unified essence, they were denying that the father, son and the Holy Spirit were three separate gods that some how joined together in the Trinity.  Instead the affirm that these three persons had always existed together as only one God. 
So Christians do not believe in three Gods, but only one God- one divine being- who exists in three persons. Traditional Christian worship has always been fully Trinitarian: we worship all persons of Trinity, and we offer songs of praise and prayer of petition to each one of them. To neglect any person of the Trinity in favor of another is to neglect God himself.

The word 'ontological' means ' relating to being'.  So we look at the Trinity in terms of being and essence in it; how the three persons of the Trinity are integrated with one another, and how they are single in essence. 
From the perspective of ontology, all three persons of God interact with each other, how they relate to one another as individual persons. In this view, each persons has different responsibilities, a different level of authority and a different assigned role with different task to perform. 
The father, son and the Holy Spirit engage in conversation with each other, make agreements with each other, and interact in many other ways. Both ontological and economic perspectives, the father is said to be the first person of the Trinity. In ontological perspective the Son is said to be generated by the father, and the Holy Spirit said to proceed from the father. From the Economic perspective, the father is said to be the first person because he has the authority over the other two persons.

In the broader sense, scripture sometime refers to God as being the father of everything he has created. Deuteronomy 32:6, Isaiah 43:6-7. Our human relationship to God as creator is often expressed in terms of relationship between a father and a son. This shows our origin and his authority. 
It was common in ancient near east to consider Kings as the father and people as their children. So God is considered as the Royal father or imperial father who takes care of people, provides and protects them . This concept is expressed in the Lord's prayer. 
More often in the OT, God is portrayed as the family head of the nation of Israel. Deuteronomy 1:31. Hosea 11:1. The same concept is prevalent in the NT too. Matthew 1:12. Passages like 1 Timothy 3:15, the Church is referred to as God's house hold and family. 
In al these perspectives God's fatherhood is referred and understood by the people through the scriptures. .

Absolute: God's authority  over the creation is absolute in the sense that he has complete freedom to do what ever he wants with his creation. Romans 9:20-21, Isaiah 29:16. 
Exclusive: God's authority as creator is exclusive in the sense that no creature possesses absolute authority. father also has the authority over the other persons of the Trinity. John 5:26-27. 
Exhaustive: By saying God's authority as exhaustive, we mean that it extends over everything he has created, in every detail. This means two things: primarily, every one is under God's authority- human, angels and demons. Secondly, everything is under his authority - all his creation function in his will. There is no segregation between sacred and secular in relation with divine authority.

His moral standards for human beings flow from  his moral character, and therefore they apply to all people in all cultures for all of history. God is love , so he commands us to love. He is holy, and he commands us to be holy. He is merciful, and he commands us to be merciful. He is truthful, and he commands us not bear false witness.

Revelation was written in a particular time  and place to particular people. Traditionally, interpreters have approached Revelation in four primary ways. 1. Preterist 2. Histrorist 3. Futurist 4. Idealist. 

We should resist "Revelation-made-easy" approaches. If we are unwilling to live with an any uncertainty. The first Christians were blessed for obeying Revelation (1:3) and the book is described as an unsealed book. even for people living in John's day (22:10).  Revelation does not progress in a neat linear fashion. The book is filled with prophetic, apocalyptic visions designed to make a dramatic impact on the reader, not to present a precise chronological sequence of the future events. For example, notice that sixth seal(6:12-17) takes us to the end of the age.

The teachings of the Sermon on the Mount have been a key element of Christian ethics. For centuries, the sermon has acted as a fundamental recipe for the conduct of the followers of Jesus. The last verse of chapter 5 of Matthew is a focal point of the sermon that summarizes its teachings by advising the disciples to see perfection. The Greek word telios used to refer to perfection also implies as end, or destination, advising the disciples to see the path towards perfection and the kingdom of God. It teaches that God's children are those who act like God.  The teaching of the sermon are often referred to as the Ethics of the Kingdom: they place a high level of emphasis on "purity of the heart" and embody the basic standard of righteousness.

When the Lord Jesus taught  His disciples the beautiful prayer known as the Lord's Prayer, He began " Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name, Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven". Spiritual kingdom in people's heart is certainly a part of it. Paul said" For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. And thus, the Church is one form of Kingdome of God, a community of people who through faith in Christ and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit serve Christ in the world. Jesus referred to His own miracles as "signs of the Kingdom" for they were bright sports in the darkness.

The kingdom of God is one of the key elements of the teachings of Jesus in the New Testament.  Drawing on Old Testament teachings, the Christian characterization of the relationship between God and humanity inherently involves the notion of the Kingship of God. The Old Testament referes to "God the judge of all" and the notion that all humans will eventually be judged is an essential element of Christian teachings.  The new Testament is written against the back drop of Second Temple Judaism. The view of the kingdom developed during that time included the restoration of Israel to a Davidic Kingdome and the intervention of God in history. The coming of the kingdom of God involved God finally taking back the reins of kingdom.

The author of Hebrews wrote to exhort his audience. Exhortation implies to summon the speakers side or to take the speaker's point of view.

The frequency of the exhortation co-relates to the urgency of the messages. These messages were implicit at times and at least 30 times they appear explicitly.

To urge - to implore, encouraging - exhorting the audience to do this or that. using imperatives, direct orders, associated with persuasive oratory.

The book of Hebrews has been characterized as highly rhetorical, can be categorized as follows 

1) Rhetorical devise called synkrisis in Greek - comparison between 2 or more things to convince the audience to affirm the speaker's point of view.

2) Another rhetorical devise of Exempla, list of illustrations or examples that follow one another to build a reasonable argument to prove a point.

3) The third rhetorical devise - Expression - gol wahomer - can be translated as light to heavy. Such arguments begin with simple explanation graduating to more complex conclusion. 

These examples help us to see the urgency of the author's intentions using different rhetoric styles to convince the audience.

Objective and subjective approaches to meaning to oppose each other in some fundamental ways. But they have something very important in common. A dialogical model help us deal more adequately with our own weaknesses and with the divine authority of the Bible. An authority dialogue model acknowledges that objective truth can be found in the text of scripture. It also avoids some serious dangers associated with objectivist extremes. Biblical theology is a Christian response to modern historicism: the belief that history hold the key for understanding ourselves and the world around us. Christians have always explored the acts of God reported in Scripture. But in the modern period, significant cultural shifts took place that led theologians to emphasize these historical interests as never before. Simply put, biblical theology is a Christian response to a prominent intellectual movement in the modern period, often called modern historicism. 

One of the most well-known Enlightenment figures who expressed this cultural shift was the German philosopher Greg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, who lived from 1770 to 1831. Hegel is best known for his proposal that every aspect of reality is caught up in logical patters of historical progress known as the dialectic. The entire universe, he thought was so ordered by God that it followed a divinely ordained historical logic. From his point of view, we understand every item in the world best when we see it in the light o f this rational patter of history. 

As a result of the cultural changes, historicism rose to prominence for many reasons; including archeology, geology, biology, and nearly every academic discipline. Historicism has had countless effect on modern Christian theology, particularly biblical theology. Theologians have either embraced historicism in ways that compromised essential Christian beliefs or incorporated historicism in ways that upheld and enhanced the Christian faith.

Modern Christians have come to approach the Scriptures through biblical theology due to the effects of historicism. Theologians have either: embraced historicism in ways that compromised essential Christian beliefs; or incorporated historicism in ways that upheld and enhanced the Christian faith. There have been many Christians in many branches of the church throughout the world who have not followed the critical rejection of biblical authority. These evangelicals continue to hold that the Scriptures are true in all that they claim, including what they claim about history. Despite these unwavering commitments to biblical authority, modern historicism has had significant effects even on the ways that evangelicals approach the Scriptures. 

According to Charles Hodge, he believed in the authority of the Scripture and his commitment to biblical authority led him to teach that Christians are obligated to base systematic theology on the findings of biblical theology. Hodge insisted that systematic theology must submit to all the discoveries biblical theology made in Scripture by putting them into logical order.

We speak of biblical history as the process by which God will be ultimately glorified by extending his kingdom to the ends of the earth because at each stage of biblical history, God had specific purposes or goals that guided his act and word revelation. Biblical theologians spend much of their time delineating these diverse goals. But at the same time, in Romans 11:36, the apostle Paul pointed to the ultimate goal of history: For from God and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever, Amen. As Paul put it here, all things are from God in the beginning. All things continue their existence now through the sustaining power of God. And all things are 'to him' that is, they are for God's glory and praise. In a word, God so orders the history of his creation that it will ultimately bring him immeasurable glory. 

God will be ultimately glorified before every creature by extending his kingdom to the ends of the earth. As Jesus taught us to pray in Mathew 6:10, 'Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven'. The divine goal of all world history is the extension of God's perfectly heavenly reign to every corner of the earth. When God's will is done as perfectly on earth as it is in heaven, every creature will bow before God and honor him as the divine king, the supreme creator of all. At that time, the ultimate goal of history will be fulfilled. The Scriptures trace how certain historical events are crucial to reaching the goal of spreading God's kingdom throughout the world.

The term 'synchronic' is defined as the occurrences that had taken place together in time or around the same time. The actual origin of the word synchronic is derived from two Greek words, 'sun' which means 'with' and the noun 'chronos' that means 'time'. When the term synchronic is referred to within biblical theology it refers to the occurrences that took place either 'together in time' or 'around the same time'. The author of the text refers to the example of how the Old Testament has a similar approach when referring to a synchronic study to that of how a movie may have one overall story or theme, but in essence each scene will display or portray a specific story or moment of the overall movie. 

With the synchronic approach illustrated within the Old Testament and within biblical theology, specific approaches are focused on within historical moments. They may vary in length of timeframe however time passes through each of these moments and allows theologians to have a relative perspective on the moments portrayed. Theologians at times actually refer to the Old Testament as a synchronic unit, and they concentrate on the theological perspectives that are established by the end of time.

The term 'synthesis' is defined as combining different components of something into a whole. The actual concept is rather difficult to comprehend, although we typically use it daily. A common example is going to work one day, and being in several meetings, and coming across your colleagues and listening to several different dialogues in the background. When coming home and sharing your day with your spouse, it will be nearly impossible to reiterate each conversation and theme, however in this instance you would synthesize and provide a recap of the day holistically. 

One of the common denials of the Old Testament's logical character was that of applying logic within each discipline. For example, theologians would believe that logic was a primary feature of what they would refer to as the 'Greek' mindset, but it was reasonably foreign to the 'Hebrew' mindset. The argument would then focus on basis that Greeks would focus on abstraction and logical order which is much like systematic theology. However, we affirm it's logical coherence by looking at a few relevant points. The first being that studies have shown that the contrasts between Greek and Hebrew mindsets were discredited. Although their mindsets were different in many ways, they were also very much similar to one another. Second, while many things in the Old Testament will remain mysterious to humans as God's thoughts are much beyond ours, the logical thinking is only a question of how it did versus if Old Testament theology involved logic.

The two worlds of interpretation for both poetic and narrative literature includes 'that world' and 'their world'. That world poetry commonly is referred to poetry that gave attention to the world that they wrote about. In writing that world poetry, objective facts about God's acts and words were provided. Another way that Old Testament poets focused on was the actual world of their readers, which is referred to as their world. The poets would work on designing their poetry to influence the lives of their beloved readers. 

In a narrative sense, that world poetry would open windows to the readers in reference to the past, present, and future. When referring to their world In a narrative sense, their world poetry can be seen in Exodus 15 when readers where encouraged to move forward with confidence to the Promised Land. The text was designed to place influence on the reader to particular ways. When reading Old Testament poetry, it should not be read the same way you read pose, instead you should recognize the unusual vocabulary and figures of speech along with its emotional impact.

When discerning historical information from the Old Testament narratives, it is important not to expect them to be like modern journalistic historical writing as it contains unusual vocabulary and syntax, it's figures of speech, imaginative concerns, and it's emotional impacts. It is important to note that within historical accounts the historical records will include every significant fact about a situation to give a balanced account. Unlike modern journalistic historical writing, all subjective evaluation that may prejudice readers will be avoided. Another important fact to point in differentiating how they will be different from modern journalistic historical writing is that they will either report details with exact precision or at least acknowledge that they haven't. 

In modern journalistic historical writing, it is very common practice to omit the actual facts and report that all facts have been included. Or, it is also notable that the writer will be bias and when reporting out the summary they will persuade the reader to be influenced in one direction of another. This will create a completely false narrative and drive a pre-meditated approach towards the reader. This will then create propogandas and religious fantasies.

The understanding that the biblical writers were only as precise as required by the didactic purposes help us overcome challenges to the truthfulness of Scripture by understanding that the no biblical passages were written in a theological vacuum. The authors would write their texts within a context of beliefs and theological structures. We must be able to grasp more fully the coherent, synthetic structurers of the historical period knowing that God may have given other special revelations that we do not have a record of. There are a variety of levels in spectrum as to simple structures versus very elaborate structures of theological structures within the Bible. 

Since  there are a variety of levels: basic level structures, middle level structures, and complex level structures there will always be a range of simple to elaborate understanding in how we overcome challenges to the truthfulness of the Scripture. As a reader continues their journey within the Scripture they are able to reflect on theological structures on many different levels. It is crucial to note that every moment of the Old Testament history was governed by logical covenant structures. These covenants help us make sense of God's particular act and word revelations.

The word diachronic is derived from Greek origin and refers to two Greek words, Dia, meaning through or throughout and Chronos which refers to time. Diachronic is commonly pointed to the way that Old Testament theology was transformed, changed or developed through time. While synchronic synthesis commonly focuses on the theological structures which emerged within chosen periods of biblical history, diachronic refers more in line with the storyline of history moving from one scene to the next. A common analogy which is made in reference to diachronic views in the Old Testament is that of watching a movie unfold from one scene to the next. 

With a diachronic approach, biblical theology is more concerned with the changes that occurred in theological structures. A diachronic approach warrants questions probing what changes occurred during a given time when God spoke or acted? Or another example would be what theological developments occurred from the time of Moses' early childhood to his call at the burning bush. It is essential to note that while diachronic and synchronic approaches may differ, they are also highly interdependent of one another as well. Meaning, you are not able to purse one approach quite extensively without the other.

The term development is used instead of simply speaking of diachronic changes to suggest two idea. The first idea is that changes in the Old Testament theological structures tend to always move towards fulfilling the purpose of God throughout history. The second reason is because theological changes only occur through God's providential involvement within history. 

Development involves divine purposes and divine providence. Within divine purposes, God's unfailing purposes for his creation is always accomplished, including everything in history and shifts within theology. This essentially translates into the fact that no matter what changes take place, history remains on course and reaches the goals that God had always ordained for it. When referring to divine providence, the Old Testament is filled with abrupt shifts which are ultimately caused by God's providence. With God's complex involvement within creation, divine revelations are connected to the historical circumstances. One example of this would many of the ceremonial practices that God had required of the Israelites within the Old Testament. God had commanded many practices in order to make his people into a holy place, and to our surprise some of these practices were marks of holiness.

Universal covenants are defined as covenants between God and all of humanity. First we see the universal covenants with Adam and Noah and it is referred to as universal because the covenant itself was made between God and all of humankind. So rather than thinking of it as a covenant just between God and Adam or God and Noah, it was more about a covenant to tell us much more about the relationship between God and all people. The universal covenant refers to the governance of divine-human relations established between God and man. 

National covenants are defined as covenants between God and Israel. The national covenants that we can see are with Abraham, Moses, and David, or his special people. God chose Israel to be the nation that would lead the rest of humanity in service to God. That is why this covenant is referred to as the national covenant, the attention is primarily focused on one group. When we look at the covenant of Abraham, the covenant emphasized promises for the increase of Israel and the promised land, and Israel was to then spread God's blessings to the entire world. That is why the covenant between Abraham and God was known as the 'covenant of promise'. Moses' covenant was respectively known as the covenant of law and David's covenant is referred to the covenant of kingship. 

New covenants are defined as the last major covenant that was mentioned within the Old Testament. The new covenants were predicted by Old Testament prophets and emphasized the covenant being established after the exile. The time when Israel would repent of their sin and God would bring history to it's final stages. The new covenant had a primary goal or design which was to govern God's people when God fulfilled his promises to re-establish his people after exile and to then spread his kingdom to the ends of the earth.

Biblical typology is essentially the study of diachronic developments between theological structures closely associated with significant persons, institutions and events in Scripture. In laymen terms, biblical typology is the study of types. For example, when the apostle Paul declares Adam was a 'pattern of the one to come.' We know from text that the the one to come is Christ, and therefore from a broader view we can see that Paul is observing that Adam was a type of Christ. 

Biblical typology is important to study as it functions as a figure of speech. When we refer to typology serving as a figure of speech, it is important to note that specifically it can be also a figure of comparison. A figure of comparison can be an indirect way of describing something by comparing them with something else. It is crucial to identify that biblical typology should be viewed as being designed to point towards futures antitypes. For example when we look at Adam being a type of Christ, it is important to affirm that in his providence, God has arranged history so that earlier persons, institutions, and events anticipated or foreshadowed later persons institutions and events. The reason that it becomes so important is that once we begin to grasp the process of reflecting, we can that identifying typologies are an important part of studying the Old Testament. In this way, you can begin to see how the theology of the Old Testament developed over time.

We should apply the Scriptures concerning aspects of Old Testament worship (sacrifice, temple, Passover meal) in church services today under the new covenant by first realizing what is the new covenant. As mentioned earlier, the new covenant was established after the exile and at the time when Israel would repent of their sin and God would bring history to it's final stage. Knowing that the church is currently living in it's final stages today at a time where the second coming of our Lord is imminent we should indeed take heed to the Scripture and apply the aforementioned teachings of Old Testament worship. 

By knowing that God has allowed for what is to come to be explained and outline within scripture, it is important to note the covenant of fulfillment regarding the coming of Christ, to spread the word, and Jesus' return. The application of Old Testament worship to be applied also coincides the the fact that God's people have to remember that they can not and should not live as they were in an earlier covenant age. And they should also never forget the wisdom of what God had taught in earlier ages, hence the Old Testament teachings. In the Old Testament, worship by humans on earth always imitated the reflection of angelic worship of God in heaven. The worship of Israel was centralized at the tabernacle around the ark of the covenant, and while we as humans reside on earth, the footstool of God is here on earth. Therefore it is essential to remember that while he died for us, we have an ultimate responsibility to worship our creator.

The twofold concept of act and word revelation has characterized biblical theology of the New Testament similar to how God had revealed himself in the Old Testament, through act revelations and word revelations. Within the New Testament, there are several reports of revelatory acts of God referencing the earthly ministry of Christ. The ministry of the Holy Spirit is also referred to in the first century church relating to revelatory acts of God. The New Testament also provides foresight into the acts of God, especially things that are to take place in the future. For example, the return of Christ is depicted several times within the New Testament, and reports on word revelations with the acts of God. 

The New Testament provides both the actions and words of Jesus , the apostles, and other Christians. God reveals his ultimate self through the actions and words of others in the New Testament, depicting the concept of act and word revelation. This can be seen throughout the New Testament, specifically in Acts and Revelations as well as the epistles. God clearly revealed himself through these passages between his actions actions and his words. These words would reference to God's actions on behalf of his people and report God's word to his people as well.

New Testament biblical theologians differ from Old Testament biblical theologians in regards to the way that they handle diachronic developments. For example, as New Testament history moved forward, theological structures also underwent diachronic changes. The earthly ministry of Christ brought forth hope of forgiveness of sins through his crucifixion. Also, as the Old Testament hoped for an entirely new creation to come in Christ, the New Testament refers to this as the clear prediction of Christ's glorious return. The primary difference though is outlined in three main obstacles. 

The first obstacle is that the New Testament only refers to around 100 years of history conceptually. This is much different from the Old Testament. It simply does not cover enough of time for major diachronic developments to occur. The second is that in the New Testament many of the instances are very similar to one another. In contrast to the Old Testament, the New Testament God spoke to the people appropriate to the situations and God's people were fairly consistent during this time as opposed to the Old Testament. Lastly, the New Testament only represents one covenant, the New Covenant in Christ, where this diminished the significance of diachronic developments within the New Testament.

Becoming familiar with the background of Old Testament eschatology helps us understand diachronic developments in New Testament eschatology. Eschatology is a theological term, which essentially means the 'the doctrine of the last days, final things, or the end times.' The Bible is very clear about certain aspects when it comes to referencing the end times. The New Testament holds great promise and biblical theologians have approached eschatology in ways that cut across the grain of debate in a traditional sense. 

In the Old Testament, the development regarding the last days developed significantly over time. It began with the covenants with Adam and goes up to the time of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David. Within the beginning of the Old Testament and in biblical history, God revealed two crucial elements of eschatology, the first beginning with the story of mankind and how humans were created to to fill the earth and subdue it. The goal for history and creation was for the earth to be a place where glory would dwell with his people. The second element was the separation brought on as a result of sin. Two groups were formed as a result of the woman eating from the tree, and the first group is in reference to the seed of the woman who remain faithful to God. The seed of the serpent would be the second group who follow the ways of Satan. 

Elements such as the one dating to the time of Adam, crossed over to the time of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David. With these diachronic developments of eschatology within the Old Testament, ewe are able to see how the last days developed even further within the New Testament. First century Judaism with a twofold view on history, along with the relationship of John and Jesus which drove advancements in the development of eschatology are noted in the New Testament. Prophecies from older times were being fulfilled within the New Testament referring to the last days.

New Testament authors were preoccupied with Jesus' three-phase eschatology because biblical theologians have demonstrated that every New Testament teaching of Jesus' was shaped by his three-phase view of the last days. Every New Testament writer was deeply engaged with Jewish theology. New Testament authors were deeply focused on Jesus' three phase eschatology and their deep interest in this was displayed in everything that they wrote. For example, when the authors would write, they would commonly refer to the New Testament as the 'last days.' Christology, referred to as the doctrine of Christ displayed Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's hope regarding the last days. Lastly, soteriology, the doctrine of salvation was shaped as well by eschatology. The New Testament authors had a similar theme in all of their writings and had displayed these three common themes within their writings as there was such a high importance around the end times and what was to come during the last days. The three-phase eschatology focused on components such as systemic theology, biblical theology and would concentrate on the application of salvation in recurrent themes, ordo salutis. 

This three-phase eschatology represents a decisive break between first-century Judaism and Christianity because Jesus' teaching about the last days represented one of the most decisive ways in which Christians would break away from first century Judaism. An important factor in this was that Jewish leaders and the general population would be extremely upset and raged against Christians in regards to their views on the last days. They were furious that Christians believed that their Messiah had already come.

My understanding of the kingdom of God shapes the way that I do my ministry in several different ways. To begin, having a strong foundational knowledge of the Scripture is vital to ministry. Unless you have a clear understanding about a subject, you are not capable to speak to it, defend it, or be able to advance it. That can be taken into consideration in any field of work, but most importantly with the Word of God, as that is something you can not merely substitute. The kingdom of God is displayed throughout the Old Testament and New Testament and the Scriptures teach us that without salvation, there is no other path to heaven. There were many themes we read in the Old and New Testament about how the perception of human kind and nature perceived the teachings of Jesus and his prophets and disciples. Many of times, it was not received. In ministry, there is no guarantee that they ears that hear or the eyes that see have to believe as we can clearly see in the Bible, however the kingdom of God is at hand and it is our dire responsibility to ensure that we clearly apply the principles that God has set forth for us to be faithful stewards even when we are not accepted. 

My ministry will definitely change because I was born into this life, I did not choose this life, rather this life chose me. I need to apply the concept of God's kingdom to all aspects of life and ministry knowing that even when God was denied by his own disciples and his people, he did not stop doing what his mission was. I will change my mindset that because I grew up in the church, everyone in the church will accept what we speak of, which is simply not true. I have to be willing to expect and accept that even members of a church and gathering may deny Christ, his teachings and what the Scripture points out. This is a cultural and mindshift for me as I move forward and advance my studies in theology.

The Apostles' Creed was developed over several centuries. The creed was composed of a collective work which would change and develop over time. It is a well known and commonly used summary of what a Christian believes in. Around A.D. 700, the creed was standardized in Latin. Although there is no evidence of such, it is believed that the Apostles' Creed was written during the first century by the twelve apostles themselves. There are many speculations on who was the original author(s) however, regardless of the author, the Apostles' Creed was widely used within the Western Churches. 

The creed that we know today was at one point referred to as the latter version of the Roman Creed as there were many similarities between the two. During the initial days of referring to the creed, the wording would vary from church to church, however in the eighth century the wording was standardized into the commonly recognized form that we use today. While Creeds are well purposed and significant articles, it is important to note that they should never be given the same importance of the Bible. The Bible is the only inspired, and infallible rule of faith and practice, breathed by God. The Creed was created and formed to assist Christians to learn and remain true to the teachings of the Bible.

The church believed it was important to create and use a creed because the Apostles' Creed was created to help Christians learn and remain true to the teachings of the Bible. During the early days, many Christians were suspicious of creeds, and questioned whether a creed held the same authority as Scripture. No creed should ever be elevated to this level whether in theory or practice. The importance of creating a creed was to have a tool that summarized the understanding of the Scripture and help Christians learn and remain true to the teachings of the Bible. 

The use of a creed was to originally look at the Scripture in it's original form, holding true to doctrine. Next the churches' traditional teachings as affirmations of Scripture were viewed and then the Apostles' Creed was used to summarize the churches understanding of Scripture. Therefore the main reason why the creed was important and created was to provide an understanding of the core beliefs of a Christian and provide a summary. The early church would rely heavily on Scripture for the basis of all its doctrine, but they would still depend on and require traditional teachings of the church to be able to summarize and understand the teachings found in the Scripture.

The Trinity in terms of persons and nature are described in the Creed on the belief that there is only one God and this God exists in three persons, yet one essence. The Trinity is one of the most important yet complex beliefs of Christianity, the belief of one essence being only one God, yet three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The first person, Father is referred to in nature as Almighty and the maker of Heaven and Earth. The Son is resembled in nature as one who went through incarnation, suffering, death, burial, resurrection, and ultimately ascension. Lastly, the Holy Spirit which allowed for the virgin Mary to become pregnant with Jesus and is associated with the experience of salvation. 

The different work attributed to each by the Apostles' Creed is clearly outlined as the creed has a lot to say about the Son, Jesus Christ. For example, several mentions of details of his earthly life and ministry are revealed in the creed. His incarnation, coming to earth as a human baby boy, living a genuinely human lift, and suffering, death, burial, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. The creed also mentions that Jesus will judge all of humanity on the last day, condemning the wicked while granting the believers eternal life. The creed may not distinctly call out each statement extensively, however the creed says enough about God and his persons to affirm the belief of Trinity and the historic Christian faith.

It is important to participate in the church and to preserve its central doctrines as the Bible clearly teaches Christians to form an actual physical community and the Creed also emphasizes the importance of participating in the church. The church is identified in prominence as Christ has appointed the church to protect and proclaim the gospel of Jesus Christ. The main and primary job of the church is to protect the truth. The Apostles' Creed refers to the church in two different phrases, one being the holy catholic church and the other being the communion of Saints. It is important to note that the holy catholic church does not refer to the Roman Catholic Church, but as a church in all its parts throughout the world. The phrase communion of saints refers to the fellowship of believers, re-affirming the need and importance of the church. 

Even in the first century, believers wanted to avoid the gathering of saints and communion of fellowship, but the Scripture teaches that the church is not only important, but necessary for Christians. The Bible teaches Christians to form an actual physical community. The community is to be like a family where people are able to interact with one another face to face. The Apostles' Creed does not teach or encourage a believer or Christian to believe everything the local church teaches, rather the Creed affirms the fact that Christ appointed the church to protect and proclaim the gospel and its truth. 

There are many false teachings around us, whether in the church or outside the church. There are many sinful practices as well. During all of this, God has never drawn back the assignment of the church, which was and is to protect the doctrine of the truth. The church has a job to do, and sometimes it is done better than other, however we have to keep trying to preserve doctrine in the church. If deny or abandon this responsibility, we are denying a major article of Christian faith.

The Apostle's Creed is foundational to Christian theology as it introduces the teachings of the apostles recorded in Scripture. Just a building requires a strong foundation, the church is symbolized as being founded on the apostles and prophets. Without a strong foundation that is true the church could not be built in a way that would honor God. Therefore, in a similar manner, Christian theology required a strong foundation on true doctrines and principles. This allows us to honor God and be useful to his people. 

The Apostles'  Creed is foundation to theology since it introduces the teachings of the apostles in Scripture. The Apostles' Creed provides a summary of the central beliefs within Scripture, and the Bible is so clear on these points that we can not compromise them. If a false teacher or prophet presents us with bad or incorrect theology, the creed is a standard that helps us remain faithful to Scripture when standing against these false teachers and prophets. The Apostles' Creed serves as an anchor even when you are up against some of the most convincing false teachers that come against you. An example of this took place during the early centuries and the teaching of Gnosticism. The Apostles Creed would confidently reject this idea on the basis of the Scripture and be able to stand against such false teachings. 

Logical Basis is the other method in how the Creed is foundational to Christian theology. We need to initially learn the big doctrines first in order to get the shape of the tree in place, and be firmly rooted in Scripture. When we are able to picture it this way, we can see the value of the beginning with the Apostles' Creed. We are able to see the relationship between different beliefs within our theological systems.

Christians say that the God of the Bible is the one and only true God because of two concepts that they strongly believe in: the singularity of God along with the simplicity of God. To begin with the singularity of God, many people believed in false gods of the Greeks and Romans in the early days. This belief was so common that polytheism was at times required by law. Polytheism is the belief in the existence of multiple gods. However as the Scripture teaches us, people of all kinds know that deep within their hearts that the universe could not have been formed without the hands and work of a divine creator. People accept and understand the existence of God in the Scripture, however through humans sin and wrong doings we refuse to glorify him and give God the thanks He deserves. Within the belief of polytheism there is a belief in multiple gods, however no one god is able to claim being the only supernatural being, which is the role of the one true God.  

The second point refers to the singularity of God. Although God, being a single being exists in three persons. Christians believe in the Trinity and worship all three persons of the Trinity. By neglecting any one person of the Trinity is to reject God himself. Father Almighty known at the creator of all things refers to the entire Trinity hence the singularity of God. 

The creed denies polytheism by using the singular form of 'god' and by dismissing any plural forms of 'god'. The Scripture also refers to the presence of God in different names, El Shaddai (almighty God), El Elyon (God most high), Adonai (Lord, Master, Ruler), and Yahweh (Jehovah, Lord). The creed proclaims that their is only one God that deserves to be called 'God' and that is the God of Christianity.

Simplicity in terms of describing God's essence refers to the fundamental nature/substance that makes up his being. God is anything but simple in nature, He is not easy to understand. However when using the term simplicity, His essence is not a combination of different substances. He is a unified whole that purely consists of a single substance. Central to the core belief of the Trinity, God has three persons but only one essence, which again illuminates His simplicity. The Scripture commonly refers to God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. However, the Scripture also states that there is only one God. So when teaching about God, we don't separate three separate Gods, but rather join them together in the Trinity allowing for three to become one. 

These three persons had always existed together as only one God. The church made it absolutely clear that three persons in one God is one divine being. The Apostle's Creed also refers to the belief of one God who exists in three persons. Even in worship we fully acknowledge and offer worship to all three persons of the Trinity. To neglect any one person of the Trinity would be to reject God himself. The essence of God is fundamental in nature, and is not a composite of different substances, rather substance that makes up his being. He is unified and simple consisting of only one substance.

Both ontological Trinity and economic Trinity speak of the same Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. However the two emphasize different aspects of the relationships between the three persons. Ontological Trinity is a perspective of the Trinity and relates to being, and essence. If you are referring to or focusing on God's being, the ontological Trinity perspective focuses on the three persons of the Trinity and how the persons are integrated into one another and share a single essence. From this perspective, all three of God's persons are eternal, infinite, and unchangeable. With each of these three persons, they also have the same essential attributes as well. They include divine attributes such as wisdom, power, holiness, justice, truth and goodness. 

Economic Trinity is also a perspective of the Trinity and relates to household management, and how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit relate to one another as distinct personalities. When we refer to the economic Trinity, we are taking into consideration how God's persons interact with one another. As well as studying how they are able to relate to one another as individual persons. Although the concept is three in one, each of the three persons hold a different set of responsibilities. They each have a different level of authority, and a different assigned role and task to perform. The three persons engage in communication with one another and act upon each other. 

From both ontological and economic Trinity point of view, the Father is said to be the first person. The reason being the Son was created by the Father and the Holy Spirit was proceeded from the Father. We can see of the Father's authority in the Scripture as the Son refers to doing the Father's will. Therefore with both economic and ontological Trinity, they both share the similarity that they accept the belief of three persons in one essence, however they differ from one another as economic Trinity is focused on the relation of Father to son and Holy Spirit and the level of authority and household versus the ontological Trinity which is the essence of one God but three persons.

Fatherhood as it relates to his role as Creator refers to God being the creator of all things. He is the father of everything he has created. Paul affirmed this idea in the Scripture by stating that to create something is to become its Father. While the creator has formed and brought all things to being, He continues to show great patience time and time again while the world that He created continues to fall into sin and grow further and further away from Him. 

Fatherhood as it relates to his role as King is revealed in the Scripture similar to how a king  at times is referred to as the father of the people he serves and the people he serves are referred to as his children. David was referred to as a King and father to his people and when the people referred to David as their father, they were referring to him as their king. Similar to this concept, God was called Father because he was the great king. The great king ruled over all of the world and because he ruled over his chosen nation, Israel, they were his children and he was their father. God is referred to as Father since he sits on his heavenly throne and rules over all of creation and leads armies into battle. This shows an authoritative father and divine king caring for us, giving us comfort and confidence. Similar to the Lord's Prayer, we refer to God as our Father in Heaven, having dominion over all the Earth.  

Fatherhood as it relates to his role as family head over his people is seen in the Old Testament in many different areas. For example, as Adam was the family head over his wife and sons, God was the head of Adam. God is also portrayed as the head of the nation of Israel, he takes care of his people and portrays his love for Israel since it's childhood. Jesus also taught in the Scripture that our Father answers our prayers in the same way that a human father provides for their children. And he also disciplines us for our own good in the same manner that a human father would discipline his children. The church is commonly referred to as God's household or family and the love he has for his children is displayed throughout the Scripture.

God's authority over creation as absolute, exclusive and exhaustive is described by his unlimited power. God has unlimited, omnipotence, and matchless power when it comes to doing anything he will do at anytime. He can create the universe while choosing to destroy everything that he has created. He can control the weather, he is able to rule and control human governments, defeat his enemies. He has and continues to save his people while performing mighty miracles. He is the Father and has the ultimate and unlimited authority and absolute power to do as he wishes. When we refer to God's authority being absolute, we can see within Scripture how God chose to create the heavens and the earth, how he chose to create man and woman, and how he also chose to wipe out the creation that he had made. This reveals his absolute reign as being the King and freedom to whatever he wishes to do with his creation. 

When we refer to the exclusive authority belonging to God, we acknowledge that the final word and authority  belongs only to the one that created everything, God. If God chose to undo or wipe out the world, he is the only one who can do so, because he is the creator of the  universe and without his authority nothing can come to be. While man and mankind do possess and hold some level of rule, no one holds the authority that belongs only to the creator. Humans have a limited measure on authority and the Father's authority is always superior to the authority of any creature or mankind. 

Lastly, God's authority as being exhaustive is described as God having authority over everything and everything is under God's authority. That means everything over the universe is subject to the authority of God. His authority extends over everything that he has created and it clearly outlines that nothing is free from the obligation to obey God. Everything that he has created was created for a concise purpose, and no matter what the subject is, there is no moral neutrality.

When the Scripture refers to the "Son of God" when applied to Jesus, it is  referring to Jesus being God's son in a unique way. The Trinity depicts this example of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and Jesus is the divine and eternal Son of God. When we refer to the deity of Christ, we must realize that Jesus is fully God and also fully man. We can not have one without the other. Jesus came in the form of man to this world and he is also fully God. This is one of the most fundamental pieces of fact that we must understand to comprehend the divinity of Jesus. 

The Scripture refers the "Son of God" commonly to talk about things in the Scripture that are not divine, for example angels, the nation of Israel, the Kings of Israel, Adam and believers were all referred to as the Son of God throughout the Scripture, and  none of these beings were divine. Jesus, being the son and part of the Trinity comes to us with authority of power, and glory to the Father and the Holy Spirit. There is nothing that can be changed, added, revised about the Trinity and Son of God, He holds the same divine attributes of wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness, and truth. Although there are three different persons within one essence, each person holds a different level of responsibility. A father can not replace a son, a son can not replace a father, and a son can not replace the Holy Spirit. The Son of God is subordinate to the Father's authority and the Son has authority over the Holy Spirit. Therefore, with each role, comes a level of authority and responsibility. 

The divine essence of the Trinity and Jesus being the Son of God is what provides the clear distinction of who Jesus is. He has always been the Son of God and is the eternal Son of God. We are told in the Scripture that Jesus was God's divine Son and is the exact representation of the Father's being. While God has three persons, there is only one essence. While the highest rank always belongs to the Father, there is no conflict between the Father and Son since the Son and Father always agree.

The title "Lord" points to the divinity of Jesus by meaning ruler or master also known as Kurios. Kurios was the term that was used in translation of the sacred name of God by Jewish scholars when they translated the Old Testament. The use of the word Kurios in the New Testament refers to the divinity of Jesus. Kurious was a common word that was used for a ruler or master and was considered a polite form of address. Not everyone who would call Jesus recognized his divinity, at times they were simply calling Him Lord out of respect. However as the Apostles Creed teaches us and as we see when the church confesses, God is indeed a full member of the Trinity. 

When the churches formally confesses that Jesus is Lord, we are affirming the biblical teachings that Jesus is indeed our God and is a full member of the Trinity. He holds the same divine attributes as the Father and the Holy Spirit. When we refer to the divinity of Jesus, it means that we should acknowledge him and worship him both in our prayers and in our songs. It also means that we should pray to him just as we pray to the Father and Holy Spirit. We can take comfort knowing that God has redeemed us from sin and we can see the divinity of Jesus.

Jesus' experiences prove that he was truly human by a few different factors. To begin, Jesus was conceived through human birth. Although Mary was a virgin and she and Joseph did not have physical relations leading to the birth of Jesus, He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born to a female. He began as a baby in his mother's worm and was formed in the same form and fashion as every other baby is molded in a mother's womb. He did not descend from heaven as a supernatural being, rather was brought into this world through his mother's womb as a human being. The next point to note is that Jesus was a real person, a real man with a physical human body. He offered his physical being to be punished, humiliated and tortured for divine judgement to atone for the sins of humankind. 

It can be a common belief for people to accept that a god could disguise himself as a human being, but that is not what Jesus did here. He actually became a human being and went through the physical and emotional parts of a human being. Which then brings us to the point of his physical form, Jesus was arrested and crucified after being flogged, spit on, forced to wear a crown of thorns. His body was one that was beaten, bruised and bled. A body that at one point from exhaustion, collapsed, and was buried in a tomb and allowed for his soul to depart. When Jesus was on the cross, he committed his spirit into the hands of the Father. We can see that when Jesus died, his physical body was buried by men, but his spirit was committed into the hands of God, the Father. When our bodies die as humans, our souls are separated from our bodies and continue in a conscious state.

The Old Testament title "Christ" means the actual title of Jesus' office, such as "king" or "judge". The word Christ is a translation of the Greek word christos which is actually another translation of the Hebrew word mashiach, or messiah which means the anointed one. In the Old Testament, the anointed one referred to anyone that was appointed by God to serve in a particular capacity. There have been many prophecies in the Old Testament that encourage people to long for the one who would deliver them, the Messiah. The Messiah would save them from their suffering and bring them into God's glorious blessings. This was referring to the coming of Christ, and was revealed as He took form of a human and was able to reveal himself as the Son of God. 

The Messiah had a few prerequisites, he had to be the Son of David, be able to atone sacrifice, and be the second Adam. The reason that he had to be the second Adam, refers to the fact that someone had to come in to succeed where the first Adam or man had failed. Adam was initially setup as the head of the entire race, but since he fell and failed, this had to established. God never changed his requirements, human beings still had to build the kingdom of God. In order to build it, we needed a human itself, so eventually the Father sent his own Son to fix the problem. And that is how Jesus is able to fulfill his office. He is able to succeed where Adam and the rest of humankind has failed throughout.

One of the areas that are disputed time and time again, is whether or not Jesus had a real flesh and human nature, or was it just a fake appearance. The human nature of Jesus and it's relationship to his divine nature has been revealed in the Scripture, and Christian theology has maintained that Jesus is fully human in every aspect. He has a body, and a soul and was subject to the same types of physical and emotional strains that every human has including sickness, injury and death. 

The areas of differentiation comes into play when we consider the birth of Jesus. We were all born into sin, however the birth of Jesus was different, therefore he was born without sin. He lived a perfect, sinless life. Before Adam sinned, he was human, and the belief is that humans are able to live a life without sinning which is was Jesus has shown us. It is possible to have a life that does not sin. When we do die, we will still be entirely human, however we will lose the ability to sin.  Jesus is the only person that possesses two natures, a human nature and a divine nature. While every other human only has one nature, Jesus is both God and man. He is fully divine at the same time as being fully human. 

He is one person with two natures, and we can not dismiss the fact that Jesus never put aside his glory or his divine nature. That is not possible, God's nature is immutable. He is not able to put aside his  nature and become separate. Jesus was able to take on an additional nature that did not replace, but merely veiled his divine nature and glory while taking on the form of man. This is how Jesus's human nature and relationship to divine nature were able to coexist while he was in human form.

Although the Apostles' Creed does not state that the Holy Spirit is divine, the Apostles' Creed does affirm that the Holy Spirit is divine in two way. First, as the Trinity hold true to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit being equals and as well as the creed's description of the conception of Jesus as being divine. The Trinitarian formula emphasizes the belief of having only one God which exists in three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. During the early church, Hippolytus explained the baptismal creed used in his day made the structure of the Trinity very explicit. For example, a person was immersed three times during water baptism. First confessing in the articles of faith relating to the Father, then the Son, and lastly the Holy Spirit. 

The second way the creed affirms the divinity of the Holy Spirit is through the conception of Jesus. When the angel of the Lord came and spoke to Mary, the angel state the Holy Spirit will come upon you, in reference to the Most High. Only God the Father can have the power of the Most High, all pointing to the work of the Holy Spirit. The Apostles' Creed affirmed the full divinity of the Holy Spirit through this conception affirming that creating the body of Jesus was specifically the work of God. With the belief and confirmation of the Trinitarian belief, we can see the expressed form of divinity as the angel states to Mary that the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. This references the magnificence of the Father as the authoritarian that will be divine and fulfill the will of the Father.

The biblical basis for the creed's teaching about the Holy Spirit's divinity can be revealed in several different ways. The creed has always been recognized as a summary of the Scripture and never to be taken in as a replacement for the word of God. The Bible however points to the teachings of the divinity of the Holy Spirit in several different ways. The areas of focus are around the names that he is called, the attributes that he possesses, the work he performs, and the Trinitarian formulas that refer to him.  In the Bible, there are several names that are connected to the Holy Spirit and and some of these names suggest the divinity of the Holy Spirit in a very clear and concise manner. Though the word holy does not in itself indicate the Holy Spirit is divine, God is commonly referred to as the Holy One which is part of the Trinity. Names that were implicit on the continuum were: Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of God, Spirit of the living God, Spirit of Jesus, Spirit of Christ, Spirit of your Father, Spirit of his Son, Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead. 

Attributes that were possessed by the Holy Spirit demonstrates the continued divinity through communication, and forms of non-communication that can be expressed. God possesses the attribute of communication with human beings. He demonstrates that we were created by a rational God that we are able to communicate with him and he to us with a form of communication. This is also relevant in a non-communication form through the omnipotence of God. While God is perfect, his power is all throughout which exemplifies the divinity of the Holy Spirit. This can also be revealed through the works that he has done, which are appropriate for God alone and none other. He is creates new life, and regenerates our spirit and is the access to the Father. There is also power behind his works and his miracles which are purely divine. 

The Trinitarian formula affirms the Holy Spirit being a member of the Trinity while being of one essence. The qualities possessed are unique to persons and includes the will of the father, intelligence, emotions and agency. There may not always be a clear distinction between the Spirit and the other persons as we have learned from previous chapters since the Father controls the Son and the Son the Holy Spirit but they are always going to be three persons with one essence. The father will always hold the authoritative power over the son and the holy spirit while being unchangeable but with divine attributes.

The Bible ascribes personal attributes to the Holy Spirit as being too many to list, however we will list a few for demonstration. To being the holy spirit does indeed have a will. This is the vehicle used to plan, to desire and to choose. If this were possible, it can not be of a simple force of power, rather of a divine nature that is able to have the ability to have a will and act upon it. If the holy spirit has a will and wishes to impart on specific people, specific gifts than the spirit must indeed be a person. Forces that are impersonal can not have plans or desires and fulfill  such actions. The holy spirit also has the personal attribute of intelligence. This intelligence is revealed in more than one ways, for example the searching and knowing the mind of God is known through this attribute. He also gives wisdom and knowledge to others. Forces that are impersonal are not able to do this and can not think, know or teach. 

These attributes demonstrate his personhood by acknowledging first and foremost that the Holy Spirit is the third person of the trinity. Not the third god or third spirit, but the third person of the Trinity. The Trinity is composed of three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The responsibility that each person holds is different from one another and each has their own authority and toles. The spirit is subject to the higher authority of the Father and the Son. Which in return means that the Father has dominion and power over the other two, although they are one essence. The mission of the spirit is to carry out the will of the father, and as we can see in the Scripture, to carry out the instruction of the Father and to glorify the Father and the Son.

The Holy Spirit is distinct from the Father and the Son as a separate person within the Trinity as there are three persons part of the Trinity. While the Trinity is composed of one essence, there is indeed three persons part of the Trinity with clear responsibilities, authority and roles for each person. The holy spirit is a subject to a higher authority to the Father and to the Son. The primary role of the spirit is to carry out instructions and glorify the Father and the Son. This is why the holy spirit is distinct from the Father and the Son as a separate person within the Trinity. The holy spirit is called the 'third person' of the Trinity. 

The scripture clearly highlights the distinction of the Spirit and the other persons of the Trinity that shows their interaction with one another in ways that emphasize their difference. The Scripture points to how the Father would send the Son first and the Holy Spirit, with each person they had an appointed role. The spirit would not begin the work appointed until the son had completed his work on earth and ascended into heaven. This makes it clear that the spirit is  separate from the son and a member of the trinity. The spirit is also our defense attorney, pleading our cases before God when we intercede with the Father. When Paul taught us about the holy spirit, he also mentioned the trinity and how  there is one person that is interceding while the others are hearing the intercession.

The Holy Spirit's relationship to the other two persons of the Trinity have been described from two different perspectives. The ontological and the economic trinity perspective have both mentioned the perspectives on the same trinity - the father, the son, and the holy spirit. When referring to the ontological trinity, the reader is focused on the existence of God, the Father. The holy spirit is equal in power and glory to the father and the son in this perspective. All of the three persons in this belief are infinite, eternal and not changeable. The have the same and divine attributes as wisdom, power and holiness. When referring to the economic trinity, you consider how the three persons interact with one another. The trinity here is described as having three different roles and assignments. The highest authority is granted to the Father and then the Son and then the holy spirit is subject to the higher two. The role of the spirit is to carry out the will of the Father and the instructions that are set forth in order to bring glory. 

The reason the holy spirit is the third person of the trinity is because he is breathed out by the father, who is the first person, and by the son who is the second person. There have been claims in other churches during the early days that it was only the father that breathed out the holy spirit, however since the creed was created before this controversy, it did not address these claims. The holy spirit does hold the lowest rank from the perspective of the economic trinity, however it is crucial to note that the he is still fully God and has complete authority over every aspect of creation. There is also a mutual deference, what one person does, they all do. They are alike and agree on everything in nature, the lower rank of the holy spirit or subordination to the Father and Son does not mean he is inferior to them, he is not, the spirit is equal to them both.

The church in the New Testament finds its roots in the Old Testament several different times. In the New Testament, the church is spoken of by using the Greek word ekklesia. However, this term was derived from the Greek translation of the Old Testament. It was commonly used to describe the gathering of the nation of Israel. Even while the the term ekklesia may be used to refer to the church, the word is originally found to refer to the gathering and assembly of the people of Israel. While there may be many differences in translation, the church does not represent a physical building or structure, rather a congregation of people here on earth. 

The church is established for a purpose and has been granted authority to establish and maintain our relationship with God. The church is equivalent to God's kingdom on Earth through which he dispenses his grace. We can see that within the New Testament, Peter refers to the church by names that were applied to Israel in the Old Testament hence finding and connecting its roots back to the Old Testament. The church was identified as a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people belonging to God, 1 Peter 2:9. One of the key differences to note between the Old Testament church and gathering against the New Testament church was that the Old Testament church was commonly depicted as the root of the tree. The strong foundation and level of the church was the Old Testament, and the New Testament was considered to the be branches of the same tree. This illustration was was identified in several portions of the Scripture and the Old Testament was the bulk of the tree consisting of primarily Jews, while the Gentile Christians were the branches of the tree.

Jesus built the church in a way that relied on but also advanced the Old Testament church. Within the New Testament there are three occasions where Jesus mentioned that he will build the church referring to the word oikodomeo, meaning build. We can also learn from the teachings of Paul that Jesus was rebuilding and restoring the church of the Old Testament. Jesus goes into details within his teachings and speaks of different attributes that the church should adhere to. For example, on one occasion, Jesus refers to the people of the church and their responsiveness. In that text, Jesus is talking about church discipline. In Mathew18:17, "If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church; and if he refuses to listen even to the church, treat him as you would a pagan or a tax collector. 

The verse mentioned in Mathew was referring to the guidance that a sinner or person  who has not repented should come before the church. The utmost fundamentals between the Old Testament church and the New Testament church remain the same. The purpose, which is to unite and turn the world into God's earthly kingdom. That is the first and foremost purpose of the church, to unite mankind and rather than proclaim a structure to be a church, gather amongst one another and assemble. This should include both believers and unbelievers. That is the verse mentioned above from Mathew, to be able to guide a sinner or unrepented person the church. 

The church is advanced throughout the Old Testament listed by Jesus and the apostles to fulfill the fundamental obligations of loving God, spreading and advancing the kingdom, and bringing him glory. Jesus is the found of the new Testament church and he is the one bringing restoration and renewal transforming the church of the Old Testament that was failing. The passages in Ephesians 5:22-23 describes Jesus as being the husband of the church.

Some of the implications of the relationship between the Old Testament and the New Testament church is that Jesus ordained the New Testament church as the restoration and development of the Old Testament church. We can see the continuum of the gathering of the people of Israel and the church described in the New Testament.
