Once the ongoing expansion was underway, God determined to fill the earth with people and humanity for a purpose that was too great for one man to accomplish on his very own (Gen 2:18). 

God then appointed man and woman to be of his service, as priests, and as vice-regents or royal representatives. This is true as they were created in the like image or likeness of God. During this time in primeval history, God assured the human race that his grand vision and purpose for them would not fail. This was known as the progress phase.

Nearly every generation of Israel has rebelled against God and suffered under the judgement of God in one way or another. However no matter how many times they rebelled, God brought Israel to repentance and would renew them. However, during the end of the Old Testament, the sins of Israel became so great that God brought down a huge curse of exile towards Israel from the promised land. During this period, hundreds of years, Israel had no homeland, no temple, no priesthood, no one to help lead them in spreading God's kingdom. 

The three stages of progress in God's kingdom during this period are covered over three main factors, the promise, exodus and conquest, and empire. When referring to promise, God made many promises about the future of the nation. Abraham is revealed as a symbolic figure, the father of many nations and his descendants would possess the land of Canaan. The second stage being Exodus and Conquest, we can see of how the Israelites praised God because he was guiding them towards his holy dwelling place. God redeemed Israel from Egypt and highlights the fact of God furthering Adam and Eve's original mission by expanding his kingdom on earth. Lastly the Empire stage, mistakenly by many interpreters, they believed God never intended for Israel to ever have a human king. However Israel was to have a human king in order to further the kingdom of God. As Christians, we know that Jesus is the perfect king who is righteous and comes from the line of David and will bring the kingdom of God to earth as it is in heaven.

The kind of kingdom that God is establishing is similar to what we read in Isaiah 66, where God's throne was in heaven, but the footstool of his throne where feet would touch earth, was the ark of the covenant in the temple. Psalm 72 reveals the ultimate goal for all the developments that took place in Israel and these stages of the kingdom were intended to fill the entire earth with God's glory. God's glorious presence would fill the whole world just as it fills heaven. 

When God's kingdom is manifested on earth as it is now manifested in heaven, life on earth will be like how Jesus and his first century apostles and prophets challenged widespread expectation. They would announce that Jesus, being the Messiah would bring the kingdom of God to earth over a long period of time. In Matthew 13:31-32, Jesus goes on to explain how the kingdom of God was going to come to earth. It would come small, like a mustard seed and over time it would grow and spread and become like a large mustard plant. The kingdom of God would extend over the entire earth and and unfold over three stages, inauguration, continuation, and consummation. This is where Christ will return and fulfill the plan of God to turn the whole world into his kingdom. He will defeat every enemy of God and the world will become the kingdom of God and of his Christ and from that time forth, he will reign forever and ever, everywhere.

Archeological discoveries can give us insight into biblical covenants by helping us grasp how the faithful Israelites were able to understand that there were fundamental connections between God's covenant and his kingdom. There are three types of royal documents from the ancient Near East which often appear within the context of biblical covenants: first, royal and parity treaties. These are considered as the covenants which kings of somewhat equal status were able to acknowledge their relationships of each other. 

Royal parity treaties in regards to divine covenants portray that although men would consider themselves of equal status to mutually negotiate the terms of covenants between, that was never the case when it came to humans and God. God never negotiated with a human being purely because they were never seen as his equal. The royal grants were writings that revealed how ancient kings would bestow land or special status towards their faithful servants. 

Much of the ancient royal documents that have allowed for continued understanding of biblical divine covenants are suzerain-vassal treaties. These ancient writings offer insight into how the authors of the bible were able to understand and grasp the relationship between God's kingdom and his covenants. These were also international agreements that greater established kings would have with lesser established kings and their nations. This would offer additional context and insight into the relationship between God's kingdom and his covenants. We are able to see within the Old Testament of how the Pharaohs of Egypt and the kings of Hittites, Babylonians, Assyrians, and even of Israel would conquer and establish their territories by controlling the weaker kingdoms.

The national covenants moved God's kingdom purposes forward starting with the covenant made with Abraham. Knowing that Abraham was the patriarch of every Israelite, God made his first covenant through Abraham. There is direct reference of this within Genesis 15, 17. Within the book of Genesis 15:18, the Lord made a covenant with Abram. God later confirmed this covenant that He made with Abraham. Through this covenant, God chose Israel to take the role of spreading His kingdom throughout the world. It was through this covenant that Abraham's descendants would spread to the ends of the earth. 

After the covenant with Abraham was made, God made his covenant with Moses. The national covenant with Moses was built on the covenant of election that God had made with Abraham. The renewal of this covenant can be seen with the second generation of the exodus in the book of Deuteronomy. This covenant stressed the requirements for what the nation needed at this time and the law of God. 

Once Israel became established and a fully supported kingdom, God made His next covenant with David. It was built on and further continued the covenant He had with Moses. His promises to David were contingent on the faithfulness to Moses' law. David and his house was required to walk within God's law and and God's covenant focused on the royal house of David. 

These national covenants would then reveal how God would advance His kingdom by establishing the house of David as the line that would eventually rule over Israel forever. This would eventually lead to the house of David remaining in control over Israel and spreading God's kingdom to the ends of the earth.

Covenant dynamics expressed in the universal covenants can be seen in a few different examples. To begin we can see that with Adam's covenant, there was an emphasis stressed around specific foundational patterns at the commencement of the world. Moving onto Noah, we are able to note the stability of nature being emphasized. The Moses covenants was structured around God's law. Lastly the covenant with David was highlighting the specific chosen royal family which was a fulfillment being stressed. 

These are all highlights of the covenants that were made, but the way that they are expressed in the universal covenants is the dynamics of living with God that is always involved. God exercised His right as king towards the implementation of covenant dynamics to ways that would fulfill His purposes. God would administer his universal covenants through the dynamics of human loyalty, divine benevolence, and the consequences for obedience and disobedience. 

The consequences for obedience can be seen through the examples of how God told Adam and Eve that they would suffer the consequences of His curse if they were to disobey Him and eat from the forbidden fruit. Noah was blessed by God for his faithfulness but God did warn him against rebellion.

The divisions of humanity within all the types of divine covenants can be described as God's covenant engaging different groups of people in different ways. When looking at within covenants, the believers and non-believers are included within God's covenants. The universal covenants that were made with Adam and Noah included all the people to God, which included both the believers and unbelievers. The national covenants that were in Abraham, Moses and David also included all people. Specifically the people of Israel, whether they had received salvation or not. 

The difference is that the Old Testament prophecies indicated that with the new covenant, only the true believers would be included. This is emphasized within 1 John 2:19 where it states that until the return of Christ, believers and unbelievers are counted among God's people. Now while all of humanity was included in the universal covenants, Gentile nations were excluded from Israel's national covenants. The reason being that during that time there were three different kinds of people in the world. The first consisted of true believers who were in Israel's covenants, the second were the unbelievers who were in Israel's covenant and lastly there were the Gentiles who were excluded from Israel's covenants. 

The divine benevolence was shown to all people through God's divine grace and outside the covenants, unbelievers have a basic understanding of their obligations to God. While unbelievers can experience temporary blessings and curses, their eternal judgment will become clear to them at the final judgement.

All biblical covenants contained consequences of blessing and cursing. There are several ways that I can see this dynamic at work within the modern world, our churches and within my life. To begin let's take a look at the modern world for example. We live within a country that was formed on the foundation of Christian beliefs and principles. Even on our monetary notes, the depiction that we 'trust in God' was emphasized with such reverence at one point in time. We also would have prayers in schools, and the Ten Commandments would sit in public buildings and federal buildings. However as time as progressed, the country has become very liberal to be 'inclusive' to all genders that they believe that exist, races, ethnicities, religions and beliefs. Although all of these people which are believers and unbelievers are children of God, there will be a judgement day where the believers will be separated from the unbelievers and judgement will fall upon them. 

Within our churches, the same methodology applies, to where we have succumbed to the Woke Culture and trying to be more inclusive to modern day practices and beliefs to gain more attendance within the church and popularity. However the church needs to call sin, as sin and teach the true meaning of repentance and forgiveness of sins. The dynamics of church have to draw more people to faith. 

Finally, towards my own conviction, I try my best to practice leading a life of separation knowing the calling upon my life. God's judgement matters more than anything and He has held me to a high standard of obedience. Knowing what I know today, I can not go back to any of lifestyle practices during my younger years, and that is the ultimate goal, to bring as many people to heaven with me as I possibly can.

The use of Canon as a mirror is justified by the character of Scripture and biblical examples through several different areas. To begin with the character of Scripture, the Old Testament is composed of smaller elements that came together to form larger sections which then eventually formed entire books. Within each of these levels and section, the contribution towards what the Old Testament book offers us was formed. Thematic analysis recognizes often draws attention to the minor topics of secondary areas. Genesis 1:1 talks about creation itself, however if there are so many topics that appear in verses like Genesis 1:1, imagine how many more topics are present in larger passages. 

When looking at biblical examples, authoritative characters and biblical writes would frequently draw attention to minor aspects of the Old Testament passages. This is demonstrated within the book of Hebrews 11 where the referenced examples of Jephthah and Samson appear. Both of these men were able accomplish victory over the enemies of God, when they had turned their faith towards God. Therefore the writer of Hebrews went ahead and drew out the positive accomplishments of these two men and looked for examples of faith within the Old Testament. The writer of Hebrews stressed minor themes that were important, but remained faithful to the book of Judges.

Synchronic snapshots function by emphasizing a specific events that occurred within a set period of time. When looking at scripture, biblical theologians would create snapshots by focusing in on a period of biblical history and then putting together a summary of the complex work of God's acts and words which took place during that period of time. There are several ways and methods to create these synchronic snapshots within historical periods, such as the primeval history, the history of the nation of Israel, and the future history of the New Testament. During the covenantal periods of time, synchronic snapshots are viewed through the period of universal covenants, national covenants, and the new covenant. This is specifically useful because it allows us as the reader to obtain specific snapshots of this time in biblical history and help identify formative events which took place. 

Diachronic traces are referenced as events or ways that something has developed over time. It connects one thought with one another over a period of time from one time to the next. We know that there are different affinities or periods of time that span over thousands of years. However with divine revelations, these ages did not contradict one another. An example of this is the covenant made with Abram, although at this specific point in time, humanity had not sinned, God expected humans to continue to strive for dominion over the earth even after the fall into sin. God continued to maintain his command to spread his kingdom to the ends of the earth. This was established as God had appointed humanity as his royal priests and instructed them to take dominion over the entire earth (Gen 1:28).

The value of a threefold focus on the writer, audience, and document in literary analysis must be studied when considering the importance of the writers of the Old Testament Canon. Beginning with the writer, it is crucial to note that we may not know everything that we would like to know about them, but we can still grasp many things that will still enable us to understand their writings. For example the authors of 1 and 2 Kings and 1 and 2 Chronicles are not known to us. We also do not know much about their psychological tendencies, so we are forced to rely on the interpretation of the book and a bit of speculation. At the same time, we are able to obtain and derive valuable information about both of these authors from the Old Testament and see that the author of Kings wrote the book during the exile of Israel in Babylon. By knowing some of the facts about the authors help us understand the differences in the their theological views and motives. We also know the authors were among the educated elite of Israel.

Next is the audience, we know of their general location from the Old Testament and the major events that they had experienced. We are also able to determine that most of the groups were faithful and some were unfaithful to the covenant responsibilities before God. When looking at the book of Kings, we know that the audience was still in exile. When looking at the book of Chronicles, they audience that had just returned to the Promised Land is addressed. Simply understanding the context of the audience helps us better understand that repentance was required before Israel could return to the promised land and align us with the literary portraits of these two books. 

Document in literary analysis are the full authoritative word of God, therefore special attention is required to the dangers and benefits of the document itself. Between the vocabulary grammar, figures of speech and structure, outline, context, genre and so on, these all contribute a great amount to understanding the original meaning and application set forth.

Understanding the diachronic trace of biblical events helps enrich my understanding of Scripture by allowing me to look at the series of events through a lens over time. Rather than looking at the scripture as an isolated series of books and themes, it is important to understand how the promises of God and covenants carried on from one period of time to the next. This can be seen beginning with Adam and how God had ordained for Adam and Eve to rule over Eden and be kings of the Earth. However due to their fall and disobedience we can see over time how God dealt with sin and trying to get His people to return to him. Knowing that Abram had a covenant with God and God has promised him to the father of many nations and for his descendants to inhabit all of the earth, that lineage continues down to the life of David and eventually Jesus. This is where the larger picture of scripture comes together. If the reader were to just look at the Israelites entering the promised land, we would not understand the promises made before that and the covenants in place. There is a certain significance to that promise and that goes back to how God had seen his people, all of humanity as his royal priests and wanted them to have dominion over earth. He told Adam and Eve to be fruitful and that they would have dominion over every living thing.

By knowing the writer's intentions, I can help determine two things to better understand Scripture. The intent and the context of the writing. The intent of the writer was to get a point or a message across to the audience. They were taking it upon themselves to document and gather the context of the information that they had witnessed, seen or were told to be able to share that with an intended audience. Whether the writer was writing an interpretation of the blessing of God or the curse of God, there is a reason that the writer took the responsibility to ensure this was document. It was to benefit the audience and provide a certain level of influence. Something that can be looked back to and referenced to see how Israel for example was referred to in Chronicles and the steps that were required to take in order to return to the Promised Land. The writer focused on the blessings that would be received for obedience and the curses that would be received for disobedience as they rebuilt their nation. Rather than question why one was blessed versus cursed, the write had an intention to allow the audience to be able to share this throughout generations to come. 

Next the context, knowing that there is some set of beliefs, and hopes that the author has, they are looking to influence their original readers and have focus more on the context versus themselves. For example the writer does not reference themselves, their bias views or opinions, rather the emphasis falls upon the need for Israel to repent, and the author of Kings emphasizes God's justice in sending his people to exile. This allows us to know that the author has the context to what is happening and what will continue to happen unless the children of God turn from their ways and turn back to God.

Romans 11:33-36 is a masterful presentation of the doctrine of God that affirms such things as His wisdom, knowledge, inscrutable judgements, and more. Because the doctrine of God is foundational to all of our theology. One is essence , three in person is the most concise definition of the doctrine of the Trinity. The Christian faith is not unitarian, confessing that one divine nature is possessed only by a single person or a single acting subject. Instead, the Christian faith says that three distinct persons are the one divine nature in its entirety. The Father possesses all that makes God who He is; the Son possesses all that makes God who He is: and the Spirit possesses all that makes God who He is. Many biblical passages teach the Trinitarian existence of God. Among the most famous of these is John 1:1-18, which says that the Word-the Son- is both identical to the Father in some way and distinct from Him in another.

According to Latin Trinitarians, God, the Trinity , is an individual rather than a community of individuals sharing the same divine nature and each Person of the Trinity is that individual. God the Father: revealed by the Old Testament to be Creator, Lord, Father and Judge. God the son: who had lived on earth amongst human beings. God the Holy Spirit; who filled them with new life and power. As per the Bible, a person is both body and soul, or more accurately, body-soul. The Old Testament supports this holistic view of persons who are not segmented into parts known as body, soul, and spirit. Genesis 1:20 uses the Hebrew expression, living soul for moving creature that has life. The revelation of the Trinity is accomplished by the coming of God himself into human history; God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16); God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5)

In monotheistic theology, the doctrine of Divine Simplicity says that God is simple (without parts). This is the idea that God does not exist in parts but in one unified entity, with no distinct attributes: that is God's existence is identical to God's essence. One such affirmation appears in James 1:5 where God is described as one who gives motives. Simplicity, divine, and human, is a central theme of the book of James. The doctrine of divine attributes, then, is set out as a reflection on Holy scripture; the One God as omnipresent, omnipotent, and omniscient, and all these as expressions of the Love who is God. Simplicity creates margins and spaces and openness in our lives. It honors the resources of our small planet.

In ways similar to the way of orthodox Christianity views the preexistence of Christ, the belief is that the Christ that was born on this Earth is same Son of God or Word who existed before this world. However, He is seen as having been created by God the Father. In the four Gospels, there is ample evidence that Jesus was fully human since He was born to a human mother ( Matthew 1:25), He experienced hunger (Matthew 21:18) and Thirst ( John 19:28), Jesus also experienced temptation (Matthew 4:1) pain and suffering (Matthew 16:21), and He died (Matthew 27:50) . Jesus name in Hebrew was Yeshua . Since the world was created out of nothing, nothing prevailed. Therefore God was idling, just existing, perhaps contemplating creation.

The Trinitarian formulas of the New Testament helps us to understand that the Holy Spirit is fully divine and fully personal. Baptism according to the Trinitarian fomula is seen as being a basis for Christian ecumenism, the concept of working towards the eventual unity of Christians. The Trinity has a very significant application to prayer. The General pattern of prayer in the Bible is to pray to the Father through the Son and in the Holy Spirit ( Ephesians 2:18). Our fellowship with God should be enhanced by consciously knowing that we are relating to a tri-personal God. The Trinity can be a model for our relationships on earth. Just as Father, Son, and Spirit are joined, so we are joined together in our families.

Although the word Trinity does not appear in Scripture, the essence of the doctrine is revealed in both the Old and New Testaments. In the Old Testament, God's triunity is alluded to rather than explicitly revealed. This is due, in part, to the preparatory nature of Old Testament revelation. Furthermore, Jesus asserts the equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19. Early Christians thought Jesus first referred to the Trinity in Matthew 28:19, by stating, " in the name of the Father, of the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In John 10:30, Jesus said, I and my Father are one. The belief in the Holy Trinity emerged during the life and shortly after the death and resurrection of Jesus.

Rev 5:1 Then I saw in the right hand of him who sat on the throne a scroll with writing on both sides and sealed with seven seals. We can't go past this verse too quickly because it holds the key to what happens in the rest of the chapter. We see that the one who sits on the throne is holding something special in His right hand. it is a scroll. A slightly odd scroll for it has writing on both the back and front and is sealed with seven different seals.
The one on the throne: This pictures God the Father who is upon His throne. He holds this scroll in HIs right hand but, as we shall see, is looking for One with the right to open it. 
The scroll: Being in the Father's right hand, this scroll is obviously very important. The Old Testament, in Jeremiah 32:6-15

The Word, a translation of the Greek, is widely interpreted as referring to Jesus, as indicated in other verses later in the same chapter. For example, the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us ( John 1:14) . John 1:1-8 is a poetic introduction of Jesus Christ. Jesus is referred to using the Greek work logos, meaning "The word" This passage clearly described Jesus as identical to God, and co-creator with God. John 1:1, establishes that the universe had a beginning, contrary to the idea that it is eternal, it also states that God has existed from the beginning. Later verses will show that God, in fact,  created all that exists.

Romans 8:27 - " And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit because the Spirit interceded for the saints in accordance with God's will ( John 14:26) But the counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom My Father will send in My name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have said to you. The Holy Spirit is divine person equal in divinity and power to God the Father and God the son. He is not a power to get hold of and use as we will but He is a loving, sensitive and Divine Person who wants to get hold of us and use us according to God's will. He is certainly not merely an impersonal force for good in the world.

The reason Jesus needed to be both God and man is that God designed humans for relationship with Himself, but ever since Adam's fall, our sin has corrupted us and broken our relationship with God. In His infinite love, God still wants a relationship with us; He wants us to be reconciled to Him. Jesus is important to us because His atonement, teaching , hope, peace, and example , He helps us change over lives, face our trails, and move forward with faith as we journey back to Him and His Father. There were several significant events which preceded the arrest of Paul. While Paul was near the end of his third missionary journey, he went to Jerusalem. The Holy Spirit warned Paul on several occasions that he would be imprisoned once he arrived in Jerusalem. Not only did the Holy Spirit warn Paul, the Holy Spirit worked among believers who would prophecy to Paul regarding his imprisonment. 

Agabus, a prophet went to the extent of binding his own hands and feet as a sign of the prophecy and warning that Paul would be arrested and bound if he were to continue to Jerusalem. As the Bible indicates, there were several warnings and prophecies provided to Paul preceding his arrest, but through it all Paul remained strong as he knew this was within the plan of God.

Paul entered Jerusalem with the great hope that the funds he had brought along with him would be received well by the Jewish Christians. Unfortunately, rumors began to float that Paul was preaching to the Jewish Christians to disregard their traditional Jewish practices (example: circumcision). While these rumors were false, and contrary to the rumors, Paul actually followed Jewish tradition while in the Jewish community. At the same time, Paul did not hesitate to behave like a Gentile while with the Gentiles. 

Paul knew that they actions he performed would affect the way that Jewish Christians perceived him along with Gentile Christians. As Paul was near the end of his purification week, he was recognized by some Jews. They were outraged and wrongly assumed Trophimus had also entered the court and were extremely upset. The angry crowd ended up chaining Paul and arresting him into custody.

During Paul's imprisonment under Roman rule, he was transported by ship heading for Asia minor. As the ship first landed in Sidon, Paul was allowed to visit some friends of his. From Sidon, the ship said to a port in Myra. From Myra, the ship sailed for Italy and during this voyage they experienced rough sailing. Eventually after many shipwrecks and troublesome voyages Paul arrived in Rome in A.D. 60 and was placed under house arrest for two years. 

During this time, he was allowed to have guests and allowed to teach them freely. Through Paul's preaching, some of the Roman Jews were converted to Christianity while others rejected his claims about Jesus. For over two years, Paul was able to boldly welcome people to his house and preach the word of Jesus Christ. Although he faced many hardships along the way, he was able to make an impact without any obstacle or hinderance regardless of his imprisonment, in the capital city of the most empire in the world during his day.

Paul's imprisonment revealed important insights about God and even about his own ministry through the awareness of suffering. For example, Paul knew he would be imprisoned and even be put to death, and he was preparing himself for it and willing to be martyred. He also was able to have the insight of the awareness of purpose. He knew his purpose in suffering ahead of time, and that if God were to allow him to go through suffering, he would also plan to use this suffering for a greater purpose. 

He was convinced that his ministry would including be imprisoned and testifying to the gospel and this would be an important talk to convert individuals. The last awareness was about blessings. Paul was very much aware of God's blessings over his ministry at that time. He was able to receive and interpret visions to protect the lives of the people that were on the ship with him that crashed on the reef. he also was aware of the blessing that came with healing the sick on Malta and all those who came to see him.

Three things that we can learn from the book of Acts about Paul's ministry during imprisonment was that he knew his responsibility and obligation to preach the gospel regardless of his circumstance. He knew that he would go through suffering and situations that would not be favorable, and he asked the Ephesians to pray for him so that he would receive the strength needed to fulfill his responsibility. 

The second thing we can learn about was that Paul was in constant prayer for the churches. He was probably able spend more time in prayer due to being imprisoned, since he had no other distractions, jobs to do and keep him busy from praying. Paul would continually pray for the Ephesians and believed that prayer was indeed powerful and hoped that God would honor his prayers. 

Lastly, suffering was the key piece we can learn from Paul's ministry during imprisonment. He was suffering on behalf of others and while suffering is typically considered a hardship and not ministry, in this sense it was minstry and as the goal and product of the suffering is a direct advancement of God's kingdom through the promotion of the gospel. His suffering did not go in vain, rather it blessed the church and increased the glory to God's people.

Three ways which Paul developed the doctrinal theme of Christ's kingship over creation include sovereignty, honor, and determination. When referring to sovereignty, we are talking about his power and authority and according to Paul when Jesus went up to heaven, God the Father vested him with this type of sovereignty over creation. The Father had granted that to Christ in this manner and with absolute power over everything, including heaven and earth. 

Christ is honored as he holds the highest position of authority, and he is perfect holy, and worthy. Not only is Jesus the rule and creator of everything, but he also established the lower offices that other rulers hold, both in the spiritual and earthly realm. Paul speaks of this in relation to the return of Christ to earth to consummate his kingdom. 

When referring to determination, Paul insisted that the future inheritance is guaranteed and that God has promised himself and will not change his mind. While the age to come will have some periods of overlap, Paul knew Christ's plan for all of creation and was determined Christ would consummate his kingdom.

Some of the implications of the believer's union with Christ is that the Christian life can be hard and it can include great suffering. However, through our union with Christ, we are united to Christ's death, united to Christ in his resurrection and life, united to Christ to his ascension and kingship, and we are united in being seated with Christ in heavenly places. 

The main indication regarding this doctrine was to ensure confidence within believers that while they may suffer for some time, they are not suffering alone and their suffering is not in vain. Paul was confident and determined that while we may suffer for some time, Christ is suffering and empathizing with the one suffering for the sake of the gospel.

The main theological truth that underlies the theological unity of Paul's prison epistles is the multifactored doctrine of the kingship of Christ over all of creation and believers to live ethically. As relating to the themes of our union with Christ and ethical living, we can use the life of Paul as the perfect example. He was on his way to Jerusalem, where he was warned by the Holy Spirit and people that he will suffer, but knowing his calling and the ultimate goal regarding his union with Christ, he pressed onward willing to be persecuted, and even put to death. When we look at the life of Jesus and how we gave his life for everyone, Paul followed the example Christ set and lived an ethical life while others created false rumors about him and imprisoned. He was willing to suffer for the gospel and the main truth is that through pain and suffering the kingdom was able to be advanced.

Paul had a very unique relationship with the Colossian church. The reason being, he never actually visited the Colosse church, however he had a deep extent of care for the them. It is possible that he may have visited Colosse prior to the establishment of the church and it is also possible that he may have never visited Colosse. However, the fact is that he did not know more of the believers personally.

Paul had an indirect relationship with the Colossians though his friendship with Epaphras, Philemon, Onesiumus, and Tychicus. And while Paul did not visit the church, letters were exchanged back and forth to one another. Paul would pray for the church and specifically asked for blessings that he knew would benefit them the most. On various individual levels, Paul had friends who were from Colosse, these were individuals who labored alongside Paul in the ministry. 

Philemon was a close friend of Pauls, and Epaphras was also another close fellow worker and fellow prisoner that was with Paul in prison as Paul was writing his letters to the Colossian church. Onesimus who was once a slave, ended up feeling away from Philemon and later ministering to Paul in prison. So while Paul had a minimal direct relationship with the Colossian church, he had strong feelings for the church and his acquaintances.

There were problems in Colosse, for example when it came to Greek philosophy, many of the beliefs and practiced based in Greek religion were advocated by false teachers in Colosse and included elements of asceticism. Their beliefs were based on the principles that aligned to the world. The Church had false teachers who would attempt to mix the church's teachings with Greek traditions. This resulted in false teachers incorporating many practices based on Jewish law.

With the Jewish law, it is true that Paul upheld Mosaic law, and for the sake of the gospel would accept and participate in Jewish practices as well. However, the false teachers were using the Jewish teachings in corrupt ways. The false teachers corrupted the laws, using idolatrous worship and pagan asceticism. They also advocated for a form of Christian circumcision and Paul would teach that once you were baptized, the need for circumcision was no longer required. 

During the time of the Colossian church, Paul wrote about the worship of angels, second he addressed the matters of rulers and authorities, and lastly he addressed the problems that dealt with the basic principles of the world. These false teachers would claim to have received false visions from angels and would go about encouraging Christians to complete the required rituals in order to receive similar visions. It is possible that these false teachers did receive visions, however instead of receiving the visions from God or God's holy angels, it may have been from demons.

Only after knowing the background of the Colossians can we truly understand the reason for Paul writing this letter. The supremacy of Christianity among all other religions of false teachings is clearly evident as Paul instructs the church of Colosse to share and instruct the Laodiceans as the intention of the can be applicable to different audiences. The Colossian church was swayed quite a bit through the teachings of false teachers and knowing this, Paul was able to provide the important aspects of the supremacy of Christ. He was able able to refute the teachings of the false prophets about how to worship, and the image of of God and the ultimate revelation of God. 

Paul's authority was far superior than that of the false teachers, in Paul's younger days, he was a zealous persecutor of the church and as time went on, the Lord Jesus appeared before him and he was converted. Though Paul was converted, he went through suffering and his suffering benefited the church by providing a powerful witness to the gospel. Through his walk with God, he would have powerful and significant revelations from God, and they were not mere human inventions like the teachings of the false teachers.

Paul demonstrated to the Colossians that Christ was supreme in several different ways, the supremacy of Christ, the supremacy of Christ's Ministers, the supremacy of salvation in Christ, and supremacy of Christian living.

Paul demonstrated and preached the supremacy of Christ as the lord and king and the superiority of Christ's ministers. Through Christian living, there is an incomparable value of salvation in Christ that allows for victory over sin. During each point of explaining that Christ was supreme, Paul was able to make it clear that what the false teachers would promise, only Christ could deliver. 

Through demonstration of how one lived, Paul lived a life by example. The false teachers were not living an ethical life, and they were not inwardly renewed by God as Paul had been. The false teachers were not even true believers to begin with and they did not follow the standards of God.

Christ's ministers were supreme over false teachers in Colosse as Christ was superior to the false gods. Paul's argument consisted of five main ideas, the reconciliation accomplished through the Christian gospel, Paul own altruism, Paul's divine commission, the revelation provided by the gospel, and the empowerment of Christ's ministers. 

The ministers of Christ are superior over false teachers as they preach a gospel that reconciles believers to God. The false teachers would encourage individuals to placate demons, and in reality no reconciliation ever took place as their gospel had no power to save. The reconciliation that we believe in, provided people with the encouragement that they were already forgiven and stood before God in righteousness.

While the false teachers relied on traditions and wisdom passed down from human hands, Paul was receiving revelations for three years in the desert of Arabia and in Damascus from God. The false teachers relied on ideas that idolatrous human beings invited, where as Paul had been granted authority to speak for God and teach the church.

Having looked at the style of Paul's teachings and the way he displays language and doctrine show a close correlation with Colossians. This would suggest that there is a possibility that Paul wrote both at the same time. According to Acts 19-21, we can see that Paul had lived in Ephesus for about two years and maintained close ties with the elders. 

The primary audience of indicates that the church in Ephesus is the target audience as it was the capital city of the Roman province of Asia. Several of the early fathers of the church had declared that Paul had sent this letter to the Ephesians. The secondary audience is the churches of Lycus valley. A significant portion of these individuals were those he had not seen firsthand and he did not contain any personal reference. Which inclines us to see that the churches of the Lycus Valley and those of the Ephesians and Colossians all faced similar problems.

Paul wrote the letter to the Ephesians because there were several problems that were being faced by the church at this time. Rather than deal with or face these problems individually, his strategy was to deal with all of the problems at once. Paul would commonly speak of Christ's work in terms of how God would pour out his blessings and curse. As Paul also believed in the manifestation of the kingdom of God, we can see that even while Paul was in prison within Rom, he wrote to the Ephesians preaching the kingdom of God. He was prepared to share the gospel or good news with topics around forgiveness of sins. He drew attention in Ephesians to citizenship and how God's people were part of God's kingdom, and the chief goal of Israel was to expand it's dominion over Earth. With that would come problems, and Paul's effort was to ensure that the church was ready to turn to the challenges that Paul addressed.

Knowing the background of Paul's letter to the Ephesians helps me better understand the letter he wrote as he was looking at the broader view of the church declaring the gospel and addressing the aspects of spiritual warfare that is to be expected. Had he focused on a single issue, than other churches would likely not adhere to his writings or teachings in this book, but rather because he wanted to address common issues among churches with the context that Christians who engage in spiritual warfare are implied citizenship in the kingdom of God. 

Based on the context of citizenship, Paul displayed that if we choose to obey and be faithful to the king, we may inherit the blessings of the covenants including forgiveness of sins and obtain eternal life. Whereas if we reject the king, and the salvation that is offered, the person no longer inherits the kingdom of God. Knowing that these topics were all written without Paul having a direct connection to the people firsthand but rather in other means, allows us to see the revelation that Paul had throughout his journey before getting to this specific place.

Paul's teaching about praise and prayer within the overall structure of the letter is worthy of attention. To begin, Paul honored God for his sovereign rule and praised him for predestining certain individuals to be his special people. Paul continues to praise God for his sovereign rule over all of creation. Paul then continues to praise God's benevolence towards his people and praised God for our inheritance in Christ. This is really important as inheritance rights only belong to the citizens of the kingdom. 

Regarding prayer, Paul's prayers repeat all the same elements. It includes strong Trinitarian theology honoring the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In reference to Christ's glorious inheritance, there is hope called for the believers. Paul is able to speak of this hope as he continues to teach within the body of his letter. Christ shared his inheritance with us, so that inheritance is for us too.

Paul's teaching regarding citizenship, administration and code for living within the kingdom of God were emphasized within Ephesians. His teachings on citizenship were divided into three sections, first the focus on the fact that fallen human beings were born into the kingdom of darkness and are enemies of God by nature. The second section speaks of how God grants us citizenship in his kingdom by transferring us from darkness into light. The third section speaks of our citizenship within the kingdom of light. 

Referring to administration, Paul was aware that false teachers would arise and create problems within the church, so he assigned the elders the right to condemn false teachers. The apostles possessed special grace from God that allowed them special revelation in their ministry that taught them infallible truth. These elders are accountable to God and to one another. God had appointed Paul to be his official representative on Earth, and this apostleship made Paul's word authoritative. 

Lastly the code for living contained many different instructions on Christian behavior. Paul emphasized how the roles of positions within leadership, influence and authority all work together for the good of all. Christ divided his gifts in what that allow the citizens of the kingdom to serve one another. The kingdom of God is to be morally as pure as possible, and reflect the character of it's king. Therefore God blesses and honors moral purity, and teaches us that by refraining from sin and doing good works, the citizens increase their blessedness and inheritance.

Christians should work to build the kingdom of God because as Christ has given us the opportunity of this inheritance, we must not take it for granted. A great king has provided the opportunity to be a part of his heavenly kingdom and to be citizens of this kingdom. However living an immoral sinful life would not qualify us to receive this inheritance. In terms of why we should work to build this kingdom, there are many reasons, but one of the major themes would be around love. The love of the father and the love to show others. If Christ loved us enough to sacrifice his own son for the atonement of our sins to live in heavenly abode with him, wouldn't we want to live that eternal life with others as well? 

By regeneration and transformation, we are made to be citizens of this kingdom. If we had an opportunity to share the greatest blessing or gift with our loved ones, should we not extend that same opportunity to others as well? Christ did not come for the holy individuals, rather the sinners and the lost people who needed to be saved. By offering obedience to the will of the father, we are claiming the inheritance that he has provided us.

My understanding of the gospel aligns with Paul's teachings of the kingdom of God in several ways. First as we learned about the citizenship of the kingdom of God, it is interesting to note the correlation between the citizens of the kingdom and the king. Unless we honor the king and keeps his commands, why would he allow us to inherit the blessings that come along with it? We have been given the solid teachings of how being called to be a part of the kingdom has expected circumstances and spiritual warfare. However the scripture also provides guidance on how to withstand such circumstances, from relying on God's word, identifying false prophets, relying on elders, to praise and worship. Paul took a practical approach to how to convey his message to the churches he had not physically gone to visit, but based on the teachings of how God would demonstrate wisdom and authority, that level of authority to a certain extent (handed to an apostle) is seen in Paul's teachings. He dealt with these issues face on and used the gifts that God gave him to send that message to advance the kingdom of God.

The three main people involved in the content of Paul's letter to Philemon were Philemon, Onesimus, and Apphia and Archippus. 


Philemon's relation to Onesimus was that Onesimus was Philemon's slave and a resident of Colosse. He lived with his master, Philemon. Philemon's relation to Paul was that Paul had brought Philemon to faith and possibly may have saved his life in some other way. Therefore, Philemon owed Paul a great deal of debt and gratitude. While we don't know for sure how they came to know of one another, we can say with confidence that they knew each other well. 

Onesimus, the slave of Philemon was a member of Philemon's household. Onesimus was not a believer and he had left Philemon's house to seek the help of Paul, who led him to faith. The last two people mentioned that we are going to focus on is Apphia, who is mentioned as Paul's "sister" indicating that she may have been a believer and Archippus, who may have been the host of the local church. We are not sure who Apphia is but she may have likely been a member of Philemon's household.

The problem that Paul was seeking to resolve by this letter was that some servants are not good servants. Some people would not accept their responsibilities and be willing to fulfill their obligations. For example, Onesimus was one of these individuals who upset his master, Philemon and it came to the point where Onesimus had feared punishment from his master so much, that he ran away. 

Paul is looking to explain that when a slave is scared of punishment and not looking to gain freedom, the Roman law would permit the slave to run away. And in this case, Paul explains to Philemon that Onesimus may have proven to be a useless or profitless slave. Paul is looking to ensure that it may be better that Onesimus is no longer a slave within the household of Philemon and good that he has run away. Through this separation, Philemon would rather benefit with Onesimus running away.

Onesimus went to the city where Paul was kept as a prisoner and knowing that Paul was under house arrest and not able to move around freely, he pursued a meeting with Paul. In Paul's letter to Philemon, he indicated that he had converted Onesimus to Christianity and that he had proven himself to Paul. He indicates that Onesimus was seeking Paul's help in the situation that he was in. 

The agreement came in the form that Onesimus was repented of all his sins that had angered Philemon and dedicated himself to ministering to the apostle in prison. Paul, in return cared deeply for this child of God and grew to love him as a son. Once favor was gained with Paul, wrote to Philemon mentioning that he is sending Onesimus to Philemon despite wanting to keep him. He asked that Philemon and Onesimus reconcile and this was fulfilled by Philemon accepting Onesimus and forgiving him.

The six aspects of Paul's petition were  salutation, where it is broken down with an explanation of Paul's role as an advocate, an explanation of Onesimus' role as a petitioner, an explanation of Philemon's role as a master, an explanation of God's role as a providential rule of the universe, and Paul's statement of confidence that the petition would be granted. 

Paul spoke as a weak man who was elderly and in need of help, he had wanted Philemon to respond to his situation with genuine love. Onesimus was returning to Colosse to petition Philemon for mercy, hoping for reconciliation and release. As a master, Paul wanted for Philemon to do the right thing, and as a ruler Paul suggested that God himself orchestrated the events in the life of Onesimus and Philemon in order for Onesimus to be reconciled. In regards to petition, Paul stood interceding for Onesimus to Philemon and with confidence Paul believe that Philemon would adhere to Paul's request.

When you appeal for mercy, you are exhibiting Christ like behavior towards others. Paul could have easily portrayed authority as an apostle, or voice of God and dictated to Philemon to forgive and accept Onesimus. However Paul took Onesimus in, mentored him, guided him to faith, talked about repentance so that not only will he change his behavior, but Philemon should see that change too. 

If Christ can change our hearts and the hearts of those who despised him as the son of God, then when a slave is able to turn from his ways and repent back to the master, should the master not heed his slaves appeal for mercy? This strategy works often when you are made to be more empathetic about a situation and if you make demands, the true motive behind the request can be manipulative. There may be other intentions driving that request, where as when you show someone mercy, it is because they have a change of heart to reconcile with one another.

Paul had a special relationship with the Philippian church as Philippi was an important city within the Roman province of Macedonia. Paul, during his second missionary journey planted the church in Philippi. The reason being that Paul had a vision of a man who was begging for him to bring to the gospel to Macedonia. As a result of the vision that Paul had, he began his journey to Macedonia moving quickly towards Philippi. During his time within Philippi, Paul had a very prosperous ministry, it was so successful that even when he left the city, Paul kept receiving monetary gifts from the Christians of Philippi. 

The church of Philippi loved Paul, and even though there were some among them who were wealthy, the general population of the believers were exceptionally poor. They were not able to help Paul as frequently as they would have liked, but they rose to the opportunity when they could and would give generously. It was not a one-sided relationship, Paul also had a deep affection to the church of Philippi as well, he enjoyed there fellowship and would commonly describe them as his closest co-workers. They were supportive of one another in nature.

The reason behind understanding the background of Philippians and knowing why Paul wrote what he did is essential because it allows the reader to know the context of the mutual respect and relationship of one another. For example, in the context of how Paul would miss the fellowship of the people he would refer to his as his closest co-workers, sends a great message about the affection he shared for this group of people. In the context of how Paul build a close bond with Lydia his hostess continues that affirmation. Paul while in prison, had a close bond with the jailor all because he had once saved his life, had we not know the relationship prior we would have thought this would be odd. Paul and the slave girl whom he rescued from demon possession is also mentioned as well, and this is all a result of how Paul had grown to love the believers of Philippi. That is why, even during their own financial challenges, they wholeheartedly gave to Paul when Paul was in need because of that mutual love they shared for one another.

While Paul was imprisoned, he suffered quite a bit, to the point that he felt that death would be his only escape. However by overcoming all of these challenges, he continued to persevere and later exhorted to the Philippians to persevere. He instructed them to continue to remain faithful to Christ no matter what and to live their lives exemplary even during difficult times in their lives. 

The types of exhortations Paul provided can be categorized into four main topics, the first being the importance of perseverance, the help that ministers provide, Paul's personal example, and the challenges to persevere. No matter how difficult the challenges were that the Philippians faced, nothing was beyond God's control. God had actually planned their suffering as a means of blessing for them. That is why it was so important for them to understand that. Paul did not want them to simply undergo this suffering, he wanted them to rejoice in the midst of it. and he continue to persevere by sending ministers to help care for them. 

Despite the hardships that Paul faced, he used himself as a positive example of perseverance in faith, behavior and mindset. Paul mentioned that purely professing faith alone is not enough to guarantee salvation, you must also persevere in faith in order to obtain eternal life. Paul stressed the importance of living holy lives, maintaining ones faith. If one is not able to persevere, then we prove that our faith was false to begin with and not genuine.

The overall structure and content of Philippians begins with highlighting the problems within the church. The church faced persecution from outside, they were threatened by the possibility of false teachings, and they struggled with conflicts among one another. Once the church in Philippi was established, we can see that Paul, being the primary author provides salutation to the Philippians which is a testament to the relationship that they had one for another. 

The next content goes onto thanksgiving, where Paul gives thanks, emphasizing his love for them which was deep and personal. Following that is prayer, which is brief but filled with expression of Christian love that honors God. Moving onto the body, where Paul talks about his suffering and his deep love for the Philippians. Paul then moves onto to talk about his perseverance, and his exhortation to the Philippians to persevere. Paul went on to advise the Philippians not to let false teachers coming among them or within the church. He went on to describe how the false teachings could invade the church and perseverance of the church. Once that is complete, is the affirmation of perseverance and final greetings.

There have been many moments in my life, where my desire was to have the individuals whom I shared fellowship with and broke bread with to impact my life by ministering to me in a time of need. Unfortunately, my response will be the opposite, which is that I did not have that experience yet in my life where I needed someone to pick me up when I needed that the most in my life. I can however share an example of how I was able to do so for a few individuals. 

There was once a fellow friend who shared some of the darkest, most personal intimate struggles with me. They confided me in more than anyone else at that time, and I was not in a position where I felt that I did anything to deserve such openness from this individual. However, the Holy Spirit guided me during that time, to spend more time with than individual, share from the word, pray with them, meditate, talk to them and offer them approaches to seek additional help. This allowed for the other individual to see a response different than what they had ever expected and would constantly ask, "why do you care so much about me?" I would never even think twice to "care" about a fellow individual who I knew was hurting and struggling, it felt natural and the "christ like" thing to do in my opinion. God has called us to partake in the good and the bad when our brothers and sisters are going through happiness and sorrow. I only pray that when the time comes, I too can experience that same love and perseverance from christ like minded believers.

When defining Christian ethics and focusing on God and his blessings, it is imperative to note that our focus is more reflective on the fact that those things which receive God's blessings are good and right. Whereas the things that do not receive his blessings are wrong and evil. This demonstrates the nature of God as being moral and the actions of God being moral as well. 

Since God is the ultimate standard of what is right and wrong, we are inclined to see God's nature as the standard model of goodness and righteousness. When it comes to his blessings, he shows his approval for what is considered right and wrong be showering his blessings upon them.

Proper motive is significant when it comes to actions because unless the work that is performed is done with the right intention or motive, it will not be a work that that God will reward with his blessings. The action must originate and flow from a heart that is purified through faith and it should come from Christian love. The type of faith that a believer holds is faith that is pure, faith that saves and faith that motivates good works. 

If proper motive is not driven by love, then the works that are bestowed are useless. The scripture states to love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. To reject God's law is to simply reject him

The threefold criteria for good works can be outlined by proper motive, proper standard, and proper goal. With proper motive, you are driven by a heart that is purified by faith. Without seeking God's blessing founded on basis of faith, we are not able to please God. Love is the next step of proper motive, everything that we do should be stemmed around the basis of love. 

With proper standard, every work that is done must adhere to the standard of God's work and his commandments. When referring to commands, there are no commands that can be bypassed or omitted, each command of God still holds true to be upheld. All scripture is basis for commands and law, and there is good reason for scripture to be used for ethical training. 

Lastly, proper goal is when the ultimate goal should always be considered. God's glory is to be a central, and foundational goal in our lives and God only rewards and approves the work of those that have his glory as their ultimate goal.

When looking at the different perspective that must be employed when approaching ethics, the first is situational. This approach can be referred to as 'teleological' because of the focus on the end result or action. In scripture we can see how Paul would encourage his readers to live a holy life and abstain from sin that they had once committed. This situational perspective creates awareness for the sake of righteousness and leads towards the reward that is mentioned for demonstrating situational perspective. 

Normative perspective is the fact that God's word is the norm or the basis of ethical standards. When considering normative perspective, you are looking to the Bible in order to be told what is the correct thing to do. This is the basis for behavior and the commandment for how people should behave in a certain way. 

Lastly, is existential which is viewing ethics through the lens of the individual's personal experience. The Scripture affirms the leading of the Holy Spirit as a valid means to determining what is right and wrong, and God moves among his people to bring them towards conviction on a personal level. When we acknowledge this, we are using existential perspective.

God serves as the absolute judge of morality as he himself is the absolute ethical norm. Goodness is a personal attribute of God and God's goodness is the ultimate standard for all goodness. When referring to personal attribute, God is the standard measure of how all morality is measured. Therefore he is the absolute judge of morality, he is not just good and right, rather he is actual goodness and righteous itself. 

God being referred to the metaphor of light enables a moral evaluation as light is commonly referred to as good and darkness is referred to evil, sin and lies. Scripture also states that no one is good except for God and within God there dwells no evil. God is also the ultimate standard for for all goodness. Scripture consistently reminds us of how the absolute standard by which all ethical issues are to be evaluated is against God's own personal goodness.

Three categories of revelation that are part of God's word include general revelation, special revelation and existential revelation. When speaking of general revelation we are concerned with the way that creation and history unravels the true things about God and his moral requirements of us. The complexity and importance of general revelation is important. Complexity speaks of how general revelation is common to all people, whereas the importance factors the character of God and what he has made, and his continual interaction. 

Special revelation is a normal that is binding on our lives, and in the complexity form special revelation is reliant on the words that are spoken, written, or communication involving God with people. In some cases, God appears to be audible and seen visibily, where in other cases he is not seen, but rather heard. In special revelations, there are also the considerations for dreams, and natural phenomenom to communicate the truth to individuals. The importance of this is that all individuals should adhere to this standard of special revelation as a norm. 

Existential revelation reflects the concept of God speaking to or revealing himself through persons. None of these presentations are considered simple, rather they contain God's revelation through human beings and are the inward leading and illumination of the Holy Spirit. This can be categorized into both the external aspects and internal aspects.

Existential revelation teaches us about God's standard by using different people and private spirits to reveal his will to his people.  While all reveal the same God and the same standard, each of these revelations are binding and authoritative. God's standard is the basis for all moral teachings and revelations. When considering existential revelations, God give to his believers the illumination of the Holy Spirit the the Holy Spirit reveals the truth about God. When referring to the illumination, we are referring to the divine gift of understanding that God grants to believers and non-believers as well. The person that has been illuminated now has the ability or knowledge that they had once lacked. God did this when he revealed knowledge to Peter at the moment that Peter did not figure out that Jesus was the Christ. While believers and nonbelievers may not grasp the truth and revelation the same way, God is able to provider the supernatural understanding of the gospel and God's truth to everyone. 

With existential revelation, human existence is also taken into consideration and humans were created in the image of God. and that is to say that in some form we are a reflection of God. The second point is that while we are created in God's image, we are able to exercise authority, revealing God's character. This authority was delegated to us by god and whatever Adam did when the animals and exercising judgment to govern and rule over them, is the delegation that we have been granted over as a reflection of the character of God and his standards.

As Christ created us in his image, and hold us to the standard that he abides by, walking in the light with Christ is also a call for separation from sin and darkness. While man was initially created by God and his image, Adam was brought into this world without sin or fault. However with the fall of temptation and man sinning, we caused all of humankind to sin and suffer through each generation. When God says to walk in his light and be a part of his fellowship, we are given the chance to be freed from this bondage of sin that was placed upon us if we choose to adhere to the teachings of Christ and be like Christ in his image and standards. That will eventually lead to the forgiveness of our sins in Christ and allow for us to exercise the divine privilege that has been granted to us to accept the grace of Jesus dying on the cross for our sins to accept and receive eternal salvation.

As the Bible derives from divine inspiration, it also carries God's authority. Since God carries all authority, whenever and however he speaks is an obligation for all to obey him. There are a few claims of this authority and it can be explained through historical examples and the way authority is claimed. In the earliest record of the Bible, we can see of how God spoke directly to humanity and how his dialogue carried authority. When God had instructed man with specific guidelines and man disobeyed God, we can see of how God's authority was demonstrated by punishing Adam and Eve. When looking at the days of Moses, we can also wee that God's spoken word was the basis for his written word and the people were obligated to obey it. 

Regarding the claims of authority, we can see how the apostles used this authority in their speaking and writings within the New Testament. Paul even carried his delegated authority from Jesus to instruct the people and churches in his writings. As the Bible is God's word, it still carries authority even to this day.

When we read and understand Scripture, we are better able to understand God and his will for all mankind. WE can see how God's will is revealed with enough clarity to guide us ethically. If one is able to study the word of God diligently, then by all means they are able to apply it to themselves and practice a lifestyle of ethical means. 

However, not everyone has the equal ability to comprehend the Bible and not everyone makes an equal effort to try and understand the Scripture. While in fact, there are some portions of Scripture that are a bit less clear than others, God's will is perfectly made clear and well known enough for us to have a standard of morality.

Scripture was written to give people a clean understanding of God's will and his character. This would allow humankind to be able to follow the ways of God and conform themselves to living a life according to God's will and character. While Scripture is clear on some matters and less clear on other matters, it is very clear on how salvation is achieved through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ. 

All of Scripture is useful and has clear implications on how it should be used. If we apply ourselves with diligence to learn the word of God, we are able to understand God's will to conform ourselves to his standards of morality. The well understanding of Scripture enables us to live a moral life with ethical decision making as God had intended. It teaches us what is right in the sight and eyes of God and allows to conform to the will of God and his character.

While the gospel was considered foolish in the eyes of some, that did not stop Paul from visiting Rome and preaching the gospel. We can see in Romans 1, how Paul reported his faith in Jesus has allowed him to have the boldness to share the gospel to all who were in Rome. He went on to explain that righteousness is revealed and achieved by faith, a faith that is blind but has great rewards, as the righteous abide by this faith. 

The implications that this for our lives today is that many people continue to reject the gospel and word of God and need to see sights and wonders to believe. But even during the time of Paul, we can see that he shared the gospel to Greeks, and non Greeks, both to the wise and foolish. He was fulfilling the commission to take the gospel to the ends of the earth and preach. In our lives today, we may not be accepted and received by all, but with that blind faith, the righteous are able to fulfill the will of God and there is power in that gospel through God's salvation.

The variety of language found in the Bible and the different uses of language notated varies in many different ways. The Scripture is full of language ranging about different forms of human communication and if we are able to understand how each of these types of languages are used, there is a strong possibility that we may misunderstand the Bible. 

Because the Bible is God inspired, many times the interpretation that is represented may be so extraordinary that it is not comprehensive for the human mind. Whereas, many Christians have testified that the extraordinary form in which scripture was written makes its language easier to interpret. While God does speak in mysterious ways, the Bible is not hidden with meanings that are not meant to be interpreted through special means, or spiritual gifts or special offices, rather it is meant to be studies and revealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. It is simply not enough to know what the Bible says, but rather how the Bible is trying to communicate with us, so that as a reader, we are able to understand it better.

The primacy of the Ten Commandments are both historical and theological. The historical primacy is dependent on the fact that these were the first set of written legal codes that were handed to the nation of Israel. Prior to this, there was no documented legal codes provided and Paul is calling special attention to this matter in Galatians 3:17. He referred to the Ten Commandments as the introduction of the law. While it is true that the people of God had many commandments and rules to follow prior to the time of Moses, such as the time of Noah where God had a standard for people to follow and they rejected God, and the consequences that followed. Hence, the written law was passed onto the nation of Israel to serve along with the Book of the Covenant which was later formed. The theological primacy around the Ten Commandments is how the law was received by Israel. The law handed to Moses was done so with thunder, lighting, smoke, clouds and heavenly trumpets. Jesus also reference the ten commandments in his teachings in a remarkable way.

Three traditional types of law that we can help apply law in the modern world include: moral law, ceremonial law, and civil law. Moral laws are revolved around God's ethical standards and are typically associated with the Ten Commandments. Ceremonial laws reflect instruction around worshipping God. Civil law is in regards to the governing of society. 

When looking to apply these to the modern world, moral law helps us as the world is rapidly changing for the worst. There are immoral things happening which directly impact the laws and ethical standards God had put in place, through Scripture and also the Ten Commandments. Ceremonial laws help us abide by the way the modern world is changing in regards to how we worship God and the forums around the challenges that we see in regards to either restrictions in the government realm and leniency in the modern churches which go against a lot of what Scripture has taught us. Civil law in regards to how society is governed was once adhered by the US constitution and forefathers, however we live in a day and age where this no longer applies and as a county civil law established by God has been diminished by mankind. Whether it has been diminished or not, the law of God around ethical standards still stand.

The word of God never changes regardless of time and society. We now live in a day and age where everything around us defies what we know is morally correct and biblically sound, however the one constant declared within Scripture is, that heaven and earth may pass away, but the word of God will never. The three most prominent theories of knowledge are:
1. Foundationalism: Foundationalism is the view that all knowledge is based on a foundation of self-evident or indubitable beliefs. These foundational beliefs are then used to justify all other beliefs.

2. Coherentism: Coherentism is the view  that all knowledge is justified by its coherence with other beliefs. In other words, a belief is justified if it is a part of coherent system of beliefs. 

3. Reliabilism: Reliabilism is the view that all knowledge is justified if it is produced by a reliable process. In other words, a belief is justified if it is produced by a process that is likely to lead to true beliefs. 

These three theories of knowledge has its own strength and weakness. Foundationalism is appealing because it seems to provide a solid foundation for our knowledge. However, it is difficult to identify any self-evident or indubitable beliefs. Coherentism is appealing because it allows us to justify beliefs that are not directly based on experience.  However, it's difficult to say how coherent a system of beliefs must be in order to be justified. Reliabilism is appealing because it seems to focus on what is important in practice. 

Ultimately, none of these theories of knowledge is perfect. However they provide us with different ways of thinking about what justifies our beliefs.
