Like St. Matthew, Luke derives much of his Gospel from that of St. Mark. generally following Mark's sequence and incorporation about 50 percentage of Mark's material into his work. 

Despite its similarities to the other Synoptic Gospels, however , Luke's narrative contains much  that is unique. It gives details of Jesus's infancy found in no other Gospel. Luke's Gospel is also unique in its perspective.

The essential difference between Jews and Christians is that Christians accept Jesus as messiah and personal savior. Jesus is not part of Jewish theology. Amongst Jews, Jesus is not considered a divine being . Therefor all holidays that have a connection to the life of Jesus and part of Jewish life and/or practice. 

Judaism originates as a result of the conventional relationship between God and Abraham. The Bible is our sacred literature. The relationship between the Jewish people and God is documented in the text. In the Bible, the history, culture, language, theology, and practices of the Jewish people are presented. 

There are notable similarities in notions of sacrifice, good works, hospitality, peace, justice, pilgrimage, and afterlife and loving God with all one's heart and soul. All three religions honor the concept of purification by fasting.

Jesus often said things "The kingdom of God is among you, is near, has come". In Luke 13:10-21, Jesus has the perfect opportunity to talk further about the Kingdom. After ticking off the local synagogue ruler for doing a healing on the Sabbath, Jesus tells two super short parable about the kingdom.

First is the Mustard seed; it's tiny , but grows huge. I've never seen this is real life. The second is about Yeast; again it is tiny, but infects a huge lump of dough. 

In the above two parables Jesus teaches that the kingdom starts small, but grows and expands with surprising hugeness. Let the Kingdom of God grow in us. By the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is our spiritual worship. Do not be confirmed to this world. but transoformed by the renewal of mind.

Eschatology is defined as the study of the last things. Especially when in consideration of theology, eschatology is referred to as the final days or end times of humanity and the study thereof. The term itself is derived from two words originating from Greek origin, meaning last or final and the second being study. This period is broadly understood to cover the timeframe which began with the life and ministry of Jesus and will be completed upon His return. 

Two historical periods are covered within this time period, the first beginning with the Old Testament and the expectations for end times. The second with the New Testament and the realizations  associated with it. Beginning with the Old Testament, Creation to redemption leading into Eschaton shows how God had plans to lay out at the very beginning of Creation which revealed an extension of God's heavenly kingdom to the point of redemption where the great son of David would rule forever in Jerusalem. 

The New Testament reveals that Jesus indeed brought the kingdom of God down to earth and He rules over it as king, and during the time from the Old Testament and the coming of Christ, Jewish theologians developed a view of eschatology that gained large acceptance. The viewpoints were divided into two ages, the first being the "this age" and the second being "the age to come" and during these contemporaries, Jesus made it clear that blessings would come to those that followed him.

The creation account of Genesis 1-2 tells us that we have specified God-ordained roles and responsibilities. In the book of Genesis, we can see distinct roles that God had ordained for humankind, the first being that we were designed to be servant kings to rule over all of creation on behalf of our King, God Himself. God being the great emperor had commanded humankind to reproduce and create humans throughout the world to work and take care of the Garden as we can see in Genesis 2:15. 

Humankind was designed to be God's royal priesthood to serve and honor him by ruling over the land that was given to them by God. Since man was created by God in the 'image of God' we were given the responsibility to rule over the land and continue to populate it and turn it into His earthly kingdom. The plan was never to just populate and be done, or just rule and be done, rather the plan was to rule, populate, and to ensure that the kingdom of heaven was brought to this earth. This was referred to as the mandate by theologians, as the purpose was not to just create and populate enough people to live in this world, but rather to create a culture throughout the world like families, government, farming, animal husbandry, and even arts and sciences.

The proto-euangelion is the 'first gospel' and is first introduced after the Fall (Genesis 3:15). This is where the plan of redemption was first introduced after the fall of mankind into sin. Due to this sin, God had cursed all of humanity and it appears that the great hope of God's eschatological kingdom appears to be lost. However that is where God appears in His mercy to introduce a plan of redemption and hope. He presents a plan of mercy and redemption that would rescue individuals from eternal damnation and through personal salvation, conviction and restoration allow for the hope of his great messianic kingdom on earth to be fulfilled. 

The reason that theologians offer this as the first gospel or the proto-euangelion is because this is where the offer of redemption takes place and the offer of salvation after the fall into sin occurs with humankind. It is worth noting that in Genesis 3:15 soon after the fall occurs, God demonstrates his mercy and promise that he will send a deliverer to deal with our sin and problems.

Five major redemptive covenants in the Old Testaments are as follows: 

Adam: after he had sinned, God extended mercy and salvation through proto-euangelion commonly referred to as the first gospel. This is where redemption was offered to humankind after the fall. Despite the redemption offered, it was made clear that there would be clear consequences for the sin that was committed. 

Noah: while the story is familiar of how God destroyed the world that Noah and his family lived in, there was a promise and covenant that was made, that until the end of the present order of creation God would spare such a harsh rebuke and not flood the earth again. 

Abraham: The covenant that was made with God and Abraham was that He would extend his redemption to the rest of humanity and establish His kingdom presence in the Promised Land and towards the ends of the Earth. This would included members from all nations on earth and the kingdom of God would not just consist of a single nation or people. 

Moses: While people would be exiled from the Promised Land and be scattered among the people and many nations, the mercy of God would not allow Him to abandon either Moses or his people forever, and there would come a time where God will fulfill his promises of blessings for his people and judgement against his enemies. 

David: with his kingdom rule and dynasty, the covenant with David was that his dynasty would rule over God's earthly kingdom forever. While the kingdom of God is a real place that is populated by real people, the expectation is that this dynasty would also be real and permanent just like each of God's words and promises.

The two great ages expected by first century Jewish theologians were "this age" and "the age to come". When referring to "this age", the characterization of sin, suffering, exile, and death were mentioned at the beginning of the fall and corresponds all the way to the age of redemption. The second being the "the age to come" when God's kingdom would fill the earth followed by forgiveness, righteousness, peace and eternal life. 

Jesus and His apostles for the most part did agree on the way that Jewish theologians characterized these ages. They were teaching that Messiah would indeed end this age and time period of sin and death while ushering in a age to come with all it's blessings. In 1 Corinthians 2:6-8, 2 and 2 Corinthians 4:4 and 1 Timothy 6:17-10 we can see how Paul would distinguish between this present age of evil and the age to come with the return of Christ, the Messiah. 

While Jesus and the prophets did agree to many of the teachings that were set forth, it is important to note that not all expectations were met, for example he did not lead armies to victory over all their enemies, and he did not restore the reign of David in Jerusalem. And during his time after his resurrection, Jesus spent time explaining why he did not do everything as his followers had expected him to do.

Biblical hermeneutics is a common word that is used frequently within theology and biblical studies derived from the Greek terminology of 'hermes' the mythological messenger of the gods. The term itself is defined as to 'interpret' or to 'explain'. Therefore when defining what is biblical hermeneutics, the meaning is simply the study of interpreting the meaning and significance of Scripture. Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834) is the father of modern hermeneutics. Biblical hermeneutics refers to the interpretation and or explanation of some type of message or communication.

The biblical roots of scientific hermeneutics can not be discounted or avoided simply because people living in biblical times were not modern scientists. Quite the contrary, they were sophisticated and had many accomplishments, and there are examples of biblical roots of scientific hermeneutics within the Bible. One notable example is the most influential figure in biblical interpretation of Origen of Alexandria. He lived from A.D. 185-253 and went far beyond scientific interpretations, and devoted himself to careful factual and rational analyses of the Bible. He crafted the Hexapla, a 6,000 page work consisting of more than 50 volumes which made a word-by-word comparison of various Hebrew and Greek version of the Old Testament. 
Another example would be Augustine of Hippo who would focus on factual and rational analysis of the Bible which at time was often painstaking. Then came Thomas Aquinas, followed by the Renaissance period which analyzed the grammar and historical contexts of the biblical manuscripts. The Protestant Reformation dealt with a thorough analysis of the Bible's grammar and historical context.

The biblical roots of devotional hermeneutics are emphasized significantly as theologians and biblical scholars have encouraged followers of Christ to read the Scripture time and time again, in the presence of God in order to bring upon enlightenment and even supernatural experiences from God. This can be displayed in Scripture, in the passage of Hebrews 4:12, where the word of God is noted to be living and sharper than any two edged sword and can penetrate the soul. 
Examples of biblical roots of devotional hermeneutics include the Letter of Origen to Gregory where Origen told Gregory that he should devote himself to the divine reading or Lectio Divinia. Throughout the medieval period, Lectio Divinia was practiced in four steps: the reading of the scriptures, the silent ponderings of the content which was read, praying to God to grant enlightenment on what was read, and then waiting for the Spirit of God to grant intuitive and deeply emotional convictions of a passage's significance. 
Calvin had insisted that when you read the Scriptures, you should be so affected as though God himself were face to face with us. Therefore you should take the initiative to read from Scripture as an all consuming, intense emotional and humbling experience in God's presence.

Two important aspects of organic inspiration are that you need to prepare yourself for when you enter the presence of God whether that is reading or meditating before God. When you get ready for God's presences you are getting your heart ready to believe in God's words as being true. For example, if you believe in false concepts and since before the word of God, without an open heart and mind, you will not be ready to accept the words that you read and you must be willing to draw near to God to read through that behavioral preparation. Another is to seek God's nearness through emotional readiness and preparation. This includes all of our attitudes, preconceived notions, and the our feelings about God, human beings, and the rest of creation. Our emotions can have either a positive or negative affect on how we approach the presence of God and whether we are ready to hear from God. 

The other aspect that you need to get ready for is the investigative piece. You have to look at the context of what the biblical authors intended with their writings and how God intends to bring that message to us. Paying attention to the detail and concepts that God and his authors intended for these writings to communicate with us must be closely tied to the organic acts of inspiration for us to be willing to accept the words we read. Lastly application, don't treat the word of God as a lifeless object, rather be willing to accept the word humbly and on an emotional level being able to apply that Scripture to our attitude and feelings as well.

The doctrine of illumination is simply answering the question of how do we receive knowledge from God/of God and how does that knowledge impact us? We have to be able to answer the question of how does God make himself known to us? By reading the word of God and allowing the Holy Spirit to help us understand the truth of God's word, we are able to understand the concepts through biblical inspiration and interpretation. This involves devout study and truth in spending time before God's word. While the Holy Spirit indwells within our lives, the Holy Spirit also allows for the guidance of all truth to be revealed as described in John 16:13-14. The Spirit will guide you on all the truth, and will reveal all that is to come. That is the illumination that the Bible teaches us about. 
By following the teachings of Paul in the writings of Ephesians, Christians are encouraged live out their faith by reading the gospel and he prays for illumination to happen in Ephesians 5:15-19. He asks that the revelation of God be revealed with his spirit of wisdom and knowledge, so that we will know what is the hope of his calling and the riches of his glory and the boundless greatness of his power towards those who believe.

The benefits that I have gained from an interpreter of Scripture has unfolded in a few different ways. For example, in my personal devotion, I always try to take the context of the writer and the audience. I then try to imagine the times in which this was written and understand the context and relate it to myself if it were me. I then try to take it in a forward thinking approach to present day and see how I can make it apply to my current day situation. The next thing I have gained is by being able to take conceptual teaching and translate them into modern day examples and be able to teach that back to my family, children, and youth group. For example, one common example is the story of Joseph and how he was abandoned by his family and taken as a prisoner, and then brought in a ruler and had the opportunity to fall into temptation. We can use that one story to describe many things we face on a day to day basis and I believe that once you are able to sit before God, in his presence and mediate, God will reveal many things to you. Another example is how I was able to learn from the life of Jonah, and many times we overlook the tiny worm that came and ate the shade that he was sitting under, but sometimes in our own lives, we overlook the creature, the worm that comes and ends up taking away the one thing that was protecting us and giving us cover. Being able to exegete the scripture, in a meaningful way is to look before the black and white text and allowing God to speak to you.

The immutable character of God helps us to see that there will always be a vital connection that occurs between the original meaning and the modern application of Scripture. We as Christians believe in the same God as the audience of Scripture as God is never changing and immutable in his promises and covenants, He continues to fulfill everything that has been sworn. This is displayed in Scripture through various aspects, beginning with Covenant Promises. When a promise is made by the Creator of Heaven and Earth, there is a certain level of weight that comes with that promise, and it is immutable. If it were simply a man that were to make a person, we are flawed and can be free to change our minds, however the Scripture uses several examples, one for example in the context of Abraham where God made a covenant that Abraham's offspring would be as numerous as the stars in the sky.

There are certain instances where God did not make a promise, and rather his words are best understood to be either threats, or even curses, and also offers of blessings. While all of this has occurred in Scripture, we as mankind continue to live in this same world that continues to evolve and change just as the days in Scripture. The first audiences lived in times where the world was not constant and change was inevitable. The people also are relatable from the first audience to those of us in today's day and age. While we are all created in the image of God, we have all fallen into sin and sinful nature. We continue to also have division amongst us, and religious quarrels. There continues to be several classes of people existing both then and now. Therefore while we may feel that we live in modern times, we should note that many of the similarities exist from the days when Scripture was written to today's day and age, however one thing remains constant, and that is God and His promises.

There are several ways that people today are similar to the original audiences from Scripture. The first is that while God had created man in his own image and intended for them to live a life of dominion over the Earth, mankind sinned and fell into sinful nature. That continues to occur day after day even in today's day and age. Every person born on this Earth, except for the Son of God share this same sinful nature. The second is religious divisions between the original and modern audience. There are three groups that are identified in Scripture, the unbelievers, the false believers, and the believers. The Unbelievers are categorized as the people who refuse to submit to God, and there were several mentions of these type of people in the Bible and we experience that even now. Then there are the false believers who make superficial committments to God and continue to do so in today's age. Lastly, the believers who make faithful committments to God, which is what we are all called to do. Lastly, there are the different classes of people that existed both in the original times of Scripture and also modern times. Many of the context around Scriptural portions are directed towards particular classes, and the connections shared between these classes can help guide mankind even in today's modern times with the use of Scripture.

There are many epochal or significant developments that have occurred over the course of redemptive history that have made our world different from the world of the Bible. For example the perspective laid out in the Bible is separated by three stages. The first being Creation, when God first made the world. The second being the Fall, when mankind fell into the temptation of sin and when sin was first committed and mankind was cursed. The last being redemption, when God showed His mercy and redeemed us from our sin. One example of how epochal developments occurred within history can be traced back to the laws regarding atoning sacrifices and how they required different things at different points in history. For example, during the time of Moses, they required sacrifices at the tabernacle, and then during the days of Solomon, they required sacrifices at the temple. In the early days of the New Testament, the required Jesus to be hung to death on a cross, and then later on in the New Testament, they ceased to be offered altogether. There have been many cultural developments between the original and modern audiences as well that must be taken into consideration, along with personal developments that distinguish people today from the audiences of the Bible.

Theologians have divided Old Testament history in a variety of ways and there are explanations for this diversity. One popular way was by associating each epoch with one of God's covenants. There are six major covenants that are notated in the Old Testament, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the new covenant that Old Testament prophets predicted would come at the end of Israel's exile from the Promised Land. Another way that theologians have divided the Old Testament history is through implications. Due to the divisions in the Old Testament, we can clearly see that God wanted his people to apply different theological themes at different times in different ways. For example, if there were a time that God had commanded a new way for sacrifice in worship, he expected that the people of God would abide by the new commandment and not ever return to their old ways.

New Testament believers should never apply the Scriptures as if they live in earlier periods of history because once God commands a new way for his people, He expects his people to never to return to the old ways. This can be seen in the example of how God had commanded his people to offer sacrifices only at the temple. In historical context, by offering a sacrifice at Moses' tabernacle would violate God's will. This would be true as well if you lived under the covenant of Moses and ended up building altars in new locations, just as Abraham and the forefathers had originally done. Once Jesus was slain for our sins, there no need for these sacrifices any longer. Christ gave us the perfect sacrifice once and for all, and  that is why when we look at the Old Testament, it is very important to study and get familiar with, however we live in a very different, yet significant time period. We should never try to disregard and ignore the old ways, however we should also not try to live and serve God as if we are still living in the original days.

Individual eschatology is defined as the study of how individual human beings experience the events of the last days. This is specifically relevant when considering the context around life, death, the intermediate state, and the final state or conclusion of our bodies an soul. 

Regenerate means being 'recreated' or 'reborn' in the terminology of theology. In terms of individuals who are spiritually alive or 'living'. While humans are considered 'born' when they receive physical life, this term is in relation to a spiritual birth which is obtained by the Holy Spirit. Our spiritual life is everlasting and eternal and that life never ends, when our earthly bodies die, our souls will continue to last forever.

Unregenerate refers to human beings who are considered spiritually dead. They are defined by three characteristics, the first being their spiritual death, the second their moral inability and the last being their enmity with God. The only way to give them life is through the Holy Spirit which would allow them to 'regenerate' allowing for a rebirth spiritually. While Adam and Eve were created with spiritual life and given dominion to rule over earth, their sin caused them to be cursed and resulted in spiritual death.

The present state of the unregenerate which is when humanity is currently living during the last days is separated by three characteristics. The first being their spiritual death, the second being moral inability, and the last being their enmity with God. When considering spiritual death, it is far different from a physical death. Physical death will result in physical decay of our flesh and cause us to return to dust. With spiritual death, your soul is still living within our bodies. Spiritual death was first brought on by Go through the disobedience of Adam and Eve when they fell into sin. God had cursed humanity with spiritual death. 

The second characteristic of moral inability is known as the fact that humans do not have the capacity to please God or obtain his blessing through merit. When considering Augustine's states of moral ability before and after the fall, he referred to Adam and Even living in a state where they were to be 'able to not sin' and they were empowered to completely avoid sin. But they also had the ability to sin, and when the did indeed sin, they along with all of humanity lost the moral ability to avoid sin.

The last characteristic is enmity with God which according to scripture refer to man loving their sin and hating God. This is called out in Ephesians 2:1-3 where Paul refers to the unregenerate and states the dead in their sins are following the ways of this world and gratify the cravings of their own desires

The regenerate come to experience spiritual life in the present state by experience a passing from death into life. This is a type of spiritual resurrection where rebirth occurs. In order for us to receive God's blessings, we have to admit that we can not do so by good works, or merits. Rather we have to undergo a second birth and that is a spiritual rebirth. John 3:3-6 refers to how no one is able to inherit the kingdom of God unless you are born of water and spirit. The Holy Spirit has to give us rebirth and render regeneration. 

It clearly affects our moral ability as we know that nothing we ever do will allow us to obtain the blessings of God through our own merit. Rather than trying to obtain your salvation, forgiveness, righteousness, and eternal life are free gifts from God which is based only on God's merit. The Holy Spirit regenerates our soul and gives us spiritual life. The Holy Spirit also allows us the ability to avoid sin and be able to pleas God to do good works. 

By being able to have this moral ability and prepare good works proves the fact that we have regained our moral ability and as a result of grace we have the Spirit dwelling in us. This then in returns allows for our good works to be rewarded with heavenly treasures and crowns, and even those who endure persecution will be rewarded. God calls us to imitate him and love each other while we keep his law. If we are to do so, our rewards prepared in heaven are great.

Unregenerate souls experience the intermediate state even after a body fails to exist and when we die. In Ecclesiastes 12:7 we read of how when the dust returns to the ground it came from, the spirit returns to God who gave it. For the unregenerate, you should be afraid, because even when your physical death occurs, your soul continues to exist and will return to God. And when that soul returns to God, it won't be to enjoy the pleasures and rewards that awaits you in heaven, rather it will be a time of judgement and punishment in hell. 

In Luke 12:4-5, we read of how you should not fear the one who kills your body, because that is the extent of what they can do to you, however the one you should fear is the one who has the power to cast you into hell even after your body has been killed. The names that are typically used for 'hell' in scripture teach us about the nature of the situation in a variety of ways. For example, in the Old Testament, the term Sheol is referred to as the home of unregenerate souls. Along with Abaddon known as a place of destruction. Bowr or pit refers to a place of punishment. In the New Testament Hades is used as a place of punishement, and Abussos refers to a place for prison or demons.

The Bible presents the experiences of regenerate souls during the intermediate state as those who are able to enjoy a sample or taste of their final blessings. In Luke 23:43, we see the thief on the cross who was promised by God to be in paradise that very day. In Revelation 6:9 we read of the souls of the martyrs being close to the altar in God's heavenly tabernacle. In Philippians 1:23 we read of how 'I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is better by far.' When the regenerate die, their bodies are put in the grave, and their souls are immediately taken into the presence of God in Heaven, where they will remain until the final resurrection. Regenerate souls have fellowship with other regenerate souls in heaven. 

In Revelation 6:9 we read of how martyrs in heaven know and have fellowship wit hone another and they continue to speak with one voice as they appeal to God to hasten the final judgement. Hebrews 12:22-23 speaks of a gathering of heavenly assembly where the spirits of righteous men made perfect assemble together.

Two predominant first-century schools of thought concerning the resurrection of the dead were between the Pharisees and the Sadducees. The Pharisees believed that there would be a general resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. While the Sadducees denied that a physical resurrection would take place for the dead. 

This is relevant to note as the Pharisees rooted their belief on the entire Old Testament, whereas the Sadducees only accepted the five books written by Moses (Genesis through Deuteronomy). When looking at Scripture and the positions that Jesus, Paul, and the rest of the early church, the view that was taken was clearly that of the Pharisees. It is clearly taught in Scripture, in Isaiah 26:19, and Daniel 12:2 that there will be a general resurrection, and this will be for both the righteous and the wicked. 

Even while the Sadducees would argue and challenge this issue, Jesus responded in Mark 12:26-27 that the Sadducees had indeed misunderstood Moses and that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were to be alive as spirits and that they would eventually be resurrected.

Divine authority is God's legal and moral right to carry out his will. If God decides to do something, it is well within His rights to do so and he never makes a mistake. Everything that He chooses to do is right. When it comes to the authority of God in regards to the general resurrection over both hell and heaven it is crucial to note that God has complete authority over hell. This is commonly misunderstood that Satan rules hell and God has no authority over hell. The people that have fallen and are suffering in hell is because God is allowing for that to happen and they are facing judgement. God rules over hell, rules over Satan, and the demons including the unregenerate souls that he has imprisoned there. 

When it comes to God's authority in heaven, heaven is the throne room of God and that is where his authority and glory are manifested openly. God has declared this in Isaiah 66:1, where He declares "Heaven is my throne." Even in the Lord's Prayer, we see that God's will is done in heaven perfectly and that is why it is the model for the new heavens and earth that will be created at the end of the eschaton.

The general resurrection will have an impact and effect on creation three different ways. It will impact the natural world, hell, and heaven. In regards to how the general resurrection will impact the natural world, God will uses events in the end time to alter how the natural world operates in order to prepare for his presence. When mankind fell into the trap of sin, the curse of God was placed upon us and it became a place of danger and death. However, in Romans 8, Paul looked forward to the general resurrection as a solution to this curse/problem. With the general resurrection, the Earth would be rescued through the resurrection of redeemed humanity. With this redemption, creation itself will be liberated. 

The impact on hell will be that when the unregenerate are resurrected, their souls will be removed from hell and then they will have their bodies returned to earth so that they can face God's judgement. However this won't just apply to the unregenerate, Satan and the demons in hell will be emptied from hell. According to some theologians, Revelation 20 teaches that Satan and demos will be released from their imprisonment in hell to participate in a final rebellion against God. 

The impact on heaven is that heaven will no longer be the residence of regenerate souls as a result of the general resurrection. While heaven is a wonder place, the intention of God was never for us to live there forever. God has something even better for us in mind in the new heavens and earth. The resurrected regenerate will return to earth in order to appear before God's judgement throne. Heaven will be emptied of it's angels and when Jesus returns, he will bring all of his angels with him and they will collect the resurrected regenerate  according to Matthew 24:31.

The three parties or groups that will face the final judgement are the fallen angels which are also known as demons, the unregenerate and the regenerate. When it comes to the fallen angels, 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 mention that the demos which at one point were angels will be awaiting their final judgement. These are the angels that rebelled against God, and abandoned their heavenly homes and his authority. The angels that did not fall, and never sinned against God will not be included in this judgement. 
The second group being the unregenerate are the wicked people that rejected God and they are separated from the righteous people that accepted God. John received these visions and it is mentioned in Revelation 11:18, and 20:11-15, Christ will indeed condemn the unregenerate. Christ will sit on his throne and separate the people one from another and say to those on the left, 'depart from me' and they will be sent to eternal punishment. 
The last group is the regenerate which is mentioned in Matthew 25:33-34. Christians are mistakenly believing that the regenerate won't be judged at all. However, unless the regenerate are part of the judgement, they would not receive their everlasting rewards.

Ecclesiastes 12:14 mentions that God will bring every deed into judgement, including every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil. God will take into consideration every imaginable piece of evidence and listen to witnesses, and weigh extenuating circumstances so that nothing will be left out and nothing will be inadmissible. This is done for perfect justice and every reward and every punishment will perfectly fit for everyone who is judged. For example, in Matthew 12:36, it is revealed that man will have to give account for every word, every careless word that has been spoken. 
However, not everyone will be held to the same level of accountability. We will be judged according to our situations, for those who have sinned blatantly, with more knowledge of God's requirements, will be judged more harshly. God will hold us accountable to our covenant obligations in the judgement, and we are bound to God and his judgement and we are obligated to obey him. We need to be very clear with this judgment as it is extremely strict.

The theological basis for giving attention to the biblical writers in our exploration of the meaning of Scripture is done so in three aspects. First the basis is giving attention to the writer, second to the original audience, and lastly to the document itself. Jesus describes in Matthew 22:41-45 that David's authorship of Psalm 110 was being referred to. This led the audience and reader to be specifically in line with the fact that a human author was acknowledged as significant. There is incredible value in understanding the original context that a writer has to understand a specific part of the Scripture. 

Second basis being the original audience, because looking back God would also allow for His Word to be delivered to His people in ways that suited their historical circumstance. God's words and ideas were revealed to his people in a way that would be understood by it's first audience. The words and ideas of Scripture were adapted to meet the needs of the current culture, technology, social structures and even the religious experiences of the time so that everyone who heard it would understand what was being said. Along every spectrum, the Scripture was written to suit the universal condition of humans. 

Lastly, the detail given to the document requires a reader to go back and look at Scripture itself. While modern translations are great and represent one of the most important teaching ministries of the church, we must be careful and wise to not be dependent on a single word of phrase which may differ from one translation to another. There is organic inspiration and the doctrine of divine accomodation which are two important doctrines that emphasis the biblical doctrines in their respective ways. With organic inspiration, the Holy Spirit inspired humans to write scripture. Whereas with Divine Accomodation, everything in Scripture came from cultural conventions of it's day.

Organic inspiration and divine accommodation helps us understand the original meaning of biblical document. Organic inspiration being Holy Spirit driven inspiration that led human authors to write the Scripture. As humans are mere mortals and make mistakes in their natural form, the only true way to understand the words of God are to go back to the original words ands translations that were set forth, because over time translations caused changes that have taken place over time and this can alter the meaning that was originally intended. One important factor to note is that the original documents of the Old Testament did not exist in Jesus day, only slight variations of the text in Hebrew versions existed at that time. 
With divine accomodation, the words, grammar, and literary style rose from the conventions of culture as it related to that day and age. If we are to pay careful attention to the ways that Scripture reflects these conventions, we are more likely to interpret it correctly. 
These two aspects are very important as the original context and scripture of God has the full authority of God, and the better that we understand the original meaning, the better that we as mankind will be able to apply it to our lives each day.

I personally find a high level of confidence in knowing that scholars today have access to many manuscripts that contain the original words of Scripture. Biblical passages can be complicated and the original intentions of the authors may at times be multifaceted. While considering the genre considerations as well, things tend to be more complicated as well. This can create several intracacies of the original meaning of the Scripture, and can then require Christians to have a complex approach when considering the meaning of Scripture. 
While there is a high level of confidence in knowing that scholars have the access to many manuscripts which contain the original words of Scripture, the greatest defeat that must be considered is that while God had spoken his inspired Word to come to life, the iterations and translations and interpretations are still being done by humans. That is where there is still room for error to be made, motives to be different and where one person can decide how the word should be interpreted. This can then create vague limitations and boundaries of the biblical passage and meanings, and the translation can vary from one person to another.

Three major approaches towards the objects and subjects of knowledge are objective, subjective, and dialogical. When considering objective approaches, scholars believe that they can impartially interpret the Scripture. With background and influence, this is achieved by scholars in obtaining an exhaustive understanding of everything that they have studied. There are both philisophical and cultural backgrounds to consider with this approach of knowledge. 
The second approach is that of subjective which is where subjectivists acknowledge human beings, the world, and matters of faith are often too complex to be discerned by scientific rationalization. Therefore many of their search for answers are relied upon heavily with emotions and intuition. For example, when Jesus said that we must love one another, there was an authoritative command with that. However as human beings, this is taken into consideration according to the weakness of mankind with emotion and intuition. 
Lastly, the dialogical approach is where dialog and discussion is required between the reader and the text. The Psalmist refers to this when they talk about spending time in the word and meditating on it day and night, this requires that a reader be able to spend time with the text and have an open dialogue to understand the context and the meaning with that Scripture.

The philosophical and cultural background of subjective approaches to interpretation were tied back to David Hume who believed that reason and scientific study can not lead us to objective knowledge, and rather our emotions and intuition will guide us to influence our thinking. Immanuel Kant believed that we only perceive the world as it appears to us and that we already have a conceptualized realization in place. When considering cultural backgrounds, romanticisim would consider that poetry, drama and music would provide an understanding of reality that is far superior to rationale scientific discourse. This is where subjective interpretors would argue that the meaning of art and literature would be included within us. Despite several backgrounds and errors, this background does allow for a significant impact in how we view and understand the Bible. God allows for a different outlook in our lives and how we understand the Bible to be able to apply it in our lives.

The authority dialog and objective models and the authority dialog and subject models can be compared and contrasted as follows. The authority dialogue model acknowledges that the objective truth can be found within the context of the Scripture. It helps us by avoiding the thought process that we can be utterly objective while approaching the Scripture. The subjective model acknowledges that our perspectives and beliefs tend to influence the way that we are interpretting Scripture. Which essentially means that if we do not submit ourselves to the authority of the Scripture, then our view and interpretation of the Scripture will be severely hindered. This is a lifelong process in the life of a Christian and will allow for us to grow and mature in our Christian faith.

Thomas Aquinas and other interpreters argued for a singular meaning of Scripture as they insisted that every legitimate spiritual interpretation was an extension of the literal sense of a passage. He taught that nothing necessary to faith was communicated without being taught somewhere else in Scripture in literal sense. During the time period of the Renaissance, Protestants would execute on the ideas that were championed by Thomas Aquinas. They would argue that all the spiritual aspects of a text were actually intended by the author and it would be for the original audience and are actually aspects of it's literal sense. 
While the Scripture is multifaceted, the passages within Scripture have meanings with many small parts and aspects that can contribute to singular, unified meanings called by literal sense.

The three types of biblical elaborations that are often used in Scripture are broken down into three parts, repetition of a facet of the original meaning, a clarification of things which were not entirely understood, and lastly an expansion of the meaning of a particular passage. The repetition of a facet is confirmed in Deuteronomy 5 where Moses is reminding the nation of the content which was within the Ten Commandments to Israel. This continued repetition enabled the people of God to remember the terms of his covenant. With clarification, we can see this example portrayed with the clarification of the commandment against murder described in Numbers 35. Moses clarifies between murder and other accidental manslaughter and the differences between the two. Lastly with the expansion of the meaning of a particular passage, an example is laid out for us in Matthew chapter 5, where Jesus criticized the rabbis of his day for incorrectly limiting the commandment's scope around murder. Jesus went on to explain the commandment that he had set out and went beyond just simple clarification. It did not just simply explain what was laid out, rather it brought additional clarification to the meaning of the commandment itself.

The more that we are able to study Scripture, the more we are able to see and decipher that the Scripture elaborates and provides clarity over and over agin. While interpreting the Scripture, we are able to make these words relevant of those in our sphere of influence without misapplying them. WE are to explore the meaning of Scripture, and acknowledge and submit ourselves to each place that the Scripture elaborates on.

The uniqueness of the biblical interpreter can lead us to multiple summaries of biblical texts and these multiple summaries are important to interpretation as they bring us as the reader closer to what the real intent and meaning of that passage was meant to be. All interpreters are different, they come with a different set of backgrounds, concerns, assumptions, and viewpoints. Their personal strength and weakness have a definite impact on how the passage is defined and interpreted. 
By having more than one summary, you are able to have more than one viewpoint on a passage and different viewpoints allow for the reader to have less of a bridge between the original meaning of the passage and the audience and what it is actually intended for. As readers, it is crucial to find summaries to the passage so that you can gain a better viewpoint and understanding of what is written. This allows for a multifaceted view and approach in understanding what is actually set forth for us a reader of the Word of God.

God is three persons in one essence, meaning that there is one substance in three persons. Our belief is that there is only one God, not three Gods. There are three persons within this one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father is the one who sends the Son and the Holy Spirit. Think of God as being the Father figure, the Father sends the Son to the Earth, and once the Son dies and is resurrected, He goes to the Father. At that time, they send the Holy Spirit. 

Being able to understand this also requires the understanding that God is one divine essence. He was never created, He was the Creator. He is the one who created the universe and all of the orders within. Many times we try to think of God as three different individuals, however they are the same essence, but with three different roles and responsibilities. The Father can not replace the Son, and the Son cannot replace the Father. Likewise the Holy Spirit can not replace the Father and vice versa. The three in one has a distinct meaning in that God has provided a clear distinction for each role of the Triune concept to understand the real meaning of Trinity.

In respect to the Trinity, a person is the distinction given to the roles of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. One thing to be clear on is that we do not mean the modern concept of an individual focused on the concept of personality. Looking at the New Testament, we can see passages of how the Father, Son and Holy Spirit speak to one another about each other. They love one another in some way that suggests the notion of communication amongst each other. While there remains one substance, you have three persons in that one substance. The persons do not have their own individual essence, rather they abide within one divine essence. 

A great example of this is displayed during the baptism of Jesus Christ by John the Disciple. When Jesus had emerged from the water, there was a sound from heaven, declaring the favor of God upon His Son in whom He was well pleased. That is the distinct person of the Father speaking directly to His Son. Then we see the example of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove coming into the scene. This is the person of the Holy Spirit within the realm of the Triuness of God. There is one essential essence, but three persons.

The reason that God's divine threeness does not violate the doctrine of God's essence is because you can not divide God into three different people. It is tricky, because people tend to confuse Trinity with tritheism, and what it makes it more difficult is that man cannot analyze him and figure this out for themselves. Theology shows us the 'simplicity' of God, and an analogy that has been used many times to describe the essence of God is related to water. With water, you can have different forms of one essence, for example when water is at normal temperature, it take the form of liquid. Under cold temperature, the water turns hard and into ice, but still remains under the essence of water. Lastly when water is boiled and heated to a certain degree, it can cause steam and evaporation which is still an essence of water. The Father will always remain the Father of His Son. His Son will always remain the Son of His Father, and that goes back to forever in time. The Holy Spirit has always been there, and the three of them are inseparable. 

In the book of Matthew, we see of Jesus talking about how if anyone regardless of who, receives 'one of my disciples in my name, they receive the One who sent me.' When you receive the disciples that were sent by the God, and has the Spirit of God in them, then you are receiving God, the Father, and the Son and the Holy Spirit. God is one but three persons that are of one divine essence.

Christ always existed, simply put he was there before time. Creation happened through Christ, existed through Christ, and continues through Christ. In the opening verses of the Bible, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the Earth" Without God, there would be no creation. If we look at the book of Hebrews, we can also see the first thing that is called out is the creation and how God appointed him the 'heir of all things.' If you are a Son then you are considered as the heir, and so as the Son, he is the revelation of the God and identifies with God and the Creation. 

Christ was the beginning of everything and the Scripture teaches us about the void before the Creation. Only after there was creation, was there the Earth, moon, and stars. Only then was there a distinction between the Earth and the waters, and only then was there any distinction of any form of being. While the word of God teaches us that 'in the beginning was the word, and the word was with God, and the word was God.' There was no other alternative to God being created, he was the beginning of all beginnings. The other factor to consider here is also faith, without the belief of faith in your Christian life, you will begin to doubt and question many things. The way to get past that is to ask, 'does this hinder my walk with God, and does it affect my eternity?' and if the answer is no, simply move and accept the word and truth of God.

The Trinitarian formulas in the New Testament help us see the equality of the Holy Spirit with the other members of the Godhead by clear distinction within the Scripture. The Scriptures mentions God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit as being equal members in the Trinity. One of these examples is portrayed in water baptism. When an individual is baptized, Scripture teaches us to baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. One name, three persons in one, and one God. When the book of Matthew ends, Scripture teaches us that Jesus ordered his disciples to go and make disciples of all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He did not command them to baptize them in just the name of the Father, or just the name of the Son, or just the Holy Spirit, but giving equal rights and power among all three to do so. 

The Great Commission and the commands given in 2 Corinthians are clear examples of how the Bible portrays the Trinitarian formulas describing the equality of the Holy Spirit among the other persons of the Triune God. With baptism, we have listed how the command is to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. And in 2 Corinithians, the command given is to depart in fellowship as 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Chris, the love of the God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with us all" which describes the three in one approach.

The Trinity is more clearly expressed in the New Testament than in the Old Testament. This does not necessarily mean that the Old Testament is wrong or less important, rather is an incomplete revelation where God did not reveal himself all at once. This occurs through progressive revelation where through the canon of Scripture and moving throughout the Scripture and New Testament we can see that in passages such as Matthew 28, where the Great Commission is outlined. Or you can take a look within Ephesians 4 and 2 Corinthians 13 where you can see the full package or depiction of the Trinity. 

When you look at the Scripture, you can see that throughout history, God is moving closer to us progressively. Before the creation, God was above us, and as time goes on, He takes steps to be closer to us, and through his Son dwelt among us. That then continues to the New Testament era where the Holy Spirit has taken a role to be closer to us and live within us. This canonical lens to understand the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is portrayed in a progressive fashion in the New Testament and not clearly identified in the Old Testament. This again helps set the context for the unfolding of our Savior known as the eternal Son of God, which is also true of the Holy Spirit as we can see.

The images of a lion and a lamb described in Revelation 5 demonstrates that the Son is a divine person that is equal to the Father. When John holds the scroll which is the secret to God's future, there is an announcement from an angel that states there is one who is worthy. The one who is worthy is the Lion, the Lion of the tribe of Judah. The symbolic gesture of a lion is royalty and with the tribe of Judah described as a lion's cub, the picture of a reigning king from the line of David is seen here. John is expecting to see a powerful lion to be depicted in this instance, however instead of a powerful lion, John sees a lamb. A symbol of sacrifice and suffering is portrayed. 

While Jesus is the conquering king and the Messiah, he accomplishes salvation by suffering and dying as the sacrificial lamb. In order to attain that salvation, the lamb must undergo suffering and sacrifice himself to pay for our sins. This is a powerful depiction of a Son being a divine person that is equal to the Father. Only the Father can redeem us of our sins, and understanding the godhood, the reader can grasp the divine essence of God. Only in this context can you see how a lamb would be worshipped within heavenly courts and while one may think this may anger God and be offensive to Him. He encourages the entire universe to worship the Lamb in front of him and that is where the full divinity of Jesus is revealed, he is not one of God's creatures, rather he is equal with God.

John 1:1 teaches us that Jesus is God because the deity of Christ is portrayed here. In the beginning was the word, the word was with God and the word was God. This is a passage that was taught during elementary sunday school days, and in the most concise way possible was described as the word being equal to God. In translation 'what God was, the word was God'. Jesus is fully God himself, he is described by John as the Son of God, the divine agent, and the one who brings life. 
As you continue to read the passage of John 1, you will see that the word became flesh and dwelt among us. John continues to go on about how Jesus is God and in John 10, you have Christ saying, "I and the Father are one." Where Christ himself is placing himself alongside the Father as one and emphasizing His equality with His Father. When the text of John 1:1 is outline, the term 'word' is not simply an abstract concept, rather it is the distinct relation to God in existence. It is a direct statement of the divinity of God and His word, which affirms that the Word is the same essence of God himself. While the word became flesh, the reference is made to Jesus and both distinct from God while being described as One.

In order to demonstrate the personality of the Holy Spirit from Scripture, we can see in John 14-16 about the Spirit doing things that only a person would be able to do. When Jesus goes on to describe that he will send forth another advocate such as himself, the Holy Spirit is the divine essence being described here. The Holy Spirit then has a role to go into the world and prosecute the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgement. Just as Jesus was a witness, the Holy Spirit serves in that capactiy as well and is identified as a distinct person in a number of passages. 

The intellect of the Holy Spirit is demonstrated in 1 Corinthians chapter 2 where the Holy Spirit is listed as searching all things and even the deep things of God. No one knows the thoughts of God except for the Holy Spirit. Another personal quality or attribute is that there are emotions involved, the Spirit is teaching, guiding, comforting, leading, all of which a person does. In Ephesians 4, we can see that we should never grieve the Holy Spirit, and knowing that grief is an emotion, this is another personality of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is able to speak to us as well just like a person, this was portrayed in Act 13 where the Holy Spirit gave specific instructions with personal communication.

It was necessary for the man Jesus to also be God because while Jesus was fully God, he was also fully human. And with his life and death through humanity, through death and resurrection we are saved. Being a human yet also being God, he is equal in power and glory to the Father and we can trust him that he is able to redeem us from our sins. Only God is able to forgive sins, yet he has to be man in order to represent us and be able to to be put through the necessity of sacrifice and death. While only God can forgive sin, Jesus had to substitute himself for us by taking the full form of human yet being without sin in order to complete this substitution. 
Being the second person of the Trinity, it's an amazing truth that he became man and lived among us. He died, rose again, and has great love for us. And because Jesus is also God, we can now have freedom to worship him and adore him for all of his power, and goodness. While he remained as the perfect sacrifice, his substitutionary atonement required that Jesus would take the place for humanity and bear the infinite wrath that God had against humankind's sinful nature. Only Jesus being fully God could have stood in the gap between God and humanity, and as a mediator reconcile us back to God. As God, Jesus had dominion and power over life and death and demonstrates his victory to believers.

If the Father has authority over the Son and Spirit, and if they disagree then what happens is the question, but one of the key fundamentals to understand is the relationship between the Father and the Son and the Spirit. We know that whatever it is that makes the Father the Father, the same is that of which the Son and Spirit is made of. They exist in unity as one God, three persons. We can see the relationship clearly identified in the New Testament where the Son gladly submits to the will of His Father and how the Spirit gladly rejoices (during the example of the baptism). 
The Bible does not depict any instance or indication that the Father and Son and Spirit disagreement or have miscommunication with one another. They always of one mind and work in absolute perfect unity in every area. 

The Father's authority is one that loves the Son and desires for His Son to be glorified, where the Son also desires for the Father to be glorified, and the Spirit is glorified as well. In the concept of God, there is unanimity of will and love, because of the unique fellowship of the Trinity. There is no area or reason within Scripture for us to think that the Father and Son or Spirit would disagree or against the will of each other. The Son obeys the will of His Father and the Spirit rejoices, and the three in one manifestation of the Trinity continues to salvation.

When we say that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, we are describing a very unique relationship which at times can be confusing to the reader. In Scripture we assume that the Son was born like every other person that was born, however in the book of Revelation we see that the Son is eternal. He always existed, and goes back to eternity. If there was always a Father, then there was alwys a Son, and this relationship goes back to eternity. There was never a beginning or start to this relationship, it always was. He was not a creature that was created out of nothing, however the son was begotten of the Father. 

The doctrine of eternal generation speak of God who is eternal and His Son. While Jesus took on the form of a full human, he was able to empty himself of his eternal manifestation of eternal glory that he had with His Father. He was still omnipotent, and omniscient, having perfect knowledge as the Son of God, however having all of this he surrendered none of them while taking on the form of mankind coming to redeem the world from sin and lead them to everlasting salvation. Since the Father was always there, so was the Son. That is what the meaning of eternally begotten is related to in the terms of this context that we read.

The early church councils affirm the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father. We are not relating this to a  procession of how a being is created or conceived through birth. Rather the Spirit is eternal just like the Father and Son and there is no beginning or end to either. So when we say that the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father we affirm the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The Council of Nicea and the Council of Constantinople defended this unique attribute of the Holy Spirit  by stating that the Holy Spirit is Lord and to be worshipped as the Father and the son. 

In 381, the Council of Constantinople met and wrote two-thirds of the Nicene Creed and regarding the section of the Holy Spirit stated, "We believe in the Holy Spirit, and the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, and with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified." It reaffirms the divine status of the Holy Spirit and the divine attributes of the Spirit. The Spirit was not created, because if it was created, then it would not be of God, because God was not created, he was God eternal and so was His Son and His Spirit. While this may come with controversy, and theologians argue that the Spirit came or proceeded from the Father and the Son, the Spirit indeed proceeds from Christ and the Son and is taught in John 16, 20, and Galatians 4.

Implications of the Council of Toledo for the doctrine of the Holy Spirit was that the Western Church added on very early to the ecumenical councils to describe the relationship of the Son to the Father, and more so the Son and Spirit relationship. The implications revolved mostly around the filioque where the argument revolved around the Father sending the Son, yet the Father and Son sending the Spirit. In Act 2, we can see the Day of Pentecost described where the the people exalted the Lord, and Jesus Christ ascends to the right hand of the Father and from the throne of authority, send the Spirit. With this depiction, the church was trying to isolate the roles and relationships between the Father, the Son and Holy Spirit. 

While some of the reasons for the division were complicated, the key fundamental is to understand that the Spirit's work is to bear witness to the Son and glorify the Father. With the council at Toledo in 589, the argument made was around the addition of "and the son" which was around the double procession of the Holy Spirit. This was done without consulting or seeking any theological input and caused a series of disputes that lasted for generations and centuries to come. And with this issues the division occurred between the East and West on the doctrine of the Trinity, speicifically around the issues of the filioque which concerned the double procession of the Spirit.

Ontological Trinity is referred to as "immanent Trinity", which has to do with the existence and personal interaction between the Father, the Son and Holy Spirit, apart from their acts of creation and salvation. When referring to ontological Trinity, we are referring to nature, that the there are three persons in one, and they are equal in substance, power and glory. While none of them are superior in this regard, the the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. They are all 100% God equally. This term also refers to the coexisting nature of all three in one, where they love one another. The Father who loves the Son, who is the beloved, and the Holy Spirit who communicate the love between them and within that being of god is given love and communicates love. 

The same God at work in creation is the Father, Son and Spirit which relates to one another eternally. God speaks to us, interacts with us, and is the same God as he always so so Trinity give us this view of ontological Trinity. The Father, which is the origin of the godhead, and the Son which was eternally begotten of the Father, sharing the same essence, and the Holy Spirit which is of the same essence as well. They all in agreement submit to the will of the Father.

Three reasons that critical scholars challenge the authorship of James is because the writer opens up chapter 1 by saying that he is a "servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ." While the writer assumed that this would be sufficient and carry enough authority, this also created reason for confusion to challenge the authorship of the book. Critical scholars have challenged the authorship by stating that there was another James but not the one who indeed wrote the book, the brother of Jesus or son of Zebedee. The second reason is because the author is aware of Hellenistic or Greek culture and James was a Jew from Palestine. However in the time of Jesus, many of the Jews from Palestine had a decent awareness and understanding of Hellenistic and Greek culture. Pseudonyimity, where the written works is assigned to someone else other than the actual author was brought up as there was no mention of the author to Jesus in the writing, and the inaccurate assumption of inaccuracies that the epistles don't match James' theological outlooks in the New Testament. 
Even with these arguments and reasons set forth by critical scholars, the argument is weak at best. The arguments of James being the author and brother of Jesus are actually much stronger than it not being evident. And due to this compelling fact, evangelical scholars affirm that James was indeed the author of the book, and the brother of Jesus.

The clues that we can gather from James' epistle about his original audience start from chapter 1 verse 2, 'the twelve tribes scattered among the nations.' This appears to be the Jews who reside outside of Israel. James also continues to go on by addressing his audience as 'believers in our glorious Lord Jesus' chapter 2:1. With these two verses alone, the reader is able to identify the audience is Jewish Christians who were living outside of Palestine. In chapter 2:2, James addresses the readers with the word 'synagoge' which is in reference to Jewish gatherings, and "kurious saboth" which is a common Old Testament name for the God of Israel listed in James 5:4. While many of the audience members were of traditional Jewish heritage, followers of Moses and the Torah, it is important to understand the audience by incorporating the fact that they are derived from a rich heritage with tradition. And James continues to talk to them about faith and living a wise life. He also goes on to explain how they should apply this into their own lives in light of the resurrection of Jesus Christ. 

Now while the audience is likely Jewish Christians, that does not avoid the fact of Gentile believers in church. We know based on the book of Acts, there were many Gentile God fearing converts who began to practice Judaism and attended synagogues. While the Bible states that the Gentile believers were regarded as "Abraham's offsprings" in Romans 8:9, they were considered as much of the twelve tribes of Israel than any of the Jews by bloodline.

James wrote his epistle likely in AD 44 to AD 62, the main consideration for these dates are anchored by the fact that Peter was released from prison in AD 44, and James was martyred in AD 62. We also know that James was a leader of the early church in Jerusalem which continues to validate the dates of origin for his writing. Acts 17 describes that James became a leader of the early church soon after Peter's release from prison. James dies at the hand of the priest Ananus in AD 62, which allows for the window of time where the book was written to be narrowed to the time of AD 44 to AD 62. James wrote his book in Jerusalem where he resided and ministered until the time of his death in AD 62. The reason behind why he wrote this epistle was to share to the church and audience of the trials and problems that he had to face and endure. James also knew that the audience that he was addressing was facing many trials as well. James was calling them to have joy and peace admist the trial, as he went on to explain that whoever is able to persevere will become mature, and complete. James goes on to say in James 1:5, 'if any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you." The trials that some were facing caused them to leave their walk with God and abandon God and pursue friendship with the world. James was teaching the audience about continuing on in joy, perserverence, and choosing humility as a path to wisdom.

By the time that James had written his book, there was a long lasting line of books and teachings about wisdom. This was clearly visible in Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiasties, and the book of Psalms. Even in the book of James chapter 5, James addresses the life and perservernce of Job, and how one should live their life similar to that during the moments of trials and temptations. In his writings, James goes on to exemplify the way that one should speak, the treatment of widows, and orphans, poverty, and favoritism. James goes on to say to the reader and audience, 'that if any of you lacks wisdom, then let him ask God who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given to him.' There are many ties to how similar the writings of Jesus are to the writings of James. Matthew 5:10 describes how the persecuted are blessed, and James writes in his book of the man who is under trial and perserveres is blessed. The structure of the letter similar to other wisdom literature of James' day was unlike any other literature of wisdom. The book of James was targeted and specific to churches and featured some of the organizational features of other New Testament epistles.

James did encourage his audience to have 'pure joy' in the midst of trials in chapter 1:2. The pursuit of wisdom in order to make something like this possible is only done through our faith and belief in Jesus Christ. The belief is that the suffering that we face, if we are to use wisdom and allow God to strengthen our confidence, then God has ordained for us the blessing of eternal salvation. Even in the book of Matthew 5, we can see how Jesus describes those who undergo trials and persecution are to be considered as blessed. While it can be rather difficult to see how suffering can lead to blessing or even see the light at the end of the tunnel, James continues to tell his audience to pursue wisdom, as that is the only means to see how suffering and wisdom go hand in hand. Neither Luke or the book of Acts clearly mentions the name of the author for the book of Acts, however there are two types of evidence, both explicit and implicit that suggest that one person wrote the book of Acts. The explicit evidence suggests that both Luke and Acts are both dedicated to Theophilus, and while Acts does refer to a former book, evidence suggests that the third gospel is what is being mentioned. The implicit evidence is that both of these books (both Luke and the book of Acts) have similarities between them which is inclusive of the orderly account, compositional structure, chronological length, the themes that are mentioned, the similar story lines and the commonalities of a redemptive historical vision, which incorporates the purpose and beliefs along with the author. The fact that there is also a connection between the two books and they are both addressed to Theophilus highly suggests the evidence that it is the same writer.

While there are explicit and implicit evidence that the writer of Luke and Acts are the same, there is also historical evidence that stems from the early church affirming that the same person wrote these two books. The Muratorian fragment (AD 170-180) confirms that Luke is the author of the third gospel, also known as the book of Luke and the book of Acts. The Anti-Macrionite Prologue which was an introduction to the third gospel, also describes the author of the book of Acts as being Luke. 
The early church leaders, Irenaeus (AD 130-202) stated, "Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the gospel preached by him." This is later affirmed by Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian and Eusebius. While all these confirmations are there, there no single indication in the literature from the early church that anyone other than Luke was the author of the third gospel and the book of Acts. Eusbius, the great church historian wrote around AD 323 that Luke was the author of the book of Acts, and while he was never designated as an apostle, the early church passed on what it had received as the truth, that Luke wrote both of these books.

Luke was immensely influenced by the Old Testament's view of history in general, and secondly was impacted by the history of Israel. Pascal's threefold outlook in history was reflected in Luke's writings of the early church in Creation, the Fall, and Redemption. In the first-fold, the Creation writings were in general and in the book of Acts. Followed by the Fall, in general, and in the book of Acts. Lastly Redemption which is listed in general and the book of Acts. When accounting for Luke's view of Israel's history, we can see how Luke's record in the context of Acts was depending on the history of Israel starting with Abraham. God had called out Abraham to be the father of many nations and through him all people on earth would be blessed. Luke reports on this as the blessing of Christ came to the Jews by fulfilling the promises of God to Abraham. Jewish Christians received the gospel and brought it to the Gentiles, which continued to fulfill the promises of God to Abraham. This then was  depicted through the life of Moses and Exodus, where Moses had prophesied that another prophet would be sent by God to redeem his people from sin. Luke points out that this prophet is Jesus and to reject Jesus was to reject the law and Moses.

Unbelieving Jews and Christians today share some similarities but also have distinct differences based on religious beliefs, cultural practices, and historical backgrounds. The similarities between the two are the ethical framework, where both often emphasize moral values such as justice, compassion, and charity which have roots in the shared scripture of the Old Testament. Cultural practices and ethical practices such as respect for Sabbath and dietary laws can overlap, although these are typically more pronounced among religious believers. Scriptural heritage, where both groups share the Old Testament stores, laws, and teachings that form the foundation for many ethical and religious concepts in both traditions. The differences lie in the belief of Jesus Christ, the most distinct difference is that Christians believe in Jesus to be the Messiah, the Son of God, where the Jews do not accept Jesus as the Messiah or divine figure. Jews also follow the Torah, and observe Jewish holiday, and traditions whereas Christians celebrate sacraments such as baptism, holidays and teachings from both Old and New Testament. By knowing the Jewish teachings, and how they view Jesus, we are able to be more impactful in our teaching and evangelism to them.
