This goes on to prove that he was qualified to be the Savior who could represent humanity without sin. Jesus showed his strength in both spirit and mind. He refused to use his divine power for selfish purposes such as turning stone to bread and he rejected satan's attempts to make him test God or bow down in exchange for power. Rather, Jesus responded to each of these temptations with Scripture which shows us his complete trust in God's Word. His victory showed that he is not only sinless but is also committed to God's plan of salvation. In addition to all of this, Jesus understands the struggles we face and can sympathize with our weaknesses because he has walked in our same shoes. His victory in the wilderness gave assurance that he is both the perfect example of obedience and the merciful savior who can help us overcome temptation.

The crucifixion was already a unique form of the death penalty that was used by the Roman Empire. Even though some might view this as a Roman execution, it was more than that. It showed God's plan to save humanity. The crucifixion was already a cruel and shameful way to die during the Roman Empire. Victims were tied or nailed to a cross as was in the case of Jesus. They were usually left to hang until death. In most cases this was reserved as punishment for criminals but Jesus was innocent and sinless. Instead of dying for his own crimes, Jesus willingly gave his life for the sins of others. This idea is called imputation. This means that God placed the guilt of humanity's sin onto Jesus even though he has never sinned. From a legal perspective, God counted Jesus as if he personally committed every sin imputed to him. Jesus took the punishment that sinners deserved, making his death an atoning sacrifice. This was along the act of divine judgment as Jesus bore the full weight of God's wrath against sin. In doing so, not only was our sins imputed on him but his righteousness was imputed on us sinners. This showed God's justice in punishing sin and God's mercy in providing forgiveness.

The resurrection of Jesus accomplished so much for God's people as well as God's plan. According to the text, Death is the greatest tragedy humans face and the most painful result of sin in this world. The good news here is that Jesus conquered death through resurrection. By rising from he grave through the power of the Spirit, he proved to all creation that he is truly God's Son in addition to being the heir to his kingdom. This also guaranteed the future resurrection and blessing of all how believe in him. This also furthered God's plan of redemption. God's covenant promise was to establish his kingdom on earth under the kingship of a descendant of David. This obviously could not happen if Jesus remained dead. His resurrection was a crucial step that allowed God to fulfill these promises. Another point to make is that the resurrection brings countless blessings of salvation to believers. You can see in Romans 4:25, it results in justification and the forgiveness of sins. Because Jesus rose of the sea, those who trust in him are now justified and made right with God and given a new spiritual life. It gives hope for the future. Just as Jesus was raised with a real physical body, believers will also be raised to eternal life. The resurrection shows that God's plan is not to abandon the world but to redeem and restore it fully.

To be honest, this is a daily challenge in my life. Trying to balance the roles of being a father, husband, brother, son, uncle, leader, musician, etc. can be very overwhelming. The responsibilities of work, family, and the calling that God as on me is always a struggle and becomes a juggling act. Working extra hours to make sure bills are paid, trying to be a loving husband, bring present for my kids, helping my parents, taking care of my health, doing ministry at church just to name a few. It is in these redundant and exhausting moments that I come to realize it's not just confessing that Jesus is Christ on a Sunday but rather how I live everyday. I have come to the understanding that life will always be busy but I have to make the intentionally effort with the opportunities that are given to men to show others the love of Jesus. This comes through treating coworkers with respect even when I get angry at them, praying for scared patients at the hospital where I work, showing grace when my kids get on my last nerve, make time to listen to my wife after a long day, being intentional about family prayer. Doing this helps me see that Jesus is at the center of my life. It is of course all about Him. Don't get me wrong, there are moments I do fail. I sometimes get too tired to pray and spend time with God everyday, I get impatient with people, etc. but despite all that I remember that Jesus hasn't given up on me and that he give me the strength to do better tomorrow. Confessing Jesus in my life isn't about trying to be perfect but it's about always pointing myself and those around me to him. I want Jesus in every part of my life. I want my kids to grow up not just hearing about Jesus but rather seeing it through the way I live my life. I want others to see despite what all might happen or what I may be going through in my circumstances, Jesus shines through it all.

The Apostle's Creed didn't appear all at once but rather is slowly developed over time during the first few centuries of the Christian Church. During the early years of Christianity, short summaries were used called the rules of faith. What these statements did was help protect the truth of the gospel, train leaders and also gave ordinary believers a clear way to understand their faith. You have to consider back then most people could not read and the Bible was not widely available so these summaries were very helpful to them. Over time these turned into creeds. These were short easy to remember statements of beliefs. Creeds were often recited during worship services and baptisms so new believers could clearly express their faith. The Old Roman Creed is one of the earliest examples of this. It closely resembled what is known as the Apostle's Creed. At first different churches had slightly different versions of the creed but around A.D. 700, it became standardized into the form we recognize today. This shows us how the early church wanted a unifying statement that could be used everywhere. It also provides a simple way to teach new Christians, help the church stay focused on biblical truth as well as offer protection against false teachings that were common at the time and are still relevant to this day.

The church believed it was important to create and use a creed for many reasons. One of the first reasons was it gave Christians a clear summery of what they believed. During the early centuries, most people were not educated to read and write and very few people had access to the Bible. These short simple statements like the Apostles' Creed made it possible for everyone to learn the essentials of the Christian faith particularly for new believers as well as those with little to no education. Secondly the creed was also important because of the commonality of false teachings during that time which in fact is still relevant to this day. Groups such as the Gnostics taught that the physical world was evil and denied that Jesus had truly come in the flesh. There were also others like the Docetists that claimed that Jesus only appeared to suffer and die but was not really human. By teaching the creed, churches during that time were able to give Christians a way to guard themselves against these false teachings. Thirdly the creed also played a major role in baptism and discipleship. Whenever new believers were baptized they were asked to confess their faith. The creed played a role here and gave them the words to express their faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as well their belief in forgiveness, resurrection, and eternal life. This was a confession and proof that they understood at least the basics of the Gospel. Lastly the creed promoted unity among the churches. Christians from different places as well as from different times may have worshiped in different ways. However by sharing the same confession they show that they belonged to the same family of faith in Jesus worldwide.

The Apostles' Creed teaches that God is the Trinity. This means that there is one God in three persons who are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. To make more sense of this you need to understand the persons and nature. A person is a distinct self aware individual. The Father, Son, and Spirit are not the same person but rather they are related to each other and do different things. Nature means God's essence or being. All three persons share the same divine nature. What this means is that Christians believe in one God not three separate gods. Going into more detail, the creed shows the different works of each person. The Father for example is almighty and the maker of heaven and earth. His role is creation and ruling over everything. The Son, who is Jesus, was conceived by the Holy Spirit born of the Virgin Mary. Jesus suffered under Pontius Pilate, then died and buried and then rose again on the third day. He is ascended to heave and rules at the right hand of the Father. Jesus will return to judge the world. His name work is salvation which was achieved through His death and resurrection. Lastly the Holy Spirit gives life and works in the church. The creed mentions Him in connection with the Holy Catholic Church, the forgiveness of sins, and life everlasting. The main role here includes creating faith, uniting believers, and applying Christ's salvation to us. In short the Trinity means one God, three persons who is working together in creation, salvation, and in the church.

It is important to participate in the church because Christianity was not ment to be practiced alone. You can see this from the start that believers came together to worship, learn, and care for one another. The Bible also warns us not to give up meeting together. This is because being with other Christians helps us grow in faith and stay strong. An example of this could be were a person might hear a sermon that helps them understand God's Word more clearly or they may be encouraged when others pray for them during a hard time. Just like a basketball team or a football team needs every player, the church needs every member to use their gifts to serve and build up the whole body. The Apostles's Creed says that we believe in the Holy Catholic Church and the communion of saints. This should tell us that the church is much bigger than one congregation. Rather, it is all believers everywhere and throughout the history of the world. Whenever we gather with the church, we are going something much larger than ourselves. It is also equally important to preserve the church's central doctrines. From the earliest centuries there have been many false teachers who have tried to distort the Gospel by denying truth such as the humanity of Christ, His resurrection, or the forgiveness of sins. This happens even today. Surprisingly even at Calvary Assembly were members of the Shincheonju Church of Jesus came. Reciting and teaching the Apostles' Creed helped the church protect these essential beliefs. Without guarding these truths the church in general could easily drift into false teachings and loose the truth of the Christian message. Participation and preservation ensures that the church remains a faithful community of believers. Gathering in worship and guarding core doctrines is the only way the church can continue its mission to proclaim the Gospel and pass it on for future generations.

The Apostles' Creed is foundational to Christian theology because it summarizes the most basic and essential truths of the Christian faith. For example, just as you need a solid foundation for a building to stand, Christian beliefs also need a solid starting point. The Creed gives the bases that is needed by setting out who is God, what Christ as done for us, the work of the Holy Spirit, the importance of the church, and the hope of forgiveness, resurrection, and eternal life. One of these ways that the Creed is foundational is that it acts as a standard for testing all other beliefs. If someone claims that Jesus was only a good teacher but not truly God for example, the Creed reminds us of the truth which is Jesus Christ is God's only Son, our Lord. In the same way if a teaching denies the resurrection, the Creeds protects us by affirming the resurrection of the body. This will help keep the true followers of Christ from being misled by convincing false ideas. The Creed is also foundational because it provides the logical basis for other Christian teachings. For example, if God is the maker of heaven and earth then he also has authority over creation and we can trust His power in our lives. If Christ rose from the dead then we can be confident that He too will raise us as well. These are some of the the basic truths which support everything Christians believe. The Apostles' Creed is foundational because it sets boundaries of authentic Christianity which anchors us to Scripture and also provides the core truths on which all other theology is built.

Christians says that the God of the Bible is the one and true God because evidence of this is found all throughout the scriptures. The Bible repeatedly teaches that there are no other gods. Many other religions call their deities gods but Christians believe that these are imaginary beings or idols that were made up. In some cases they could also be evil beings or spiritual forces. The Bible explains that from the beginning of creation you can see where God has made evidence showing his existence clear for all the world to see. You too can see this evidence of His power and divine nature in creation itself. The sad fact of the matter is that humans have fallen into sin and because of this they refuse to honor God and choose to instead worship false gods or other created beings. The belief that Christians have is the belief in one God which is called monotheism. Similar to and extent to Judaism and Islam which also believe in monotheism. However, there is something different with Christianity that both Judaism and Islam rejects. Christians believe that this one God exists in three persons which are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These three persons are not separate gods but share the same divine essence. This God is what Christians believe to have the power to create everything from nothing. Also having the power to ultimately rule over all and save people from their sin. This is clear in the Apostles' Creed when it states that "I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth."

When you use the term simplicity it is easy to fall into the narrative of sounding like it means easy to understand. The truth of the matter is that that is not the case at all. Instead it describes God's essence which is completely unified and not made up of different parts. God is not a mixture of pieces that you put together like love, power, and justice but rather he is one perfect and complete being. All of His qualities are fully present in everything that He does. An example of this that was explained to us to help us understand is the example of a glass of pure water. Pure water is completely water and nothing else. You can by all means add dirt and then it becomes mud. This is then a mixture of two different substances. However, God's essence is not like this at all, His essence is like the pure water which is entirely one and undivided. This is very important to understand especially when Christians believe in one God even though God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit exists. The three persons are not separate gods joined together but rather they share the same exact divine essence. This is what it means to Christians believing in one God while also affirming the Trinity. God's simplicity means that He is unchanging and perfectly consistent. All his attributes work together in perfect harmony. For us believers this means that God can always be trusted. He will always act according to His good and perfect nature.

Both of these terms, "ontological Trinity" and "economic Trinity" are used in a way for Christians to describe the relationship between God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. The ontological Trinity primarily focuses on who God is in His being. The word ontological means related to being. This term focuses on God's essence showing that all three persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, share the same divine nature. Each person is fully God as well as equal in all power and glory as well as all divine attributes. This helps us remember that there has never been a time when one person has existed without the other. The economic Trinity on the other hand focuses on what God does. In other words, it helps us understand how the three persons relate to each other. This view describes the roles each person has. An example of this is seen when the Father sends the Son into the world. The Son obeys the Father and accomplishes salvation. When then the Holy Spirit applies that salvation to believers. The Father has authority over the Son and the Spirit but is not because He is more powerful or more God like than they are. It is because of their roles to one another. These two views are similar because they both describe the same God and affirm that the Father, Son and Spirit are one. However both are different in respects to the ontological Trinity explains God's being while the economic Trinity explains his actions and relationships.

The scriptures show that God is our Father in three different but important ways which are as a creator, as a king, and as the head of His family. First let's look at how God is a father because He is the creator. According to the Word, God is the creator of everything. Just as a human father gives life to his children, God gave life to the world and to everyone in it. The Word says that from one man God made al nations and gave them places to live. This means that everyone is God's child because we come from Him. Like a good father God cares about what he has created and shows patience and mercy towards people even when they turn away from him. Secondly let's look at God the father as the King. In the ancient times, the kings were called the fathers of their people because they were supposed to protect and provide for them. God is the perfect royal Father because He rules from heaven defending His people and defeating their enemies. Jesus also taught His disciples to pray to "Our Father in heaven" which also serves as a reminder to the fatherhood of God as the King. Last but not least, God as the head of His family. The Bible calls us believers His children and describes the church as His household. Similar to loving parents, God guides us, provides for us, and disciplines us so that we may continue to grow in faith and become who He wants us to be for His glory and purpose.

God's authority over creation as absolute, exclusive, and exhaustive help explain just how complete His rule is. First let's discuss how God's authority is absolute. This means that there is no limits to His power or control. He has made everything by His words including everything in heaven and on earth. Because of this, everything belongs to Him. Nothing can stop God from doing what He has planned. This was very clear in the scriptures. You can see many examples of where He clam the storms, raise the dead, and even changed the hearts of kings. God authority is not shared with anyone and no one can overrule Him. Second we see that God's authority is exclusive. This means that He has the right to rule creation. There is no one that can claim to be the Lord of the universe. There are many other false gods, spirits, and idols but they have no authority. Most if not all of these so called gods are still under God's power. Last but not least you see that God's authority is exhaustive. This means that it covers every part of creation. There is no place, no situation, no moment in time that is outside of His control. From the largest galaxy to the smallest detail of our life we can have assurance that God is in charge of it all. Even if things happen to us that may feel as if they are random or accidental, they are all under God's sovereign will. With all of these truths in minds, we can be at peace knowing that everything is in God's hands. This should also give us the confidence that his plans will always come to pass.

Whenever the Bible uses the term or call Jesus the "Son of God" it means that Jesus has a very special and very unique relationship with God. You can see in different parts of the Bible when the words "Son of God" is used, it also refers to angels, kings, or even believers. For these examples, it just means that they belong to God or that they were chosen for something special or important. However, when the title is used for Jesus it's different. It means so much more. Jesus is not just close to God but rather He is actually God's eternal Son. He has always existed with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. That makes Jesus equal with God. He has the same power, wisdom, love, and holiness as God the Father. The scriptures goes further and shows us this in two distinct ways. The first is that Jesus is fully God, the same as the Father and the Spirit. Secondly, it explains that Jesus took on a role where He chose to obey the father to save the world. Don't misunderstand this by thinking that it makes Jesus less than God, on the contrary it shows the Father, Son, and Spirit work together but have different roles.

Whenever the Bible calls Jesus "Lord" it is showing that He is truly God. In the Greek language, the word "Kurios" is used in reference to "Lord." This means master, ruler, or someone with authority. However, when you look at the Old Testament whenever the Jewish scholars translated God's name "Yahweh" into Greek, they used the same word "Kurios." So what this tells us is that when the New Testament calls Jesus "Lord" it is not just for the sake of saying that he is a respected teacher or even a leader but rather that He is equal to God. Calling Jesus "Lord" shows that He has authority over all people and all creation. It means that He rules as King and is worthy of worship like God the Father. We pray to Jesus and worship Him because we believe that He is divine. If Jesus was only a man then it would be wrong to worship Him, but because He is God, this makes it right. The title of "Lord" also shows that Jesus is the one who saves His people. You can see in the Old Testament that God is the one who redeems His people from sin as well as from slavery. In the New Testament you can see that Jesus takes on this role. By calling Him "Lord" the writers of the Bible makes it clear that Jesus is the same God who has the power to forgive sins as well as bring salvation.

This life of Jesus shows many clear signs of how He was truly human. This was not the case of God just appearing in disguise. Let's first look at His birth. Yes He was conceived by the Holy Spirit but He was born as a baby by the Virgin Mary.  Even though His birth was a miracle, He still grew inside Mary's womb just like every other baby. He did not just magically appear but rather he went through the normal process of being born. Secondly, Jesus had a real human body. He grew up from that baby to an adult. He ate food, got tired, and even felt pain. He could bleed, suffer, and eventually die. All of which are the same things that normal humans go through. The Apostles Creed even mentions that He was crucified, died and was buried. All of these experiences are only possible if He has a real physical body. Next you can see that Jesus had a human soul. Just like everyone else, Jesus had emotions, thoughts, and a spirit. While Jesus was on the cross He prayed to God the father and gave up His spirit. this shows that His inner life was truly human as well. Last looking at his resurrection, this proves His humanity. When He rose from the dead, it just wasn't a spirit that was floating away but rather it was His real human body that was raised and reunited with His soul. You can even see where he showed his disciples his wounds and even at food with them after rising from the dead. This proves that He was a real man. All of these experiences, the birth, body, soul, suffering, death, and resurrection, shows that Jesus was fully human.

Often times there are many who misunderstand the word "Christ" and think that it is the last name of Jesus. This is not the case. The word "Christ" is a title. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word Messiah and the Greek word Christos both mean anointed one. This title was given to people who were chosen by God for a special job. You can see throughout scriptures that kings, priests and prophets were sometimes anointed with oil to show that God had set them apart to lead, serve, and guide His people. The Old Testament also promised a future great king who is a descendant of King David. This king would be the "Anointed One" or the Messiah. This messiah would rule with justice, save God's people and bring peace to the world. Israel waited and hoped for this Messiah for hundreds of years. Jesus fulfills this office in every way. He is the true Christ and the Messiah that the Old Testament points to. As a descendant of David, Jesus is the rightful King. As a priest, Jesus offered Himself as the perfect sacrifice to pay for our sins and still represents us before God. As a prophet, Jesus revealed God's truth very clearly by teaching people about God's Kingdom and how to live in it. Jesus fulfilled all of these roles, prophet, priest, and king. This shows us that Jesus is the Christ. He is not just another leader or another teacher but rather He is the one that God has promised to send, the Messiah.

Jesus is unique because he has two natures. You see that he is fully human and he is fully divine at the same time. This idea is called hypostatic union. This means that in one person Jesus has both a human nature and a divine nature. The human nature of Jesus was just like us in many ways. He had a real body that had the same types of experiences that we do as well. For example he could get hungry, tired, and feel pain. He had a mind that could learn and grow and he also experienced emotions like job, sadness, and compassion. He suffered and died as well. All of which humans can do. This shows us that Jesus was truly one of us and that He shared in our struggles and because of this He is able to relate and understand what we are going through. Now at the same time He is also divine in nature. This means that He is God. He has all the attributes of God. He is eternal, all powerful, holy, and perfect. Because He had all of these attributes, he could do things that no other person was able to do. Examples of this are found throughout scripture where He preformed miracles, forgave sins, and rose from the dead. What is important is that both of these natures are not mixed together. Jesus is not half of a God or half of a man but rather he is fully God and fully man at the same time. His human nature and His divine nature remain distinct and are united perfectly in one person. This means that Jesus can bridge the gap between God and humanity. As God, Jesus has the power to save us at the same time, as man He can represent us before God.

The Apostles' Creed affirms the Holy Spirit's divinity in an indirect manner. You can see in the Apostles' Creed where it says, "I believe in the Holy Spirit." Even though it may appear brief it has a very powerful meaning. The Apostles Creed is written in three main sections. It covers God the Father, Jesus the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This Trinitatian structure shows that the Holy Spirit is placed on the same level as the Father and the Son. By doing so, the Apostles' Creed treats the Holy Spirit as fully divine and not as a lesser being or anything of that nature. The Creed also mentions that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit. This can be found in the Gospel specifically in Luke where the angel tells Mary the power of the Most High will come upon her. That power mentioned is God's alone. When the Holy Spirit performs this miracle, it shows that He shares God's divine power and nature. The Bible itself also calls the Spirit by divine names like "Spirit of God" and "Spirit of Christ." You can see that this credits the Holy Spirit with divine works such as creating the world, inspiring Scripture and renewing believers' hearts. The Spirit's divinity is not only shown in two main ways by first its Trinitarian structure which places Him equally with the Father and Son and by describing His role in conception of Jesus, an act only God could perform. Together these truths affirm that the Holy Spirit is not just a helper or some kind of influence but rather is truly God Himself.

The Apostles' Creed teaches us that the Holy Spirit is fully God. This belief comes directly from the Bible. You see the Apostolic Creed by itself is not meant to replace the Word of God but rather what it does is summarizes what the Bible already says about the Holy Spirit's divine nature. The Word shows the Spirit's divinity through His names, characteristics, and actions. You can see throughout Scripture the different names of the Holy Spirit. The Bible reveals who He is. He is called the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Lord, the Spirit of Christ, and the Spirit of the Living God. These titles show that the spirit is not separate from God but one with Him. You can also see an example in the Book of Acts where Peter was telling Ananias that lying the Holy Spirit is the same as lying to God. This makes it very clear that the Holy Spirit is God. Next the Bible gives the Holy Spirit divine qualities that only God can have. You see throughout Scripture where it mentions that He is eternal, meaning He has no beginning or end. He is all knowing meaning he understands even the deepest thoughts of God. He is also all powerful and present everywhere. The Holy Spirit's work also reveal His divinity. He took part in the creation of the world, giving life to all living things, inspiring the writers of the Bible, and changing people's hearts by bringing them to faith in Jesus. These are examples of thing that God can only do.

The Bible shows us clearly that the Holy Spirit is not just a spiritual force or some kind of an energy but rather a real person with a mind, a personal will, and real emotions. He speaks, as well as teaches and guides and shows love. This shows that He has personal qualities that only a living being can have. These traits reveal that the Holy Spirit is a divine person and not just a power or symbol of God's presence. An example of this can be found in 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 where the Word says the Spirit "searches all things, even the deep things of God." This helps us see that the Holy Spirit has intelligence and understanding. This means that He knows and understands the thoughts of God perfectly which no created being could ever do. He also teaches believers spiritual truth reminding them of what Jesus said. This shows actions of a thinking person where the Spirit has knowledge and communicates it to others. You can also see where the Spirit also has a will. In 1 Corinthians 12:11 it goes on to say that the Spirit gives different spiritual gifts to believers "just as He wills." This means that the Holy Spirit makes decisions based on the purpose and wisdom He has which goes on to prove that He acts intentionally. Another example you can find is in Ephesians 4:30 where the Holy Spirit is showing emotions. Here we can see where Christians are warned not to "grieve the Holy Spirit." This shows that the Holy Spirit can feel sorrow when the people sin or reject God's ways. On the other hand you can see in Romans 15:30 where Paul speaks of the "love of the Spirit." This shows that the Spirit feels and expresses love towards believers. Lastly were can see where the Spirit takes personal actions as He guides people, intercedes for them in prayer, speaks to believers, and calls people to serve. Again these actions are that only a person can accomplish and not that of some being of energy or power.

The Bible teaches that God is one in essence but exists in three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These three persons are equal in power, glory, and divinity. Even though they are equal they are distinct from one another in their roles and in their relationships. The Holy Spirit is fully God just like the Father and the Son but He is also a unique person within the Trinity. You can see specifically that the Holy Spirit is distinct in His identity. As stated clearly in John 14:16-17, the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, and the Spirit is not the Father. Jesus said that the Father would send another Helper. He was referring to the Holy Spirit as the another person. The Spirit is the one who will continue the work of Jesus among His believers. Next you can see that the Spirit is distinct in His roles and in His functions. You can see in the Scripture that each person of the Trinity carries out specific works. The Father plans and sends while the Son accomplishes redemption through His life, death and resurrection. The Holy Spirit now has a role that applies that salvation to the believers by giving them faith, transforming their hearts, and guiding them in truth. In addition to this the Spirit intercedes for believers by speaking to God the Father on their behalf. This clearly shows the interaction between distinct persons. Lastly we can see that the Spirit is distinct in relationship. In the "Economic Trinity" where it describes how the persons of God work tother, the Spirit carries out the will of the Father and of the Son however in the "Ontological Trinity" all three are equal in being and in glory.

The relationship of the Holy Spirit to that of the Father and the Son is shown in unity and cooperation within the Trinity. The Trinity means that God exists as one divine being in three equal and eternal persons. These persons are as the Father the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Each of these persons is fully God while still sharing the same divine nature but yet they are still distinct in their roles and relationships. Looking into their relationships, you can see that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are completely equal in power and in glory but they relate in different ways. Starting with the Father, He is often seen as the source or the origin. He sends the Son into the world and later sends the Spirit. The Son in turn willingly obeys the Father and accomplishes the work of salvation through His life, death, and His resurrection, The Holy Spirit's role here is to carry out and apply the will of the Father and the work of the Son. The Spirit brings God's presence to believers and gives them a new spiritual life and even guides them in the truth. You can see in John 15:26 where Jesus describes this relationship where "When the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, He will testify about Me." This shows us that the Spirit comes from both the Father as well as the Son. Not only that but it also shows that the Spirit works to glorify them as well. You can also see in Romans 8:9-11 where it explains that the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ dwells in believers. This shows the unity and the harmony that is between all three persons. Even though the Holy Spirit is called the third person of the Trinity, it does not mean that He is any less important. Rather on the other hand it shows the traditional order in how God's work is revealed. The Father is usually mentioned first as the sender, next is the Son as the Savior, and then comes the Holy Spirit as the one who applies God's power and presence to believers. The relationship here to the Father and the Son is that of quarry divinity and shared purpose with a distinct role.

The church in the New Testament grew out of God's people in the Old Testament. It was not something new that was created. God had chosen Israel to be His special people. They worshiped Him, as well as followed His commands, and lived as an example to other nations. They were called an assembly which is similar to the word church. This shows us that God has always had a group of people set apart for His purpose. When Jesus came into the world, He didn't start a completely different group of people but rather He continued and completed what God had already begun with Israel. Jesus spoke about building His church. What he ment by this is that He would restore and strengthen God's people. You can see that the apostles also showed this connection as well. An example of this is where they used Old Testament titles like holy nation and royal priesthood to describe Christians. The purpose also were the same. You can see in the Old Testament that Israel was called to love God as well as obey him and to be a light to the world. Throughout the New Testament the church can be seen receiving the same calling by preaching the gospel, living holy lives, and the mission to spread God's Kingdom. Paul goes on to explain that the believers from all the nations are like branches added to Israel's tree. This is showing that the church shares the same roots as well as the same promises. In this manner, the New Testament church is not a. separate story but rather the next chapter.

Jesus built His church by continuing what God started in the Old Testament. He didn't stop there but rather He went on to bring it to its full purpose. In the Old Testament God formed a covenant people who were Israel. They were chosen and set apart to worship Him and represent His kingdom on the earth. They had leaders, laws, worship, and a mission. However, over time, you can see throughout scripture that they failed to live faithfully. Jesus didn't come to destroy this foundation but rather He came to complete it and restore it. First you can see where Jesus relied on the Old Testament church by honoring its teachings, traditions, and scriptures. He worshiped in the synagogues and taught from the law and from the prophets. He went on to affirm God's covenant with Israel. He also choose 12 disciples which symbolizing the 12 tribes of Israel. He not only did this but he also advanced the church beyond its Old Testament form. How was this possible? He fulfilled the prophecies about the Messiah and offered salvation not just to the Jews but also to all nations. Even though Israel was just one nation, Jesus opened the covenant to everyone who believed in Him. He gave new authority to the church saying that I will build my church and the powers of death could not defeat it. He went even further by sending the Holy Spirit. Unlike the Old Testament where the Spirit only came to certain leaders, here in the New Testament the Spirit was for all believers which empowered them to spread the gospel across the world.

The relationship between the Old Testament and the New Testament church carries several important implications. First you can see that it shows that God has one continuous plan for His people. The church as not some last minute ideas that began in the New Testament but rather a continuation of God's covenant that started with Israel in the Old Testament. What this basically shows us is that Christians are a part of the story that began with Abraham, Moses, and the prophets. Secondly we can see where this continuity reminds us that the church has a clear purpose, which is to spread God's kingdom. In the Old Testament, Israel was called to be a light to the nations, in addition to that also showing God's truth through obedience and worship. You can see similarly in the New Testament where the church carries the same mission by preaching the gospel and to living out the love of Christ. Thirdly you can see that both the Old and New Testament communities have a mix of believers and unbelievers. Just as Israel has faithful people as well as people who decided to turn away from God, you see the in today's church as well. There are plenty of people who may appear religious but lack true faith. This is important because it shows us that we must continue to preach the gospel within the church and to examine our hearts. Lastly you can see Israel's ongoing obligation and commitment to love God, obey His laws, and glorify Him. The New Testament church has these same responsibilities.

You can see in the Apostles Creed that is uses the word catholic. You may think it refers to the Roman Catholic Church but it does not. It comes from the Greek word which means "universal." When Christians refer to using this word by saying that they believe in the "Holy Catholic Church," what they mean is that they believe in the universal church made up of all true believers in Jesus across every place and time. In the earliest centuries of Christianity, churches were spread across different regions, cultures, as well as many different languages. They did not all look the same or even share the same leadership but they were united by one faith. The word Catholic was used to remind believers that the church is bigger than any single local congregation or denomination. It includes all who choose to follow Jesus sincerely. No matter where you are whether it be a large city, small village or even in secret. This idea is inclusive not exclusive. This means that any church holding to the core truths of the Christian faith is part of the one true church. Churches may have different traditions or different customs but they are still united together with Christ as the Head.

The visible Catholic Church refers to all the congregations around the world that outwardly professes faith in Jesus and gather together in His name. It is called visible because it can be seen through the gatherings, worship, teaching, sacraments, as well as the church life. This will of course include all the different denominations and traditions as long as they acknowledge Christ as Lord and follow the core teachings of Christianity. There are three key signs that Christians have traditionally looked for to decide whether or not the church should be embraced as part of the universal church. This is called the marks of the true church. The first mark is faithful preaching of God's word. A true church teaches the Bible accurately especially the message of salvation through Jesus Christ. It does not deny essential truths like the Trinity, the divinity of Jesus, or the resurrection. The second mark is the right administration of the sacraments. A true church practices baptism as well as the Lord's Supper in a biblical way. The third mark is the practice of church discipline. This is where the true church takes holiness seriously. It corrects serious sin and encourages repentance. It also seeks to protect the community from false teaching and harmful behavior. If the church in question holds to these core practices and beliefs. it should be recognized as part of the wider body of Church even if it differs in worship style, culture, or secondary doctrines. There are two extremes that are present that believers must recognize to avoid. The first is accepting every group that simply calls themselves as Christians and secondly rejecting all church except our own.

The problem with sin is that it separates us from God and it brings His judgement on all of humanity. Sin isn't just doing something bad but rather it is disobeying God and breaking His law. You can find this in the scriptures as "lawlessness" meaning that it goes against what God says is right. Whenever we sin, we choose our own way instead of God's way. What this does is break our relationship with God because He is holy and perfect. Because of this, He is not able to just ignore sin. Sin is the reason that people feel guilt, shame, and spiritual emptiness. Essentially it is the case of all the brokenness in the world. Sin originated from the Fall. This is were Adam and Eve disobeyed God int he Garden of Eden. God told them that they could eat from any tree expect one but they instead decided to listen to the serpent's temptation and ate the fruit anyway. By doing this they chose to rebel against God. Because of this act of disobedience, it brought sin into the whole human race. From that point on, every person has been born with a sinful nature. The consequences that is associated with sin is essentially death. Spiritual death is being separated from God. In addition to this, it also brings corruption which affects both our hearts and our bodies. This in return leads to pain, sickness, and selfishness. Because of sin, physical death became a part of life and people also face the danger of eternal separation from God after death. Sin just ruined the good relationship people once had with God and it affects every part of life. Because of this is why we all need God's grace and forgiveness through Jesus.

To begin, divine grade is the free gift of forgiveness and salvation which involves all three persons of the Trinity. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit though all have different roles, they all work together in unity to show God's love as well as His mercy and desire to save humanity from sin. Starting with God the Father, you can see that He is the source of divine grace. The Father is the one who planned salvation from the beginning. Out of His deep love for us, He chose to send His Son, Jesus to redeem the world. The Father didn't act out of anger but rather out of compassion. He wanted to restore the broken relationship between Himself and His creation. His plan shows that grace starts with God's initiative and not any of our efforts. We cannot ever earn forgiveness. This is the reason why God the Father provided a way through His Son Jesus. God the Son, Jesus Christ carried out that plan. Jesus stepped into this world as both fully God and fully man to accomplish what was never done. He lived a perfect life without sin and died as a sacrifice for the sins of humanity. He took it upon himself to endure the punishment that we deserved and made forgiveness possible for everyone who believes in Him. Through His resurrection, Jesus conquered death and opened the door to eternal life. He was not done quite yet. God sends the Holy Spirit next. The Holy Spirit helps people understand the truth about God, feel genuine sorrow for sin, and believe in Jesus. After one accepts Jesus, the Holy Spirit continues to live in them and helps them by guiding, teaching, and strengthening their faith.

Individual responsibilities plays a very important role in the forgiveness of sins. Even though forgiveness is a free gift from God, it requires a personal response from each person. God will offer His grace to everyone but it is up to us to choose to respond with faith, repentance, and a humble heart. The scripture teaches us two main conditions that are needed for forgiveness which are faith and brokenness. Faith means believing and trusting in God as well as his power, trusting in His mercy, as well as submitting to His will. It is about truly depending on Him and believing that Jesus died to save us. Brokenness means that being truly sorry for our sins. Don't get it mistaken, it's not about just feeling bad because we got caught but rather because we know we have disobeyed God. It's about realizing that sin hurts our relationship with God and us wanting to change. Whenever we admit our wrongs and come to God with a sincere heart, He is ready to forgive us. God has also provided ways for us to receive forgiveness. Some of the main ways is through prayer, faith, and the sacraments. Prayer is how we confess our sins and ask for forgiveness. Whenever we pray honestly and with faith, God cleanses our hearts and restores our relationship with Him. There are also times where prayers that are made on behalf of others, also called intercessory prayers, can also bring forgiveness and healing. Lastly the sacraments such as baptism and the Lord's Supper reminds us of what Jesus did for us and it also helps us experience His grace again. Forgiveness depends on God's mercy but each one of us have the responsibility to respond. Through faith, repentance, and prayer, we open our hearts to receive the forgiveness that God has freely given through the price that was paid by Jesus.

When humanity fell into sin it affected every part of our lives not just our souls but also our bodies. Before sin came into the picture, God created humans perfect and good. You can see in scriptures where Adam and Eve lived in harmony with God, with each other and with the rest of creation. They were essentially free from death, pain, and suffering. However that all changed when they disobeyed God int he Garden of Eden. Their sin not only broke their spiritual connections with God but also brought physical corruption and death into the world. The fall into sin first corrupted our souls. We are all spiritually dead, which means that we are separated from God. Our thoughts, desires, and emotions are no longer pure. People began to struggle with selfishness, pride, fear, and guilt. The image of God that was in us was damaged. Instead of naturally desiring to obey God, we because drawn to disobedience and rebellion. This spiritual corruption is what the scriptures call the sinful nature. It didn't stop there, sin when on to affect our bodies as well. When Adam and Eve sinned, God's curse included pain, sickness, and eventually death. The body which was once perfect and free from decay, began to age, weaken, and eventually die. Disease, suffering, and physical imperfections all came into the procure because of sin's entrance into the world. Even nature became broken and out of balance.

Bodily redemption is part of God's plan to heal and restore humanity. It does not just apply to the spiritual side of things but to the physical as well. When sin entered the world, both our souls as well as our bodies because corrupted. This brought in pain, sickness, and death. However through Jesus, God promised full redemption. This will occur in three main stages, renewal in this life, peace after death, and complete restoration at the resurrection. The first stage of the bodily redemption because in this life when a person puts their faith in Jesus. When this occurs, the Holy Spirit comes to live within them and brings new spiritual life. Even though our physical bodies still experience weakness, aging, and sickness here we see God slowly starting to change our hearts. The Spirit helps us resist sin and gives us strength to follow God's will. At this point, our physical suffering may not go but it helps bring hope that our pain and struggles are only temporary. It helps us start a lifelong transformation that prepares us for eternity. The second stage happens after death. When a believer dies their body remains in the grave but their soul goes to be with God. In this state, the soul is freed from sin, pain, and fear. Believers experience comfort and joy in God's presence while waiting for the day when their bodies will be raised again.The last stage will happen when Jesus returns. This is when God will raise the dead and give believers new glorified bodies. These bodies will never grow old, get sick, or die. They will be perfect and eternal in addition to completely being free from the effects of sin.

Christian ethics focuses on mainly and solely on God and His blessings by focusing on all moral understanding in who God is and what He has done for humanity. We tend to base things on right and wrong on human reasonings and cultural standards but rather Christian ethics begins with the belief that God is the ultimate source of truth, goodness, and authority. This means that ethical behavior is not just about following a set of rules but rather its about living in a way that would reflect God's character. Since God is holy, loving, and just we are called to act in ways that would mirror those same qualities in our lives. The blessings of God also play a central role as well. The Christian life is not motivated by the fear of being punished but rather it is full of gratitude for God's grace and the blessings that He provides. These blessings include salvation through Jesus, the guidance of the Holy Spirit and the promise of eternal life. Because of all of this, we as Christians are inspired to live ethically. We are not here to earn God favor but rather live in a way that shows thankfulness for His generosity. When you look at it this way, through your obedience it becomes an act of worship and moral living. We start to understand that God's moral laws is designed for human flourishing. God's commands are not burdensome restrictions but rather it is a blessing that is meant to bring peace, justice, and harmony. When we decide to follow His will, we start to experience the fullness of life that comes from living according to divine wisdom.

A proper motive is significant in Christian ethics because God not only cares about what people do but also why they choose to do it. You see, actions alone do not define righteousness but rather the heart and the intent behind those actions determine their true moral value. A person might do a good deed such as helping the poor, donating, attending church, etc. but if it is done for selfish reasons like praise, recognition, or guilt it looses its spiritual worth. While we may look at these actions, God looks beyond the outward behavior and judges the inner motives. The reason for this is because genuine righteousness comes from love and faith not from obligation or personal gain. Christian ethics emphasizes integrity of heart as much as obedience in action. Proper motives are those that align with God's character and His purpose. It comes down to the love you have for God and the love you have for others. Jesus taught that all the commandments come from these two principles. When we act out of love for God, we should desire to please Him, reflect His goodness and express gratitude for His blessings. At the same time, when we act to show love for others, we show compassion, kindness, and humility, seeking the well being of others before ourselves. Proper motives comes from a heart that is transformed by God's grace. We are not called to act out of fear, pride, or duty alone but rather out of sincere devotion to God. Whenever motives are pure, actions become an expression of worship and ethical living becomes a joyful response to God's love rather than a burdensome task.

The threefold criteria for good works in Christian ethics teaches us that a truly good action must meet three key standards. These are as follows; the right standard, the right motive, and the right goal. Each of these works together to make sure that an action is pleasing to God and not just outwardly good by human standards. The first criteria is the right standard. This means that good works must be based on God's revealed will. Christians do not need to determine what is right and wrong by personal opinion, cultural trends or even by emotions but rather by Scripture. The Bible provides the moral foundation for all ethical behavior because it shows us God's commands and it also reflects on His perfect character. Actions that ignore or are contradicting to God's Word can't be considered good even if it may appear to be noble to others. The second criteria is the right motive. Even if someone appears to obey God's commands outwardly, their actions are not truly good unless they come from a sincere heart of love and faith. You see, God looks at the inner reasons behind what we do. That is why proper motives come from gratitude from God's grace, love that we have for Him, and a deep desire to worship Him in everything that we do. Acts done for selfish reasons such as pride, fear of punishment, or the desire for approval all fall short of this. The last criteria is the right goal. This focuses on glorifying God. The ultimate purpose of every good work is not personal benefit or social recognition but rather it is honoring God and advancing His kingdom. When Christians have this goal in mind, the works that are done reflect His character and as a result it will point others to Christ.

The three perspectives that you must keep in mind when considering ethics are the normative, situational, and the existential perspectives. Each one of these are designed to help believers see moral decisions from a different but complementary angle. This helps give a fuller and more balanced understanding of what it means to live righteously before God. Together they show that Christian ethics involves not only knowing God's standard but also applying them wisely and sincerely in real life. Starting with the normative perspective, it focuses on God's law and his commands as the standard for right and wrong. Here we can see the questions being asked, "What does God say?" or "What rules or principles apply here?" This perspective helps remind us that moral truth comes from God's revealed Word and not from our reasonings or emotions. The Bible sets the standard for ethical living because it expresses the character of God and His will. The second perspective is the situational perspective. This perspective considers the circumstances and the results of an action. The questions one might ask here is "What are the outcomes or effects of this choice?" or "How can I best show love in this situation?" Here we see this perspective emphasize wisdom and discernment. This helps us understand how to apply God's commands appropriately in different context. The Bible gives us unchanging principles even though we may encounter situations in life that are diverse and complex. We as believers must thoughtfully evaluate how to act in ways that show God's intended good. The last perspective deals with the heart and the person that is making the decision. The questions that come here are "What kind of person am I becoming?" or "Am I acting out of faith and love?" This perspective focuses on motives, integrity and spiritual maturity. Ethics is not only about external actions but rather it is also about inner transformation.

God serves as the absolute judge of morality because He is the Creator, the Lawgiver, and the ultimate standard of what is right and wrong. Since God made the world and everything in it, all moral truth comes from Him. His character defines what is goodness, justice, and love. Unlike human standards which change over time and also differ from culture to culture, God's standards are perfect and unchanging because they reflect who He is. What this means is that morality is not something that people can invent or decide for themselves but rather it is something God has revealed and continues to uphold through His Word. God has the final and absolute authority to declare what is right and wrong. His commandments that are given in the Scriptures are not suggestions but rather what is expected of His righteous will. They are based on His wisdom and holiness showing humanity how to live in harmony with Him and with one another. Because God knows all things perfectly, His judgements are always fair. He not only sees people's actions but also their motives and thoughts. What this means is that His evaluation of morality goes deeper than any human judgment. God also serves as the final judge who holds everyone accountable for their actions. At the end times He will judge all people according to His perfect standards. This should remind us all that ethical living is not just about pleasing others but rather its about honoring God. In other words, God is the absolute judge of morality because He is the source, standard, and the enforcer of all moral truth. His perfect character guarantees that His judgment are just and His authority is final.

The three categories of revelation that are part of God's Word are decrees, commands, and works. Each of these forms of revelation communicates God's truth in a very unique way. It helps believers understand His will and character. First looking at God's decree, this refers to His eternal plans and purpose. This is showing us what He has determined will happen throughout history. This decrees reveal God's sovereignty and control over all things. From creation to redemption, everything happens according to His divine plan. An example of this is where God decreed the salvation of His people through Jesus Christ before the world was made. By studying God's decrees, we can learn that He is all powerful, wise and faithful. This helps remind us that nothing happens by chance and everything serves His divine purpose. Secondly we can see God's commands. These are God's moral instructions that He gives His people. These include the laws, principles, as well as teachings. God's commands show us that His holiness and how to live in a way that would honor Him. They tell us what is right and wrong as well as what is good and evil. Examples of this can be found with the Ten Commandments as well as the teachings of Jesus. Lastly we see God's works. Here we find God's actions in creation, providence, and redemption. Everything God has done from the beauty of the world that He created, the order of the universe, and not to mention the work of Jesus providing us salvation, all shows us God's glory and His goodness.

Existential revelation teaches us about God's standard by showing that His truth is in our hearts and we experience it personally in our everyday lives. This means that God does not only reveal His standards through the Bible or the world around us but rather through our inner sense of right and wrong. Because we are all created in the image of God, each one of us has a conscience that helps us recognize good and evil. When we feel joy for doing what is right or guilt for what we do wrong, it shows us that God's moral law is active within us. This inner voice helps remind us that God's standard is not just a set of rules but rather it is part of who we are in Him. Even though sin can cloud our understanding and lead us to ignore God's truth, our conscience will continue to point us back on the right track. For the ones who follow Christ, this becomes even stronger because the Holy Spirit works within our hearts. It helps us understand God's Word by convicting us when we disobey and guides us toward a life that is pleasing to God. Instead of just obeying to follow rules, we learn to do what is right out of love and faith.

In 1 John 1:7 it says, "But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin." What this shows us is that our obligation to obey God's standard is closely tied to our forgiveness in Christ. The reason for this is because both come from the same source. Walking "in the light" means living according to God's truth. We do this by showing that we have truly been forgiven and transformed by Christ. John also points out that obedience is not what earns forgiveness but rather it is the natural result from being forgiven. Once you have received salvation, your heart as well as your desires begin to change. You no longer live for yourself but rather you start to live for God. Obedience becomes an expression of gratitude and love, not a way to gain acceptance. It shows that a person's faith is real and that they are living in fellowship with God. Forgiveness in Christ removes the barrier of sin that once separated us from God. When our relationship is restored we are called to live in the light. You can see here where John links obedience and forgiveness as two parts of the same. For those of us who are forgiven will seek to obey and those who obey have been forgiven and made new through Christ.

The Bible teaches us that it has divine authority because of the fact that it is not just the work of human authors but rather it is the Word of God Himself. You can see this in 2 Timothy 3:16 where Paul writes that "All Scripture is God breathed..." This means that God inspired the human writers so that every word reflects God's truth and His purpose. Because of this, it makes the Scriptures completely trustworthy. God cannot lie or make any mistakes. The Bible holds a unique place among all writings. It stands as the ultimate source of truth and moral guidance. Since it comes from God himself, it carries His authority and not just human opinion or cultural wisdom. The implications of this are very important for how we live and think. You see if the scriptures truly speaks with God's authority, then we must approach it with humility and with obedience. It's not something that we can debate or try to adjust to fit our modern preferences. Rather it is the standard by which everything should be measured. Secondly, the authority of the scriptures gives us confidence and stability in a changing world. We all know that human ideas, governments, and even cultures rise and fall but the Word of God remains firm and unchanging. It tells us what is right and wrong, what is true and false, despite the fact that everything of the world's values may change. If we understand this, we have to study the Word thoughtfully and seek to understand its true meaning and apply it faithfully in our lives.

When it comes to making ethical decisions, we benefit from understanding the characteristics of Scripture because it gives us a solid and a dependable foundation to stand on. The Bible isn't just another book filled with human thoughts or moral lessons but rather it is the inspired Word of God. This means that every word in Scripture comes from God Himself, who used human writers to communicate His truth. When we read the Bible, we are hearing God's wisdom and not just human opinions. The Scriptures are also authoritative. This means that it carries ultimate power over our lives. It tells us what is right and what is wrong. It also teaches us the truth that outweighs our personal feelings, our traditions, or even cultural trends. Whenever we recognize this authority, we start to learn to base our moral choices on what God says rather than what we think society accepts. This will help us keep grounded when the world's stands keep changing all the time. Thirdly the Scripture is sufficient. The Bible gives us all the knowledge we need to live in a way that honors God. It will not cover every single issue directly but rather it provides principles that help us make better, wiser, and faithful decisions in any situation. Last but not least, the Scripture is clear and unified. You can see from the beginning to the end, its message points us to love God and to love others. It does not contradict itself or allow us to be in a confused state. When we start to understand the qualities of God's Word, we can approach every moral decision with humility, confidence, and peace. We start to understand that we are not left along to just figure things out but rather God has already given us everything we would need.

The Scripture helps us become more like God by showing us who He is and what He cares about. The Bible isn't just a list of rules but rather it is a message from God that reveals His heart and His desires for His people. We can see this through the stories, instructions, and the promises all throughout the Word. We learn about God's love, His mercy, justice, and holiness. As we dive deep and study the Scriptures, we begin to understand what is pleasing to God and what isn't. The Word gives us a clear picture of God's character and it helps us see how we can reflect that character in our own lives. One of the biggest ways that Scripture helps us grow is by changing how we think. We see in Romans 12:2, "Be transformed by the renewing of your mind." This only happens when we read and start to apply God's Word in our lives. The more time we spend in Scripture, the more our thoughts start to align with God's truth instead of the world's opinions. It teaches us to see life through the lens of God. It helps us value what He values and to reject what goes against His will. The Bible acts like a mirror by showing us both our weakness and the areas where we need to grow. Whenever we face decisions, it reminds us of God's wisdom and it helps us choose what is right. In addition to this, Scripture also gives us the strength to live according to God's will. It continues to encourage us when we're tired and weak and corrects us when we are wrong. Not only that, it comforts us when we might be struggling as well. As we follow the examples of faithful men and women found in the Word and continue to trust in God, we being to change from the inside out. We start to love what God loves and hate what He hates.

In Romans 1:15-16, Paul says that he is eager to preach the Gospel because he is "not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes." Even though there were many people in his time that thought the message of Jesus's death and resurrection was foolish or weak, Paul knew that it was the only message that could really change lives. The Romans valued wisdom, strength, and status. To even think about the idea of a crucified Savior sounds ridiculous. However, Paul understood that what seems foolish to the world was actually the exact news they needed so desperately. The Gospel revealed God's plan to save humanity from sin and give eternal life through faith in Jesus. This is what Paul was compelled to preach because he himself had a personal encounter with God. Once a persecutor of Christians and being transformed by Jesus Himself, how can he keep quiet? That transformation gave him an unshakable confidence that the Gospel does work. It really does have the power to rescue people and change hearts. Paul wasn't motivated by fame or comfort but rather he preached because he loved God and wanted others to know the true God. Paul's example for us today reminds us not to be ashamed of our faith. Even though it may seem unpopular or mocked by the world, we must be bold and remain strong spreading the good news. Life Paul we are called to share it boldly trusting that God's power will work through His Word touching the hearts of the unbelievers.

The Bible is filled with many different kinds of languages because it was written by many different people, in different times, and for different purposes. Even though all of these factors are at play it is written all under the inspiration of God. You can see throughout Scripture there is poetry, stories, songs, letters, proverbs, laws, as well as prophecies. Each of this type of writing helps us understand God in a unique way. If you look at Psalms for example, it uses poetry and vivid imagery to express emotions like joy, fear, and sorrow. The historical books tells real stories of God's people to show His faithfulness. The Gospels share the life and teachings of Jesus through storytelling and dialogue. You can also see that Paul's letters use thoughtful reasonings to guide believers in their faith and in their moral living. This wide variety of language shows that God speaks to people in ways that touch both the mind and the heart. Some of these passages use extraordinary language such as visions, miracles, and prophecies. These are used to help reveal God's power. When Isaiah describes seeing the Lord on His throne or when John writes about heaven in Revelations, the language that is used helps us understand that it is beyond ordinary. It gives us a sense of God's greatness as well as mystery. At the same time, much of the Bible uses ordinary or everyday language. You can see that Jesus often spoke in parables about simple things like farmers planting seeds, and shepherds caring for sheep, or even the example of a father welcoming a lost son. 
All of these stories make a deep spiritual truth that anyone would be able to understand. By combining both the extraordinary and the ordinary language it allows us to be reminded that God's Word is both majestic and approachable. It reveals divine mysteries but at the same time also meets us in our daily needs.

The Ten Commandments are important both historically and theologically because they show how God has guided His people through time and revealed His moral standards for everyone. You can see historically that the Ten Commandments were given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai after the Israelites were freed from slavery in Egypt. This event was turning point for them because it marked the beginning of their life as a nation chosen and led by God. The commandments were more than just a set of rules but rather they were the foundation for how Israel were to live. They were written by God Himself on stone tablets showing that they were permanent and carried divine authority. These laws were placed in the Ark of the Covenant and kept in the center of Israel's worship. This helped remind them that obedience to God was at the heart of their identity. Theologically, the Ten Commandments reveal who God is and what He values. The first four commandments teaches us how to love and honor God by worshiping only Him and avoiding idols, respecting His name and keeping the Sabbath day holy. The last six teaches us how to treat others like honoring our parents, valuing life, being faithful in marriage, respecting others property, telling the truth, and being content with what we have. All of this together reflect God's character. If we look at it even today, the Ten Commandments are a guide for how to live a moral and faithful life. They remind us that doing what is right isn't about following just an empty set of rules but rather it's about loving God and as a result loving people.

You can see in the Old Testament that God's law is often understood in three traditional categories which are the moral law, civil law, and ceremonial law. Each of these types of laws have a special purpose. The moral law includes God's unchanging standard of right and wrong. Similar to those found in the Ten Commandments. These laws reflect God's character and apply to all people for all time. They teach us how to love God and how to love other. This is done by honoring our parents, speaking truth, avoiding theft, murder, and adultery and most of all worshiping only God. Even though we live under grace, the moral law still guides our behavior and shows us what pleases God. Next is the civil law. This was given specifically for ancient Israel as a nation. These laws governed daily life, justice, and social order. It handled issues with things like property rights, punishment for crimes, and rules about how to handle debts. While these specific laws don't necessarily apply to our present day, they still show God's concern for fairness, justice, and compassion. If you dive deeper, you can find principles that would help shape our views and how we treat others. The last is the ceremonial law. This specifically deals with worship sacrifices, rituals, festivals, and cleanliness. When Jesus came, He fulfilled these laws through His life and His sacrifice. We no longer have to follow these laws literally but they still teach us important truths about holiness, forgiveness, as well as God's desire for relationship with His people. If we can understand these three categories, we can wisely start to apply God's law today.

Even though it may seem a little confusing at first, the key idea to keep in mind is that the Old Testament civil and ceremonial laws have expired in their original form but their principles still apply today because they reveal God's character and His values. The civil laws were given specifically for the nation of Israel when it was both a religious and political community. These laws covered things like property rights, punishments, and community justice. Even though modern societies are not bound to follow these exact laws, the principles behind them such as fairness, honesty, justice and care for the vulnerable all reflect God's heart. We can still learn how God wants His people to act justly and how God wants us to treat others rightly. The ceremonial laws were about worship and sacrifice. These would include things like temple rituals, animal sacrifices, and purification practices that helped Israel stay in right standing with God. All of these laws were fulfilled by Jesus who because the ultimate sacrifice for sin. Because of Jesus, we do not need to offer sacrifices or follow those rituals anymore. However, the meaning behind them such as God's holiness as well as the seriousness of sin and the need for forgiveness all still applies to this day. So even though all of these laws may have expired because Jesus fulfilled their purpose, they still apply spiritually because they teach eternal truths about who God is and how we should live.

To make ethical decisions it requires understanding the situational content of God's revelation. What this means is that we must pay attention to what is happening around us and how God's truth speaks into that situation. There are three types of this situational content; facts, goals, and means. The first, facts, describe what is actually true in the situation that we face. This includes the people involved, the events that are taking place, as well as the responsibilities or the relationships that shape. At the same time, we must keep in mind the spiritual realities as well such as God is always present, always ruling, and always faithful to His people. When you are able to understand all of this, it helps see the situation more clearly and avoid making decisions based on fear or confusion. The second type of situational content is goals. This is the purpose or outcome that we are hoping for. God uses His revelation to teach us what goals we should be pursing. There will be many situations that seem complicated but God gives clarity through His Word by showing us what truly matters. The most important face we must remember is that our goals must be shaped by what God values and not by what feels good or convenient in the moment. The last is by means. This referee to the methods or the actions that we use to reach our goals. God doesn't just tell us what to aim for but rather he shows us the proper way to pursue those goals. We should not choose sinful or selfish methods but rather do it the right way. God cares not only about our goals but how we achieve them as well.

Facts are things that are very true in any situation. They can include what has happened in the past, who is involved, and what responsibilities we have. Facts are not just our feelings or our guesses. They are actually details that describe what is going on. Facts also include the spiritual truths that are found in God's Word. These are things that we could never figure out on our own such as God's character, His promises, and the truth that He is always present and in control. Knowing this is important because good decisions must be based on truth and not on any type of concussion or assumptions. If you and I were to misunderstand what is actually happening, we could make a wrong choice that might hurt someone or lead us away from what God would want us to do. Facts help us assess our situation more clearly. It keeps us from acting too quickly, over reacting, or even reacting with fear or anger. When we start to understand the real situation, we can make wiser and more responsible choices.
