Knowing important facts about God such as how God is loving, wise, powerful, and always with us helps us change the way we face our decisions. Knowing who God is gives us the courage to do what is right even when it might be very difficult. His promises remind us that obedience brings blessings. He controls everything and makes everything work together for our good. Knowing this helps bring us comfort and peace in any decision we make. Putting Him first in all thing will make our decisions just that much easier.

Goals are the purposes and the outcomes that we try to aim for whenever we make decisions. It is what we would like to accomplish or what we hope will happen because of our actions. Some goals are small and immediate such as fixing a problem, keeping peace with someone or finishing a task. Others are much bigger and long term such as building a strong family or growing in faith. Goals help give us direction to our choices. Without goals, we would just be reacting to life instead of making thoughtful and intentional decisions. Trying to understand biblical goals is very important because not every goal we want is good, wise, or even pleasing to God. Most of the time our desires are often shaped by comfort, fear, pride, or even the pressures around us. If we only consider what feels right in the moment then we will choose goals that will be either selfish or short sighted. However, God reveals goals that help us see what truly matters. God's Word teaches us that our highest purpose is to honor God, love our neighbor, and live in a way that reflects His character. When we start understanding these biblical goals, our decisions that we make become more clearer. Our questions will change from "What do I want right now?" to "What would honor God in this situation?" Biblical goals helps us see beyond our immediate emotions and start to think about the bigger picture of God's work in our lives. They also help us avoid choices that might seem helpful in the moment but later would lead to harm.

An overly rigorous approach to revelation happens whenever someone treats God's commands in a harsh, strict, or an overly literal way that actually goes beyond what God actually requires. This will more than often add extra rules, create heavy burdens, or even demand one correct answer in situations where the Bible allows freedom or requires wisdom. Instead of using God's revelation to guide and help share our decision, a rigorous approach turns it into a rigid system that leaves little room for prayer, judgment, or even grace. When you fall into this type of mindset you may believe that you are protecting obedience but more often than not you end up making God's law seem stricter than He made it. This in fact is very dangerous because it can distort God's character. When you add strict rules, we may start seeing God as harsh or demanding instead of wise, patient and loving. A rigorous mindset can make people feel full of guilt and fear because they will feel like they can never meet the impossible standards placed on them. It can create pride as well because people who keep the rules will feel superior or better than others. Instead of growing in wisdom, humility and faith you will be focused on strict rule keeping. This by all means can be avoided by remembering that God's revelation always points us to wisdom and love and not rigid legalism. Even though the Bible tells us to obey it also teaches us to use good judgment.

Jesus teaches us many different things throughout the Sermon on the Mount. There was one important theme that He spoke about as well which was the Kingdom of God. He describes what the kingdom is like, who belongs to it, and how people in the kingdom are called to live. In the first section you can see Jesus highlights the kingdom in the Beatitudes. He starts by describing the kind of people who receive God's blessing. You can see that He mentions twice "theirs is the kingdom of heave." This shows that the kingdom is not just something in the future but rather it has already belongs to those who follow Him. The Beatitudes shows us a picture of the kind of character that fits in God's kingdom. This helps remind us that God values the heart more than outward success. Secondly you can see Jesus emphasizing the kingdom when he teaches about righteousness and the law. He says that those who belong to the kingdom must have a righteousness that is deeper than that of the religious leaders. Instead of just obeying the rules outwardly, kingdoms people obey from the heart. They refuse anger, lust, dishonesty, and revenge. True righteousness comes from a transformed life. Living under God's rule means letting His character shape every part of our lives. Lastly you can see that Jesus spoke about the kingdom when He teaches about worry and priorities. He tells His listeners not to be anxious about food, clothing, or daily needs. Instead what we should do is not be controlled by fear. Jesus says to "seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness." When the kingdom becomes our first priority, God promises to take care of our needs.

The Kingdom of God has three main components that work together to help us see what life under God's rule is meant to be. These are God's rule, God's people, and God's place. The first component of God's rule is that the kingdom exists whenever God's authority is recognized and obeyed. God has always ruled over the wold but His kingdom becomes visible when people accept His rule in their hearts and live it out in their lives. This plays out practically when we trust Him and obey His commands, living the way He has called us to live. God's rule is the foundation of the kingdom. The second component is God's people. A kingdom must have citizens and God's kingdom is made up of those who belong to Him through faith. These are the people who hear God's voice and have a desire to live according to His will. They live out their lives to reflect His character. It is through these people that His kingdom become visible on earth. The third component is God's place. What this is in reference to is the environment where God's rule is displayed. You can see in the Old Testament that this place was the land God gave Israel. Likewise in the New Testament, the place of the kingdom expands to the whole world because God's presence is with His people wherever they go.

The outline of the historical developments of the kingdom of God in three major periods show how God has worked through history to establish His rule among His people. These periods move from creation to the fall and God's work to the restoration of all things in Christ. Each of these periods build on the one before it. The first is the original kingdom at creation. God created the world as His kingdom and everything He made was good. Adam and Eve lived under God's rule enjoying His presence and carrying out His commands. They were called to fill the earth and care for it. Even though it was the early stage, God's rule, His people, and God's place were all perfectly aligned. Humanity lived in harmony with God as well as each other and the creation. The second period is the fallen kingdom and God's work of restoration. After sin entered the world through Adam and Eve, the perfect order was damaged. Humans no longer obeyed God's rule. As a result, relationships were broken and suffering entered creation. Despite all this, God did not abandon His kingdom but rather He became restoring it through covenants. First it was with Noah, then Abraham, Israel, and later with David. Through all of these covenants, God formed His people, gave them His law, and placed them in a land where His rule could be seen. This period shows God patiently rebuilding His kingdom despite the fallen world. The third period is the fulfilled kingdom in Christ. This has both a present as well as a future reality. Jesus announced that the kingdom of God has arrived because He is the true King. Through His life, death and resurrection, He defeated sing and began renewing God's people. The kingdom continues to grow as people turn to Christ and one day it will be completed when He returns.

When I think about God's law, I don't see it as a burden or something irrelevant but rather a way to help shape us into the people God created us to be. I understand what the lessons and the text say such as God's law shows His character, protects us from harm and teaches us how to love Him and others. Still I know at times it is a struggle because it can feel demanding or difficult to follow all the time. These are areas where we need to strive to improve. I used to see it as rules that take away freedom and even avoiding it altogether. Influence from culture shapes our thoughts and without strong biblical teachings and understanding is makes us confused or allows us to believe in ideas that are skewed. But after growing in faith a more biblical way to think about God's law is to see it as something that brings joy and life. It is meant to guide us and not crush us. The problem is not the law but rather our heart. When we rely on our own strength and our own ways it feels too heavy to bear. However when we trust in God, the law becomes a path that leads us closer to Him. Instead of feeling trapped we start to experience the freedom that comes from living the way God intended for us to. Don't get me wrong, I still have alot of growing to do myself. I need to understand more that God's commands are not random but rather they show what matters to Him. I need to examine my heart everyday with the help of the Holy Spirit to make sure I am living the way God intended for me to live. I am not blinded in any way and be able to live in His freedom ultimately drawing closer and deeper relationship with Him.

Loving allegiance to God means being loyal to Him. This would look like to shaping our lives around Him and accepting the responsibilities that along with that. First of all, Loyalty means that you stay faithful to God no matter what. It is choosing Him as our King and not letting other things take His place in our hearts. When we choose to be loyal, we trust God, depend on Him, and keep following Him even when life is difficult. This kind of loyalty isn't just about keeping rules but rather it comes from loving God because He has already loved us. Secondly, loving allegiance shapes our orientation. In other words it shapes the overall direction of our lives. When we love God, our thoughts, choices, and goals are tuned in toward what pleases Him. Instead of living for ourselves, we begin to ask what God wants. His Word becomes our guide and keeps us pointed in the right direction. Even when we mess up or get distracted, this helps us turn our hearts back to God. Lastly loving allegiance includes responsibility. When we choose to love someone, it affects how we act. In the same way, loving God means that we take responsibility to obey Him, love others, and live in a way that reflects His goodness. This isn't meant to weigh us down but on the other hand it's to show our love in action.

God's atoning grace and God's common grace gives us powerful examples of how we should treat people in our day to day lives. Starting with atoning grace, this is the grace God shows when He saves us through Jesus. This is something that we did not earn and we did not deserve but God freely gave it to us. This teaches us that our love for others should also be generous and willing to sacrifice. When God forgives us, He does not hold things over our heads but rather He lets them go completely. We should also try to forgive others the same say. Atoning grace reminds us to be patient, kind, and willing to show mercy even when someone has hurt us. Now common grace is the everyday goodness God gives to all people. He sends sunshine, rain, beauty and blessings to everyone not just His believers. This shows us that we should treat all people with respect and kindness not matter who they are. If God is good to everyone then we should also look for ways to be good to everyone. This can be done by being fair, helpful, and generous. Common grace helps us see the value in every person because they are all made in God's image.

When I honestly reflect on my on heart and what motivates me, I see a mix of good and not so good reasons. There are times that I do what is right because I want things to go smoothly but there are also other times I act out of habit rather than real convictions. Even though both of these still lead to outward obedience they don't always come from a heart that is fully focused on God. I try to make it my goal. I am still a work in progress and I hope that one day it is second nature. A heart truly committed to God is one that acts because it trust Him. I would say I have learned through many experiences that now majority of the time I do trust God. However there are moments when my obedience is shallow and moments when my heart is not fully aligned with God's purpose. This is where the Holy Spirit nudges me and it helps remind me that spiritual growth is a process. God doesn't expect perfection but He does invite me to keep returning to Him. When I slow down, pray, and focus on His grace, my motives begin to change and I start wanting what He wants and not just acting out of pressure or convenience. At the end of the day, I do want my obedience to grow from a heart that is more committed to God and His Word. I know that He can help me get there as I stay close to Him.

I do remember what it was life when I first came to the faith. In the beginning I was full of excitement and passion. Everything felt new and I was "on fire" for God. my motives were simple and strong. I wanted to please Him, learn as much as I could, and share my faith. Obedience felt joyful and doing the right thing came more naturally because my heart was overflowing with gratitude. However as time went on and life brought challenges, there were seasons when my motivation faded and times when I struggled with doubt, fear, and disappointment. Some situations pulled me away from God and other times I just felt tired spiritually. My motives were always clear and my behavior didn't always match what I knew was right. These ups and downs didn't mean that my faith was gone but rather they just showed that the Christian journey is not always smooth. Over the years though, God's faithfulness has been steady. He has shown love, protection, and grace to me and my family again and again. Seeing His care in real life situations has changed me. It has deepened my motives and made my faith more mature. Now my desire to follow God is stronger than before. I want to be right with Him not out of fear but rather out of love and respect. Today, I feel more in tune with God than I ever have and I want to grow closer to Him each day. My journey isn't perfect but it has brought me to a place of deeper trust, gratitude, and genuine devotion.

Imagination is the ability that God gave us to picture things in our minds even when we can't see them with our eyes. It helps us think about ideas, possibilities and situations that are not always right in front of us. Imagination is not just for art or for stories but it is an important part of how we learn, understand, and make sense of life. Our imagination is very important when we think about God. Since we can't see God physically, we use our imagination to understand what He is like. When we read the Bible, our imagination helps us picture the stories, teachings, and the way God works. It helps us see His love, power, and care in a way that feels real and meaningful. Imagination also helps us apply God's Word in our lives by picturing how we should act, speak, and respond to different situations. Imagination also helps us understand the world. It helps us to think ahead and plan and consider the results of our choices. When we imagine different outcomes, we become wiser and make better decisions. Imaginations helps us learn new things because we can connect ideas and think beyond what we already know. Imagination also helps us understand ourselves. It lets us picture who we are becoming and how God is shaping our character. We can imagine the kind of person we want to be and how we can grow in faith, love and in obedience.

Assessing knowledge is important when we make ethical decisions because it helps us make choices based on truth and understanding and not just on our feelings or guesses. When we take time to think about what we know, we can make wiser and more thoughtful decisions. Assessing knowledge helps us figure out what is true. We get information from many places such as friends, family, social media and even from our own experiences and our emotions. Not everything we hear or think is correct. By checking what we know and asking if it is reliable, we avoid making decisions based on wrong information. This in return helps us from acting in ways that might hurt ourselves or others. It also helps us slow down. Ethical decisions are often complicated and if we act too quickly, we might choose something that might be unwise. When we take the time to stop and examine what we understand about the situation, we become more careful and less impulsive. This gives us time to think about the consequences of our actions. Assessing knowledge also helps us see the bigger picture. It encourages us to think about how our choices affect other people and our relationship with God. Instead of focusing on what we want right now, we start to think about what is fair, loving, and responsible. Lastly it also reminds us that we need God's wisdom. We don't know everything so we look to the Bible and in prayer we seek wise advice to help us make good decisions.

The will is the part of us that makes choices. It is where our thoughts, feelings, and our desires come together so we can decide what to do. Our minds helps us understand information and our emotions help us feel and react but the will is what actually chooses the actions we take. Throughout the decision making process the will plays a major role. It first looks at what we know. This would include what we've learned, what we believe is right or wrong and what God teaches in His Word. It then considers our motives such as why we want to make a certain choice and what we hope will happen because of it. After thinking through these things, the will makes the final decision. The will also shows what we truly value. It is possible to know the right thing and even feel strongly about it but the choice doesn't become real until the will says yes. This is where if our hearts are focused on God and we want to please Him, our will becomes stronger and more able to choose what is right, even when it's hard. However, if our hearts are distracted or set on selfish desires, our will follows those instead.

Reflecting on Luke 6:45 "A good man brings good things out of the good stored up in his heart, and an evil man brings evil things out of the evil stored up in his heart. For the mouth speaks what the heart is full of." 

When I think about what Jesus says here, it reminds me that my actions and words show what is really in my heart. So when I look honestly at my own life, I can see signs of what I'm truly committed to on the inside. There are times when my works and speech show good things. When I'm patient, kinds, or willing to help someone. Or when I choose to forgive or when I speak gently instead of reacting in anger. These moments point to a heart that care about God's will. They show that I am trying to live a way that honors Him. These moments my heart feels focused on God . On the other hand, there are also times when my actions and words show weakness. There are times I complain, get frustrated too quickly, or say things without thinking. This becomes clear that my heart still struggles. These moments show that I don't always trust God as much as I should. They show areas where I need to grow and let God change my heart. My works and speech show a mix of these good and bad moments. I still need God's help everyday. I truly do want to honor Him but I am not perfect. Seeing both the good and the bad reminds me to keep seeking God everyday so that my He can shape my heart so that my actions and words are more clearly aligned with Him.

God's authority, control and his presence helps shape our ethical responsibilities in meaningful ways. First, looking at God's authority means that He has the right to tell us what is right and what is wrong. Because He is our creator, moral rules are not based on personal opinion or even cultural trends. Rather, they come from God's character and His commands. What this means for us is that our ethical responsibility is obedience. We are called to listen to God's word, respect His commands, and submit our choices to Him even if it seem difficult or even unpopular. Acting ethically isn't about doing what feels the best to you but rather its about honoring God and doing what is pleasing to Him. Second, God's control reminds us that nothing happens outside of His power and His plan. God rules over everything, including history, circumstances, and outcomes. This does not take away our responsibility but rather it strengthens it. Because God is in control, our decisions matter and are part of His purposes. It is our responsibility to act wisely and faithfully, trusting God that He can use our choices for good. Even when the circumstances that we face may seem confusing or challenging, we have to continue to do what is right knowing that God is able to work through our obedience. Lastly, God's presence means that He is always with us. We never make decisions alone. God sees our thoughts and motives and actions even when no else does. Our ethical responsibility is to live the same way in our private lives as we do in public. God's presence is always there to bring us comfort in knowing that He helps us make wise and Godly choices.

The preternatural realm is the created spiritual world that exists beyond what us humans can normally see or touch. It is not the same as God's divine nature because God is uncreated and He is eternal but at the same time it is also not part of the physical universe. This realm includes spiritual beings that God created and it works under His authority and control. The preternatural world reminds us that reality is bigger than just the material world that we live in every day. The primary beings that inhabits the preternatural realm are the angels and the demons. Angels are good spiritual beings created by God to serve Him. Their purpose is to carry out God's commands, worship Him, and even at times help or protect people according to His will. Angels are powerful, intelligent, and moral beings. However, they are not all knowing or all powerful. They only exist to glorify God and support His purpose int he world. Demons on the other hand are fallen angels who rebelled against God. They rejected His authority and chose sin. This in return separates them from God. Demons can still exist within God's control but they go against His work and choose to deceive and harm humans spiritually. Their main goal here is to lead people away from God by promoting lies, temptation, and creating confusion. They do not have unlimited power and they can only act within the limits God has allowed. The interactions that occur within the preternatural realm are full of real conflict. Here Angels and demons are apposed to each other because they both serve completely different purposes. This struggle is not equal though since God's authority is absolute and the outcome of the battle is already determined. Even though this is the case, it still affects the human world. Spiritual beings can influence thoughts, events, or circumstances. Despite that, humans still remain responsible for their own choices. It is still our responsibility to live wisely and faithfully to God's plan.

The natural realm is the physical world that God has created. This is the world that we live in and that we can experience with our sight, touch, hearing, smelling, etc. This realm includes the earth, plants, animals, and human beings. It works in accordance with the laws of nature that God has established. The natural realm was created good and orderly reflecting God's wisdom and His purpose. Humans hold a special place in this realm because they are made in His image. What this means for us is that people have a moral responsibility, the ability to reason, and the calling to rule over all of creation in a way that honors God. The inhabitants of the natural realm include all living creatures but humans are unique. Animals act according to instinct while us humans are capable of moral decision making and meaningful relationships with God. People were created to live in harmony with God and with one another. The work we do, rest, creativity, and community were all originally part of God's good design for life in the natural realm. However, over time the situation of the natural realm has changed because of our sin. When humanity rebelled against God, sin entered the world and disrupted the original order. The natural realm became affected by suffering, decay, and death. The relationships between people were damaged, work became more difficult and creation itself began to experience brokenness. We started to see more natural disasters, disease, and hardship. All of these were signs that the world is no longer as it was originally intended to be. Despite all of this, the natural realm is not abandoned by God. He still continues to sustain us and work within this realm to accomplish His plan and His purpose. You can see all throughout history God has been guiding events toward restoration. The Bible says that one day the effects of all this sin will be removed and creation will be renewed. Until that day comes, we are called to live responsibly in the natural realm by making ethical choices that reflect God's plan and purpose for us.

The preternatural realm and the natural realm are both part of God's creation but they are very different in nature and purpose. The natural realm is the physical world that we live in every day. This includes humans, animals, plants, etc. It operates according the physical laws like gravity, space, and time. People experience this realm directly through their senses. Human are given a moral responsibility within it because they were created by God in His image. The preternatural realm on the other hand is the spiritual realm created by God. It includes angels and demons who do not have physical bodies like humans do. This realm is normally unseen by humans but it is just as real and it also exists under God's authority. While humans live mainly in the natural realm, spiritual beings operate in the preternatural realm and serve either God's purposes or oppose them. One of the major similarities between the two realms is that both are fully under God's control. Neither one operates independently from Him. However a  key difference is how they function. The natural realm follows physical laws while the preternatural realm functions spiritually. Humans belong to the natural realm but are affect by the preternatural realm while the spiritual beings do not belong to the natural realm. There are several ways that these realms influence each other. First you can see that angels may protect or guide people int he natural realm as part of God's plan. At the same time, demonic influences can lead to temptation, deception, or moral confusion which impacts human decisions and behavior. Lastly, prayer connects the natural realm to the preternatural realm. Our prayers are used by God in spiritual activity beyond what we can physically see. Bringing this all together we can see that these interactions show that ethical choices in the natural realm often have spiritual significance beyond the physical world.

Humanity is described as good because people are created in the image of God. What this means is that human beings reflect God in a special way that no other part of creation does. People can think, make choices, create, and form relationships. Because of this, every human life has value and has dignity. No matter who you are or what you do or even what you have done int he past, they matter to God. Humans being made in God's image also means that humans are responsible for living in a way that shows God's character. Some of these are love, truth, justice, and the compassion to care for others. God also gave His blessing to humanity. This blessing was more than just kind words but rather it gave people the ability to grow, thrive, and enjoy the world God created. God's blessing showed that He wanted humans to succeed in their role. Because of this blessing, people are meant to depend on God, be thankful, and trust in Him every day. This blessing reminds us that life comes from God and is meant to be lived for Him. Along with being created in God's image and receiving His blessings, we were also given a cultural mandate. This is God's command for people to rule over the earth in a caring and in a responsible way. Humans were called to work, build families as well as communities in addition to taking care of the world. We must not use what God have us in a selfish way but rather be good stewards who protect and develop what God has made.

The fall has deeply affected humanity's ability to clearly understand and follow God's commands. When sin came into the picture through human disobedience, it did more than damage behavior, it also damaged understanding. Unredeemed human beings are no longer able to see God's truth clearly on their own. Sin darkened human thinking. Because of this people naturally misunderstand, ignore, or even reject what God has said. Instead of trusting God's wisdom, humans tend to rely on their own judgement. This often times leads us away from God's standards. Because of the fall, our hearts are also affected. People are not neutral when it comes to God's commands. Sin has caused us to resist God's authority and prefer independence. Even when God's rules are known, unredeemed people often twist them to fit their own desires or excuse their sinful behavior. This moral rebellion makes it difficult for people to accept that God's commands are good and are ment for their benefit. We start to see that pride and self-centeredness replaced humility and obedience. The fall also affects how people interpret the world around them. Without redemption, we may recognize right and wrong in a general way but we fail to understand God's commands as part of a loving relationship with Him. God's law is often seen as restrictive. Because of this, people follow cultural rules and personal feelings instead of God's truths. Lastly, the fall separates people from God spiritually. Without God's guidance, human reasoning is limited and its flawed. Proper knowledge of God's commands require a heart that is renewed and that is willing to listen. Until a person is redeemed, sin will continue to block clear understanding making it impossible to fully know or obey God's commands as He as intended.

Christians can find great comfort in knowing that God's attributes are immutable. This means that they never change. In a world were everything is uncertain and constantly changing, God remains the same. His love does not fade and His promises do not fail. In addition to all this, His character is always trustworthy. This gives believers the stability and the peace we need. When circumstances are confusing or painful, Christians can be confident that God's goodness, wisdom, and His faithfulness are exactly the same as they have always been. God will never just suddenly stop being loving or just or even act in a way that goes against His nature. God's immutability also brings comfort because it means that His moral standards do not change. What God calls right and wrong does not change with culture or with time. Christians can trust that God's commands are consistent and reliable. Even when we live in a society that may pressure believers to compromise, we can rely on God's unchanging truth as a steady guide for life. This reassurance helps Christians make ethical decisions without fear or confusion. There is also comfort in knowing that God's attributes never conflict with one another. God is never loving at the expense of justice or just without being loving. His wisdom, power, holiness, mercy, and love all work together in perfect harmony. What this means to us is that everything God does is completely good and completely right even when there are times that we don't fully understand it. When we face suffering or unanswered questions, we can trust that God is not divided or confused. He never makes a mistake or acts unfairly. Knowing this we can be at peace and have confidence in Him, trusting His plans are loving, wise, and purposeful in every situation we go through.

In Christ I know that I've been given the ability to live in true goodness again but I still struggle with sin every day. One of the most helpful strategies that I've found in resisting sin is prayer. When I pray honestly and often, it helps remind me that I can't fight sin on my own and that I need God's strength. Reading the Word has also been important for me. When God's Word fills my mind, it helps me recognize temptation more clearly and respond with truth rather than emotions. Another strategy that has helped me is accountability. Having trusted Christians in my life who encourage me, pray with me, and speak truth when I'm struggling makes a big difference. Sin is much harder to fight when it stays hidden but by bringing struggles into the light helps weaken its power. I've also learned that avoiding situations that lead to temptation is wise, not weak. Setting boundaries protects my heart and keeps small temptations from turning into bigger failures. Relying on the Holy Spirit instead of my own strength has been especially important. When I depend only on willpower, I usually fail and feel frustrated. I started to realize that growth happens when I ask God to help change my desires not just my actions. Some strategies have not worked well for me such as ignoring sin or minimizing it only makes it stronger. Guilt without turning back to God leaves me discouraged and comparing myself to others often leads to pride or shame. What helps me the most is staying honest with God, trusting in Him, and continuing to walk forward even after I have failed.

There are three main reasons that the majority of interpreters believe that Paul was not the author of the Book of Hebrews. The first is that Hebrews is completely anonymous. You can see in Paul's other letters that the book never names its author. Paul on the other hand always introduced himself at the beginning of his writings. This is seen in the book of Romans and in Corinthians. He was also careful about false letters being written in his name. Because of this, it would be very unusual for him to leave out his name. The second reason is that the themes in Hebrews are very different from Paul's usual focus. You see Hebrews spends a lot of time explaining Jesus as the High Priest, the role of the tabernacle, and the significance of Melchizedek. All of these topics are either missing or only briefly mentioned in Paul's letters. While Paul wrote deeply about salvation and grace you can see in Hebrews that it uses a different approach and emphasizes Old Testament priesthood and sacrifices in a unique way different from Paul's. The third and the most important reason is that the author of Hebrews places himself in a later generation of believers. You can see in Hebrews 2:3 "So what makes us think we can escape if we ignore this great salvation that was first announced by the Lord Jesus himself and then delivered to us by those who heard him speak?" The writer says the message of salvation was confirmed by those who heard Jesus. This means that he received the gospel from eyewitnesses and not directly from Christ. Paul on the other hand strongly taught that he received the gospel directly from Jesus himself. This can been seen in Galatians 1:11-12, "Dear brothers and sisters, I want you to understand that the gospel message I preach is not based on mere human reasoning. I received my message from no human source and no one taught me. Instead, I received it by direct revelation from Jesus Christ."

The book of Hebrews was written to a specific group of believers and it gives us a clear clue about who there were for. First, the audience was mostly Jewish. In Hebrews 1:1 the writer talks about the Old Testament people as "our forefathers," which shows us that both the author and his readers shared a Jewish background and understood the Scriptures well. Secondly, we can conclude that they were Hellenistic. This means that they were influenced by Greek culture and likely lived outside of Israel. The ideas and teaching style that are found in Hebrews fit with  Greek speaking Jewish communities. This shows that they were part of that environment. Thirdly you can see that they were spiritually immature. In Hebrews 5:12, the author tells them that they should be teachers by now but instead they still need to learn the basic truths again. This shows that they had not grown in their faith like they should have. Fourthly they were facing persecution. In Hebrews 10:32-34 it explains how they suffered publicly, lost property, and stood with others who were imprisoned. This shows us that their faith came with very real hardship and pressure. Last but not least they were close to turning away from Christ. In Hebrews 10:26-27, the author warns his readers about the dangers of continuing in sin after knowing the truth. This shows that some were at risk of abandoning their faith. With all of these characteristics, it helps us understand why the writer speaks so strongly. His main goal was to encourage them to grow, stay faithful, and not give up on Jesus.

The author of Hebrews used many different methods and literary devices to express and reveal his exhortations to his audience. They were very clear and powerful ways to speak to them and encourage them to stay faithful. His goal was not just to teach information but rather was to move people to take action and stay strong in their faith. First he used strong encouragements. He often said things like "let us hold on" or "let us draw near." These phrases are ment to include the readers and push them to respond. It shows that the message is personal and urgent and not just some general teaching. Secondly he gives clear commands. He told the readers to persevere, obey their leaders, and stay faithful to Jesus. These commands made it clear that their situation was serious and that they needed to act right away. Thirdly, the author used comparisons to help explain his message. He compared Jesus to angels, Moses, and the Old Testament priest. Each time he showed that Jesus is greater and this helped the readers understand why they should not go back to their old ways. Fourthly he used examples of faithful people. In Hebrews 11, you can see that he lists many people from the Old Testament who trusted in God even during hard times. These examples were meant to encourage the readers to do the same. Lastly, he used a "lesser to greater" way of thinking. This means if something was important in the past, it is even more important now because of Jesus. By using all of these various methods, the author was able to make his message very clear to his readers.

Hebrews 5:12, "You have been believers so long now that you ought to be teaching others. Instead you need someone to teach you again the basic things about God's word. You are like babies who need milk and cannot eat solid food." This verse reminds us that the original audience had not grown in their faith like they should have. It also challenges me to think of ares in my own life where I still need to grow. At the top of my head I see that there are two important areas for me, one is gaining a deeper understanding of Jesus and second becoming a better father by reflecting how God cares for His children. First I want to grow in my understanding of who Jesus truly is. I know that Jesus is my Savior, but Hebrews teaches that He is also our High Priest who stands before God on our behalf. He understands our struggles and helps us in our weakness. I want to go beyond just knowing facts about Jesus and really understand how His role affects my daily life. This means trusting Him more, depending on Him in hard times, and seeing Him as someone who is always present and working for my good. Secondly I want to grow in being a better father by showing my kids the same kind of love and patience that God has shown me. God is patient, kind, and full of grace even when I make mistakes. I want my children to experience that same kind of love through me. This means being more patient, listening better, guiding them with wisdom, and leading them toward God in both my words and actions. These are some of the areas of practical grown that reminds me that spiritual maturity is not just about knowledge but rather it's about living out my faith every day.

The author of Hebrews wrote to encourage believers to reject false thinking and to stay faithful to Jesus especially when life is difficult. In my own life, one false mindset I face is becoming complacent because life feels busy and overwhelming. Even though I am currently in Bible School, I know that I delayed starting and even when I was enrolled I moved slower than I should have. I allowed the responsibilities of life to slow me down and made excuses instead of stepping forward when God was calling me. It is easy to stay comfortable and move at a slower pace when things feel chaotic but that can keep me from fully walking in what God has for me. Another struggle I face is getting discouraged or mentally checking out when life gets hard. When challenges come, it is easy to feel frustrated or distracted and lose focus. Instead of pushing through, I can sometimes feel like giving up or even pulling back. This kind of thinking can weaken my faith if I let it continue. To remain faithful to Christ I am learning to stay consistent even when life is not perfect. I remind myself that God's timing is still good even if I started later than I wanted. I focused on being faithful where I am now instead of looking back with regret. I also try to stay grounded in prayer and staying consistent in God's Word. This helps me to keep the right perspective. Most importantly, I am learning to take steady steps forward trusting that God is still leading me and growing me daily.

The author of Hebrews used the Old Testament to support his theological views by making it as the main focus for his teaching. He didn't create new ideas but rather he showed that everything about Jesus was already pointed out in the Old Testament. Since the author and his readers already believed that the Old Testament was God's Word, all he had to do was to prove that Jesus is the true fulfillment of God's plan. A few examples of how he accomplished this was first he used historical facts to explain deeper truths. An example of this can be found in Hebrews 7:2 where he explains the meaning of Melchizedek's name which means "king of righteousness" and "king of peace." This shows how Jesus is the greater king and the greater priest. Another example that can be found is how he used theological truths that were already known. If you read Hebrews 1:7 it says that the angels are servants while Jesus is the son. This shows that Jesus is greater than angels. Another area is how he reminded them of moral lessons. This can be seen in Hebrews 3:7-15. In this passage the author warns his readers not to harden their hearts like Israel did in the wilderness. The author also points out prophecies about the future as seen in Jeremiah 31 which speaks of a new covenant. He shows that this promise is fulfilled in Jesus. Last but not least, he showed that Jesus fulfills the ideal king from David's line by perfectly living out what earlier kings could not. All of these different examples show that the Old Testament and Jesus are fully connected and furthermore shows that Jesus is the center of God's plan.

The author of Hebrews teaches that Jesus is superior to angels by showing his readers both who Jesus is and what He as done. You see in the Old Testament angels where highly respected because they delivered messages from God. As a result of this there were some people that even began to elevate angels too highly. This is where the author makes it clear that Jesus is far greater than angels in every way. He does this by first showing that Jesus is the Son of God and not a servant. Angels are described as servants who carry out God's work but Jesus on the other hand is the one who rules. Hebrews points to Old Testament passages that call the Song "God" and place Him at God's right hand. This position that is given is the position of power and authority. This shows that Jesus has a much higher status than angels. Secondly the author explains that Jesus brings God's final and greatest message. You see in the past God spoke through prophets and sometimes through angels but now God has spoken through His Son. What this means is that Jesus is not just another messenger but rather He is the complete and final revelation of God. Next the author shows that the angels worship Jesus and not the other way around. This is very important because it proves that Jesus is above the angels. You see angels are created beings but Jesus on the hand is the one that they serve and honor. Last but not least the author explains that Jesus became human and died to save people from their sins. Angels never did anything like that. Jesus took on flesh, suffered, and paid the price for sin so that people could be saved. By using all these  evidences by showing that Jesus is the Son, the final message, the one worshiped by angels, and the Savior, the author makes it very clear to his readers that Jesus is far greater than angels in every way.

The new covenant is superior to the old because it is built on the perfect work of Jesus. You see the old covenant given through Moses. While this was good because it came from God, it could not fully solve the problem of sin. It showed people God's law and it also included sacrifices and priests. However, it could not completely cleanse the heart or bring final forgiveness. But what it did do was point forward to something better that was still coming. The new covenant is better because Jesus is its mediator. Under the old covenant, human priests served in an earthly tabernacle and offered animal sacrifices again and again. These sacrifices were ment to be temporary and had to be repeated because they could not take away sin. Jesus on the other hand is our perfect High Priest. He serves in the true heavenly sanctuary and not an earthly one. Another example of how the new covenant is better is because Jesus offered Himself once for all. Instead of bringing the blood of animals again and again, He gave His own life as the final sacrifice for sin. Because His sacrifice was perfect, it never has to be repeated. This is one of the greatest differences between he old and the new covenants. The old system reminded people of sin again and again but Jesus brings real forgiveness. Another reason the new covenant is greater is that it fulfills the promise of Jeremiah 31. You can see here that God said that He would make a new covenant, write His law on His people's hearts, forgive their wickedness, and remember their sins no more. The author shows us that this promise is fulfilled in Christ. Because of the new covenant, believers can now draw near to God with confidence, have real hope, and rest in the finished work of Jesus. The new covenant is better because Jesus is better, His sacrifice is better, and His covenant brings what the old covenant could only point towards.

The book of Hebrews makes it clear that the Old Testament is extremely important and honestly I have to admit that I am not as familiar with it as I should be. For a long time it has been easier to focus on the Gospels and the New Testament because they feel more direct and easier to understand. However through this study I am starting to see that the Old Testament is not just background it is the foundation of everything we believe. Because of this, I am trying to be more intentional about reading through the Old Testament and spending time studying it. I realize now that if I skip it, I am missing a huge part of God's story. The Old Testament teaches about who God is, His holiness, His faithfulness, and His patience with His people. It also helps me understand why Jesus had to come and what His work really means. We all know of the inspiring accounts, examples and lessons in the Old Testament stories like David, Jospeh, and Moses but there are more detailed lessons and examples we can really learn if we spend the time to dive deeper. There are many real life examples of trusting God in difficult situations and these are not just stories but incredible lessons that can be applied in my life today. In my life and ministry I want to grow in valuing the whole Bible and not just leaning towards one part of it. This means that that I continue to study the Old Testament and learn how it all points to Jesus. An additional bonus is using this to teaching my family as well as when I get opportunities at Children's Church. Overall, I am not where I want to be yet, I am still a work in progress but I am taking the steps to now and give the Old Testament the importance it truly deserves.

One of the main messages of Hebrews is that Jesus is completely enough. It teaches that He has fully paid for sin and nothing else needs to be added. In my own life and ministry, I want to clearly communicate that truth in simple and practical ways. One of these ways is that I can communicate the sufficiency of Christ by how I live my daily life. You see people are always watching, especially my kids. If I am constantly stressed, trying to control everything, or acting like everything depends on me then I am not showing trust in Jesus. However, when I trust God and stay steady during hard times and rely on Him instead of myself, it shows that Christ is truly enough for me. Secondly, I can communicate this truth by teaching and speaking about it clearly. It doesn't matter if it's with my family or others around me, I can still express that the sacrifice that Jesus made for us was complete. He does not need our good works to finish what He already did. The book of Hebrews teaches that His sacrifice was once and for all. That in itself should give us the confidence and peace we need. Another example is that I can point people back to Jesus instead of to performance. What I mean is that it is easy for people to feel like they have to earn God's love to fix themselves first. It is a good reminder that Jesus already did the work. Our role is simple, just trust Him and follow Him. Lastly in my role as a father, I can model this by showing grace, patience, and consistency. When my kids see that love is not based on performance, it reflects how God treated us. Overall my life, my words, and the leadership positions that I am in should point people to the one truth, Jesus is enough.

Before Paul was arrested there were several important things that happened to help paint the picture for us to better understand the situation. Near the end of his third missionary journey, Paul was traveling back to Jerusalem. His main goal was to bring money to help Christians there who were suffering from a famine but you see this gift was not just about helping people financially. Paul also hoped that it would bring unity between the Jewish and the Gentile believers and also help them see each other as one family in Christ. As Paul was making his way to Jerusalem, he kept getting a lot of warnings. The Holy Spirit made it clear to him that he would face trouble, suffering, and even imprisonment when he arrived. In a place called Miletus, Paul told the church leaders that he did not know exactly what would happen but he knew it would not be easy. Even with that knowledge, he still felt strongly that God wanted him to continue. In other cities like Tyre and Caesarea, there were people who also warned Paul not to go. One powerful moment happened when a prophet named Agabus took Paul's belt and tied up his own hands and feet. This was a visual way of saying that Paul would be arrested and bound if he went to Jerusalem. The people who loved Paul were very concerned and begged him not to go because they did not want him to suffer. Despite all of this, Paul did not change his mind. He understood that these warnings were not meant to stop him but rather it was to prepare him. He trusted that God had a purpose for everything, even if it were to involve pain. You see Paul was committed to his mission that he said he was ready not only to be arrested but even to die for the name of Jesus. With this in mind, Paul chose to follow God no matter what the cost may be. As a result, that decision led to his arrest.

Paul's arrest in Jerusalem happened because of a lot of unfortunate misunderstandings, accusations, as well as growing tension between different groups of people. You see when Paul arrived in Jerusalem, he met with James as well as the church leaders. They were very glad to see him but they also had their concerns. The reason for this is because there were rumors going around that Paul was teaching Jewish Christians to stop following their traditions like the laws of Moses. Even though this was not true, there were many people believed it. Paul actually respected those traditions and was willing to follow them when it helped share the gospel. To calm the situation down, the leaders asked Paul to take part in a temple ritual with four men who had made special vows. They wanted Paul to show publicly that he still honored Jewish customs. Paul agreed to do this because he wanted peace and unity especially between the Jewish and the Gentile believers. However, that did not go according to plan. You see while Paul was in the temple, there were some Jews from Asia that saw him. They had previously seen him with a Gentile man named Trophimus. They wrongly assumed that Paul had brought this Gentile into a part of the temple where only Jews were allowed. This was actually a very serious accusation and it made them very angry. Now because of this false assumption and accusation, a crowd quickly formed. The people started becoming violent, grabbed Paul and dragged him out of the temple. They were so upset that they were ready to kill him right there on the spot. It was at that moment a Roman soldier stepped in and stopped the mob. The commander arrested Paul. It wasn't because he was guilty but rather to bring order and stop the chaos. So all in all Paul's arrest wasn't because he broke the law but rather because of the false accusations and misunderstandings about his teachings and the anger of the crowd.

Paul's imprisonment in Rome came after a very long and difficult journey. This turned out to be one of the most important seasons of his ministry. After being held in Caesarea for about two years, Paul used his rights as a Roman citizen to appeal his case to Caesar. What this meant was, he had to be sent to Rome for his trail. The trip to Rome was not easy at all. Paul traveled by ship under Roman guard. Along his journey the entire crew as well as Paul faced dangerous weather. Even though Paul warned the crew not to continue sailing, they went ahead and were caught in a violent storm that lasted for many days. Eventually the ship was wrecked near the island of Malta. Everyone survived just as Paul had said that they would. While they were on Malta, Paul continued to serve others. He healed the sick people and showed God's power even though he was still a prisoner. After a few months passed, Paul finally arrived in Rome. Instead of being placed in a dark prison, he was kept under house arrest for about two years. This meant that he lived in his own rented place but he was always guarded by a Roman soldier. Despite the fact that he was not free to leave, he was allowed to have visitors to come and visit him. Even though he was restricted physically, he was not spiritually. He continued to preach the gospel and teach about Jesus, as well as encourage people who came to see him. There were many people who heard the message of Jesus because of this situation. Paul also used this time to write letters to the various churches as well as to individuals. These letters later became part of the New Testament and have impacted Christians even to this day. Despite the face that Paul was in chains, his ministry didn't stop but rather reached even further. Paul's imprisonment in Rome shows that God can use difficult situations for a greater purpose. What looked like a limitation actually became a very powerful opportunity to spread the gospel.

There are a lot of things here to uncover. Paul's imprisonment teaches a very powerful truth about God and Paul's ministry. From the outside, Paul's situation looks like a complete failure. He was falsely accused, attacked by a mob, and stuck in prison for years without justice. However, when you take a closer look you can see that God was still fully in control and working through every part of it. One important insight about God is that He is sovereign. This means that God is in control even when life seems unfair or confusing. Paul's arrest was not an accident. God used every part of it to move Paul exactly where He wanted him to be. Throughout all the trails, court hearings, and even on the dangerous journey, Paul was eventually brought to Rome. This allowed the message of Jesus to reach people it might not have reached otherwise. It shows that God can use even the suffering and the injustice to accomplish His plans. Another point to consider is that God's plans are not stopped by hardship. Even though Paul was in chains, the gospel was not. Paul's situation was used to help spread it even further. This teaches that God's work does not depend on perfect circumstances. He can use any situation for good. Paul's imprisonment also reveals a lot about his own ministry. First of all, Paul did not see prison as the end of his calling. He continued to preach, teach, and encourage others. He also continued to speak boldly to leaders, guards, as well as visitors. He also spent a great deal of time praying for others as well as writing letters that would later become part of the Bible. Secondly, Paul understood that suffering was part of following Jesus. He was not at all surprised by the hardship that he faced but rather he accepted it and trusted that God had a plan and purpose for it. The attitude towards it showed courage, faith, and a deep commitment. All this to say that Paul's imprisonment showed us that God is always working even in difficult times and that true ministry continues no matter the circumstances.

There are three things the book of Acts teaches us about Paul's ministry during his imprisonment. These lessons helps us understand how Paul continued to serve God even though he faced very difficult situations. First of all, Acts shows that Paul was fully aware of the suffering that was coming. He was not surprised when he ws arrested or when he was put in prison. Before going to Jerusalem, Paul had already been warned many times that he would face some hardships. Instead of running away from it, he accepted it. He understood that following Jesus would sometimes lead to pain and sacrifice. This shows that Paul's ministry was build on courage and obedience. He chose to follow God not matter the cost even if that meant that he had to suffer. Secondly, Acts shows use that Paul had a strong sense of purpose. He believed that God would use his imprisonment for something greater. Even though Paul was a prisoner he didn't stop sharing the message of Jesus. He spoke to crowds, religious leaders, governors, and even kings. Every time he was given a chance to speak, he would use it to tell others about Christ. Prison did not stop his ministry but rather it gave him new opportunities to reach people he might never have met otherwise. Thirdly the book of Acts shows us that Paul experienced God's blessings even during his imprisonment. God continued to guide him, protect him, and work through him. An example of this can be seen when Paul was able to encourage others during a dangerous storm at sea. He even healed people when he was on the island of Malta. These are the moments that show us that God was still with Paul and God was still using him in powerful ways. Even though these are just a few examples, the Book of Acts teaches that Paul's ministry was full of suffering, but it was driven by purpose and supported by God's ongoing presence and blessings.

Paul developed the idea that Christ is King over all creation in three main ways. This helps us understand who Jesus is and why it matters especially during Paul's time in prison. First of all Paul taught that Jesus has complete authority over everything. This means that Christ is not just a spiritual leader but rather a true ruler of all creation. After the resurrection and return to heaven, Jesus was given power and authority over the entire world. Even though earthly leaders like the Roman Empire seemed powerful, Paul made it clear that Jesus is above them all. This truth was especially important because Paul himself was in prison under Roman authority. Secondly, Paul emphasized that Jesus deserves the highest honor. Since Christ is not only King but also God, He is worthy of worship, respect, and obedience. Paul wanted believers to understand that Jesus is not just important but also supreme over everything. this means that people should respond to Him with their whole lives. They should honor Him not only with words but also through their actions, choices, and attitudes. Thirdly, Paul taught that Christ is determined to complete His rule. Right now not everything in the world fully obeys Jesus but there is coming a day that will change. Paul goes on to explain that Jesus will return and fully establish His kingdom. This gives believers hope for the future. No matter how broken the world may seem, there is coming a day that Christ will rule and will make it complete and perfect.

Pauls idea of being united with Christ is a pretty simple idea when you break it down. He's saying that when someone follows Jesus, they're not just believing in Him from a distance but rather they are closely connected to Him, almost like their lives are joined together. A way to think of it is when Jesus died, Paul teaches that it's like our old life died with Him. The person we used to be especially the part of us controlled by sin, doesn't have the same power anymore. Then when Jesus rose from the dead, we were given a new king of life. So being a Christian isn't just about trying harder but rather it's about becoming a new person on the inside. Paul also explains that because we are connected to Jesus, we share in what he has. Jesus has authority and a place with God and in a spiritual sense, we are connected to that. That means our identity changes. We are not defined by our past mistakes anymore. We are defined by being connected to Christ. This has some really important effects on how we live. First it gives us confidence. If we are connected to Jesus then e are secure in Him. We don't have to constantly worry about losing that relationship. Secondly, it changes how we act. If we are connected to Jesus, our lives should start to look more like His. What that means in showing love, being humble, and making better choices. Not because we have to earn anything, but because we've been changed. Finally it gives us hope. Just like Jesus was raised to life, we know that our future is also secure in Christ.

The main theological truth that ties all of Paul's prison letters together is this simple but yet power idea that Jesus is Lord over everything and believers are connected to Him. Everything Paul writes comes back to that. Even while he was in prison, Paul kept pointing people to the fact that Jesus is in control, not Rome, not circumstances, or anything else for that matter. This truth connects directly to Christ's kingship. Paul teaches that Jesus is the true King over all creation. That means He has authority over the whole world even over rulers and governments. Even though Paul as sitting in prison, he know Jesus was still on the throne. That gave him confidence and peace because he understood that God was still working behind the scenes. This also connects to our union with Christ. If Jesus is King and we are united with Him, then we are closely connected to the One who is in charge of everything. That changes how we see ourselves. We are not just trying to follow rules but rather we are living in a relationship with Jesus, sharing in His life. Our identity comes from Him not from our past or the situations that we face. Because of that, it naturally leads into how we live. This is where ethical living comes in. If we are connected to Jesus and He is our King then our lives should reflect that. We should live with love, humility, patience, and obedience. This isn't to earn anything but in the end it's because we belong to Him.

Paul's relationship with the Colossian church was somewhat unusual because he had never met most of the believers there in person. Unlike the other churches such as Philippi or Corinth where Paul spent alot of time teaching and ministering, the church in Colosse was different. Even though Paul likely never visited them, he still cared for them deeply and was very concerned for their spiritual well being. This shows us something vvery important about Paul's heart. He did not only care about people he knew personally but he also cared about all believers and wanted to see them grow in their faith and remain faithful to Christ. Most of Paul's connection other the Colossian church came through trusted friends. The most important person was Epaphras. He was probably the one who stared the church in Colosse and shared the gospel with the people there. Whenever false teachers began influencing the church, Epaphras traveled to visit Paul in prison and told him what was happening. Because of Epaphras' report, Paul wrote letters to the Colossians. He spoke very highly of Epaphras and described him as a faithful servant of Christ who cared deeply for the church and prayed for them often. Paul also had a close friendship with Philemon who was a respected Christian who lived in Colossee. Paul called him a beloved friend and fellow worker. Another important person was Onesimus who was a slave who had run away from Philemon but later became a Christian through Paul's ministry. Onesimus eventually because a valuable helper to Paul. Apphia and Archiuppus was also likely involved in the church and there is a strong change that they may have been part of Philemon's family. These relationships help us understand why Paul wrote with such passion and concern. He was not just writing as a distant teacher who knew nothing about the people but rather through his friendships and connections. He genuinely cared about the Colossian believers. He wanted to protect them from false teaching.

One of the biggest problems that were facing the Colossian church was the influence of false teachers who were mixing Christianity with ideas from Greek philosophy, Jewish law, and the worship of spiritual beings. These teachings may have sounded wise and spiritual but they were actually pulling believers away from the truth. The truth that Paul tried to emphasize was that Christ is completely sufficient for salvation and spiritual growth. The first problem was Greek Philosophy. During the time of Paul, philosophy was not just about learning or education. It many times included secret knowledge, mystical experiences, visions, and hidden wisdom. The false teachers claimed that they had access to deeper spiritual truths that ordinary Christians did not know of. They promoted asceticism which involved harsh self denial and sound make someone more spiritual. Paul strongly disagreed with all of these teachings. He went on to explain that these human rules could not change a person's heart or defeat sin. True wisdom and spiritual growth are found in Christ alone. You will not find it in some secret knowledge or self made religion. The second problem was that of the misuse of Jewish law. The false teachers emphasized food laws, religious festivals, Sabbaths, and circumcision as though these practices were necessary for spiritual maturity. Paul was not trying to attach the Old Testament law but rather he was trying to explain that these practices were only shadows pointing forward to Christ. Now that Church had come, believers should focus on Him rather than the symbols that pointed to Him. The third and most serious problem was that of spiritual beings. The false teachers encouraged people to worship angels and fear spiritual powers. They claimed these beings could provide special wisdom and protection. Paul then responded by reminding them that that Christ created every ruler, authority, and spiritual power. Not only that but Christ had already defeated the powers of darkness through His death on the cross. Because of this believers did not need to worship, fear, or seek help from spiritual beings because everything they needed was already found in Jesus. If you see, all of these messages were pretty much concluding to the same thing, "Christ is not enough."

Understanding the background of Colossians is very important because it helps us understand why Paul wrote the letter int he first place. If you only read the letter without knowing what was happening in the church, some of Paul's teachings might seem random or even difficult to understand. Once you learn about the problems that the Colossian believers were facing, then Paul's message becomes much clearer. The church in Colossee was bring influenced by false teachers who were introducing the idea that were not part of the true gospel. These teachers were mixing Christianity with greek philosophy, Jewish religious practices, and the worship of spiritual beings such as angels. They claimed that believers needed more than Jesus in order to become truly spiritual. According to them, people needed secret knowledge, special spiritual experiences, strict religious rules, and help from spiritual powers. This became a very serious problem because it cased people Tod out whether Christ alone was enough. Knowing this background helps understand why Paul focuses so much on the greatness and the supremacy of Christ throughout the letter. Paul wasn't just teaching theology just for the sake of teach but rather he was responding directly to the false ideas that were spreading through the church. When Paul says that charts is the image of the invisible God, the creator of all things, and the head of the church, he is showing that Jesus is far greater than any angel, philosophy, or religious system. When he says that all wisdom and knowledge are found in Christ, he is answering the false teachers who claimed to have secret wisdom. The background also helps us understand Paul's personal concern for the church. Even though he had probably never met most of the believers in Colosse, he cared deeply about them. Paul knew what was happening and wanted to protect them from teachings that could harm their faith.

Paul demonstrated to the Colossians that Christ was supreme by showing them that Jesus is greater than everything the false teachers were promoting. The false teachers were encouraging people to trust in philosophy, religious rules, mystical experiences, angels, and spiritual powers. Paul responded by pointing the believers back to Christ and showing that everything they were looking for could already be found in Him. One of the most powerful ways that Paul demonstrated the supremacy of Christ was by describing who Jesus is. He said that Christ is the image of the invisible God. What this means is that if someone wanted to know what God is like, they should look at Jesus. Christ perfectly reveals God because He is God in human flesh. Paul also called Jesus the firstborn over all creation. This does not mean that Jesus was created but rather it means that He has the highest position, authority, and honor over everything that exists. Paul went even on to teach that Jesus is the creator of all things. Everything in heaven and on earth, whether visible or invisible, was created through Him and for Him. This also includes angels, rulers, authorities, and spiritual powers. The false teachers were encouraging people to focus on these spiritual beings, but Paul reminded them that those beings were created by Christ. They were not rivals to Jesus but rather they were under His authority. Paul also explained that Christ is the sea of the church and that all the fullness of God dwells in Him. There is no human teacher, religious tradition, or spiritual experience that can take His place. Paul also taught that Christ alone can reconcile people to God. Through His death on the cross, Jesus provided forgiveness, peace, and salvation. There was no ritual, angel, or philosophy that can do what Christ has already done.

Paul taught that Christ's ministers were superior to the false teachers because their ministry was build on truth, sacrifice, and God's power rather than human ideas and empty promises. The false teachers in Colossee claimed to have special wisdom, secret knowledge, and deeper spiritual experiences. They tried to impress people with their philosophies, visions, religious rules, and teachings about spiritual beings. Paul on the other hand showed that true ministers of Christ had something far greater than impressive sounding ideas. They had the true Gospel. First, Church's ministers were superior because they preached a message that actually saved people. The false teachers offered rules, rituals, and spiritual experiences. They could not reconcile people to God. Paul preached Christ and through that message people received forgiveness, salvation, and peace with God. The Colossians themselves were proof of this because their lives had already been transformed by the gospel before the false teachers arrived. Secondly, Christ's ministers demonstrated genuine love and sacrifice. Paul pointed to his own suffering as evidence of this. While the false teachers were seeking influence and recognition, Paul was sitting in prion because he had devoted his life to serving Christ and His church. He was willing to suffer so that others could hear the gospel and grow in their faith. His ministry was marked by humility and self sacrifice rather than personal gain. Thirdly, Paul explained that Christ's ministers had a divine calling and authority. Paul was not teaching ideas he invented himself. He had been personally called and commissioned by Jesus. The message he preached came from God's revelation not from human imagination or philosophy. The false teachers relied on traditions, speculation, and human wisdom but Paul's authority came from God. Lastly, Christ's ministers were empowered by God Himself. Paul said that he worked with the strength that God provided. His ministry was effective because God was a t work through him. The false teachers depended on human efforts and world wisdom but Paul deepened on God's power.

To completely understand why it is believed that Paul wrote Ephesians you have to look at the clues left behind in the letter and in early history. There are some modern scholars today that think that it was a student of Paul who wrote Ephesians after Paul died just to keep his ideas going but the evidence shows that Paul himself was the real author. Knowing that Paul wrote it is a big in itself because it means that the letters carries real apostolic authority from an official representative of Jesus. The first big rule of this is right at the start of the letter in Ephesians 1:1 where it explicitly says it is from "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God." If anyone else wrote it and put Paul's name on it, that would be fake. Why this matters is because Paul hated forgeries. In another letter, he warned Christians not to be tricked by fake letters that pretended to be from him. It makes no sense that a loyal student of Paul would try to honor him by doing something that Paul explicitly told people not to do. Also, the way Ephesians is written sounds like Paul's other letters, which all were written around the exact same time while he was stuck in a Roman prison. These letters talk about the same deep theological topics and use the exact same vocabulary to show that Jesus rules supreme over all spiritual powers and demonic forces. Finally, Paul had a massive history with the city of Ephesus. The book of Acts tells us that he planted the church there and lived with them for 2 years. He as close friends with the leaders so the people in the church would have instantly recognized if a letter was fake trying to sound like him. in addition to that, very early church leaders from history completely agreed that Paul was the true writer. When you look at internal clues and historical facts, it is clear that Paul wrote Ephesians to teach Christians how to live and follow Jesus.

To fully understand why Paul wrote the letters to the Ephesians you have to look past the fact that he was just writing to write random theological essays and consider the fact that he had a heart for these peoples as a paster. While he usually wrote letters to fix specific local problems in one exact church, Ephesians was written to be a circular letter that was passed around to multiple congregations. This includes churches like Colossee and Laodicea. Because he was addressing several churches at once, his strategy was to give all of them a single universal framework. He wrote this letter to teach these believers how to understand their new identity and how to successfully live, build, and thrive as citizens under the rule of Jesus. First of all Paul wrote to help Christians transition out of their old lifestyles. He reminds them that before salvation they were spiritually dead and trapped int he kingdom of darkness completely controlled by sin and Satan. Since many of the readers came from pagan backgrounds like Ephesus, which already was a major hub for occult practices and worship of the goddess Artemis, they struggled to change how they thought and acted. Paul wrote this to show them that because God gracefully transferred them into he kingdom of light their because had to match their new citizenship. They needed to drop their old sinful habits and put on a pure code for living that reflected the holy character of Jesus. Secondly, Paul wrote to solve intense racial and ethnic divisions between Jewish and Gentile believers. Before Christ, Gentiles were treated as outsiders and completely excluded from the national citizenship of Israel. Paul wrote to demolish any sense of cultural or spatial superiority by expelling that through the blood of Christ, the dividing wall of hostility has been torn down. He wanted them to know that Jews and Gentiles are not full equal co-citizens in one body. Finally, Paul wrote to prepare the churches for ongoing spiritual warfare.
